# Advances in Information Security, Privacy, and Ethics (AISPE) Book Series

Manish Gupta (State University of New York, USA)ISSN: 1948-9730 |
| --- | --- |

### Mission

As digital technologies become more pervasive in everyday life and the Internet is utilized in ever increasing ways by both private and public entities, concern over digital threats becomes more prevalent.

The Advances in Information Security, Privacy, & Ethics (AISPE) Book Series  provides cutting-edge research on the protection and misuse of information and technology across various industries and settings. Comprised of scholarly research on topics such as identity management, cryptography, system security, authentication, and data protection, this book series is ideal for reference by IT professionals, academicians, and upper-level students.

 
| 

### Coverage

*   Electronic Mail Security
*   CIA Triad of Information Security
*   Risk Management
*   Access Control
*   Tracking Cookies
*   Information Security Standards
*   Cyberethics
*   IT Risk
*   Internet Governance
*   Privacy Issues of Social Networking

ABOUT THE SUBJECT

The internet as we know it, brought humans closer to their peers at a speed never seen before at the civilizational level. With this transformation new elements appeared, and others resurfaced in the form of activities less licit like cybercrime, having been the object of successive and insufficient measures of correction. These are not the only characteristics of a technological society, fully computerized and where terrestrial borders matter little in limiting the active agents, harmful or not, of this system, because in this new era, information represents money and practically everything represents information, especially, personal data and personal activities and its respective detailed interconnections.

The last decade has demonstrated that technology is without any kind of doubt mankind’s most challenging endeavour where society is defied by sudden change with social, political, economic and high environmental costs. This volatility implies strong consequences for the (in) security of societies and organizations due to new technological offers, trends, products, problems and solutions, razing a disruption that already has today an impact virtually impossible to contain or hide.

Day in and day out people, companies, nations depend of the most important information highway that is the Internet, and it is impossible to disassociate the internet with the vast unknown army of harmful subjects that plot against security to obtain any kind of advantage in the misuse of information.

It is throughout is highly technical actions that cybercrime takes place and mostly because people depend on the use of technology but lack the means to comprehend it in its many subjects, being the most critical, security.

THE MISSION

For the information security practitioners, the constantly changing landscape of Cyber Security, Cyber Crime and Information Privacy makes it challenging to stay informed of the field’s most up-to-date research. That is why the authors and editors are pleased to offer this second and enhanced version of the Handbook of Research on Cyber Crime and Information Privacy, a vastly and complete one volume edition, full of top of the line research and references that will empower students, researchers, and academicians with a strong understanding of critical issues within Cyber Security and Information Privacy.

This book emergent studies and research provides both broad and detailed perspectives on cutting-edge theories and developments. This reference is designed to act as a single reference source on conceptual, methodological, technical, and managerial issues, as well as to provide insight into emerging trends and future opportunities within the discipline.

ORGANIZATION

This handbook of research is organized in 33 chapters, co-authored by 81 contributors belonging to 43 different organizations from 14 countries of the five continents. This significant participation gives us the possibility to claim a diversity of visions that contribute to the soundness of this book.

We are grateful to all the authors for their excellent contributions: this handbook of research reflects the result of their relevant work and deep knowledge on the Cyber Crime, Security and Information Privacy domains.

All these works express a positive contribution to the scientific domains of the handbook. We would like to welcome feedback and comments about this handbook from the readers. Comments and constructive suggestions can be sent to the Editors of IGI Global at the address provided at the beginning of this Handbook of Research.

We hope you find it useful. Enjoy your Reading!

*   The editors,

We express our gratitude to IGI Global for the opportunity to edit this handbook of research and for the excellent support of their team of professionals. We express our appreciation and gratitude to all the authors for their excellent contributions: this handbook encloses the result of their relevant work and deep knowledge on the domain of cybercrime, security, and privacy.

# Chapter 1

*   Carlos Alberto M. S. Teles  
    Federal Center for Technological Education of Rio de Janeiro (CEFET-RJ), Brazil
*   Carlos Roberto Gonçalves Viana Filho  
    Federal Center for Technological Education of Rio de Janeiro (CEFET-RJ), Brazil
*   Felipe da Rocha Henriques  
    Federal Center for Technological Education of Rio de Janeiro (CEFET-RJ), Brazil

ABSTRACT

Information security is gradually becoming an area that plays an important role in our daily lives as information and communications technology assets grow with increasingly connected environments. Increasingly we have information from society having their data leaked due to information security flaws in both hardware and software of ICT assets. To identify failures of ICT assets, through the detection of malicious traffic, this chapter proposes a black-box-based framework that aims to detect malicious traffic. The black-box method allows monitor the network without accessing the software or hardware details. In the proposed framework, information security and network resource usage are used together in order to provide a reliable detection of malicious traffic. Firstly, the authors collected network traffic information, generating a dataset from open source networking tools. The proposed detection scheme can identify risks and threats like malware, suspect traffic, and others. The scheme was validated verifying the correlation between network security alerts and network resource usage.

INTRODUCTION

The security of today's technological environments is highly dependent on the proper behavior of the various Information and Communications Technology assets that make up them – where ICT assets are used to contemplate all kind of hardware and software capable of performing computational processing and engaged in information technology and communications activities. The term ICT refers to the combination of computer with telecommunications technologies and has in computer networks, and especially on the Internet, its greatest expression (Miranda, 2016). In fact, the inadequate functioning of a simple element of a computer system, whether hardware or software, can compromise the entire security of that system. It is therefore essential to develop mechanisms to ascertain and attest that ICT assets meet desirable security requirements. This objective, however, is a huge challenge, as the ICT assets used in today's computer systems become increasingly complex. ICT assets are at into increasingly critical activities and relevant to the society's well-being.

One approach that has gained increasing strength in the compliance of products, services, processes, systems and people to regulatory requirements is the implementation of Conformity Assessment Programs (CPAs) (Fernandes, 2011). These programs deal systematically, using traditional quality management techniques, such as inspections, tests, sampling and audits, to analyze compliance with pre-established requirements in standards and regulations, for each product, process, service or professional under evaluation. Conformity Assessment programs are already used in various areas to verify compliance with the most diverse types of requirements, including calibration of measurement instruments, energy efficiency, electromagnetic compatibility, radiation detection, thermal insulation, ergonomics and civil construction (Inmetro, 2019).

In the area of ICT asset security, the use of CPAs to verify compliance with cybersecurity requirements has gained a strong impulse in the last decade with the publication of international standards ISO/IEC 15408-1:2009 (Information technology - Evaluation criteria for IT security) and ISO/IEC 19790:2012 (Information technology - Security techniques - Security requirements for cryptographic modules) (Leszczyna, 2018). However, even if the area of information security is moving towards international standardization and the search for systematic testing procedures for conformity assessment, the evaluation of ICT assets includes advanced technical challenges arising from the complexity of the behavior of such assets, which requires research to develop systematic and conclusive tests.

In recent years, there have been cases of compromised ICT assets (Kirtley & Memmel, 2018). Several models of babysitting suffered security incidents, where in some cases there was the sending of scary audios to children, in addition to the theft of access credentials to Apple and Google stores, and the improper obtaining of the authorization of other users to remotely view and control the monitor. According to (Cziesla, Kemper, Muntermann, & Sinanaj, 2015), several companies have had their data breached by the NSA through security breaches in ICT assets. In (Restuccia, D'Oro, & Melodia, 2018), it has been proven that internet-connected cars, through Internet of Things (IoT) devices, can be controlled remotely. More worrying cases, however, involve medical devices and can have fatal consequences in the event of failure (Restuccia, D'Oro, & Melodia, 2018).

Addressing information security issues of ICT assets has become an important issue. Thus, the U.S. Senate recently proposed the 2017 IoT Bipartisan Cybersecurity Improvements Act, which aims to boost Information Security on Internet-connected devices (Restuccia, D'Oro, & Melodia, 2018). According to a study by (Chen, Woo, Brumley, & Egele, 2016), through the extraction and evaluation of vulnerabilities in embedded devices, it was found that the highest incidence of failures is in the network layer. Thus, the monitoring of network traffic has become an important aspect (Goncalves, Faria, Vieira, Silva, & Mascarenhas, 2017), so that malicious packets do not penetrate the security of companies and institutions, which could lead to failures in ICT equipment and assets.

In this work, we propose a black-box framework based on open source tools that allow the collection of network security data, in addition to making it possible to detect malicious traffic in real time. Through the environment, proposed, real data from home and corporate network were collected and a database was generated. Through the correlation between security information and the use of network, (we call it as network performance) malicious traffic detection can be performed reliably.

Thus, we can summarize the contributions of this work through the following items:

*   • Development of an ICT asset-testing environment based on tools of virtualization. The proposed environment differs from the observed proposals in the literature, since it enables the instantiation of sophisticated test environments, including the use of virtualized ICT assets. The environment is publicly available as a software product in https://github.com/carlos-teles/etsg/ so that the academic community can reproduce the experiments.
*   • Development of a methodology for conducting systematic tests with a focus on security. The proposed methodology differs from those observed in literature, since the safety and performance tests allow to evaluate both the security flaws that allow assets to be attacked and allow to identify possible malicious behavior by the owner device under evaluation
*   • Construction of a reference database for the study of events security and attacks on ICT assets from traffic captured by monitoring during the experiments.

This chapter is structured as follows: we firstly initiate the theme of this chapter in the Introduction Section; the Background Section presents some fundamental concepts considered in this work to implement our proposal; the Related Works Section situates our proposed framework within the literature; the Section called Black-Box Framework Proposal for Malicious Traffic Monitoring presents the proposed framework for malicious traffic detection in ICT environments; the Section of Experimental Methodology presents the computational setup used to implement the experimental environment; the obtained results are discussed in Section called Results; concluding remarks are presented in the final section of this work.

BACKGROUND: BASIC CONCEPTS

In this section, we present the basic concepts used in this work, such as software testing, monitoring and behavior analysis of systems and network.

Software Tests

In (Khan, Khan, & others, 2012), software tests identify errors, flaws, or errors in code that must be fixed. We can also define software testing as a process of accessing the functionality and correction of software through analysis. Software testing is a key component for quality assurance and represents a review of specification, design, and coding. Its main objective is to affirm the quality of the system, systematically testing it in carefully controlled circumstances. In addition, another goal is to identify its integrity and suitability, and ultimately discover undiscovered errors. The three most important techniques for finding errors are: (i) white-box test, (ii) black-box test, and (iii) gray box test.

White-box tests are performed through a detailed investigation of the internal logic and structure of the code. In these tests, it is necessary for a tester to have full knowledge of the source code of the software. Black-box tests are performed without knowledge of the internal workings of the software. This test examines the fundamental aspects of the system and has little or no relevance to the internal logical structure of the software. Intermediate tests, between the white-box and the black-box, are the gray-box tests, which use a limited knowledge of the internal components of the software. In principle, this could mean that the tester knows some parts of the source code and not others, but in practice this usually means that the tester has access to more detailed design artifacts than specifications or requirements (Michael & others, 2013).

Below, we can mention some important characteristics, presented in both white-box and black-box tests, as a comparative summary.

*   1\. Black-Box Test: 
    *   a. It is not suitable for algorithm testing.
    *   b. It uses a trial and error method.
    *   c. It is less exhausting and time consuming.
    *   d. It is based on external exceptions, and the internal behavior of the program is ignored.
    *   e. Final users, testers and developers (User Acceptance Testing) execute it.
    *   f. It has a low granularity.
    *   g. We need to know only fundamental aspects.
*   2\. White-Box Test: 
    *   a. It is suitable for algorithm testing.
    *   b. It can use other methods, as well as trial and error.
    *   c. It is more exhausting and time consuming than the black-box test.
    *   d. The internal behavior of the program is not ignored.
    *   e. Both developers and testers perform it.
    *   f. It has a high granularity
    *   g. Full knowledge of software and hardware is required.

System Monitoring

To monitor a system is an important issue in computer networks, the Internet, and the most modern data-centers. This is so, because it helps to encounter many problems before they cause any trouble that affects your end users and can impair service availability. In addition, it helps plan for growth based on the utilization of your current resources. The collection of different metrics from many data sources is not enough; it is still necessary to tailor the monitoring of systems to meet your business needs and security, in order to set the right alerts so that any abnormality in the system should be avoided (Girish & others, 2018).

Behavior Analysis

Behavior analysis of an ICT asset is a task that can be divided into two main points: network connectivity and monitoring.

The connectivity provided with the network to an ICT asset must be transparent, so that it knows that it is in use, or rather in operation. Some devices have a “test”, demo or “store” mode. This type of operation demonstrates some features of the device, but mainly as a view of its core features. However they can also hide features. Another existing way in ICT asset is putting devices in standby. Generally, when a device is in any of the above modes, its connectivity is not transparent, that is, it may be transmitting and/or operating in a way that hides functionality.

One can cite the case of Volkswagen (Blackwelder, Coleman, Colunga-Santoyo, Harrison, & Wozniak, 2016), where the company admitted to installing a software in cars, where results on pollutant emissions were changed. The software has been installed in more than 11 million diesel vehicles worldwide, in models of various brands belonging to the group. The mistrust stemmed from the difference between emission levels found in shooting tests and officers. After investigating, the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) concluded that the software installed by the automaker detects when the car is being inspected to check the level of pollutant emissions and, only then, starts to control the gases that the vehicle releases into the atmosphere. This control is turned off in normal shooting situations, causing cars to pollute far beyond the required level in the country. Thus, monitoring an ICT asset should be aware of all its forms of operation as non-compliance, which will be briefly described below.

According to the World Trade Organization (WTO), the conformity assessment encompasses any procedure used, directly or indirectly, to determine that the requirements pertaining to technical regulations or standards are complied with. In addition to this definition, the Brazilian National Institute of Metrology, Quality and Technology (Inmetro) understands that: “Conformity Assessment is a systematized process, with pre-established rules, properly monitored and evaluated, in order to provide adequate degree of confidence that a product, process or service, or even a person, meets pre-established requirements in standards or regulations, with the best possible cost benefit for society” (Inmetro, 2019).

A non-compliance can be defined as not meeting a requirement, that is, when a company, institution, or person does not operate according to the requirements. This requirement does not necessarily need to be defined only in the ISO standard, and may also be a customer requirement, an internal procedure or even failure to meet a legal requirement, which when not met, becomes non-compliance. We can also state that a product when it exhibits behavior outside its specifications or that it presents functionality against its specifications is in non-compliance.

In addition, we may have a suspicious behavior, that is, even if speaking of product, it goes through a behavior or functionality presented that does not explicitly go against the specifications, but that may represent potential vulnerability of safety or malicious action.

In this work, we analyze the behavior of ICT assets (or computational environments), performing network monitoring. Thus, it is intended to detect and block external attacks before they can affect equipment and computer systems.

RELATED WORKS

In the literature, there are environments that were already implemented and consolidated for monitoring ICT assets, but not all of them have the characteristics we need. These are the characteristics: monitoring of all network traffic (with vision of information security and performance) where the ICT asset is located; possibility of virtualization of ICT assets in multiple architectures; and exporting data for statistics.

In our search for environments with these characteristics we found that GNS3 (Welsh, 2013) is a network software emulator, which allows one to combine virtual and real devices to simulate complex networks. It has the tools: KVM/QEMU (Goto, 2011) for virtual machines and the Dynamips environment.

SIMOC (Machado, 2018) is a simulator to train military fighters from the digital space. This is employed by the Electronic Warfare Instruction Center (CIGE), in the formation of the Brazilian Army Cyber Warfare Course, and can be used for training civilians. It has, as theoretical advantages, the possibility of scalability, the low cost of implementation and the reduction of time for training. As disadvantages, it was identified the limitation of the use of a simulator based on a network virtualization solution with the main ICT assets. Thus, the scenarios created can become very theoretical, diverging from the objective of training, which is to make use of corporate networks with ICT assets.

The Docker Security Playground (DSP) (Perrone & Romano, 2017) is the implementation of an architecture that uses a micro-service-based approach to building complex network infrastructures specifically tailored to the study of network security. This was conceived as a tool to teach information security in computer networks with a practical approach. Multiple labs can be instantiated, and it uses operating system-level virtualization via Docker.

Corelab (Nakao, Ozaki, & Nishida, 2008) proposes a new network testbed and it is based on a hypervisor as a virtual execution environment (VEE) for network services to run. It uses a prototype based on KVM/QEMU.

Comparatively, GNS3 and DSP could be adapted to our research; however, they would need to change in source code, more memory, CPU, and storage. DSP and Corelab do not have an associated monitoring platform. SIMOC and DSP use only x86 and x86-64 architecture, not instantiating others (arm, mips, and so on).

Therefore, this work differs mainly from the works presented in this section by enabling: (i) inspection of packages of all ICT assets in the environment with security event/incident detection; (ii) performance analysis of all ICT assets in the environment; (iii) extraction of performance and security data for analysis and history.

BLACK-BOX FRAMEWORK PROPOSAL FOR MALICIOUS TRAFFIC MONITORING

After the presentation of the main basic concepts, we now will describe our proposal for black-box testing for the detection of malicious traffic in ICT assets. We will divide this scheme into a monitoring environment and an environment of ICT assets, as depicted in Figure 1.

Generally, in the ICT asset environment (lower right side of Figure 1) there may be virtualized elements, in addition to physical elements, that must simulate Internet access, simulate access to the local network, and simulate connection to the ICT ASSET UNDER TEST (IAUT). Thus, the basic idea is that all connected elements, cable or wireless, and with Internet access, will be monitored. The network connection will be performed by an ICT asset prepared to capture and copy all the information that passes through the network; that is, all data from the ICT assets to be monitored will be copied to another environment that will process this information in order to identify whether there is suspicious, malicious (or non-compliant) behavior.

In addition to the ICT asset environment, there is a monitoring environment. This will receive a copy of all traffic, inbound and outbound to the Internet or Local network, from the ICT asset environment. This information will be processed by the Information Security and Performance components. From the investigation of such information, aiming to identify non-conformities, e.g., behaviors, unspecified requirements and functionalities incompatible with the specifications of the IAUT. It is worth mentioning as a contribution of this work that this information will be processed by the monitoring environment, without the help of the source code of the IAUT or its engineering documentation. Thus, the monitoring environment will identify any deviations, only by observing the behavior of the ICT asset.

Failures Sought in Non-Conformities

From the configured and Internet-connected black-box testing environment, we can identify the following non-conformities and/or failures in the ICT assets being tested: (i) unauthorized remote access; (ii) remote software update of the IAUT; (iii) hidden devices (Interfaces not initially detected or declared); (iv) scanning of doors, services and protocols; (v) extrusion of information by the IAUT; (vi) Botnet infection and; (vii) Malware Infection.

According to (Michael & others, 2013), there are several techniques for safe black-box testing. Each of them, according to its functionality, we can classify according to the tools used: (i) fuzzing, (ii) syntax testing, (iii) exploratory testing, (iv) data analysis, (v) test scaffoldings and (vi) monitoring the behavior of Software.

In this work, our proposed approach has the classifications: “Exploratory Tests”, which are tests without a specific test plan, based only on observation about the results; and “Software Behavior Monitoring”, when many tests are applied automatically.

Proposed Malicious Traffic Detection Algorithm

Algorithm 1, described in Figure 2, presents the steps of the detection of malicious traffic used by the system proposed in this work. Variable n represents the instant of measurement of the data; d is the number of devices on the network; the Boolean variable A[r] receives the value of 0 when there is no security alert, and receives the value of 1 when there is a security alert. In this case, when A ← 1, the system checks the performance (or resource usage) of the network; the variable L[r](d) defines a lower limit to identify that there are attacks, based on the number of devices connected to the network, that is, when there is an increase in traffic due to intrusion attempts, there is also a consequent increase in network flow or the number TCP connections. L[r](d) is proportional to the number of connected devices, because if there is an increase in the number of connections on the network, the traffic also increases, augmenting the detection limit. Note that the detection takes place in two steps, one referring to the identification of an alert (with A[r] = 1) and other referring to the verification of an increase in the use of network resources, through the analysis of D[r]. These two steps aim to make the detection system robust, so that there is no false-positive. In addition, when there is detection, a countermeasure is carried out by the system, which can represent the activation of a firewall or even the shutdown of an ICT asset.

EXPERIMENTAL METHODOLOGY

In this section, we describe an environment for black-box testing on ICT environments. Hereafter, we present the components and tools used to build such an environment. Installation and configuration details can be found in the Project GitHub repository - https://github.com/carlos-teles/etsg/doc\_orient.pdf.

Network

Regarding to the experimental setup, some basic premises are suggested: (i) Internet connectivity, (ii) Internal IP addressing plan, (iii) Equipment to provide Internet connectivity and IP addressing plan, (iv) Server for installation of the Monitoring Environment; and (v) Server for virtualization environment installation. The definition of an IP addressing plan will help identify the IAUT and ICT assets that will not be tested. We suggest identifying the MAC addresses of all ICT assets, as they may change IP within this range. For automatic addressing of the environment's ICT assets, in IPv4 and IPv6, use a DHCP server. The same should be associated with one of the ICT assets that will provide connectivity. This suggestion aims to make ICT assets interpret that they are in operation and not in test mode. (Droms, 1997)

Port Mirroring (Switched Port Analyzer) is a network traffic monitoring that involves sending a copy of each packet from a switch source port to a destination port. (Orebaugh, et al., 2006) (Ornaghi & Valleri, 2019)

Sniffer is a software used to monitor and analyze network traffic to detect problems. It captures all network traffic, including unencrypted data. It must be installed on some ICT asset connected to a local network, and should not be installed on the IAUT (Orebaugh, et al., 2006).

Port mirroring and sniffer are ways we can use to capture network traffic. We emphasize that it is considered the most “elegant” way to capture traffic; however, it is necessary that the ICT asset, for network connectivity, have such capacity. In this case, for port mirroring, two network interfaces are required, one through which all network traffic (inbound and outbound) passes through and the other that will receive a copy.

Monitoring

The Monitoring Environment must be installed on a Server with Linux operating system. The installation script it is available at https://github.com/carlos-teles/etsg/install-only-etsg.sh. It is prepared for Ubuntu versions 16 and CentOS 7. Once all packages are installed, it is necessary to verify the processes that must be running.

The Influxdb, Telegraf, Grafana, Suricata, and Evebox packages are installed from the script (https://github.com/carlos-teles/etsg/install-only-etsg.sh) and they must be configured in advance. Below is a brief description of these packages, as they will present the Performance and Information Security information.

Performance

For performance collection there are several tools; some, for example, use SNMP, as CACTI and LibreNMS. However, such tools are usually used for measurements in every 5 minutes (we call this frequency as granularity). In this work, we indicate tools that consider lower frequencies with respect to the granularity.

Telegraf and Influxdb are components of the TICK ecosystem, developed by the company InfluxDATA, and, in our research, we will use them in the open source version. Telegraf is a server-based agent used to collect metrics and data. It has plug-ins to send metrics to a variety of services and message queues, including InfluxDB, Graphite, Kafka, MQTT and many others. InfluxDB is an open source time series database and it is written in the Go programming language, and has a query language similar to SQL On the other hand, Grafana, which is used in this work to show the data collected via Telegraf and Influxdb, is an open platform for data analysis and monitoring. It has a vast documentation and availability of control panels ready, for visualization of data collected via Telegraf and Influxdb. (Naqvi, Yfantidou, & Zimányi, 2017).

Information Security

Intrusion detection systems (IDS) are tools that, like other measurements, such as antivirus software, firewalls and access control, aim to strengthen the security of information systems. One of the main features of an IDS is that it recognizes an intrusion into a particular ICT asset and saves the IPv4 or IPv6 address and the mac address in a message (IDMEF). (Stallings, 2017)

According to (Hallstensen, 2017), a Network Security Monitoring (NSM) can be seen as a loop of repetition, consisting of collecting, detecting and analyzing network security data to address four main elements, that are: (i) Protect the network; (ii) Detect threats to the network; (iii) Block threats on the network and; (iv) Sustain the operational capabilities of the network.

The Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) is an extension of an IDS that includes the ability to try to block or prevent detected malicious activity. As an IDS, an IPS can be host-based, network-based, or distributed. This can use anomaly detection to identify behaviors that are not from legitimate users or signature to identify known malicious behavior. When an IDS detects malicious activity, it can respond by modifying or blocking network packets on a perimeter or on a host, or by modifying, or blocking system calls by programs running on a host. Thus, a network IPS can block traffic, such as a firewall, but it makes use of algorithms that are developed for IDSs to determine when to perform the blocking task (Stallings, 2017).

In this work, we considered the Suricata (Gupta & Sharma, 2019), because it has the functions of IDS, IPS and NSM. It is used to inspect network traffic using rules and signatures language. It is also able to handle high network traffic and email alerts; it supports Multi-Threading; it provides built-in hardware acceleration, so we can use graphics cards to inspect network traffic; it supports Lua scripts to detect complex threats; and it works in various operating systems such as Unix, Linux, FreeBSD and Windows..

The information collected by Suricata should be indexed. Thus, we will use the Evebox framework, which allows one to view collected data. It is a web-based event and alert management tool. We can configure it for simple searches with SQLite, Postgresql or even Elasticsearch indexing databases. (Ish, 2017)

Virtualization

All virtual machines are managed and controlled by a virtual machine manager. These are generally referred as hypervisors, and their main focus is to provide abstraction to the underlying hardware. The system on which the hypervisor is installed or run is called the host machine, and all other virtual machines running within the host machine are called guest machines. The host and guest machines generally use the same interface that is used for different applications. The host machine and all available guest machines are independent of each other (Yadav, Garg, & others, 2019).

For the configuration of the virtualization environment, we suggest to use some basic premises: (i) internet connectivity and; (ii) the configured Monitoring Environment.

The virtualization environment must be installed on a Server with Linux or Windows operating system. Each of these environments can be used for a virtualization purpose. In order for the IAUT not to be considered under test, in our case, we use each of these environments for the following purposes: (i) Virtualization of devices for simulation of a real network, that is, the ICT asset can verify its neighborhood and given that there are a number of other ICT assets (the same is not considered in testing); (ii) Virtualization of surrounding devices to simulate access to the ICT asset and for monitoring environment to check network traffic and; (iii) Virtualization of the IAUT, if possible.

Our suggestion for the open source-based hypervisors are the Oracle VirtualBox, KVM, and QEMU. KVM/QEMU packages work together in virtualization on Linux systems. From these tools, there are several ways to create virtual machines. In our example, one of the system requirement was to start several virtual machines within the network of IAUT.

Oracle VirtualBox

This tool can be installed on various operating systems, and it is available in https://www.virtualbox.org/. It currently belongs to Oracle Corporation, and aims to create virtualized environments, such as the x86 and x86-64 architectures, for the installation of different operating systems. (Oracle, 2018) (Dash, 2013)

KVM

The Kernel-based Virtual Machine (KVM) is an open source virtualization technology based on Linux. With KVM, Linux can be used as a hypervisor, allowing a host machine to run multiple isolated virtual environments, called guest machines or virtual machines. This kind of virtualization allows inheriting all Linux features, without additional engineering. (Goto, 2011)

QEMU

QEMU is virtual machine emulator software that can run an operating system, such as Windows or Linux and its applications, on a virtual machine. It supports several hosted operating systems, such as Linux, Windows, and Mac OS X. Hosted CPUs and guests may be different. In addition, QEMU is integrated with a Linux user mode emulator. Its main features are: (i) CPU and device emulator; (ii) debugger; (iii) graphical interface; (iv) multiple architectures such as x86, x86-64, mips, arm, etc. (Bellard, 2005)

RESULTS

In this section, after the presentation of the suggested tools, for the construction of the experimental environment, we will have the components configured according to the architectural suggestion presented in Figure 1

To validate the proposal of this work, two scenarios were constructed, called as: (i) Home Office; and (ii) Internet. A different network topology and ICT assets characterize each one. For the scenario (i) we have the following experimental setup: one Wi-Fi Router, three Smartphones, one server, one desktop, one Multifunctional Printer, one network extender, one Smart TV, one Cable TV decoder and one firewall. This environment is a local network. The server has the Monitoring Environment and a network card, where it provides connectivity and receives all network traffic for analysis.

In the scenario (ii) we have the following experimental setup: one switch, one IP camera, one server for monitoring, one server for honeypot and there is no firewall. This environment is connected directly to the Internet. There is a server with the Monitoring Environment installed and it has two network cards; one that provides connectivity to the environment and the other network card that receives all network traffic for analysis. This is done via Port Mirroring on the switch to the Monitoring Environment server.

Results were obtained from the experiments related to the described scenarios. All evidence is made by querying via Evebox, Grafana or graphs with information extracted from the InfluxDB (Grafana) and Postgresql (Evebox) databases. They are available in https://github.com/carlos-teles/etsg-results, in a database built from network monitoring. However, it is not possible to expose all the evidence. Thus, in this section we will describe the most significant obtained results.

In scenario (i), from queries to events generated by Suricata and published on Evebox, we identified on the desktop, in one of the IAUT, undue access of an application that was no longer used for at least 1 year. This application was by the security module of monitoring environment and identified through a DNS event, referred as 'guardiao.itau.com.br', as shown in Figure 3. One can confirm DNS traffic by the UDP datagrams, queried in Grafana, from the information depicted in Figure 4. We also extract, from performance monitoring, the daily packet averages on the network, as packet inputs presented in Figure 5, and packet outputs depicted in Figure 6. We extract, from information security monitoring, the total numbers of alerts and DNS per day, from alert events presented in Figure 7 and DNS events, in Figure 8.

Results obtained from both experimental scenarios showed the correlation between information security and network performance (or network resource usage). When there is an attempt of malicious traffic entering in the network (reflected in the number of alerts), one could expect to have an increase in the network resource usage, which can be reflected by the number of packets through the network. Our proposal explore this correlation in order to detect possible threats, referred as malicious traffic

Scalability Analysis of the Proposed Malicious Traffic Detection System

Once we have identified malicious traffic from scenarios (i) and (ii), we performed scalability tests in our solution. Using the infrastructure already configured in scenario (ii), we added a server with KVM and QEMU virtualization solution. In this scenario, we added 08 virtual machines and performed the following test with denial of service attack:

*   • 01 virtual machine from 16:00 on 04/12/2019 with interval every 01 hour;
*   • 02 virtual machines from 23:55 on 04/12/2019 with interval every 01 hour;
*   • 04 virtual machines from 08:55 on 05/12/2019 with interval every 5 minutes;
*   • 08 virtual machines from 17:30 on 06/12/2019 with interval every 5 minutes;
*   • End of tests with shutdown of virtual machines at 00:00 of 07/12.

Results of the scalability experiment are presented in Table 1, that by increasing the number of virtual machines and decreasing the attack interval (potentiating the attack), we verified an increase in the number of alerts as well as a number of packets. In addition, we verified an increase in the volume of data with the scalability of virtual machines. To solve this problem, the collected data had to be transposed to another server.

Table 1. Scalability test for the proposed malicious traffic detection system

| Item || 01 Virtual Machine || 02 Virtual Machines || 04 Virtual Machines || 08 Virtual Machines |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Number of alerts (maximum) || 2,488 || 2,413 || 1,202,136 || 3,577,547 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Number of packages (maximum) || 2,155 || 2,598 || 3,863 || 11,010 |

Thus, we can observe, from results presented in Table 1 that the system proposed in this work was able to detect attacks, combining information security data and the use of network resources, even in a scenario with scalability, that is, with more devices connected to the network. This analysis is even more important thinking about IoT scenarios in which the number of connected devices tends to be increasingly high. However, it should be noted that the amount of data to be analyzed is directly linked to the processing and storage capacity of a detection system.

CONCLUDING REMARKS AND FUTURE DIRECTIONS

In this work, we proposed a Black-Box framework for detecting malicious traffic in ICT environments. We have established concepts and suggestions of tools for implementation of the environment. An experimental methodology was presented with the implementation of two scenarios. Results from both scenarios, obtained through the collection and analysis of performance and information security information in the IAUT, validated the proposed methodology.

The obtained results were considered to be satisfactory and reveal the ability of our proposed environment to detect malicious traffic, in addition to non-conformities, and information security events and alerts. Compared to the environments mentioned in the literature, none of the other environments so far can perform such collections and queries to the point of analyzing the data and verifying the identification of non-conformities, events or information security alerts on ICT assets

As one possible future direction to be considered, one can apply some machine learning techniques on data collected by the system proposed in this work in order to classify the traffic from the external network, categorizing it as malicious or not. Moreover, one can identify at which moments of the day there are more attacks on the network, and use this information to try to anticipate these problems. Another possibility to be explored in a future work can be the evaluation of the proposed malicious traffic detection system in an Internet of Things environment, which tends to be an interesting work, especially because of the energy and memory constraints presented in the devices that composes this kind of network. These constraints probably will influence the way the data will be stored and used by the detection algorithm.

KEY TERMS AND DEFINITIONS

Black-Box Test: Test performed without knowledge of the internal workings of the software in which it examines the fundamental aspects of the system.

Conformity Assessment: It encompasses any procedure used, directly or indirectly, to determine that the requirements pertaining to technical regulations or standards are complied.

Cybersecurity: It is the organization and collection of resources, processes, and structures used to protect cyberspace from security events.

ICT Assets: All kind of hardware and software capable of performing computational processing and engaged in information technology and communications activities.

Information Security: It is the practice of preventing unauthorized access, use, disclosure, disruption, modification, inspection, recording or destruction of organization's information.

Malicious Traffic: Any suspicious connection or content created or received over the network. Malicious traffic is a threat that creates a security event.

Network Traffic: It refers to the amount of data moving across a network at a given point of time.

Network Traffic Analysis: It is the process of intercepting, recording, and analyzing network traffic patterns.

Security Event: Any observable or detectable occurrence relevant to information security. This can include attempted attacks or lapses that expose security vulnerabilities.

Virtualization: It allows you to use a physical machine’s full resource by distributing its capabilities among many users, environments, or virtual machines.

# Chapter 2

*   Suzana M. B. M. Moreno
