Integrating Privacy Requirements Into System Design

The term ‘Privacy by design’ (PbD) was first coined and conceptualized by Ann Cavoukin (2009). Later, around 2010, the framework for integrating privacy into system design was developed. Subsequently, different researchers have proposed their own methodologies for integrating privacy within the system design; in fact, this is a mandatory clause in the General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), which is a regulation in EU law on data protection and privacy in the European Union (EU).

As design techniques can vary widely and quantitative comparison among different design techniques is not possible, the pros and cons of each technique are identified in this survey. This will help system developers to choose the appropriate design technique as per requirements.

Langheinirich (2001) discussed the importance of PbD in ubiquitous computing and provided a set of well-formed guidelines to be considered while designing any system in this domain.

Schaar, (2010) tried to quantify the objectives and approaches towards PbD. The paper lists a set of PbD objectives to be followed by different enterprises. These generic objectives include data minimization, controllability, transparency, data confidentiality, data quality, possibility of segregation, etc. The objectives have been verified by analyzing three different examples. Although the paper did not propose any implementation mechanism, the basic objectives of PbD have been clearly identified.

The term ‘Privacy by Design’ was first coined by Cavoukian. It comprises technology, business practice, and physical design. In the paper by Cavoukian (2011), seven basic Pbd principles have been identified and applied in all three areas. These principles are: prevention of privacy breaches before they occur, privacy as the default setting, privacy embedded into system design, full functionality, end-to-end security or full lifecycle protection, visibility and transparency, and respect for user privacy. This paper does not suggest technical privacy measures for system design; however, this is the earliest paper where goals of PbD are clearly and unambiguously mentioned.

Gürses, Troncoso, and Diaz (2011) have shown how data minimization can help to engineer privacy by design. The paper suggests a four-step methodology for including privacy in the design phase. The first step is to perform a functional requirement analysis, which is mostly a manual process. The second step is to identify the datasets required to fulfill the functionalities identified in the first step. The minimal set of required data should be identified manually. The third step is comprised of a risk analysis with respect to the datasets for identifying appropriate threats and vulnerabilities. The final step is to implement the solution that fulfills all of the requirements with minimum data revelation.

Antignac, Scandariato, and Schneider (2016) demonstrated how legal texts, stating privacy regulations, can be included in the system software design, and how these can be verified. Standard DFD notations have been extended to take privacy principles into account. A privacy aware DFD system, PA-DFD, is comprised of three main external entities namely, the Data subject, the Data Controller, and the Data processor, as they are the major entities that handle personal data at any stage of the data lifecycle. Purpose binding and other privacy clauses have been considered. This is a very basic model and it is not practicable to implement the principles of different privacy regulations, such as GDPR and HIPAA, using the proposed notation.

Hoepman (2014) attempted to develop privacy design strategies in line with software design patterns. The approach is based on the framework proposed by Spiekermann and Cranor (2008) and a balanced mix of two perspectives, i.e. providing privacy by architecture and providing privacy by policy. The aim of this work is to derive privacy design patterns from existing data protection laws and privacy frameworks, such as OECD guidelines (OECD, 2002) and ISO/IEC 29100 (ISO, 2011). The approach is to first identify when and how privacy can be violated, and then attempt to prevent those violations. The paper specifies four data-oriented privacy design strategies, namely: minimize, hide, separate, aggregate, and four process-oriented privacy design strategies, namely: inform, control, enforce, and demonstrate. The major drawback of this research is that it does not provide any specific guidelines for choosing a particular strategy and related privacy pattern.

Colesky, Hoepman, and Hillen (2016) bettered Hoepman’s 2014 approach by adding an additional layer of abstraction called privacy tactics between privacy strategies and privacy design patterns. The authors identified different tactics for each privacy strategy identified in their previous paper. They have shown how these tactics can appropriately be used for implementing different data protection acts while designing a software system. However, the strategies and tactics are too generic and, therefore, cannot be chosen automatically based on privacy requirements.

Perera, McCormick, Bandara, Price, and Nuseibeh (2016) proposed a PbD framework for assessing Internet of Things (IoT) platforms. This framework enhances Hoepman’s framework of PbD by providing a set of guidelines based upon the lifecycle phase of data at each IoT node. Software engineers are free to choose the appropriate guidelines based on other requirements of the system and assess the privacy capability of IoT platforms. The major drawback of this approach is that the legal and business aspects of privacy requirements have not been fully addressed. Additionally, the process is mostly manual, making it difficult to verify whether the chosen guidelines are correct.

Through analyzing the existing research on the different approaches for integrating privacy requirements into system design, it can be concluded that PbD is more of an abstract constraint, and while researchers have attempted to conceptualize this into some tangible forms and different guidelines have been provided, no concrete methodology for choosing an appropriate privacy-enhancing technique has been proposed thus far. Moreover, socio-cultural privacy risks, and risks emanating from requirements of different stakeholders, have not been considered. All of the proposed approaches need some manual intervention, which is both tedious and prone to errors. Table 2 classifies the approaches in terms of methodology, usage of privacy enhancing technology, extent of manual intervention, and their merits and demerits.

Privacy Impact Assessment

Privacy impact assessment is an integral part of ‘Privacy by Design.’ The basis of PIA is ‘risk assessment’ involving risk identification, evaluation, and analysis. Available research works related to PIA can be classified into two broad categories: (1) guidelines on organizational and management level tasks related to PIA and; (2) guidelines focusing only on privacy risk assessment methodology. Several countries have developed their own guidelines for conducting PIA. In this section, a comparative study of available PIA techniques, especially which provide implementation-level instructions, is presented.

The privacy risk assessment framework (PIAF) project reviewed various existing PIA processes and methodologies and formulated an optimized PIA process (Wright, 2013). It can be considered a high level guideline, and although it specifies that risks should be assessed in terms of likelihood and impact, how those details can be captured is not mentioned.

In the PIA guidelines proposed by the Commission Nationale de l’Informatique et des Libertes (2012) assessing risks depends on the severity and likelihood of the risk. Severity is measured in terms of potential impact of privacy breach on personal data and likelihood is measured in terms of risk sources and supporting assets involved with the data. These guidelines use a semi-quantitative approach and the final outcome is privacy controls for identified privacy risks.

Wagner and Boiten (2018) proposed a PIA methodology wherein they expressed privacy risk value as a distribution instead of an average score. They proposed a systematic methodology for the quantification of impact and likelihood of risk. These values were then combined to obtain a risk distribution for the enterprise as a whole. However, the authors did not provide any specific method for combining these values.

PRIAM (De, Le Métayer, 2016) defines a risk model where privacy harms, privacy weaknesses, risk sources, and feared events are considered. The risk level for privacy harm is assessed in terms of severity and likelihood. Harm trees are constructed to represent the relationship among key factors, privacy weaknesses, and risk sources. This model uses a quantitative approach for measuring the likelihood of privacy harm and a qualitative approach for measuring severity of the same.

Alshammari and Simpson (2018) presented another risk assessment approach expanding the core concept of PRIAM. Here, the assessment of exploitability and severity of vulnerabilities are influenced by context-relative processing norms. The assessment of motivation behind a threat is analyzed using the value of the personal data and the motive behind processing the data.

Trabelsi, Salzgeber, Bezzi, and Montagnon (2009) proposed a tool for identifying disclosure risk of a dataset having sensitive data. The tool is not only capable of identifying re-identification risks for a proposed disclosure, but also suggests a safe combination to aid the user during information disclosure. All possible correlations between different data items of the dataset and risk values associated with each combination are defined beforehand. Depending upon the user’s disclosure request, privacy risks for those selected attributes are estimated and it is decided whether the disclosure is permissible.

Spiekermann and Oetzel (2012) proposed a PIA model and tested the same in the field of radio-frequency identification (RFID) technology. This is one of the earliest works for standardizing privacy impact assessment and it has been established as a guideline for the development of privacy-aware RFID applications. In the proposed methodology, privacy requirements are expressed in terms of privacy targets, and targets are weighed and assigned protection demand categories. The threats to each privacy target are assessed and controls are identified to mitigate those threats.

A comparative study of different PIA methods is presented in Table 3.

Privacy Compliance

Implementation of privacy in an enterprise is not only about technical measures, but also about proper management of those techniques. Several researchers have focused their privacy research on how the privacy-enhancing techniques are implemented such that they comply with relevant legal frameworks and privacy policies of the enterprise.

Mont, Pearson, and Thyne (2006) described an integrated suite of privacy technologies to help enterprises automatically enforce privacy policies and check the compliance of implemented policies with privacy requirements. The solution has been integrated with an existing identity management system. The operational aspect of privacy is comprised of the principles proposed by the Fair Information Practice Principles (FIPP); the compliance aspect is about ensuring that data is processed according to legal and contractual requirements, business requirements, and expectations of users. This approach is comprised of an access control-based obligation enforcement technique that checks for necessary control implementation; whether the controls are in place; whether these are configured correctly, et cetera. The major drawback of this solution is that it does not provide any automated technique or guideline for the conversion of generic privacy policies to tangible privacy goals. In addition, while analyzing privacy obligations, privacy-specific properties such as anonymity, unlinkability, undetectability, and others, are not considered.

Guarda, Ranise, and Siswantoro (2017) presented a declarative framework to support the specification of information system design, purpose-aware access control policies, and the legal requirements derived from the GDPR in a coherent and uniform manner. It is meant to address the privacy of customers, along with the security of the information system. It uses first-order logic for specifying access permissions based on different combinations of security attributes. The access control policies and legal requirements are formalized for compliance checking. However, it does not consider other aspects of privacy.

Research by Pasquier et al. (2018) discussed how audit data for privacy compliance can be gathered and managed in a large-scale IoT system, and how graph-processing tools can be used effectively to query the audit data. The researchers proposed capturing provenance data to assess actual system behavior. This can be compared with expected system behavior (derived from legal and contractual requirements and users’ expectations) for compliance checking. The approach is suitable for IoT systems only.

A recent work by Diamantopoulou, Androutsopoulou, Gritzalis, and Charalabidis (2018) suggested a methodology for making a system GDPR-compliant in cases where crowd sourcing is used. The researchers identified the privacy needs for crowd sourcing approaches with respect to GDPR and suggested privacy design patterns for the same. The paper does not propose any new privacy enhancing technique, but suggests selecting one from the available techniques. The major drawback is that it caters to a specific domain and regulation only (crowd-sourcing and GDPR), and cannot be customized for other privacy domains and standards.

In another recent work, Alshammari and Simpson (2018) proposed a privacy-engineering model, named the Abstract Personal Data Lifecycle (APDL) Model, to express privacy requirements in terms of states, roles, and operations. The paper also provides an UML-based solution for maintaining compliance with the identified requirements. For purpose binding, purpose is decomposed into actions and events. The requirements of different privacy standards and expectations of stakeholders are considered by the model. The model considers privacy compliance as a purpose binding issue and, therefore, proposes a design mechanism for the same. The main drawback is that it works only at the design level and the process is mostly manual.

A summary of the research papers is presented in Table 4. It can be seen that there is a lack of a generic framework for the verification of privacy compliance of an enterprise information infrastructure. In addition to research papers, there are several standards for data privacy. Privacy standards are collections of frameworks, best practices, and controls, for privacy management. If an enterprise follows one or more standard(s), its data privacy needs can be properly managed.

Popular Privacy Standards

ISO/IEC 29100 (ISO, 2011) provides a privacy framework applicable to organizations dealing with Information and Communication Technology Systems where privacy controls are required for the processing of PII. It specifies a common privacy terminology and defines the actors and their roles in processing PII. It also describes privacy safeguarding considerations and provides pointers on privacy principles.

ISO/IEC 29151 (ISO, 2017) provides controls and guidelines for the protection of PII. As per this standard, privacy requirements are generated from three different sources, namely enterprise policies, legal and contractual requirements, and privacy risk assessment. An enterprise should identify the important requirements as per its risk management criteria and budget, and select relevant privacy controls for the same. The standard also mentions that the current lifecycle stage of PII should be considered while choosing controls. There are approximately 14 control categories that are almost similar to those detailed in ISO/IEC 27002 (ISO, 2013) standard. ISO/IEC 29151(ISO, 2017) contains an additional 13 control categories, which are specifically applicable for the protection of PII while in the custody of an enterprise.

ISO/IEC 27018 (ISO, 2019) deals with protection of PII that is processed in a public cloud. It provides a set of controls, in addition to those of ISO/IEC 27002 (ISO, 2013), aimed at cloud service providers. It helps service providers comply with applicable obligations while the data is in their custody. It also helps enterprises to implement appropriate privacy controls by providing specific implementation guidelines.

ISO/IEC 29101(ISO, 2018) describes a high-level architecture framework and associated controls for safeguarding privacy in Information and Communication Technology (ICT) systems that store and process PII. It provides guidance for planning, designing, and building ICT system architectures that safeguard the privacy of PII by controlling the processing, access, and transfer, of PII. It shows how Privacy Enhancing Technologies (PETs) can be used as privacy controls.

NIST SP 800-122 (McCallister, 2010) provides guidelines for a risk-based approach to protecting the confidentiality of PII. It explains the importance of protecting the confidentiality of PII in the context of information security and explains its relationship to privacy using the Fair Information Practices. It provides context-based guidance for identifying PII and determining the level of protection that is appropriate for each instance of PII. The standard also suggests safeguards that may offer appropriate levels of protection for PII, and provides recommendations for developing response plans for incidents involving PII. Enterprises may customize the recommendations to meet their specific privacy requirements.

Modeling Privacy in an Enterprise Information System

In this section, a survey on available holistic models for integrating privacy in the implementation of enterprise information systems is presented.

Modeling is a popular technique that is used in security and privacy research to understand the working of an enterprise and its security and privacy requirements. Generally, modeling approaches are grouped into three broad categories: formal models, BPMN (White, 2004) or process models, and modeling-language based approaches.

One of the earliest models for implementing privacy was proposed by Karjoth and Schunter (2002). They proposed an access control-based model, extending a flexible authorization framework (Jajodia, Samarati, Sapino, & Subrahmanian, 2001) to accommodate principles related to privacy. Other than authorization, they also introduced the concept of administrative domains and showed how authorization can be applied to the same. Privacy principles such as consent and purpose binding have been modeled using extended authorization. The model is implementable and verifiable. However, it does not consider enterprise business processes while defining purpose binding and consent.

In a paper by Barth, Mitchell, Datta, and Sundaram (2007), the authors developed a general framework for specifying and verifying privacy and utility goals of business processes. Privacy is considered only as a confidentiality requirement. The framework is capable of identifying privacy violating agents. Thus, it can be said that the model is audit-compliant with respect to data disclosure to agents. However, it does not consider consent, consent revocation, and purpose binding. Also, it focuses on data storage and disclosure phases, but not on collection, archiving, and deletion phases.

Researchers Xia et al. (2015) attempted to model the adversaries in an enterprise network. The authors argue that attack by adversaries is not a one-time affair, but a series of attack scenarios. They proposed a re-identification-based risk framework that formalized potential penalties and information uncertainty that are present in a real world scenario where a de-identified dataset is present. They concluded that whether the record of an individual is exploited not only depends on the availability of the de-identified datasets, but also on how easily the data can be linked to available external records. They have also shown that an attacker is probably going to exploit all the records in an equivalence class. The advantage of this model is that it considers deterrence mechanisms. The major drawback of the model is the unavailability of external records while evaluating risks.

In research by Witt, Feja, Speck, and Prietz (2012), the authors presented a privacy modeling and validation technique that is integrated with an existing business process model. The paper also proposes a multi-view concept, i.e. views with concentrated and reduced privacy. The aim of this paper was to integrate privacy aspects with a process modeling architecture. The authors used an example to show how a process can be modeled along with its privacy needs. Privacy rules are expressed formally using Graphical–Computational Tree Logic (G-CTL) (Del Bimbo & Vicario, 1999) that specifies temporal behavior of the system. The researchers presented how privacy requirements like deletion of data, collection minimization, etc., can be expressed using G-CTL.

Jung and Kim (2015) studied the need for continuous privacy protection and monitoring in an enterprise environment and proposed a framework for an information privacy program. The framework consists of four domains, eighteen indicators and fifty-nine metrics to cover the necessary components of information privacy. This is based on the business models of ISACA and Gartner. The proposed framework is divided into two major domains: oversight and implementation. Implementation domain consists of people, process, and technology. The oversight domain consists of three sources of privacy requirements, i.e. privacy governance, risk management, and privacy compliance. With the inputs from the members of a core privacy expert group, the researchers attempted to measure the feasibility and materiality of each of those metrics. The major contribution of this study is that it has identified the privacy research areas needed to be addressed immediately.

Lam, Mitchell, Scedrov, Sundaram, and Wang (2012) tried to formalize the privacy policies of a healthcare organization and show that for any formalized healthcare policy of a certain form, there exists a finite model under certain assumptions. They also provided an algorithm for creating the finite representative model. This can eventually be used for deriving training materials. The researchers attempted the conversion of policies in logic form into a form of policy associated with cryptographic access control.

In a 2017 paper, Ahmadian, Strüber, Riediger, and Jürjens (2017) proposed a model-based approach to support the analysis of the design of a system concerning privacy. The model can be used from an early stage of system design and development. The researchers integrated different modules for addressing privacy elements, such as purpose binding, visibility, granularity, and retention within a security analysis tool.

Researchers Geng, Liu, and Bryant (2010) proposed a personalized framework that would help individual users manage their privacy preferences effectively. The framework converts standard privacy policies to comprehensible texts, highlighting the clauses where the user is expected to make privacy choices.

Angelopoulos et al. (2017) provided a platform called ‘VisiOn’ that enables public administrations to analyze privacy from different viewpoints such as requirements, threats, trust, legal perspective, etc. It also considers ‘preference of users’ for e-governance systems. The framework is comprised of four major components: Desktop Framework, the Web Framework, the VisiOn Database (VDB), and the Visualization Tool (ViTo). Although the framework has taken a holistic approach for privacy implementation, it relies mainly on access control mechanisms and considers privacy as a confidentiality requirement only.

Researchers Martiny, Elenius, and Denker (2018) proposed an ontology-based policy framework, which is useful for data sharing and deciding whether to allow a specific data request. While requesting certain data, the requester should specify parameters such as policy authority to be queried, data requester, requested data items, and the time of request. For each request, the policy engine would check whether a rule exists to allow or deny that particular request, and returns the decision accordingly. The policy engine also provides an explanation for the decision in natural language, such that it can be understood easily by the data requester. The overriding mechanism, in case of policy conflicts, can also be specified.

Researchers Agrafiotis, Creese, Goldsmith, and Papanikolaou (2010) attempted to represent privacy requirements formally. The paper identifies the points of conflict and ambiguities among those requirements. It proposes two approaches for modeling consent and revocation of consent; one is based on access control and the other on Hoare logic. In the access control model, consents and revocations are formalized using labeled transition systems. Here, users and their privacy preferences are the main elements, and consent and revocations are perceived as dynamic modifications of preferences. In the Hoare logic-based model, consent and revocation have been modeled with a set of rights. Ambiguities related to consent and their revocations were also considered.

Research by Abe and Simpson (2016) proposed an access control-based formal model to address the gap between privacy policies, written in natural language, and their implementation. Privacy is perceived as a constraint on processing personal data, and the implementation model is based on role-based access control. The major drawbacks of the model are: (1) it needs considerable manual intervention to assign permission to roles, such as assigning process identifier values, etc.; (2) it focuses primarily on obligations on data sharing, but not spatial or temporal obligations; (3) it does not consider privacy parameters other than confidentiality and major privacy goals, such as purpose binding, consent revocation, etc., were not considered.

In a study by Decroix, Lapon, De Decker, and Naessens (2013) the researchers suggested a formal approach for the analysis of privacy properties of complex electronic services. Their typed first-order logic-based framework is flexible and capable of formally modeling the services. The main elements of the model are: user; user’s credentials; an identifier for the user; the service provider organization; and the trust relationship between customer and service provider. Based on the different trust levels assigned by users, user profiles are created and grouped, and privacy requirements of different levels are identified. The positives of the model are that it considers data storage, processing, distribution, and new data generation from existing private data.

Researchers Datta et al. (2011) introduced a logic approach for representing privacy policies and a semantic model of the same for representing contextual information. Contextual information comprises of disclosure event logs, roles’ database, and data attribute information, etc. The logical framework restricts the flow of personal data, which are not appropriate as per the given privacy policies, by modeling each privacy rule as a combination of data, user roles to access those data, past provisions, and future obligations. The researchers also proposed an algorithm for auditing system logs for privacy violations. The major drawbacks of this research paper are: (1) it focuses mainly on confidential data flow, but does not focus on other properties like anonymity, unlinkability, undetectability, etc.; (2) although it focuses on audit mechanism, it does not stress on accountability and (3) the privacy risks generated due to hardware and other supporting assets were not considered.

A review of the different privacy models shows that most of the formal modeling approaches have used access-control based techniques. This means that privacy has been considered as a ‘confidentiality’ requirement only. In process model-based approaches, though different extensions of process modeling notations have been used, there is no generally accepted approach for modeling privacy. There are few techniques that can model actual privacy principles, information systems and data together, as well as suggest an appropriate privacy solution. Thus, there is lack of a comprehensive model of privacy in enterprise information systems.

FUTURE RESEARCH DIRECTIONS

In this chapter, surveys on different phases of privacy engineering have been presented and respective research gaps have been identified. From the identified gaps, it is obvious that there exists no comprehensive and holistic framework for protection of data privacy in an enterprise. Such a framework is needed for enabling enterprises to address data privacy issues, combat cybercrime, and maintain compliance with relevant laws and standards. The framework should be able to capture the privacy requirements of all stakeholders; convert those requirements into technical and implementable requirements of the enterprise information system; implement the same; and evaluate the compliance of the system with privacy requirements.

CONCLUSION

From previous analyses, it is understood that expressing privacy requirements, assessing privacy impacts, and modeling data privacy for an enterprise information system considering all privacy properties i.e. confidentiality, integrity, availability, anonymity, unlinkability, undetectability, and unobservability, will provide a holistic solution. However, the surveys presented in this study, suggest that almost no approach has considered all of these properties together while proposing a solution. It is also understood that there is no holistic framework available for ensuring that privacy requirements are formally captured, privacy risks are identified, and appropriate measures are taken to mitigate those risks. It is hoped that this study will assist researchers who are working towards diminishing the research gaps in various phases of privacy engineering.

KEY TERMS AND DEFINITIONS

Privacy by Design: An approach where privacy should be taken into account throughout the entire engineering process.

Privacy Compliance: An enterprise’s conformity to some established privacy guidelines provided by standardization organizations.

Privacy Modeling: The process of developing an abstract model to understand, conceptualize, and implement privacy, in the system design.

Privacy Requirement Engineering: The process of defining and eliciting, documenting, and maintaining privacy requirements, throughout the system design phase.

Privacy Risk Assessment: The overall process of risk identification, risk analysis, and risk evaluation, with regard to the handling of personally identifiable information (PII).

ABSTRACT

Coronavirus has affected China massively. This creates dread among the peoples in the world. Cyber criminals tend to take advantage of fear through malicious activities. Cyber criminals generate a phishing and spam campaign to trick the people in the name of Coronavirus. According to current analysis, the criminals hide malware behind different documents that are shared for creating awareness for the people regarding Coronavirus. Kaspersky technologies discovered that such documents contain viruses, trojans, worms, etc. (malwares) that can infect other files on victims’ systems and corrupt or encrypt them. In this chapter, the nature, behavior, and types of different malware and their impacts are analyzed. An analysis is performed on how attackers’ attacks using that malware to misuse the victim’s data and what the techniques used to perform the attack are. In this chapter, an experimental analysis is performed to detect these attacks, and also measures and guidelines are proposed to prevent these types of attacks.

INTRODUCTION

Cybercrime involves crime using computers, network, internet communication and any digital devices connected to the Internet. Cybercrimes are performed by the criminals having bad intention to damage, steal or modify data or information stored in computer or any other digital devices. There are several types of cybercrime attack. Phishing attack is one of the type of cybercrime attack. Some examples of cyber-attacks are discussed below:

*   a. Denial-of-Service (DoS): sends flood of packets to exhaust the resource.
*   b. Man-in-Middle Attack: here attacker act as intruder between server and client communication.
*   c. Phishing Attack: In this type of attack, the attacker sends spam and malicious email that pretend to be from trusted network.
*   d. Password Attack: In this type of attack, hacker tries to crack the password.
*   e. SQL Injection Attack: Here hacker tries to hack database by executing invalid SQL queries.
*   f. Cross-Site Scripting: Here cyber-criminal runs some script on a vulnerable web browser and hack the web browser.
*   g. Eavesdropping Attack: In this type of attack, the attacker grasps some confidential information that an individual is sending through network.
*   h. Malware Attack: Cyber criminal’s motive is to spread malware like virus, trojan, worms etc. to a victim’s system or network.

Phishing attack is a type of cyber-attack where cybercriminal collect or gather the information or credentials like user name and password and other details through fake websites or spam emails. Phishing attack is a type of social engineering attack where cyber criminals gain the trust of a victim through fake website and spam emails. Steps of Phishing attack are shown in Figure 1.

| Figure 1. Steps of Phishing attack |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch004.f01](i/ch004.f01.png) |
| --- |

Types of Phishing Attacks:

*   a. CEO Fraud/Business Emails: Cyber-criminal sends emails to lower level employees who works in accounting or finance department. The goal of these emails is often to get their victim to transfer funds to a fake account. In this attack the attacker clones a authenticated message and send it to a victim
*   b. Domain Spoofing: In this attack the attacker creates a fake website and ask user to enter their credential.
*   c. Evil Twin: Attacker creates a fake Wi-Fi access point which appears as authentic. If any victim connects itself to this access point the hacker collects all the information from the packets travelling through this point.
*   d. HTTPS Phishing: In this approach the cybercriminals send spam emails that pretends to be authentic to victim. This email contains malicious links in the body. If a user clicks on the link it gets hacked
*   e. Smishing: Here attacker sends malicious payloads with the text messages and convince victim to download that infected file and in turn it gets infected.
*   f. Spear Phishing: Hacker sends a bulk of spam messages with malicious content pretending as a campaign to the individuals of an organisation.
*   g. Vishing: Cyber criminals call through a phone to a victim and try to collect confidential data by gaining trust of the victim.

Malwares are nothing but a malicious code which exploits the vulnerabilities of a system. These malicious codes may hide themselves in packets to bypass the Antivirus, Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) or Firewall. These malwares may attach themselves in some documents, program codes to spread themselves over the internet. Cyber criminals develop such malicious code and target a vulnerable system to attack and exploit the system. Various types of malwares are as follows:

*   a. Virus: It is a self-replicating virus. It attaches itself with some document, program code but it requires human activity to spread themselves over the internet.
*   b. Worms: It is same as virus but it doesn’t require any human help to spread themselves. It exploits vulnerable operating system.
*   c. Trojan: These malwares attacks in disguise. They gain the trust of the user and force them to download and install such malware. Using trojan malware malicious hacker gain access of a targeted user and steal confidential data.
*   d. Bot: It is automated malicious code. A controller is needed to run these bots. Multiple Bots forms a Botnet which leads to Botnet attack.
*   e. Adware and Spyware: Adware are pop-ups advertisement which are seen in a website. They are gaining information for revenue purpose. Spyware is a malicious code. These codes are hidden in a adware and a user when clicks on such pop-ups the spyware gets installed into the system. These spyware notes every activity of victim and send it to the attacker.
*   f. Ransomware: Malicious actor locks and encrypt victim by running malicious code and demand a ransom or pay against that data.
*   g. Rootkit: Cyber-criminal obtains administrative privileges of victim system using rootkit malware.

During COVID-19 the malicious actors are mostly using Trojan malware to hack system.

BACKGROUND

Phishing entices victims to visit fake sites and reveal their private data through fabricated messages. In phishing, hacker creates a fake website and sends the hyperlink of this website to user via email or instant messaging. User is unaware of such site and opens the hyperlink unknowingly and shares the information with it.

The type of phishing without enticement is known as Pharming. A hacker hijacks a computer system and installs malicious code that causes the system's website traffic to be transferred to the hacker's fake site. This happens without victim’s permission. The hacker then takes private and personal information entered on these fake sites.

There are two types of phishing:

*   1\. Manipulation of Link: In this method, hacker manipulates the links in such a way that user is not able to easily identify the page has opened from genuine website or fake website.
*   2\. Website Forgery: In this method, the address bar is altered by hacker. Hacker does this by the following tricks: 
    *   a. Hacker hides the address bar
    *   b. Make use of script to alter the contents of address bar
    *   c. On legitimate URL, image is added over address bar

In current situation Coronavirus disease has affected worldwide. The disease is so infectious that it is spreading very fast all over the world. This creates a panic situation among the people in the world. People are searching lots of websites related to this virus to get the knowledge and awareness about the virus. They are also forwarding messages or various documents regarding these viruses to create awareness. Similarly, several government and private health organisations are also sending messages or documents through emails or websites. Cyber criminals misuse these opportunities to get confidential data or credentials through Phishing attack. Cyber criminals use malware to perform Phishing attack. Such type of attack is named as Coronavirus malware attack.

PROPOSED WORK

Phishing attack is a method to steal credentials and other confidential data by gaining trust in disguise of the victims. In Phishing attack cyber criminals generally have motive to steal username, password, bank account information or other confidential data. It is said that if a system is totally secured then also it can be hacked through phishing attack. Phishing attack are performed in two method. In the first method attacker send spam emails which contains malicious file attached with it. Hacker may spoof domains of a trusted organisation and send such emails. They use these spoofing techniques to gain trust of the victim. A victim which when clicks or downloads these files these malware gets installed and infects the targeted system. In second method hackers create a fake URL and send these links through emails. A victim when click on these links a malicious page is opened which asks for the credentials. Victim on providing these credentials may lose confidential data. These fake websites contain Trojan which gather the credentials entered by a victim and uses the credential for data theft.

The methodology is as follows:

*   Step 1: The phishing attacks are performed in two ways. Firstly, creating a fake URL & sharing the URL to a victim. The victim on clicking on the fake URL enters the credential that is captured by the attacker. Secondly, sending spam emails which contain malicious documents attached with it.
*   Step 2: Detection Techniques of the above-mentioned phishing attacks. Several syntactic, semantic and pragmatic techniques are discussed in this chapter. Also, the techniques to detect phishing emails, URLs and web pages are discussed. The techniques of malware analysis are discussed.
*   Step 3: In this chapter prevention guidelines are mentioned from such type of phishing attacks. Preventive measures are steps that can be followed to avoid any theft due to such attack.

2\. Phishing Detection

Phishing attacks can be performed using email and website/URL. In all the categories of phishing the syntactic, semantic and pragmatic features are used to detect the phishing techniques.

*   i. Syntactic Technique: In this it features the correctness of the syntax of the email id, website and URL. For email id, there should be local-part, @symbol and a domain. For example, abc@example.com. So, in the example ABC in the local-part and domain is example.com. So, for a valid email id it should have a valid domain name (El Aassal et al., 2020). Top level domain name is .com or .net. Hacker sometimes uses fake domains .app, .ooo, .xyz, .online, .site, .club, .top, .info, .icu, .website etc. For URL and website, the valid syntax is scheme: //host: part/path? query-string#fragment-id. Scheme is the protocol used to access the Internet like http, https, ftp, mailto. Host is the hostname where the resource is present. Path is the path where the resource is present. Query string consist of the data that is to be sent to the server. Fragment id contains the location within a page where fragment is present. So, hostname is the local domain name to access the resource. For example, www.example.com. Here www is the host’s machine name and example.com is the domain name. The hackers uses fake URL for Phishing attack. For example, the registered name is “google” but instead of that they used fake that is “goggle”. URL are shortened by URL shortener. For example, https://goo.gl/rkmzol. Such URLs may be malicious. Also viewing the header of a suspicious mail it can be detected that from where the email has actually send. The Figure 7 shows a phishing email about covid-19 data. In Figure 8 the header information of the specific email is shown in Figure 8. It is found that the email is not authenticated and a fake email is send using a email shortener emkei.cz.
*   ii. Semantic Techniques: In this technique, the main motive is to check the meaning of the text in the content of the email, URLs and websites. These semantic techniques help to find the hidden objects meaning within the content of the email (El Aassal et al., 2020). They check whether there is any information regarding updation, verification. In the term like “Click here” or “Act on” etc (El Aassal et al., 2020). The following Figure 9 is an example of semantic attack on eBay In semantic technique special character @ in URL or email is also checked (El Aassal et al., 2020). The following example shows how cyber criminals can link one website with the other. http://www.example.com@www.phishing.com. In this URL the example com links with phishing.com, which is another URL. If a victim clicks on the URL thinking that it is forwarding to example.com instead it will get forward to a fake phishing webpage that is phishing.com. So, care is taken for such type to features. Hackers use characters having almost same representation for phishing attack. For example, www.bloom.com. In this URL instead of “oo” hackers use “00” and create a fake link. A victim misunderstood “00” as “oo” and clicked on the link. Similarly, the small letter “l” and the digit “1” are almost same representation. In Semantic techniques such letters should be considered.

*   iii. Pragmatic Techniques: Sometimes the age of a registration page, details of any website are disabled by the cyber criminals so that a victim can’t check. In pragmatic technique such type of feature is detected. Sometimes a hacker disables the HTML source code view options of a webpage so the victim cannot be check whether it is authenticated web page (El Aassal et al., 2020).
*   iv. Lexical Techniques: Such features use the semantics and syntactic features to detect a phishing website and URL. In this technique, it detects a fake website or URL on the basis of backlisted words, whitelisted words, the malicious content within the email. Lexical techniques are the bottom level of syntactic, semantic and pragmatic techniques (El Aassal et al., 2020).
*   v. Network Techniques: In this technique, it checks if the port number in present in the URL and features extracted from the HTTP protocol of a website. In the above-mentioned cases network techniques acts as the bottom level of Syntactic feature. Under semantic feature network technique checks the match between the port number and the protocol used within URL. Similarly, it verifies the download time on the basis of the type of the content attached in websites. Under pragmatic features network techniques checks Autonomous number and who is information (El Aassal et al., 2020).
*   vi. Scripts Techniques: under syntactic features it checks the escape, eval, etc. in the script in URL and also checks the number of external scripts in websites. Under semantic features it checks which file extensions are present in the URL path and also checks whether there is any malicious file or any other suspicious behaviour in the website. Under pragmatic features it checks the loading time of the script of URL and checks whether a website loads in proper way (El Aassal et al., 2020).
*   vii. Email features: A phishing email can be detected on the basis of analysis of Email headers, Body of the emails, Text features, Email URL features and attachment features. In email header analysis the lexical technique is applied to gather information about some suspicious blacklisted words in subject, information of message IDs, and checks whether content of the emails is in plain text. After applying the network features it verifies the sender and receiver path domains and finds whether there are any mismatches in the IP addresses in the path. It also verifies the domain keys. In body feature techniques consist of text class and URL class. In text class, the lexical features are applied to find the text from the email content and HTML and is verified whether there are any blacklisted words. Network features and Script techniques are applied to text class to find the features like website pages. In email URL class it verifies the features of the URL, secure connections, the difference in URL domains from the sender address and the number of URL with same IP address. Email attachment type of attachment whether malware is present or not (El Aassal et al., 2020). The following Figure 10 show how an individual can check the header of a suspicious email. Here mxtoolbox.com site is used to check the email header content.

*   viii. Malware Analysis: Malware are detected using Antivirus or Anti malware systems. Intrusion Detection/ Prevention Systems (IDS/IPS), Host Based IPS (HIPS), Firewall are also used to detect malware. These systems used signature based, behavior based and anomaly-based approaches to detect a malware. Malware analyst generally used two types of approach: 
    *   A. Static analysis: Malware analyst analyses the code and tries to find any hidden actions are there in the code. They use to disassemble the code to find any malicious action within the code. Antivirus, while performing static analysis, does reverse engineering i.e., they use disassemblers, debuggers and debuggers. In static analysis antiviruses try to find and match the signatures from malware databases. So static analysis is a signature-based analysis.
    *   B. Dynamic Analysis: It is a behavior or heuristic based approach. While performing dynamic analysis, malware analyst checks the behavior of the malware by executing it in a sandbox environment. This sandbox environment helps the analyst to prevent the malware to infect the systems. Again, this environment also provides a rolled back mechanism which help the system to rolled back to the clean state after analysis.
    *   C. Hybrid Analysis: It is a combination of both static and dynamic analysis. In this approach, malware analyst first detects the malware using dynamic analysis and then analyze the code using static analysis. It is observed that hybrid analysis is better to use for new type of malware.

Malware used packers to hide themselves so that Antivirus will not be able to detect. Also some of the malwares are encrypted themselves in a packer such that if they are detected then also these malwares cannot be encrypted by the malwares. Unpacker tools are used to to detect such malwares who hides themselves. Several disassembler or debugger tools are also used to static and dynamic analysis. Some of the tools used are:

*   A. PE Explorer: This tool is used to disassemble the code.
*   B. WinDbg: It is a debugging tool
*   C. OllyDgb: A debugging tool
*   D. GNU debugger: A debugging tool
*   E. Prodump32: A unpacker tool
*   F. Reverse Engineering Compiler: A Compiler tool
*   G. WinHex: A Hex editor

STAGES OF MALWARE ANALYSIS

Generally, four stages of analysis are there:

*   A. Fully Automated Analysis: In this stage a malware analyst detects a malware using fully automated tools. It is an easiest way to detect malware and can be done quickly. This analysis generates detailed reports on the network traffic, file activity and registry keys. But this analysis does not provide as much information as a malware analyst. Cuckoo is an opensource fully automated toolkit used for analysing malwares. Other automated tool are Zone Wine, Buster Sandbox Analyzer, Malheur, REMnux etc. (Mastering 4 Stages of Malware Analysis, n.d.)
*   B. Static Properties Analysis: A full in-depth knowledge can be provided through static properties analysis. Here a malware code is analysed using static analysis approach. Several properties like PE header information, hashes, embedded strings, embedded resources are analysed in this stage. It provides an easy way to detect a malware. Virustotal is one of the efficient online tools to detect malwares and it uses static properties analysis (Mastering 4 Stages of Malware Analysis, n.d.).
*   C. Interactive Behaviour Analysis: Malware analyst executes malwares in a isolated laboratory to observe the behaviour of the malware. The analyst monitors the behaviour of the malware frequently and periodically. They try to find the way how malware infects the system or how it attaches itself to any host to spread themselves. This help a malware analyst to draw an opinion regarding the behaviour of the malware which is difficult for fully automated analysis stage. (What is malware analysis? Defining and outlining the process of malware analysis, n.d.)
*   D. Manual Code Reversing: Reverse engineering process is used in this stage. Reversing the code means to extract valuable features which cannot be found in Interactive Behaviour Analysis. Reverse-engineering includes the steps like decoding of encrypted data stored or transferred by the malware, Determining the logic of the malicious program’s domain generation algorithm and also understanding other capabilities of the sample that didn’t examine themselves during behaviour analysis. Debuggers or disassemblers tools are used for manual code reversing stage. This stage is used during memory forensic analysis to detect a malicious code. This method is time consuming and also expert skills are needed to do reverse-engineering. So many malware analyst doesn’t use this stage. (Mastering 4 Stages of Malware Analysis, n.d.)

A malware is a malicious software which when gets downloaded and infects the system. Basic components of a malware are, Crypter which is software to protect malware from getting detected through reverse engineering, a downloader which help malware to download, a Dropper which install other file of the malware, an Exploit code which misuses vulnerabilities, an Injector which helps malware to inject in other files which are vulnerable, an Obfuscater which helps malware to hide, a Packer which compress the malware file, a Payload which performs different activities like modifying data, delete data etc what a malware does and a malicious code like Java Applet, ActiveX controls, Browser plugin etc. Two types of malware analysis can be performed, first is Static analysis where a code is analysed. In this type of analysis binary executable code is analysed but purpose of the malware is not taken under consideration and second one is dynamic analysis behaviour of malware and its impact is analysed. In malware analysis we analyse several techniques like malware file fingerprinting, local and online malware scanning, performing string search, Identifying packing, Identifying file dependencies, Malware disassembly. As from Figure 14 the first two bytes have a value 0x4D and 0x5A in hexadecimal format. These two values denote MZ. The starting MZ signifies it is a PE header. Using the PE header an analyst comes to know whether a malware is for 32-bits or 64-bits Windows machine. From the header it is also analyzed whether any packer is used by the malware. Using PE explorer, the malware code is disassembled a shown in Figure 15. Here PE explorer unpacks a malware if it hidden in a packer as shown in Figure 16 and disassembled the malware code. PREVENTIVE MEASURES

Various ways we can prevent Phishing are as follows:

*   i. Anti phishing techniques are used to detect as well as prevent Phishing attacks. The Antiphishing techniques are: 
    *   a. Attribute based Antiphishing: In this method different attribute checks are performed like image attribute check, certificate check, and URL check. In this technique checking is done like a URL allocated to a page is relatively new. It verifies the image of a suspicious website and compares its similarity with the authenticated site (Malware detection of Coronavirusmap.com.exe application, n.d.).
    *   b. Genetic Algorithm based Antiphishing: Here Genetic algorithm logic is used. These algorithms generate a simple rule on the basis of principles. Using these a fake or phished website can be differentiated from the original one. The advantage of these technologies is that it can detect phishing email before it is opened (Malware detection of Coronavirusmap.com.exe application, n.d.).
    *   c. Character-based Antiphishing: In this type of technology URL is checked whether URL has any hidden destination embedded within it. It also verifies whether there is any hidden dotted format destination IP address within the URL. Using this method both known and unknown phishing techniques can be avoided but sometimes this technology gives false positive result (Malware detection of Coronavirusmap.com.exe application, n.d.).
    *   d. Content-based Antiphishing: In this method it detects the website which have short live and low ranking but make their ranking high (Malware detection of Coronavirusmap.com.exe application, n.d.).
    *   e. Identity-based Antiphishing: This technology checks a phishing website based on some features of the identity of the website (Malware detection of Coronavirusmap.com.exe application, n.d.).
*   ii. Handling the emails: Every individual should be educated about the phishing ideas and while handling with emails they should be careful. 
    *   a. To know how the email has reached.
    *   b. Whether it is an authoritative website is to be verified.
    *   c. Personal or financial information should not be shared unless it is sure.
    *   d. Links or URLs should be checked several times before clicking.
    *   e. Some portion of the suspected email can be pasted in google browser to check whether there are some reports against those emails are present.
    *   f. Mobiles, computers, laptop should be updated regularly.
    *   g. A strong and unique password should be used by the user.
    *   h. Extra level of security should be used like 2 way authentication, using of updated antivirus software etc.
*   iii. Content of email: An email having content of illogical meaning and of poor quality may be fake. An individual must be sure about the email before downloading anything from the email. Any text “Click here” or “Act on” should be avoided.
*   iv. Any email telling about reward should be avoided.
*   v. Any website asking for personal details should be avoided.
*   vi. Any email asking individual to renew any policy or update any licenses may be a fraud email. Care should be taken for such cases.
*   vii. Any email where a warning message like “Your system is hacked. Click on this to recover the data” is dangerous. Individual should not click on such emails. Rather they should contact an authenticated Ethical Hacker.
*   viii. Any URL shortened using URL shortener should be avoided.
*   ix. SSL provides a secure communication channel. Any site which do not have valid SSL certificate may be a fake website. Care should be taken for that.
*   x. Individuals should avoid pop-ups. No credentials should be entered in pop-ups.
*   xi. Updated antivirus should be installed in an individual system so that these antiviruses will prevent any malware for getting downloaded.
