KEY TERMS AND DEFINITIONS

Adversarial Learning: A research field that combines machine learning and computer security.

Anonymization: A technique to sanitize information for privacy protection by encryption or removing identifiable information.

Attribute: A characteristic or a property of a specific object.

De-Anonymization: A technique to re-identify the anonymized (encrypted or generalized) information.

Game Theory: Is a mathematical discipline that studies the strategic interaction among rational individuals.

Inference: A process of deriving a result using evidence and reasoning.

Privacy: A state of being apart from monitoring.

Reinforcement Learning: Is an area of machine learning that learn for the experience in order to maximize the rewards.

Utility: The ability of being useful.

ABSTRACT

With the rise in usage of social media, large quantities of data like pictures, videos, audio, and computer graphics are created. As the data is shared over the network, security and privacy become important concerns. Social networks are most popular and have become a medium for instant information sharing. Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp are the most popular social networks. There has been extreme increase in the usage of audiovisual data over the social network. When multimedia data are stored in a networked environment, billions of users get connected to it for different purposes. The privacy challenges are personification, harassment, password sharing, location-oriented services, and privacy vs. marketing. The other challenges are data semantics, content management rights, and false information. There has been significant contribution by the researchers in development of security systems against these threats; still, the problems of clickjacking, short URL, phishing remain unresolved for some network architectures.

MULTIMEDIA DATA OVER SOCIAL MEDIA

As per the work stated by Naaman (2012), presently, several Web-based sharing and public services are used by mobile users. Some examples, such as YouTube and Flickr have made a massive growth with fast growing amount of multimedia content over the web. These contents are continuously available online. The multimedia contents uploaded by individual participants with private/public sharing options. These multimedia contents are accompanied by diverse types of metadata. YouTube have enormous collection of videos in different categories. Sharing of videos over YouTube have shown drastic increase in the business. Many individuals are running their channels on YouTube. The usage of smart devices has been increased and this is the reason for increase in the multimedia content over the internet. These smart and handy devices are making media sharing easy and has become a popular activity across the users. However, all the present social networks offers images/video sharing abilities, many of them are lacking in offering privacy concerns according to Temmermans et al. (2017). With the initiation of internet and social networks, the quantity of multimedia data communication is rapidly increasing. The evolution of social media data, as demonstrated by social networks such as Instagram, YouTube and Facebook, united with developments in multimedia content analysis and underscores potential risks for malicious use. The illegal copying, piracy, plagiarism, and misappropriation. Therefore, secure multimedia sharing and traitor tracing issues have become critical and urgent in social network, C. Ye (2014).

Multimedia forensics supports set of scientific tools for analysis of multimedia data with an aim to reveal the history of multimedia contents. The main purpose of these scientific tools is to retrieve the information from multimedia data. Generally, the digital forensic techniques are verified with freely available image and video datasets. Most of the freely available datasets does not represent the real world scenarios and they are outdated in case of videos. This fact motivates and indicates the need for heterogeneous and large datasets of multimedia data as a benchmark to verify the digital forensic techniques. In the work stated by Shullani et al. a new set of images and videos captured with 35 latest smartphones and tablets. The authors collected 11,732 real images. 7565 images (with high and low quality both) were shared through Facebook. Those images were also shared through WhatsApp. Furthermore, authors picked up 648 videos with 622 videos shared through YouTube with higher resolution and set of videos shared through WhatsApp. The name of the dataset acquired by the authors is VISION dataset. This dataset is acquired from the devices with specific procedure. This dataset is more suitable for multimedia source identification applications. The authors organized the data collected from each device in two folders: images and videos. The images folder contains the social media images. These images have flat surfaces so there are no restrictions on scenario or orientation of images. The videos folder contains the social media videos which are captured in landscape mode. The videos in this folder represents indoor and outdoor scenarios. As an extension of the work, authors gave the procedure used for uploading and downloading the images and videos on social media. Although the VISION dataset is huge representation of images and videos, it is important to have extension of this dataset with different video formats, Dasara Shullani et al. (2017). The protection of multimedia contents over internet has become critical and the system cannot rely on the classical security and protection mechanisms. The additional protection mechanism is required to encourage the authorized distribution of the contents. The mechanism of multimedia fingerprinting is a novel method of protecting multimedia contents. It provides a mechanism to identify the unauthorized users and unauthorized access of data, Z. Jane et al. (2014). Visual cryptography is acts as a powerful technique when secret information sharing happen over internet especially images. It has been observed as a robust technique to share confidential images and documents. Visual Cryptography is an art of encrypting the multimedia contents such that decryption requires no mathematical computations. Visual cryptography encrypts the multimedia secret into number of shares and these shares are distributed among set of participants. The revealing of the multimedia secret information takes place just by superimposition. Though the method is powerful and robust, the space complexity is high because of the number of shares getting generated for each multimedia content, Weir J. et al. (2012). There has been drastic increase in usage of online food services by the users. In food related services, the visual information is important with respect to the search service for particular dish/recipes. Significant amount of research is promoted in food services using food images with different datasets. However, there are some restrictions to these datasets including the type of image set, the momentary capture of the image irrespective of the cooking process and no linking of the images to the recipes. Cookpad Image Dataset in turn is a novel dataset of food images serving the largest recipe search. This is image collection for food research infrastructure. This dataset has approximately 1.64 million images which are taken after cooking. There are approximately 3.10 million images which are taken during cooking process. The Cookpad is also linked with the existing recipe corpus, Jun Harashima et al. (2017).

The term multimedia security is defined as protecting the multimedia data (images, audio’s, video’s) and multimedia systems from unauthorized access, unauthorized use, unauthorized modification or destruction in order to provide integrity, reliability, confidentiality and availability. Integrity means protecting against improper modification or destruction of multimedia data. Reliability indicates the trust about multimedia data and its usage. Confidentiality preserves author’s rights about access and protects as well as preserves the personal and proprietary information. Availability ensures timely access to the user. Multimedia security is required because the applications of technology to multimedia systems creates risks. Multimedia data might be improperly disclosed, modified in wrong way, lost or destroyed which can result in loss of the reputation or damage to the reputation. In context of social media, disclosure of the information is a major risk to the organizations/companies. There are homogenous groups in social media. These groups focuses particular area of interest and can leak the significant amount of the sensitive information. The privacy and confidentiality can be preserved better if one does not join such homogenous groups. It is observed that the users underestimates the dangers of openly made available posts (publically) on the web. As a common behavior, users trusts on the security and the privacy of the websites of the social media assuming that these websites protects the personal data. This blind trust is becoming a significant risk for the industries and the organizations. The people who shares the information too freely over the social media are being rejected by the organizations when they apply for the job or being fired due to unwanted posts sharing in social media and the posts leading to threats. This is a security analysis organization point of view indicating that the people who are too free to share information may result in the security and privacy risks. The multimedia security principles needs to be expanded to incorporate responsibility, trustworthiness and ethics. The protection levels in multimedia security should also be expanded with respect to the individuals and their social relationships. These protection levels should cover the private roles of the users as well as the public roles. As stated by Hekkala Riitta et al. (2012), the post important challenges to the multimedia security caused by the social network is multimedia data integrity and the confidentiality. According to their findings, the important challenge types and the risks are: outside attack on a company or employee, employees unawareness, and the role challenge. The security risk to the outside attack on a company are malware, spam, untrusted applications and unsafe internet connection. The security risks at employees awareness phishing, scams, identity theft, information leakage and reputation damage. The security risks related to the roles are social network tool, private identity and professional identity.

There are intrusion detection systems to monitor social networks for malicious activities that takes the help of security and multimedia information management systems. These systems are signature based or anomaly based. In case of signature based systems, the detection of attack can be done by monitoring the specific pattern such as sequence of bytes over the network. It is very difficult to detect the new and unknown attack with signature based method and has many challenges. In case of anomaly based systems, the concept of machine learning is used to detect unknown attacks. It deals with the malicious insider as well as targeted external attack. However there are significant challenges to anomaly based systems such as noise (which can limit the effectiveness of the intrusion detection system), no clear distinction among false alarm and the real attack and the problem with encrypted packets. As stated by Negandhi P et al. (2019), intrusion detection systems performs better if they are implemented with machine learning algorithms. Such systems are able to detect real time network attacks. Still some of the security challenges are not resolved. The wide range of security and privacy challenges is discussed below in detail.

Privacy

According to Staff Writer (2018), certainly, there are privacy issues with the social media. The top five privacy concerns are given below.

Impersonation and Hacking of Account

The social networks are targeted by the hackers, intruder and online criminals thus the privacy gets compromised. In this case, the online criminals can impersonate the user. They are interested in users account in order to spread the viruses, spam messages and the malware. The people trusts the messages received over social media by their friends and it is more likely to click on the links that can infect the user’s computer system.

Harassment

Online harassment and the cyberbullying is the most dangerous threat and over social media such threats are easily executable. The harassment very often comes from the strangers and from the people who are less friendly over the network. On the other side, some social networks allows advertising on the user’s wall irrespective of the interest of the user. In this case, reduction of the usage of the social media is more likely.

Password Sharing

As the amount of information shared by the user on social media increases, there is a need to strengthen the security and the privacy of an account. Password sharing is one of the major challenge to the privacy and security of multimedia data. The administrative passwords are pervasive in all the organizations of all the sizes. The administrative passwords are very powerful and majority of these passwords are used in shared environment, i.e. the group of administrators uses the same password to access the shared resource. The account privileges are accessible to all the members in that environment. Apart from this fact, the users often shared the official password with their colleagues for some or other reason. The most common reason for such pattern of the sharing is an emergency on someone’s absence. Thus mismanagement of the password leads to multimedia information theft and information manipulation without the trace.

There is a need to put a stop to the password sharing in the organizations. This will reduce the risk of the organization associated with internal as well as external threats. There are three steps to be followed to implement this mechanism. First is implement and communicate strong organization policy. Second, enforce the policy with controls and third, monitor the logs. It is always good to avoid the password sharing at administrative level and thus an ideal solution. Easy mitigation of threats associated with shared password can be implemented using standard set of software’s.

Privacy vs Marketing

Many social media companies are adapting a practice of posting the advertisements through user’s login. There is no financial incentive for the user against the advertisement. It is more likely that the advertisement is seen by the user many times and led to the sale of particular product shown in advertisement. Even user recommends the product to the friend in turn growth in the sale of product is observed. This type of marketing is targeted marketing and have a close association with the privacy of an account. The marketers must be aware of the privacy and security threats to their customers and the business. The general data protection regulation by European Union unify and strengthens the data protection for all the users in European Union. This regulation defines following rights: consent, right to be informed, right to data portability, erasure right, access right, rectification right, restrict processing right and withdraw consent right. On the other side, there is a concept of behavioral marketing. In this, the marketer targets the consumers based on their behavior on social media and the websites. These marketers targets the consumers and sends the advertisements in particular categories. There are security and privacy issues with behavioral marketing.

Location Oriented Services

Most of the users assesses the social media services through smartphones. The social media takes the benefit of the location of the smart devices and recommends the user nearby services or facilities available. Because of this the threat to the privacy and the security increases. The location data of most of the users of smart devices is easily available. Social media applications heavily uses this data.

Data Semantics

Consistent form of multimedia data gives correct information and correct semantics of the media. The correct sense of the images and videos is one of the important challenge faced by social media. Six types of images are used over social media, Roy Olende (2016).

*   • Photos: The post popular type of image over social media. It is found relatively easy to capture a photo through smart phone and to upload over the social media. The challenge is that the uploaded photo is the edited version of the captured photograph and it becomes difficult to observe the real texture of particular object present in the photograph.
*   • Collages: Collages allows to describe a story through set of photographs.
*   • Text over Background: These type of images are used for quick communication with heavy text embedded with an image. The challenge with text over background is that the phrasing of the text over image needs to be carefully designed to maintain the consistency of the data shown by the image. Also the synchronization to be maintained among the phrases and the visual information in an image.
*   • Text over Photo: This is a facility for visual story telling.
*   • Icons and Illustration: They gets added easily with the images over social media. The challenge with this type of images is that the wrong icons may get placed in an image.
*   • Screenshot: The most common type of image allowing to put the latest scenario on the screen.

Cross Site Scripting and De-Anonymization

In this attack, malicious email, website, program or a blog is open on the user computer. This malicious entity makes use of the users’ browser to get connected to another website and then uses the login credentials (indicating that the valid user is interacting at this point). The cross site request forgery is the most common attack usually performed with RESTful API. This API is used to interact between the applications and the social network. The social networking websites have API’s for such applications that retrieves the user related information (for ex. Facebook). A. A. Obiniyi et al. (2014) states the concept of de-anonymization. In case of anonymization, the users can hide the personal information that makes user known over the social network. Such information includes users, profile photo, name, address, contact number and other sensitive data. The purpose of anonymization is to protect the user from advertisers, data hackers, researchers from data miming area and the application developers. However, de-anonymization of the users on social network is possible attack. Combination of the information can be generated from different social networks and can be used to extract the sensitive information. This form of attack is bypassing the user’s privacy settings.

Content Management Rights to Users

The rights, privileges and permissions are correlated terms. Right defines the type of activity a user can perform. Privileges defines how one user can handle the group of users to get involved in the activity while permission defines how user can access the data (read, write, delete, localize). Very first need of the content management right is: right audience at the right place. Billions of users exists over the social media and the media contents are managed by the media users. It includes uploading, downloading, editing, liking and sharing. As the user reserves the content management rights, the challenge faced is an authenticity of user generated content. The mass media contents are being available on the social media leading to different interpretation of the same contents. Such contents creates ambiguity among the media contents and the confidentiality of the contents becomes weak. Liu et al. (2003) states the digital content management rights over social network. This model of content management rights includes the elements: content provider, content distributor, consumer and the clearinghouse. The authors used cryptographic mechanism in the model to strengthen the security concern. These cryptographic mechanisms are, symmetric and asymmetric encryption, digital signatures, one way hash functions, digital certificates and digital watermarking. This digital right management system is used to protect the digital assets with high value and also used to control, distribute and use the access to these digital assets. It offers strong content protection against unauthorized access to the digital contents, also a limited access to the permitted set of users. This model is flexible to manage the user’s rights for different kinds of multimedia contents (e.g. Music files, digital books, videos, images).

False Information Detection

The circulation of fake media (images and videos) over social network is a biggest challenge and growing day by day. The business and commercial media editing tools allow any user to add, clone and to remove the objects from the media. Also these editing tools allows to remove the people from media. Such type of editing generates the false information by generating false images. These images are known as fake images. Several methods have been proposed to identify the fake images but there stands a new attack every day against the method proposed. The most dangerous element over the social media is image to image translation. Such kind of translation changes the meaning of the image thus affecting its semantics. The image to image translation is based on the Generative Adversarial Network. It is dangerous because the context of the image can be changed at any moment. The image forgery detection methods exists to identify the image translation still the methods have challenges over the network, F. Marra et al. (2018).

Clickjacking and Survey Scams Abound

Many social networking websites makes money through the advertisements. For example, Facebook shares many advertisement without prior permission of the user. The most common threat on Facebook is clickjacking. It is also known as likejacking which is based on the UI redressing. This type of attack tricks the users into the confidential information and takes the control of the user’s device when user clicks on the web link. Clickjacking also led the survey scam. In this, the users are asked to install the application through a spammed web link. Because of the awareness among the mobile users, this form of attack is ineffective. Survey scam and the clickjacking are appearing on regular basis over the social networks. These attacks may cause the leakage of the personal information of the user.

Shortened URLs

Twitter is real time information network and it helps is raising and solving the issues. Since the real time information is available, it may misused by the attacker for the personal gain. Twitter uses frequently shorten URL’s. This is done to keep the tweet in specific range of the characters. These small URL’s gives no direct information of the website and directs the users to malicious websites. If such links on twitter asks the user for Facebook or Twitter password then it is always secure to exit out immediately. Some twitter messages are fake which takes the user to some false page and by clicking on such false page, the use account can be easily hacked, Sophos (2020). Social Engineering Attacks

Many social media users are not conscious about the importance and the value of data they are producing. These users pay less attention to keep their data safe against different attacks. The attacker takes benefit of this behavior of the users and tries to reveal the confidential information by executing different mechanisms. In case of reverse social engineering attacks, the attackers establishes the connection with the user by trying different techniques with the higher degree of trust. Fake account creation is the most common practice followed by the attackers. Social engineering attacks are performed through different mechanisms like phishing and pretexting. In case of phishing attack, the attacker enforces the user to do the activities as if they are authentic activities through authentic source. Spear phishing is the special type of phishing attack in which the attacker targets the particular group of high profile users. In spear phishing, attacker starts to collect the personal information of the targeted set of users through different resources. Email address guessing is the most common step by attackers observed in spear phishing. Pretexting is a method in which attackers enforces the user to release the confidential information.

Social Engineering assaults are multifaceted and incorporate physical, social and specialized perspectives, which are utilized in various phases of the real assault.

Physical Methodologies

Katharina et al. (2015) mentions, as the name infers, physical methodologies are those where the assailant plays out some type of physical activity so as to assemble data on a future casualty. This can run from individual data, (for example, standardized savings number, date of birth) to legitimate certifications for a PC framework. A regularly utilized technique is dumpster plunging i.e., looking through an association's rubbish. A dumpster can be a significant wellspring of data for aggressors, who may discover individual information about workers, manuals, reminders and even print-outs of touchy data, for example, client accreditations. On the off chance that an aggressor can access a focused on association's workplaces e.g., in open-plan workspaces e they may discover data, for example, passwords composed on Post-it notes. Less modern physical assaults include burglary or coercion to acquire data.

Specialized Methodologies

With specialized methodologies, it has been noticed that the Internet is particularly intriguing for social specialists to gather passwords, as clients frequently utilize the equivalent (basic) passwords for various records. Many people are likewise not mindful that they are unreservedly giving assailants (or any individual who will scan for it) with a lot of individual data. Aggressors regularly use web crawlers to assemble individual data about future casualties. There are additionally apparatuses that can assemble, aggregate the total data from various Web assets. One of the most mainstream devices of this sort is Maltego. Social systems administration destinations are turning out to be important wellsprings of data also.

Identity Theft and Spamming

Identity theft is the attack of obtaining the financial or personal information of the user for the purpose of assuming the users identity. The high level identity thieves are performed by the attackers over corporate databases to steal the customer’s information. He methods used to perform the identity theft includes phishing, unknown friend request acceptance, account details sharing, poor privacy settings, clicking unnecessary links and getting directed towards unknown websites and free applications downloading. This attack may originate inside the network as well as outside the network. In spamming, the attacker send unnecessary emails in huge number over the network. The purpose of the attacker here is to gain the sensitive information from the users and to use this information to advertise the product and to increase the sell of the product. Cyberbullying is another serious challenge the social network is facing. It is the type of attack which targets the users by sending offensive or harmful information and material. The material may include text, images as well as videos. Once such material reaches to the large set of users over social media, it is very difficult have a control over it and to remove it from the network. Another important aspect about cyberbullying is tracing of the origin of such offensive information because such material is posted often anonymously, Deliri S. et al. (2015).

CONCLUSION

Though the presence of social media have become essential, right methodology to be followed by the users of the data over the network. The usage of multimedia data have been increased drastically over the social network demanding security and the privacy. Security and privacy challenges are reported in this chapter. Data semantics are required to be preserved over the network. As the content management rights are given to the users, duplication of data increases. False information detection has been reported as the important challenge. The act of clickjacking (likejacking) caused the scams related to the business. The act of advertising the products through user accounts is a challenge to be addressed. Usage of Shortened URL’s over real time data may take user to malicious page, thus, its usage needs to be restricted. The strategy of social designing reported some genuine instances and describes the attacks over social network. The method of handling social engineering attacks described in this chapter covers the physical methodologies and specialized methodologies. Protecting real time multimedia data over media sharing networks is observed as a future of multimedia data. Technologically, steganography, cryptography and watermarking stands at their best for protection of multimedia data, still there are threats in real time environment to multimedia data and there a need for enhanced multimedia systems to handle these real time challenges.

# Chapter 8

*   Michelangelo De Bonis

ABSTRACT

During investigative activities in the field of contrasting tax evasion and fraud, it is known that law enforcement agencies are increasingly encountering digital documents, which are slowly replacing the paper ones. The chapter has the purpose to explain as data, extracted from an electronic device, turns into evidence in court. The authors describe how hidden data (metadata) can become forensic evidence. In particular, the chapter examines the metadata contained in digital photos, which conceal a mass of data whose existence is not normally suspected. The second part of the chapter consists of miscellaneous cyber-attack descriptions in which computer forensics can be applied. It is finally described how one can protect systems against a cyber-attacks.

INTRODUCTION

The information required during investigation activity that once led to the production of photocopies, folders, paper documents to be examined now frequently ends with the acquisition of many data saved on CDROM or hard disk and a few paper documents.

It is equally known that there is no official methodology that describes the forensic acquisition procedures, still relying on best practices, ISO standards, RFCs and some legislative adjustments ratifying 2001 Budapest Convention (Council of Europe, 2001).

Computer forensics hardly finds a univocal and exhaustive definition that can correctly describe it in all its nuances. As a first approach, computer forensics could be defined as the technical-investigative activity aimed at identifying, acquiring, protecting, managing, analyzing and interpreting digital traces, found inside electronic devices and their correlation to the facts, circumstances, hypotheses and traces of any nature, related to the investigated fact (Osterburg & Ward, 2010). In addition, the heterogeneity of electronic media hides traces and clues, the constant technological evolution and every situation in which an investigator must confront, unfortunately does not allow to identify a univocal and universal procedure for digital evidence acquisition (Reyes et al., 2007).

The theme therefore clearly refers to the procedures and dynamics that some digital evidence can bring to the case resolution. An accurate application of digital forensics procedures ensures the integrity, authenticity, truthfulness, non-repudiation and completeness of the test, which are the basis of computer forensics itself.

The steps that characterize the computer forensics activity can be summarized in the identification, preservation, acquisition, analysis and correlation of the data assumed, as well as in a complete and exhaustive documentation of what has been done in the individual phases.

Before starting to deal with this topic, it is necessary to give some definition. We have to distinguish two fields in this subject. The first one is Digital Forensics (Reith et al., 2002) and the other one is Computer Forensics.

Digital forensics is the science that allows, through the use of specific methodologies (Beebe & Clark, 2004; Carrier & Spafford, 2003) and tools the identification, storage and analysis of digital evidence. An important concept before continuing to explain the topic is the definition of a “digital proof”. It’s an information, with probative value, that is either stored or transmitted in a digital format.

Computer Forensics is another point of view. It is the discipline that deals with the preservation, identification, study, documentation of computers, or systems information in general, in order to highlight the existence of evidence in the course of an investigative activity (Casey, 2009).

For lawyers, Digital Forensics means to examine digital media and technological systems in order to extract the evidence required to demonstrate or refute the question that has been asked.

We are going to describe which is the accurate application of digital forensics procedures ensuring the integrity, authenticity, truthfulness, non-repudiation and completeness of the test, which are the basis of computer forensics itself.

First of all, we characterize the computer forensics activity summarized in the identification, preservation, acquisition, analysis and correlation of the data assumed, such as a collection of a complete and exhaustive documentation of what has been carried out in every step of process.

In second part of the work we analyze kinds of data that are usually an attack target, such as identity, medical, work, educational, financial data and so on. Today, these data are also well protected by General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) (European Commission, 2018), but in the last five years, since 2014 to 2019 we had an increasing cyber Crime Activity. Of all cyber attacks in 2019, 83% were due to cybercrime compared to 63% in 2014. Technical community is particularly concerned and attentive. In consequence of intensive use of ICT (Shiuh-Jeng, 2007), especially during COVID-19 pandemic, IT fraud further increased. This period was hard test for ICT infrastructure, but it also shows we are not completely protected in software technology against cyber attacks. Moreover, Internet surfers and company employees (Willison, 2006) do not generally apply any security policy, so many ICT frauds happen due for naivety and lack of knowledge. So, we thought it appropriate to describe all Cyber attack techniques in this work.

BACKGROUND

Phase 1: Devices Identification

The immateriality of digital evidence is supported by the materiality of the medium where it is stored. For some type of media it should not be difficult to identify them, for example if you consider pen drives, or hard-disks, or even solid-state memories such as SD and Compact Flash memory cards. Unfortunately, we can find problems related to the identification of devices if they are not easily identifiable as supports containing digital evidence (Carrier, 2005). In fact, there may be “hidden” information stored inside non traditional or ad hoc created media.

Phase 2: Preservation and Isolation

This phase is defined “the descriptive phase”, in which an inspection with a precise inventory of the evidence found, and a technical phase with preventing any interaction of the evidence found with the surrounding environment until the next acquisition phase. However, the most important rule that should always be at the basis of any type of intervention is to avoid accessing the device in any way, because this fact could damage the evidence found on the crime scene. In fact, just turning on a computer, mobile phone or any device that has computational capabilities, causes an interaction between data, memories and the operating system which, in terms of management of forensic evidence, must always be considered as an alteration of such data and therefore of the find itself.

In this context, there could be many operative aspects for a correct acquisition of all the necessary data. For example, without going into details, but just to focalize the problem, we can ask some questions.

How to preserve data stored in RAM memory, or in a system cache? In fact, RAM memory is also defined as volatile memory, that means it continues to store data as long as the power source is on. This could conflict with the above rule: if we access the system to retrieve information, we change the state of the system itself.

How to retrieve the traffic data about active connections in a specific time on the computer system (or router, server, etc.) we are inspecting? Some of this information, such as routing tables, is stored in temporary memories which may undergo changes during time flowing (Casey, 2001).

Whenever a user interacts with the operating system on a device, there is a series of operating system actions which result “invisible” to the user that modify a series of accessory data (invisible information), called “metadata”.

We can define Metadata “a speaking data”, such as title, author, publisher, year of publication of a book, the caption of a photograph, the technical data of a photograph, the image of the poster of a film, the description of a movie in a movie dictionary, the ID3 tag of an MP3 song, or the whole series of EXIF ​​tags regarding a digital photo.

Phase 3: Data Acquisition

The most important aim during data acquisition is to assure data transfer respecting its integrity, authenticity, truthfulness and non-repudiation (Casey, 2004).

To reach this target, we realize that it is not possible to access the system without compromising it (Heisenberg effect) (Chisum & Turvey, 2014; Lee et al., 2001). In order to acquire the data correctly, an operating system is generally used with the “noswap” characteristic. This feature, usually based on Linux, consists in loading the files into RAM memory only, without accessing hard disk. One of the most famous operating system aiming at this goal is Kali Linux, often used also as an operating system to perform penetration testing analysis. Another one is DEFT Linux, an operating system created and used by expert technicians in computer forensics.

The acquisition of digital evidence consists in the creation of the so-called “bit stream image”, generally called “bit to bit” copy of the device under investigation. This data acquisition procedure must consider its physical structure and its logical allocation (partial, deleted, overwritten, interrupted, ... documents). It is not important to understand the meaning of a document. In addition, the access to the external unit used to acquire data, must take place in a “read only” mode such as maintaining intact its inner data, guaranteeing the preservation of the data itself and its subsequent correct analysis.

Once you have obtained the digital copy of the data, the correct procedure requires that you conclude with the calculation of the hash function. This function is a seal, a signature that, through a mathematical algorithm, provides an univocal demonstration of an unmodified data acquisition integrity.

In every acquisition, a hash code is uniquely associated to the acquired data. We can consider a hash code like a fingerprint linked to data. So, if only one bit is modified inside the acquired data, its calculated hash code is not equal to the original one. This is a proof of a data corruption.

The hash functions most frequently applied for digital forensics are typically identified in the following:

*   • MD5
*   • SHA-1

The acquisition of digital evidence is certainly to be considered as the most delicate phase of the whole procedure. In the past, the problem was focused on repeatability or unrepeatability of the evidence in court. Before hash code using, a proof acquisition was not easily repeatable, because the acquisition was destructive for data. Hash code assures proof immutability.

The acquisition presents significant problems, but today there is also a series of standardized procedures indicated by the best practices that make it possible to produce a forensic copy in terms of absolute repeatability. Although the local laws of the countries do not always require the use of specific software application and do not impose any restrictions on the software to be used, it is however clear that referring to products whose code could be checked at any time can provide a greater and better guarantee for this purpose.

Phase 4: Data Analysis and Correlation

Unlike the acquisition, where it is possible to define standard procedures to operate in complete safety, in the analysis phase, every case study can be different, so different kind of analysis are defined depending on objects to be analysed (Beebe & Clark, 2004; DeBrota, 2005).

What does the analysis of an electronic computer reveal to us? First of all, it needs to know in detail the different structure of the operating systems, not only the families they belong to: Windows, Linux, macOS, but also their specific versions. Then for every version we have to analyze the user profile, the related metadata, access, mail, configurations, cloud, browser (in normal and private browsing), PDF documents, eBooks, social networks, connected USB devices, temporary files, Wi-Fi connections and much more.

If we consider the analysis of a portable smartphone or tablet device, the problem is very different to solve, because the objects to be analyzed are very different. In this case the operating systems to be familiar with, in order to search for the necessary information, are Windows Phone, iOS, Android. The information that is available from an analysis of mobile devices are: (outbound/inbound) calls, contacts, browsers, emails, messages, chats, GPS (storage of positions), reading, purchases, social networks, cloud, etc.

From Data to Evidence

Finally, the data becomes a computer proof and needs caution in its conservation (Casey, 2009). The computer proof presents the characteristics of extreme lability, such as the chemical-biological findings which by their nature are easily perishable. The digital data may be modified due to the device on which it is stored. It will therefore be necessary to pay more attention according to the type of element that has undergone reporting. However, the management does not end with the mere drafting of technical and legal documentation, but it must include a series of procedures to be implemented in order to prove that all the seized IT supports and the data contained inside, subjected to analysis, have been preserved and adequately protected by damage or possible alterations throughout the investigation.

In recent years, computer evidence has taken on an increasingly important role in the field of judicial investigations and the introduction of information technology in the criminal world, although relatively recent, has undergone an immediate spread at all levels, from the single to the most sophisticated organizations.

Computer forensics is based on precise scientific foundations and has the typical prerogatives of the investigative activity. So, it is not a simple activity of supporting the law enforcement, but – on the contrary – computer forensics has the role of providing as precisely as possible, with scientific method helping, a space-time situation of the investigated event defining facts, refuting alibis, correlating elements or events.

The most important target in the analysis of digital evidence is to correlate the facts, the different elements, the clues that characterize the “puzzle” of the entire evidentiary framework.

It is easily understood that the forensic biologist from the examination of a genetic fragment can scientifically demonstrate the presence or absence of a subject on the crime scene. However, this circumstance must necessarily be correlated with other elements acquired during the investigation process that establish how, when and why there is a presence of a specific biological trace. The example of the forensic biologist, translated in the computer field, consists of managing digital proofs, not only limiting to the acquisition and analysis of the digital data but also considering the analysis of the facts that must be related to the other investigated elements. Everything requires science and experience for data becoming a proof. Computer forensics is a discipline and a science that must focus on legal fundamentals.

The ratification law of the Budapest Convention on Cybercrimes, which expands the legal institutes about researching sources of evidence, has introduced the cardinal principles of computer forensics in every country. The law is deficient in the specific technical procedures to be adopted, however it affirms the fundamental principles of the conservation, integrity and non alterability of the IT test even in emerging situations, providing application of correct procedures in order to avoid the alteration of the digital element.

Guidelines suggested in Budapest Convention on Cybercrimes invite the modern investigator in a situation of continuous training to deal with new technologies in order to be able to provide a certain, precise and meticulous answer to the fact being investigated. For this reason, the investigator must operate on the basis of codified procedures and not exclusively on the basis of personal intuition, improvisation or experience.

METADATA

We previously mentioned that in computer forensics two central topics are very important: data and relative context. But, if we want the understand the context, metadata are to be analysed (Buchholz & Spafford, 2004).

A first way to better explain the importance of metadata is to define them in an easier way. Edward Snowden suggests we replace the word metadata with “information about activities”. For example, the metadata of a digital document is creation date/time, or last modification date/time, the name of its author, etc. For another kind of digital document, for example a photo, the inside metadata can be information concerning the taking picture activity: type of camera, shooting parameters (time and aperture), shooting date/time and geographic coordinates of the place where the photo was taken.

But what could we deduce from the analysis of photo metadata? During a computer forensics process can we list the steps we have to follow in a digital photo analysis?

Let’s look at an example and comment on its related metadata analysis.

| Figure 1.­ |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch008.f01](i/ch008.f01.png) |
| --- |

The photo (see Figure 1) was taken in San Marco square, Venice lagoon. What can we analyze from the metadata inside this photo? Metadata are not difficult elements to locate or discover; on the contrary, they are perfectly extractable data, living in conjunction with real data. In fact, every modern operating system provides access to all over metadata. To carry out this analysis example, the photo was opened with the Preview program of a macOS Operating System and the “More information” screen has been requested. The program provides four summary sheets.

The tabs available are four: General, Exif, GPS and TIFF.

In the sheet number 1 (see Figure 2), we find general information about the file: the size of photo, the fact that it was taken by a device with a rotation of 180° (that is, in an inverted position respect to the correct position).

| Figure 2.­ |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch008.f02](i/ch008.f02.png) |
| --- |

The second tab (see Figure 3), Exif data, provides data on the actual shot. The abbreviation Exif stands for EXchangeable Image File, that is, image interchange file. It is a format used to combine each digital photo with a set of additional information, metadata, shared by all camera manufacturers.

| Figure 3.­ |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch008.f03](i/ch008.f03.png) |
| --- |

The advanced information can be divided into two large sets. The first one is the static information, such as camera or device brand and model that takes the photo. The second one is dynamic information, which change from photo to photo, such as the values ​​used for opening, shutter speed and ISO or the photo date it was taken. EXIF data is recorded with each shot and incorporated into the image. From the analysis of this photo we see that the information clearly reports, about static component, that the photo was taken by a smartphone mobile device and, about dynamic component, that the shutter speed is quite slow. What does it mean? Is there a low light? Was it taken during a dusk? Do these data correspond to the data relating to the shooting date and time?

The third tab (see Figure 4) is related to the GPS position. The device had the GPS detector active and it was possible to geolocalize the shot. From the latitude and longitude coordinates it is verified that the shot was taken in the Venice lagoon. This seems to support the veracity of the photo, in fact the perspective from the sea to the square.

| Figure 4.­ |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch008.f04](i/ch008.f04.png) |
| --- |

Finally, the last tab (see Figure 5) provides information on the saved image. For example, the rotation of the device can be an element used as an additional criterion to transform the photographic evidence analysis. We have to contextualize this element to support a complex investigative activity: the person in the event is using to take photos with the rotation of the device itself. This attitude can be important during the investigation analysis, for example to identify the person.

| Figure 5.­ |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch008.f05](i/ch008.f05.png) |
| --- |

This is just one of the possibilities that the analysis of a simple digital photo can provide. But we find metadata in every digital environment with an increasingly massive way.

Another field in metadata analysis is about instant messaging communications, such as the most common app for mobile systems: WhatsApp.

WhatsApp is one of the most popular apps and offers end-to-end encryption to all users. In this app all messages are encrypted from source to destination device. WhatsApp cannot decipher and read them. This technique leads users to have an illusion of security and tranquility which is certainly not true. How can metadata be exploited, considered unimportant, especially when cryptography is involved in a context of forensic computing?

The typical objection, but also the most incorrect, is that if the content of a message (of a conversation) is secret, it does not matter whether someone has access to their metadata. For example, WhatsApp has full access to user message metadata, but what could it do with them? Even if he knew that Alice and Bob talked to each other, it wouldn't know what they said.

Here are some examples where we only know the information about the activities, therefore only the metadata about some users. These examples are illuminating, because they show us how, by carefully reading metadata, it is possible, although not knowing the content of the conversations, to reveal the conversations themselves.

*   • The metadata show that a pupil of school X sent messages to a national number against bullying, immediately after school time, when the pupil himself was still near the school. But the topic of the conversation remains secret.
*   • The metadata show that an underage student from school Y exchanged numerous messages with her gynecologist, and subsequently called the local counseling center. But nobody knows what they talked about.
*   • The metadata show that a photo taken with the front camera was sent to a cell phone number connected to the same cell. But the content of the photo is unknown.
*   • The metadata show that a message is sent every night to a number in the address book, corresponding to a smartphone located in another city. Immediately thereafter neither the first device nor the second one are active until the following morning. But the content of the message is unknown.
*   • These examples concretely show that the work of computer forensic science is an activity that requires multidisciplinary specializations and knowledge.

Skills go beyond the classic watertight compartments that can be learned from traditional department and training courses such as Engineering, Computer Science or Law. This new frontier requires a new and innovative environment in which skills are mixed with new knowledge in order to be sensitive, precise and scrupulous experts to be able to apply their specific skills to rigorous and scientific methodologies and procedures.

CYBER ATTACK AND COMPUTER CRIME

Computer Forensics is widely applied in Cyber security and Cyber attack (Perilli et al., 2019).

What does it mean Cybersecurity? Cybersecurity represents a constant commitment to protect interconnected systems and their data from unauthorized use and accidental damage. A distinction is usually made between computer systems and data.

Information systems are computers, or a set of computers, servers, databases, switches, routers, modems, interconnected by network, through a basic client-server architecture, which offer functionality and services to users. IT systems are often referred to as corporate information technology (IT, IT infrastructure) or corporate information and communication technology (ICT, IT and telecommunication infrastructure). Cybersecurity in this area must protect and guarantee correct and continuous working of corporate ICT in order to continue providing service to users.

Data, on the other hand, can be distinguished in personal data and public or private company data. In the first case, it is necessary to safeguard person identity, or better personal identity data. In private company, all employees are responsible to protect company online reputation, data and customers. Finally, in public company, we have to consider security of an entire nation and protection of citizens. Referring to personal data, we often talk about online identity (von Solms et al., 2013). Before Internet age, personal identity was a set of data associated with physical person with whom friends and relatives interact daily at home, at school and at work. This kind of data are name, age, address, etc. ... Online identity belongs to cybernetic world and maps a set of personal data that a person shows to others in this online dimension. Only a limited amount of data is concerning real person. What kind of personal data do others observe online? What data is to be protected? Which personal data can we show online? Which kind of protective measures have we to use?

Here above we list data we can find in an on-line dimension:

*   • identity data
*   • medical data
*   • work data
*   • educational data
*   • financial data
*   • visited places data
*   • food consumption data
*   • spare time data
*   • hobbies data
*   • Internet surfing data.

Otherwise, in addition to personal information employees, company data also include intellectual property and financial data. Personal information can be inherent job offer proposal, job offer joining, job contracts, etc... Intellectual properties, such as patents, registered trademarks, design plans or new product development plans, allow company to obtain a possible economic advantage over competition. This intellectual property can be considered a commercial secret and relative information lost would be disastrous for the future of company. Financial data, tax return, balance sheet and cash flow statement of a company can offer a real overview of health of company (Kshetri, 2006).

Furthermore, corporate or private information, accelerated its online diffusion thanks to presence of Internet or Things (IoT, Internet of Things). In fact, amount of data to be managed and therefore “protected” exponentially increased. IoT is a large heterogeneous network made up of physical objects, such as sensors, various equipment and devices, as well as traditional computer networks. Connectivity increasing, daily use of “clouding” services (network storage), virtualization services expansion, led to a growth in data generated and transmitted on network. This data has created a new concept in technology, called “Big Data”. High speed data transmission, big data volume generated by the IoT and daily business activities, concepts like confidentiality, integrity and availability of such data become vital for survival of company itself (Defense Authorization Act, 2000).

Now we are going to define who, through particular skills, manage to access private information, devices (smartphones, computers, IoT, etc...) or make corporate services inaccessible, such as company e-commerce website. This figure is commonly called “hacker”. However, there are three types of hackers: “white-hat”, “gray-hat” and “black-hat” (Gold, 2014). The former, “white-hat” hackers believe in a safer computer society and make their skills available to discover any vulnerabilities and to improve system security. These, also called ethical hackers, use their programming skills for good, ethical and lawful purposes. “White-hat” hackers can implement system penetration tests, in which they try to compromise networks and systems, using their skills on cyber security systems to discover vulnerabilities. Critical issues identified by “white hats” are reported to company developers for debugging, before they can represent real threats to systems and networks.

Another less noble type of hacker is identified as “gray-hat” hacker. This category includes people who commit crimes, but not for personal profit. They seek networks or websites vulnerabilities, without company system access authorization. In case of critical issue discovered, they communicate problem to company to solve it. Finally, “black-hat” hackers are cyber security experts, who unscrupulously violate server security, networks, archives where information is stored, to gain personal profit or to block company services. “Black-hat” hackers exploit vulnerabilities to compromise network, computer systems, and to steal confidential user information.

CYBER ATTACK TECHNIQUES

To understand attacks complexity and their consequences we can find into cyberspace, it is important to analyze some of the main attack techniques and to mention defense principles that can be implemented for protection and prevention (Perilli et al., 2019).

Social Engineering

Social engineering is an information security field that deals with manipulating people in order to perform illegal acts or steal confidential information. This technique exploits people weaknesses to overcome increasingly sophisticated and more complicated protection systems (Perilli et al., 2019).

Social engineering develops in these sectors:

*   • collection of information (confidential information)
*   • computer fraud (use of information for scams)
*   • unauthorized access to data (access data with stolen username and password)

Social engineering uses following techniques to capture information:

Phishing

It consists of a practice based on sending deceptive emails. For example, hacker pretends to be a bank employee who informs victim of his account or credit card blocking, following probably irregular activities. The fake employee invites victim to enter their credentials in order to verify and unlock them.

Pretexting

A cybercriminal pretends to need personal data to verify recipient identity. It is a very similar to phishing but uses a different medium, for example an interview on a phone call.

Shoulder Surfing

It is a technique whereby user who enters credentials is “spied behind shoulders”. It is usually committed by a hacker who pretends not to be interested, but looks at keyboard while user typing credentials, storing in mind username and password observed.

Dumpster Diving

It is a technique based on analysis of “garbage” produced by victim. Receipts, magazines, every single object can be useful to hacker to reconstruct victim lifestyle and habits.

Spear Phishing

It consists of a technique in which cybercriminal creates a targeted and personalized phishing attack for a specific user in a company, whom analyzed his habits using previously Dumpster diving technique.

Spam

It is a technique whereby spam emails are used to deceive a user into clicking on an infected link or downloading an infected file.

Eavesdrop

It consists in intercepting a conversation in secret, in order to capture confidential information.

Wiretap

It consists of a real environmental or phone interception, but using the most modern instant messaging and e-mail systems.

Quid Pro Quo

A hacker leaves a physical device infected with malware, such as a flash drive usb, in a public place such as corporate lobby or toilet. An employee finds device and put into his computer to see who is owner. This action inadvertently installs a malware.

Most of this information collected aim to user identity theft, in order to perform actions on his behalf. Identity theft really has huge implications, ranging from credibility loss to criminal and civil liability for criminal actions or administrative infringements.

In our opinion, if we want to defend from social engineering attacks, we have to adopt some basic precautions such as:

*   • never disclose personal and business access credentials;
*   • lock computer when leaving your position;
*   • always ask strangers to identify themselves and verify the declared identity.

Every company is working hard around the world to prevent and raise awareness of its employees best practices.

Man-in-the-Middle

Man in the middle is one of the most effective ways to steal private data without victim noticing. As you can imagine from name of this attack, hacker is man who places in the middle of a “conversation” between two users. The purpose is mainly to steal data from a conversation. The Man in The Middle attack, often called “MITM”, is very effective and difficult to detect. It is a kind of attack easy to implement, but difficult to detect. Hacker enters conversation between a client and a server, intercepting their conversation, and takes place of either server or client, without the other interlocutor noticing.

In most MITM attacks, hacker uses a Wi-Fi network. to steal data. In fact, it happens to find free hotspots observed by hackers. If you connect to one of these networks and visit specific sites, such as home banking sites, hackers can steal your login, to steal money or highly private financial information. You can find this attack technique in many software technologies.

Man-in-the-Mobile

Today everyone is connected by a smartphone. In recent years, the main intent of cybercriminals has moved massively towards an attempt to infect mobile devices, through man-in-the-middle attacks, in order to intercept SMS traffic. Main aim is to bypass two-factor authentication used especially in various financial institutions. In this way hacker manages to obtain authentication codes sent by SMS.

Man-in-the-Browser

Hacker inserts malware into victim's computer. This malware acts on browser in order to record data exchanged between user and websites, in order to steal private interesting data.

Man-in-the-IOT

Internet of things is a reality, as previously mentioned. There are thousands of devices connected to network: TVs, washing machines, thermostats and many other household appliances. These devices are highly “intelligent” but also highly vulnerable. Among threats to which smart devices are exposed we have man-in-the-middle attacks, which can be used to intercept private data concerning user, collected by each device connected to web.

Man-in-the-App

Applications are also not immune to critical issues and vulnerabilities. Hacker falsifies security certificate that user app uses to communicate safely and securely with website. This way allows him to communicate directly with application and to steal all user data.

It is clear that it is difficult to realize that you are a victim of an MITM attack, essentially due to various forms which this attack is launched. User can take a series of measures to try to protect their data and private information.

A series of best practices to avoid a MITM attack could be:

*   • never use unencrypted or free Wi-Fi access points, especially for home banking transactions for example;
*   • make sure to use encrypted version of a websites, checking URL starting with “HTTPS”, because it means that HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) protocol is used in communication within an encrypted connection, through asymmetric encryption, provided by Transport Layer Security (TLS) or by Secure Sockets Layer (SSL). These techniques provide authentication of website visited, protection of privacy (confidentiality) and finally integrity of data exchanged;
*   • set a password for home Wi-Fi by most secure and recent encryption and change default password for router access;
*   • periodically update antivirus and operating system to latest version;
*   • do not visit websites when browser warns us about problem in security certificate;
*   • activate two-factor authentication in every account, for e-mail, banking systems, social media and so on.

DDoS Attacks

A real attack for cyber security experts, which is able to make servers, data centers and content distribution networks unusable in a few minutes are called “Distributed Denial of Service”, DDoS. These attacks are malicious attempts to make a website or web application unavailable to legitimate users, overloading site with a huge volume of traffic, causing it to stop or work extremely slowly. Although DDoS attacks are one of the oldest threats to websites, they are constantly evolving, making defense against them difficult. Today, hackers use huge armies of automatic “bots” (robots), computers that have been infected with malware and that can be controlled remotely, to create very large-scale DDoS attacks (Perilli et al., 2019).

DDoS attack is a large DoS attack (Denial of Service). Goal is not only to hit a single website or a small server, but to make an entire data center or a server farm or DNS services (Domain Naming System) unreachable and unavailable. So, hackers launch a DDoS attack exploiting a greater number of routes and devices than a “normal” DoS attack. In this way it is possible to “neutralize” target within a few seconds, causing damage that persists over time, from a few hours to a few days, depending on reaction capacity of company providing service.

A DDoS attack success is a large network of devices infected by malware and Trojan horses, remotely controlled by a single hacker or a group of hackers. This is botnet (a net of robots), a portion of Internet nodes composed of compromised devices that can be used for many different purposes, including DDoS attacks. Many years ago these devices were also called “zombie” computers, systems infected by a particular type of virus capable of transforming the infected machine in a sort of puppet.

Today, however, set of devices that can join a botnet has expanded exponentially. Alongside classic desktop and laptop computers we have smartphones, tablets, routers and network printers. But, as we above noticed, list of smart devices connected to network is grown exponentially in recent years, thanks to Internet of Things. Smart TVs, smart thermostats, smart appliances, cars and various smart sensors scattered on street corners can potentially be infected and used to carry out attacks on servers.

Depending on target they choose, hackers can decide to conduct their attack using different techniques and different strategies. In particular, DDoS attacks can be grouped into four macro-categories: TCP connection attacks, volumetric attacks, fragmentation attacks and application attacks.

TCP Connection Attack

Hackers exploit functionality of TCP (Transmission control protocol) protocol to quickly saturate target network resources. Target can be a data-center or a services distribution network. In this case a botnet sends a connection request flood which are not followed up. In this way, IT system resources quickly run out, making it impossible for any other user to access inner service contents.

Volumetric Attacks

These attacks aim to saturate communication band available to a node on network by simultaneously sending a large number of access requests to most of contents. In this way, hackers create an incredibly high and unmanageable traffic volume, so that server or service distribution network are forced to refuse any other connection attempt.

Fragmentation Attacks

In this attack hackers do not try to saturate network, but try to consume all target computing resources by sending requests broken up into many fragments. Server or distribution network use much of its computing power in an attempt to reconstruct fragmented data, without success.

Application Attacks

Hackers have recently moved their target from network level to application level, where attacks are more difficult to detect. Software programming bugs are exploited, to make application unstable and, consequently, unavailable.

HOW TO DEFEND FROM HACKER ATTACKS

DDoS attacks, increasing in volume and sophistication, are very difficult to fight. Today large companies started up security policy, but infrastructure implementation is difficult to grow up in response to a massive DDoS attack.

DDoS attacks are targeting web service providers and no single users. Therefore, if a user falls as victim into web service attack, a cyber security expert of web service company will mitigate attack and limit unavailability. Listed below are some techniques that experts adopt to protect and reduce inefficiencies.

Server Protection

A well-done server hosting configuration is one of the main methods to mitigate a DDoS attack. A system administrator can limit resources that an application can use in such a way that an attack on application level does not affect entire IT system, but only blocks application functionality.

Sinkholing

This technique consists of diverting all traffic created by botnet to a digital dead end. In this way it is possible to prevent a DDoS attack from making service completely unavailable, even if it works slower.

Intrusion Detection

Specific software and hardware technology, used by IT security experts, identify attempts to access network and neutralize attacks before they are successful. Intrusion detection systems constantly monitor incoming and outgoing data traffic and are able to identify when network operation protocols are used for other purposes. This software technology is usually combined with hardware firewalls using. This device can block incoming data traffic, limiting and neutralizing their effects.

Redundancy

This technique is widely used in hardware and software technologies to assure uninterruptible services. It consists in duplicating infrastructures by cloning them. In this way, even if a part of service distribution network is not available, it is still possible to continue to provide service by moving traffic towards the “cloned” part, so as to be able to mitigate attack and try to restore service.

CONCLUSIONS AND FUTURE RESEARCH DIRECTIONS

2017 was the worst year in terms of evolution of “cyber” threats and their impacts, both for quantitative and qualitative point of view, highlighting a growth trend in cyber attacks, their severity and consequent damage, which in the world is persisting without interruption.

In last years, level of cyber insecurity has recorded an impressive increase in the world. Cyber ​​attacks are the single greatest threat to global stability, risks arising from cyber attacks are ranked third among the major global risks, immediately after natural disasters and extreme weather events.

Cyber-security is not just a word but a mentality. In the world it needs to radically modify investment model in the field of ICT security. In the last period, Europe has issued regulation, called General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) (European Commission, 2018), to protect privacy, Network and Information Security (NIS) (European Commission, 2016). However, it is true that they are a step forward in the cyber security mentality by forcing companies and individuals to make the theme of security a structural element of corporate behavior and processes, transforming the theme of data protection and cyber security from a mere bureaucratic question to one of direct responsibility. European Directives, GDPR and NIS, are a sign of cultural change.

Underestimating the risks of cyber attacks on personal, company or national data, postponing the adoption of adequate countermeasures and relying on the “good luck” or goodwill of individuals, is not the correct way to proceed. Starting to become aware of the dangers of cyber insecurity and understanding the attack and defense methodologies at stake are the first steps to be taken to increase the security level starting from the conscious use of individual personal tools to arrive at the strategic management of digital infrastructure for global security.

KEY TERMS AND DEFINITIONS

Availability: Characteristic of hardware or software systems to be always available.

Clue: A sign or some information that helps you to find the answer to a problem.

Completeness: The quality of being whole or perfect and having nothing missing.

Confidentiality: Private content in data communication between users.

Digital Evidence Acquisition: Data extracting from a device to provide an evidence.

DNS: Hierarchical and decentralized naming system for computers, services, or other resources connected to the Internet or a private network. It provides the translation of URL address into network IP address.

HTTP: Application protocol for distributed, collaborative, and data communication for the World Wide Web.

Integrity: Non-corruptibility feature that a message has during transferring from source to destination.

Internet of Things: Every object is going to be connect to a network, so internet network becomes internet of objects (things).

Investigation Activity: Set of actions that investigator implements to find clues.

Non-Repudiation: Non-repudiation is the assurance that someone cannot deny the validity of something.

Router: Device that routes data packets on a network.

SSL, TLS: Cryptographic data protocol that assures authentication, privacy, and integrity during transmission on TCP/IP networks.

Traces: Clues having significance for the investigation.
