# Chapter 10

A Bibliometric Approach

*   Josélia Mafalda Ribeiro da Fonseca  
    Faculty of Social Sciences and Humanities, University of the Azores, Portugal
*   Maria Teresa Borges-Tiago  
    Faculty of Business and Economics, University of the Azores, Portugal

ABSTRACT

In less than two decades, social media has become a part of life for many people, increasing the positive and negative effects of social relationships. In a sense, the traditional offline behaviors moved into a ubiquitous environment, enhancing the social phenomenon of cyberbullying. Thus, it attracted much attention from different fields within academia. To understand how research has been conducted in the last 20 years and the topics addressed, this study applied a bibliometric analysis to academic literature from 2000 to 2020 related to cyberbullying in social media, using techniques such as citation analysis, co-citation analysis, and content analysis. The growing interest of the field is confirmed, and some research gaps are unveiled. Since this is one of the first studies to explore cyberbullying that occurs in social media networks, it is hoped that this chapter will stimulate further research on this topic reinforcing the gaps found.

INTRODUCTION

Bullying is a human behavior, exercised from a self towards another human being, which is perpetuated in time, inflicting harmful effects on the victims. In fact, bullying is an attack on human sustainability, understood in this context as the set of political, social, educational and ethical conditions and behavior’s that favor the process of developing balanced, dignified and responsible human life.

The widespread use of new communication technologies, alongside with the web evolution led to a new form of bullying: cyberbullying. Nowadays, through the internet, computer, mobile, tablets and other devices, social networks can be easily accessed and allow perpetrating violence against others, humiliating them, attacking their self-esteem, leading them, creating an environment of hopelessness, depression and psychosocial problems, the loss of self and of their identity.

The growth of the phenomenon of cyberbullying in the 21st century has aroused the interest of researchers, from different areas of knowledge, and, consequently, has motivated and increased by research in this field. Thus, it is important to understand how the research process of cyberbullying developed, analyzing which countries, areas and time periods registered the greatest difference in studies at this time.

In this article we present a study that involves a bibliometric analysis of cyberbullying in the academic bibliography of the specialty, from 2000 to 2020, carrying out a survey of the areas, authors and countries that have been dedicated to the study of this theme and a content analysis of 2289 research works referenced in Web of Science.

This study aims to promote a wider understanding of a violent phenomenon raised in the 21st century - cyberbullying, identifying which domains have been mostly studying, which concepts, contexts and behaviors have been associated with it and identifying the gaps in the literature, in order to develop a prophylactic investigation, inducing the promotion of improvement and prevention of cyberbullying behavior, particularly in educational contexts.

BACKGROUND

As technology advances are widely adopted by people, social interactions tend to change from face-to-face to virtual exchanges. When looking at both theoretical and empirical research studies on social networks it can be found that traditionally they are an interdisciplinary endeavor (Zych, Ortega-Ruiz, & Del Rey, 2015). Thus, this phenomenon has its starting point as a broad range of social phenomena present since the begin of humankind history, has been complexity crosscutting multiple levels of analysis, especially since the birth of online social networks.

Social network sites have been present on the Internet for almost 20 years, and in the last eight years have deeply affected relationships established between users. According to Marwick and Boyd (2011) social media should be ruled by a social norm of personal authenticity. Thus, in this networked world, people post tweets, likes and become fans, explore millions of mobile apps, and search, create and share content; people tend to actively live virtually. which encourages youths to share aspects of their personal life with their social network (Marwick & Boyd, 2011). Users stay connected through multiple devices which increase efficiency, convenience, access to information, a wider spectrum of information, and broader selections of data sources (Fotis, Buhalis, & Rossides, 2012), changing communication flows and information ownership (Berthon, Hulbert, & Pitt, 2005).

The users’ communication empowerment occurred alongside with internet evolution, not only modifying information access, but also shaping users’ behaviors and motivations. In the early years of Internet, Web 1.0 appeared as a tool linking documents and turning them electronically available on the Internet. This allowed users to search and read a wide range of information. At this point Tim Berners-Lee noted that the web could be compared to files extensions as “read-only” (Tiago & Veríssimo, 2014). With Web 2.0 and Web 3.0 communication flows in both directions, allowed users to interact and share information among each other, users, enabling the creation of virtual communities of users and social networks (Singh, Iyer, & Salam, 2009). This new reality may enable bonding and communication among users, but it also leaves users susceptible to less positive reflections on offline human relational phenomenon (Kwan & Skoric, 2013; S. Wang, 2020).

The evolution of the Web and its functionalities has led to the migration of bullying from the classroom and school context to the cyberspace context, with an incidence that transcends the school and the borders of the city, district and country, we talked about cyberbullying.

Cyberbullying is understood to mean acts of violence between humans that occur through electronic devices. According to some authors such as Picoli et al (2020, p. 260), citing Smith et al (2008) reference, “cyberbullying refers to «an aggressive, intentional act carried out by a group or individual, using electronic forms of contact, repeatedly and over time against a victim who cannot easily defend him or herself»”. The cyberbullying “(…) involves sending harassing or threatening messages (…) posting derogatory comments about someone on a Web site or social networking site (such as Facebook or Myspace) or physically threating or intimidating someone in a variety of online settings.” (Hinduja & Patchin, 2010, p. 208).

Nevertheless, there is still a lack of consensus regarding to the cyberbullying definition (Bauman, 2012; Betts, 2016; Davis, 2017). As noted by Smith, del Barrio, and Tokunaga (2012), these difficulties arise from the specific characteristics found in cyberbullying, that weren’t present in traditional bullying: the anonymity (Menesini et al., 2012), the publicity (Coyne, 2015), the multiplicity of Information and Communication Technologies available and used (Menesini et al., 2012), the permanency of data, and the unlimited number of bystanders (Hayashi & Tahmasbi, 2020).

Nonetheless, there is a conceptual similarity between cyberbullying and bullying, defined as the presence of aggressive acts of Man, or groups of Men, towards the other human being, causes many authors (Olweus & Limber, 2017; Vaillancourt, Faris & Mishna, 2017) consider that both concepts are not completely different. Fanti, Demetriou and Hawa (2012, p. 167) understand this even when they define bullying and include in their definition aggression through the electronic devices: “Bullying is an international, widespread phenomenon occurring in different social contexts, such as the schoolyard, the workplace, and more recently in technology.”

Although both report aggressive acts perpetrated by humans against their counterparts, the fact that they are developed through different means - bullying occurs face-to-face, cyberbullying happens through electronic devices - makes bullying and cyberbullying different concepts, making the latter much more dangerous and aggressive. “Cyberspace makes bullying easier, more accessible, and inflicts greater harm than traditional bullying” (Ansary, 2020, p. 1).

Cyberspace makes acts of violence more aggressive, as they are not developed face to face, which in psychological and moral terms makes them much easier and simpler to perpetuate. There is no direct confrontation with the victim, nor with any embarrassment that the victim's suffering may cause, there is no trace of pity, nor possible rebate of conscience on the part of the aggressor.

The lack of social censure that cyberbullying enables through the absence of face-to-face interaction means that many of the social restraints associated with traditional direct bullying are not in play for cyberbullying. This enhances the role of personal regulatory factors in cyberbullying that are particularly salient in the linkage between bullying and morality (Bussey, Fitzpatrick & Raman, 2015, p. 31).

In cyberbullying, the aggressor/victim relationship is mediated by electronic devices, which leads to an intensification of violence because the aggressor, since he avoids face-to-face, feels morally uncommitted (Fang et al., 2020; X. Wang, Yang, Wang, & Lei, 2019). In bullying situations, the aggressor has a very low level of moral obligation, that is, they do not show any kind of compassion, respect for the dignity and integrity of the victim. This level of disengagement becomes even lower in cases of cyberbullying in which the victim's vulnerability becomes more and more indirect to the aggressor (Runions & Bak, 2015). While in the context of bullying the aggressor is forced to look away in order not to have compassion, although he continues to feel the environment of vulnerability that the victim expresses, through electronic means violence becomes much easier, without bringing any trace of guilt, because you don't see, you don't hear, you don't even feel the other's (victim's) look of suffering.

If bullying already makes the aggressor powerful, because it is capable of subjugating someone, although this can bring an insignificant feeling of guilt, cyberbullying makes the aggressor a hero who dominates the victim, without any feeling of guilt, with the aggravation that can display internationally and infinitely from your domain. X. Wang et al. (2019) posits that cyberbullying perpetration relation to family factors, such as parental supervision and/or childhood maltreatment, have received little research attention.

The number of viewers in cyberbullying is much greater than in the cases of bullying, “a material bullying can be sent to hundreds of people with a single text message and each recipient can become a bystander.” (Hayashi & Tahmasi, 2020, p. 2). As mentioned by Lazuras et al. (2019), adding to bullying common traits, cyberbullying also shares common features with indirect bullying. And, for indirect bullying, the authors considered rumour/fake news or misleading information spreading, social exclusion, and denigration of the victim. All of these can be found online, related to the different bystanders profiles that can be found online: some will be able to distinguish the “bad intentional” content; others think they are able to, even when not; and others simply rely in all the information available online (Borges‐Tiago, Tiago, Silva, Guaita Martínez, & Botella‐Carrubi).

Adding to that, in cyberbullying, viewers play a completely different role. “(…) In traditional bullying, bystanders are often present during cyberbullying situations, and they can take one of the three actions: assisting or reinforcing the bully, supporting or defending the victim, and remaining outsider.” (Hayashi & Tahmasi, 2020, p. 1).

Looking at the studies examining cyberbullying predictors, it can be found different perspectives, including parental supervision (Camerini, Marciano, Carrara, & Schulz, 2020; Dehue, Bolman, & Völlink, 2008; Ho, Lwin, Chen, & Chen, 2019), media exposure (Akbulut, Sahin, & Eristi, 2010; Ho et al., 2019; Van Ouytsel, Walrave, Ponnet, Willems, & Van Dam, 2019; S. Wang, 2020), childhood maltreatment (Emirtekin, Balta, Kircaburun, & Griffiths, 2019; X. Wang et al., 2019) or other personal factors (Barlett & Coyne, 2014; Holfeld & Grabe, 2012; You, Lee, & Kim, 2016), and environmental factors (Holfeld & Grabe, 2012; Modecki, Minchin, Harbaugh, Guerra, & Runions, 2014). Given the increasing rates of technology adoption and the panoply of cyberbullying predictors, the parents and educator’s task to contain or mitigate cyberbullying is daily challenge (Guo, 2016).

Cyberspace allows bullying to have no borders, the threat and fear perpetrated on someone can be seen anywhere in the world (Fanti et al., 2012). Cyberspace also allows aggression and threats to be eternal, once on the net it can never be erased from it.

The use of electronic devices in aggressive acts broadens the context of bullying. This is no longer limited to the school context (Casas et al., 2013), nor is it limited to the period of pre and adolescence, but it is possible to apply it in any space of life in any age group.

Back in 2010, Tokunaga tried to end with the controversy on whether cyberbullying is a category of bullying, stating that cyberbullying is more than the traditional bullying taking place in a new context; it can be considered as an umbrella term that integrates in line concepts such as electronic bullying and internet harassment, and can occur through multiple devices and platforms. This umbrella acceptation lead to the development of a diverse set instruments to assess cyberbullying (Berne et al., 2013). To be able to develop and implement anti-cyberbullying programs and assessment instruments a clear notion of the context is needed.

A decade ago, Bampo, Ewing, Mather, Stewart, and Wallace (2008) restated the need to look more closely at the users’ motivations and drivers to participate in digital communications, or simply to be bystanders in peer interactions. Recent research on users’ behavior in social media found that (i) not all users are equally active online (Borges-Tiago, Tiago, & Cosme, 2018; Correa, Hinsley, & De Zuniga, 2010; de Vries, Peluso, Romani, Leeflang, & Marcati, 2017; Vollenbroek, de Vries, Constantinides, & Kommers, 2014), and (ii) content is generated by a small number of users with specific motivations (Crowston & Fagnot, 2018; Naab & Sehl, 2017).

There are currently different users exploring the web in distinctive ways (Kaplan & Haenlein, 2010), including viewing and creating content, participating in discussions and viral communication, sharing knowledge with peers through thematic social networks or digital communities, or simply acquiring knowledge shared by others (de Vries et al., 2017; Naab & Sehl, 2017). Whenever a user becomes a producer of shared content, he/she becomes a prosumer.

Hartmann (2016) notes that it is important to acknowledge and understand the attitudes of this new tech-savvy category of users, who are said to be enthusiasts of new technologies such as mobile web access, digital convergence, blogs, online web pages, and social media connectivity. Back in 2012, Yar addressed the fact that new media challenge commonplace criminological assumptions and rule-breaking behavior (written-verbal, visual, exclusion, and impersonation). Thus, besides posting mean comments online, there are other formats of digital harassment that are used by cyberbullies as spreading rumors, posting sexual remarks, unwanted forwarding of private communication, use of aggressive and pejorative words, threats, profile hacking, or photo-sharing without consent.

Hayes and Luther (2018) recalled that “Crimes are committed online, law enforcement investigates the social media accounts of alleged perpetrators, and questions are being asked about the responsibility of new media in crime control responses”. Nonetheless, the high-speed rate of evolution of these rule-breaking behaviors challenges society as an all, and not only new media.

Publications are very suitable sources of data to understand the relevance and interest of a specific topic to the society. Social media networks seem to be a “fertile” environment to the occurrence of cyberbullying. However, when looking at the panoply of research studies conducted regarding to cyberbullying in social media networks, there seems to be an underestimating and delimitation of the fields of analysis. Thus, through a careful analysis of the articles published can shed to light into to this matter. To do so, (a) a well know database was chosen and current data up to publication year 2000 was retrieved and (b) analyze the data across all disciplines.

Research Methodology

1.1. Data Gathered

The data extraction comprised two phases. In the first, a total of 2043 cyberbullying related research works published from January 2000 to January 2020 were retrieved from both online databases, using “bullying” and “social media” as search keywords. The retrieved articles were systematically analyzed, and two criteria were adopted in choosing the articles to be included in the second phase; these criteria were as follows:

*   1\. Articles must have been published in recognizing academic journals with peer review between 2000 and 2020;
*   2\. Articles should also be empirical research works, focusing digital peer victimization or cyber bullying. All studies that only consider bullying, mobbing or school violence (unspecific) was excluded, following a similar procedure to the one followed by Zych et al. (2015).
*   3\. Reviews on cyberbullying mixed with other phenomena or cyberbullying outside social media were also excluded from the sample.

Subsequently, the authors of the present study refined the analysis, rescanning the database using the “cyberbullying” keyword, instead of bullying, and use the same time period, in order to validate the final solution retrieved. The full text of each article was reviewed to eliminate articles that were not fully related to cyberbullying in social media network sites. Through this procedure, 356 full articles and research notes were selected. These articles were used to conduct the following analyses: citation analysis, co-citation analysis, and content analysis. From this last process, 10 different clusters of authors and research stream were determined.

1.2. Bibliometric Analysis on Cyberbullying in All Different Disciplines

Academic research on cyberbullying has grown significantly over the last decade (see Figure 1).

With 291 items the right-hand (red) cluster is the biggest cluster and is centered on the user’s role within the network and the content produced. When analyzing this cluster formation over the years, it can be noted that it changed from a more technology-driven approach to a detection-driven approach (see, Figure 5).

| Figure 5. Key concepts within the biggest cluster over the years |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch010.f05](i/ch010.f05.png) |
| --- |

Initial studies were mainly conducted by computer scientist, aiming to unveil the technological adoption patterns and motivations. More recently, the studies shifted to development of tools to detect and prevent cyberbullying, being the last studies related to the Artificial Intelligence use to conduct automatic cyberbullying detection (Rosa et al., 2019).

The left-hand bottom side (dark green) with 264 items represents research linked to the theoretical and practical evidences of bullying victimization related to the use of social media, especially related to younger users. As earlier noted, cyberbullying shares with bullying common defining characteristics, that led many researchers to study the similarities and differences between the phenomena. Most of these studies found support in empirical evidences related to a young person’ behavior over social media and compared them with school context evidences (Casas et al., 2013; Zych et al., 2015).

The third cluster, on the top left-hand side (dark blue), aggregates 237 items are related to the cyberbullying perpetration. Considering that generally cyberbullying is considered as encompassing both perpetration and victimization, it was expected to find a strong connection between these two concepts in prior studies. Nonetheless, in the last five years, this link was overlapped by the relationship between cyberbullying perpetration and moral disengagement, such as the works of Charalampous, Ioannou, Georgiou, and Stavrinides (2020) and Fang et al. (2020).

Looking closer to the center of the graph, seven small clusters can be found integrating different approaches: cyberbullying as an academic issue (166 items); attitudes toward sexual-related cyberbullying (146 items); aggressor-victim relationship (93 items); predictors and emotional response using mobile and instant messaging (92 items); gendered bullying (70 items); antisocial internet behavior (42 items); and ethical media competences (17 items).

An overall look into this database led to conclude that over eighty percent of the studies conducted related to cyberbullying focus on young people (children, adolescences and young adults). With the rise of cyberbullying among adults, particularly in workplaces, and the more intense use by seniors, it will be expectable to see in the future a decrease of focus in young people.

Analyzing the contribution by the first author, the following graph is obtained (see Figure 6).

As presented in Figure 6, there are nineteen groups of authors. The three main groups of authors (the two at the center of the graph – green and red; and the bottom right-hand clusters) are leading the research on this topic with publications since 2004 and are from different disciplinary fields (computer science and psychology).

After the first set of bibliographic analysis, a second round of analysis was conducted considering only those articles that analyzed specifically the cyberbullying on social media. The initial results present a much clearer graph solution, with less clusters and stronger relations between clusters (see, Figure 7).

| Figure 7. Key concepts network visualization using cyberbullying in social media |

Figure 7 shows four major clusters: the bottom left-hand side (green), with 176 items, are dominated by victimization, gender differences and psychosomatic problems, while the top left-hand side (blue), with 56 items, features the instruments and scales development. The academic reviews conducted related to the subject are represented by 45 items in a disperse cluster (olive green).The right-hand side (red), with 266 items, features the individual, which is the main node, and integrates a wide set of themes concerning the social and learning problem and the detection, classification and the distinctive approaches to cyberbullying. Comparing the two network structures (Figure 3 and Figure 7), the ethical concerns have missed in this last one and the educational and parenting supervision/values transmission is relatively minor within the top left cluster.

Most research focuses on the United States (122 articles), followed by Canada (30 articles), the England (26 articles), and Spain (22 articles).

| Figure 8. Map with research works density |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch010.f08](i/ch010.f08.png) |

Cross-analyzing this data with the social media adoption rate by country (Statistic.com), it can be noted that countries with high social media penetration-rates and with better internet access are the ones presenting the highest number of studies. These results corroborate existing research that shows that time spent online enhances the likelihood of being involved in cyberbullying (Frison, Bastin, Bijttebier, & Eggermont, 2019; Hinduja & Patchin, 2008).

Trying to unveil the research gaps in the field, the main differences found in the cyberbullying were listed and compared with the traditional bullying, and their reference in the cluster analysis presented.

Table 2. Different approaches and cluster identification

| Traditional bullying || Cyberbullying in Social Media || Cluster |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Lower self-control || Self-control is not a decisive fact, but the ability of the disinhibition provided by the online environment || Bottom left-hand side cluster – green cluster |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Moral disengagement, but sometimes the bullies have some empathy || Moral disengagement associated with low empathy || Bottom left-hand side cluster – green cluster |
| Home is a safe place || Home is not a safe place || Minor disperse reference |
| Time is contextualized, just when aggressor and victims are together || Aggressor is available 24 hours, 7 days a week || Minor disperse reference |
| Space are contextualized || No boundaries || Minor disperse reference |
| Aggressor and victims have a different role || Victim in traditional bullying can be an aggressor in cyberbullying || Bottom left-hand side cluster – green cluster |
| The victims are, normally, school students || The spectrum of victims has increased, anyone can be a victim of cyberbullying || Bottom left-hand side cluster – green cluster |
| Depression is the major health condition post-victimization || Victims present higher evidences of mental illnesses, such as depression and suicide attempts || Bottom left-hand side cluster – green cluster |
| Parents and school are the main agents of detection || Social media, AI machines, parents and school are responsible for detection || Right-hand side cluster – red cluster |

Research on cyberbullying has been carried out for two decades. Nonetheless, the number of cyberbullying studies conducted in a social media context is quite small, compared with the number of users and cyberbullying complained acknowledge by users (Statistic.com) and compared with general cyberbullying studies. The high number of studies is still concerned with a more conceptual approach, lacking the empirical evidences. When looking at the specificities of social media and the intense nature of social interaction establish among users, the context assumes an increasing importance in the attraction, adoption and behavior of users. Therefore, it can be identified gaps of empirical studies concerning the users´ profiles on social media and online risk behaviors, ethical concerns, educational and parenting supervision/values transmission and bystanders’ responses to cyberbullying.

FINAL CONSIDERATIONS

In the last two decades, cyberbullying is on the rise worldwide, powered by people massive adoption of technology and by the enable of fast data access in multiple devices. Cyberbullying might seem as the digitization of traditional bullying, since it their ground bases are similar (Casas et al., 2013; Davis, 2017; Smith et al., 2012). And, this conceptual proximity has led researchers to consider as a framework of analysis similar models to the ones adopted to analyze traditional bullying (Pearce, Cross, Monks, Waters, & Falconer, 2011). However, as pointed by Casas et al. (2013) there are many divergent predictors between cyberbullying and traditional bullying, which implies the need to develop a wider understanding of cyberbullying.

LIMITATIONS AND FUTURE RESEARCH DIRECTIONS

Regardless the richness of data gathered on Web of Science database, this study has some limitations. Firstly, the research and analysis are carried out on papers belonging to the Web Science database, leaving some relevant works aside. Secondly, the research focuses on the keywords cyberbullying and social media. That was important to delimit the scope of the analysis, because allow us to have an intensive study in this field, but also can be limit the analyses outcome, since some papers may not include due to the keywords used.

Thus, in future works we intend to broaden the scope of the investigation, which I use from other platforms, either by using more comprehensive keywords, in order to understand the level of coherence between the results obtained now and the conclusions we will reach in this future work.

In addition, and based on our conclusions, we intend to develop research in the field of education, ethics and the role of the family in order to understand what the role of education and parents should be in preventing cyberbullying, and what measures should be taken to achieve this prevention.

CONCLUSIONS

In the last twenty years, there has been a concern with a conceptual mapping of cyberbullying, always taking as a reference and starting point the concept of bullying, establishing a similarity between these two concepts (Casas et al., 2013; Davis, 2017; Modecki et al., 2014; Perren & Gutzwiller-Helfenfinger, 2012; Smith et al., 2012). Although it has already been concluded that bullying and cyberbullying are distinct concepts, that the latter transcends the former, the reality is that we are still at a stage of characterizing the protagonists in terms of ages, genders, ethnicities, behaviours, psychosomatic problems of the victims and aggressors, types of cyberbullying, scales used in their study (See, Figure 7).

When looking at the main results found in the bibliographic analysis conducted (see, Table 2) we can see that, despite the interdisciplinary dimension that the study of cyberbullying involves, the truth is that most of the articles are in the area of the computer sciences, which denotes a concern to understand the phenomenon of traditional bullying in a new context, the electronic devices and social media. Thus, it is understood that areas such as psychology, research in education are also areas of investment in scientific production, since the purpose of the articles produced was in reality to understand whether the protagonists of cyberbullying continued to be students in school periods (Alfandari, 2019; Buelga et al., 2015; Fanti et al., 2012; Hinduja & Patchin, 2010; Van Ouytsel, Lu, Ponnet, Walrave, & Temple, 2019), people who have, in psychological and moral terms, the same characteristics, such as the low self-control and the moral disengagement (Bussey, Fitzpatrick, & Raman, 2015; Perren & Gutzwiller-Helfenfinger, 2012; Vazsonyi et al., 2012).

The analysed articles are limited to a descriptive dimension of the current situation, neglecting a prospective stance, which seeks a prophylactic action. In our point of view, this explains the disinvestment in research in the educational field (See, Figure 7), either formal education (at school) or in the informal context (within families), in the ethical and moral training of students. Research in these areas will allow not only to characterize the context of cyberbullying from the point of view of these domains, but also to stimulate action-research projects that enhance educational improvements and investment in the formation of a moral and axiological awareness of students that would facilitate the construction of an autonomous and balanced identity and the establishment of healthy interpersonal relationships, guided by values such as solidarity, tolerance, equality and justice.

Adding to this, there is still a lack of empirical studies that profile both cyber victims and cyberbullies in social media and identify online risk behaviours. This last point links to one other research gap related to parenting supervision/values transmission. At this point, the difference between technology adoption by generation seems to result in parents' underestimation of their own child's cyberbullying risks, experiences and behaviour. Parents as well as other bystanders still are learning how to respond to cyberbullying.

Although the field of cyberbullying is relatively new, as is shown in the literature, it has the potential to continue to develop insights into different disciplinary areas, as well as provides evidences in other domains, such as firm-related cyberbullying or ethnic cyberbullying, as seen recently during Coronavirus initial spread. The need to explore semantically rich links between data retrieved from heterogeneous sources arises as relevant to victims, families, schools, social media firms and policy makers, that are daily challenged by new formats and extensions of cyberbullying.

KEY TERMS AND DEFINITIONS

Bibliometric Analysis: Consists in the use of qualitative and quantitative statistical methods to analyse publication’s contents, references, citations and (co)authorships.

Bullying: Comprehends an aggressive human behaviour against another human, which is perpetuated in time, inflicting harmful effects on the victims.

Cyberbullying: Comprehends an inimical behaviour to harm others by an individual or a group, perpetrated by the electronic devices, inducing psychosomatic problems.

Moral Disengagement: Term used by social psychology to refer to the process according to which the self does not recognize the ethical-moral norms as applicable to itself, in any context. People with moral disengagement do not show any kind of empathy, pity for the vulnerability of their victims.

Power Imbalance: Is one of the major differences between bullying and cyberbullying, based on the fact that one single malicious act may be repeatedly disseminated over the time and viewed by multiple users that can become active or passive bullies.

Psychosomatic Problems: Human disease, some kind of physical or mental human's disorder.

Social Media: Are internet-based forms of communication, such as social network sites and microblogging, that allow users to establish social networking relationships.

# Chapter 11

*   Salma P. Z  
    NSS College of Engineering, Kerala, India
*   Maya Mohan  
    NSS College of Engineering, Kerala, India

ABSTRACT

One of today's important means of communication is email. The extensive use of email for communication has led to many problems. Spam emails being the most crucial among them. It is one the major issues in today's internet world. Spam emails contain mostly advertisements and offensive content, which are often sent without the recipient's request and are generally annoying, time consuming, and wasting space on the communication media's resources. It creates inconveniences and financial loss to the recipients. Hence, there is always the need to filter the spam emails and separate them from the legitimate emails. There are a lot of content-based machine learning techniques that have proven to be effective in detecting and filtering spam emails. Due to a large increase in email spamming, the emails are studied and classified as spam or not spam. In this chapter, three machine learning models, Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), and Bidirectional LSTM (BLSTM), are used classify the emails as spam and benign.

INTRODUCTION

Electronic mail or email is one of today's most prominent and fastest methods of exchanging messages between people using digital devices over the internet. Email is one of the easiest and most common means of communication in our time. One of the major communication platforms in today's age is the internet and hence emails are considered to be the fastest and essential way of communication means. Email communication contributes to the major part of conversations in almost all domains. It is one of the most effective and commonly used sources of communication. The cost-effective and speed in communication made email communication popular among the users.

Spam emails, often known as junk email, is the unrequested messages which are sent in bulk through email communication. These unwanted emails are generally annoying and time-consuming and wasting space on the communication media's resources. Spam emails result in many issues such as reduced performance of the email engines, occupation of unnecessary space in the mailbox, and destroying the stability of mail servers. In certain cases, it also contains viruses, trojans, and other materials that may be potentially harmful to certain categories of users (Shrivastava and Anju, 2017). There have been several studies on spam emails and it shows a steady growth of spam emails by 90% from the early 1990s till 2014. Issues related to spam mail has also been growing exponentially over time. Users receive hundreds of spam emails with new content and new sources and these spams are generated by spammers using automatic robot software. The organizations face an influence financially due to the proliferation of spam emails. Spam emails not only invade the user's email but also produces a huge volume of unwanted data thus limiting the network's usage and capacity. Email spamming is also the first step in targeted attacks in organizations, which is currently an important issue. Email spam is not merely an innocuous waste of time (Alurkar et al., 2017). It is a tool for malicious activities such as spear phishing, whaling, clone phishing, website forgery, and much more. Classifying emails as spam or ham is thus of utmost importance from a security perspective for the user. The issues related to spam mails are escalating with the increased usage of the web. The fact that out of 80 billion emails received every day, 48 billion of them being spam highlights the importance and urgency of implementing effective classification procedures for emails (Harisinghaney et al., 2014).

With the increasing network bandwidth and improving technology, spam emails have become more sophisticated and it is necessary to use advanced algorithms to create efficient spam filters. Despite the huge amount of research work that has taken place in this sphere, there is no spam filter that is 100% efficient. Hence, there is a need to develop a more sophisticated and accurate classifier model to eliminate the problem of spam emails. All emails share a common structure i.e. subject of the email and the body of the email. Spam emails are identified through the contents of the email, based on the assumption that the content of the spam mail is different than the legitimate or ham mail. The frequently used words in spam emails are words that are related to any product, the recommendation of services, dating related content, etc.

The process of spam email detection can be broadly categorized into two approaches (Ma et al., 2009): knowledge engineering and machine learning approach. Knowledge engineering is a network-based approach in which IP (internet protocol) address, network address along with some set of defined rules are considered for the email classification. This is a fruitful method but bares the limitation of time consumption. The updating of rules and maintenance are also tedious for users. As an alternative, machine learning techniques can be used which does not involve any set of rules. Comparatively, it is much efficient than the former method (Guzella and Caminhas, 2009). Several classification algorithms are used which classifies the emails based on its content and attributes.

BACKGROUND

H. Karamollaoglu et al. (2018) explained the detection of spam emails with machine learning methods. In this study, the content information of emails written in Turkish were analyzed with the help of Naive Bayes Classifier and Vector Space Model from machine learning methods to determine whether these emails are spam emails and classify them. Both methods were subjected to different evaluation criteria and their performances was compared. In this study, an application has been developed in the Java environment. With this application, the username and password of the known email accounts with Gmail extension, email accounts provided by Google, email IMAP support has been accessed. In order to determine the performance of the study, the data set named Turkish Mail (Ergin et al., 2018) which is composed of Turkish content emails was used. Based on the analysis, emails were classified as spam email and ham emails. Although it was seen that both methods have achieved high performance in comparison, the Naive Bayes Classifier method was more successful in the classification process according to the Vector Space model.

Sharma et al. (2018) proposed a machine learning-based hybrid bagging approach by implementing two machine learning algorithms: Naive Bayes and J48 (decision tree) for the spam email detection. The results were collected from three experiments and compared. The Naive Bayes J48 algorithm was used for doing the two experiments (Tang et al., 2016). The third experiment was the proposed Spam Mail Detection (SMD) system implemented using a hybrid bagged approach. The SMD system exhibits strong classification ability by utilizing the hybrid bagged approaches. The correlation-based feature selection mechanism was used for feature selection. The novel hybrid bagged approach was used for classification. Matrices such as precision, recall, accuracy, F-measure, true negative rate, false-negative rate, and false-positive rate were found and compared and the performance of SMD was evaluated.

Olatunji et al. (2017) explained the wide use of two machine learning methods, extreme learning machines (ELM) and Support Vector Machines (SVM), for both classification and regression problems of recent. The experimental procedures implemented here followed strictly the computational intelligence approach. The acquired dataset was first divided into training and testing set in the ratio 7:3 respectively using the stratified sampling approach. Then the training dataset was first introduced to the models for training and validation. Thereafter the reserved 30% of the dataset was then used to test the system to ascertain the performance accuracy of the proposed model. Experimental results from simulations indicated that the two proposed, developed, and compared ELM and SVM models showed an improved accuracy when compared with earlier models used on the same dataset. Empirical results also indicated that the proposed SVM based scheme outperformed the ELM in terms of accuracy while ELM outperformed SVM in terms of speed of operation.

Alurkar et al. (2017) proposed a system that attempts to use machine learning techniques to detect a pattern of repetitive keywords which are classified as spam. The system also proposed the classification of emails based on other various parameters contained in their structure such as Cc/Bcc, domain, and header. Each parameter would be considered as a feature when applying it to the machine learning algorithm. This method provided an alternative architecture by which a spam filter can be implemented. A three-tier architecture which is also a client-server architecture was incorporated in the proposed model. The first module is mainly used for the processing of data. Here, the first step of acquiring emails from an email server and data formatting was performed. In the second module, the fundamental logic behind the classification of spam/non-spam emails was implemented. The proposed system trained the algorithm and classified emails by learning from a previously classified dataset, and then extends that functionality to classify incoming emails and display them in an organized manner. This not only resulted in an increase in productivity by reducing the distractions and clutter caused by spam but more importantly it protect the user from malevolent attacks.

Shrivastava et al. (2017) described spam mail detection through data mining techniques. The method proposed in this paper involves creating a spam filter using binary and continuous probability distributions. The algorithms implemented in building the classifier model are Naive Bayes and Decision Trees. The effect of overfitting on the performance and accuracy of decision trees is analyzed. Finally, the better classifier model is identified based on its accuracy to correctly classify spam and non-spam emails. This paper presents an approach to spam classification using Bernoulli's and continuous probability distribution. The spam classifiers were tested on three benchmark datasets and the experimental results revealed that the classifier models perform better with Bernoulli's probability distribution than with continuous probability distribution. There is inherently no superior classifier model between Naive Bayes and Decision Trees. The performance of classifier models varies and depends on several factors such as the probability distribution used, dataset, and the problem involved.

DeBarr and Wechsler (2009) explained a spam detector system making use of the random forest algorithm. The density-based and uncertainty-based clustering methods on term frequency and inverse document frequency were used here. Clustering was performed using the Partition Around Medoid algorithm (Nguyen and Smeulders, 2004). The proposed method was verified on the TREC spam email corpus. The receiver operator characteristic curve was plotted and the area under the curve was analyzed. Another work in targeted malicious email detection was proposed by Amin et.al (2012). Targeted emails are spam emails that are sent to single users or a small group of users. The Random Forest technique to differentiate legitimate emails from such targeted emails was presented here. The true positive and false positive values were found. The machine learning model using general descriptive features in detecting spam emails was presented by Cohen et.al (2018). The features were extracted from the emails itself. An integrated detection rate measure was defined for the machine learning classifiers used here and the Random Forest algorithm showed a higher detection rate. Nizamani et al. (2014) discussed the method to detect fraud emails using advanced features of email. Various relevant feature sets were extracted from emails and different machine learning algorithms were applied using the WEKA tool (Witten,2005). The accuracy of the classification of each machine learning algorithm was analyzed. Aski and Sourati (2016) explained the machine learning approach using C4.5 decision tree classifier, Naïve Bayes classifier, and multilayer perception model. The model was evaluated using the WEKA tool considering the header, and white and black list keywords of emails. The efficiency and accuracy of the model was tested and analyzed. The advanced machine learning technique known as reinforcement learning was used by Samdi et al. (2018) in the detection of phishing emails, a type of spam email. The model proposes a novel algorithm named, feature evaluation and reduction, to explore the new changes in the behavior of emails and to adapt to these changes. A dynamic evolving neural network using the reinforcement learning is used here for classification. This was the first work to use reinforcement learning for spam email detection and showed high performance in accuracy, precision, and recall. A different approach using fuzzy clustering technique is proposed by A.W Wijayanto and Takdir (2014). The Fuzzy C-Means algorithm (Havens et al.,2012) is used here for classifying the spam emails. The simple and popular k-medoid method is used here for fuzzy clustering. The implementation of this model in the cybercrime domain is explained here and gave promising results in the classification.

Saidani et.al (2020) proposed a semantic based approach in spam email classification. A two-level classification is used here. The emails are initially categorized into different subject domains using a supervised classifier and a semantic feature space is built through feature extraction using the CN2-SD method (Lavrac et.al, 2004). Different machine learning algorithms were used for classification, and accuracy, precision, and recall of each method was found. Another semantic approach is explained by Bahagt et.al (2018). The feature reduction is performed here using the semantic relation and similarity measures of the semantic ontology, WordNet (Hristia, 2013). The reduction module includes the semantic discovery, weight function, and feature selection steps. Different machine leaning algorithms were used for classification and the performance was analyzed.

An analysis in intelligent detection of spam emails is done by Kareem et.al (2019). The analysis focused on four parts of the email structure. The spam detection methods using Artificial Intelligence (AI) and regular non-automated methods are discussed here. The accuracy of each method was found and compared. Alli et.al (2018) described a method in detecting the Advanced Fee Fraud (AFF) (Ofulue, 2010), (Garrett, 2014), which is a type of spam email. A linguistic analysis technique using self-referential pronouns was used here. The pronouns used in emails were detected using a text analysis software known as Diction (Hart,2001). Chae et.al (2017) discussed the combined use of information gain and context of emails in filtering spam email. The template graphs (Aery and Chakravarthy, 2005) are formed from emails and are used in email classification. The accuracy of the model was found and analyzed.

Diale et.al (2019) proposed an unsupervised feature learning method for filtering spam emails using small feature sizes. The distributed bag of words model and distributed memory models (Le and Mikolov, 2014) along with cosine similarity and autoencoders were used here to captures the word ordering and semantics of email for learning. Machine learning models such as Support Vector Machine, Random Forest, and C4.5 were used and the performance was analyzed. An extension to the bag of words method is explained by Douzi et.al (2017). A paragraph vector distributed memory technique is used here to overcome the limitation of word loss in the bag of words (Le and Mikolov, 2014) method. The embedded information in the email context was extracted and the emails were represented as feature vectors. Neural networks were used for learning and classification. Faris et al. (2018) proposed a method to identify relevant features of email for spam detection. The method was implemented using the Genetic Algorithm and the Random Weight Network (Schmidt et al., 1992). This hybrid model identified the relevant features and the classification was performed.

A hybrid model combining the Negative Selection Algorithm (Balthrop et al., 2002) and Differential Evolution is presented by Idris et al. (2014). The negative selection algorithm is used to generate detectors in the spam space and the differential evolution is integrated to avoid the problem of overlapping of detectors and to efficiently cover spam and non-spam space. The performance of the model was measured using different matrices such as accuracy, positive prediction value, negative prediction value, and correlation coefficient. An extension of this approach using particle swarm optimization was explained by Idris et.al (2015). The particle swarm optimization method was implemented using a local outlier factor (Sajesh and Srinivasan, 2011). A fitness function was used for generating the detectors. This method improved the random generation of detectors in the spam space and performance than the traditional models.

MACHINE LEARNING MODELS

Machine learning can be defined as the scientific study of algorithms and the statistical models using which computer systems can perform the tasks efficiently and effectively. The study relies on specific patterns and inferences and does not involve any explicit instructions. Machine learning is a subset of artificial intelligence. The machine learning algorithms make use of the training data, a sample data extracted from the input dataset, to build a mathematical model that can make predictions or decisions without the help of any explicit programs. Machine learning algorithms find application in a variety of areas. It is used in email filtering and computer vision, where it is infeasible to develop an algorithm of specific instructions for performing the task.

Types of Learning Algorithms

Machine learning algorithms can be classified based on the approach used, the type of input data and output data, and the type of task or problem that is intended to solve using the machine learning algorithm. The different types are:

1\. Supervised Learning

Supervised learning algorithms (Caruana and Niculescu-Mizil, 2006) is used to build a mathematical model of a set of data. It contains both the inputs as well as the desired outputs. This set of data is known as training data and consists of a set of training examples. For each training example, there are one or more inputs and the desired output. The output is also known as a supervisory signal. Supervised learning algorithms can learn a function that can be used to predict the output associated with new inputs, by using the iterative optimization of an objective function. An optimal function is the one that will use the algorithm to correctly determine the output for inputs that were not in the training data. Supervised learning algorithms include techniques such as classification and regression. Classification algorithms are used when the outputs are restricted to a limited set of values, and regression algorithms are used when the outputs may have any numerical value within a range. One of the areas of supervised machine learning that is closely related to regression and classification is similarity learning but here the goal is to learn from examples by making use of a similarity function that measures how similar or related two objects are. It has applications in the ranking, recommendation systems, visual identity tracking, face verification, and speaker verification.

2\. Unsupervised Learning

Unsupervised learning algorithms (Barlow, 1989) take a set of data that contains only inputs, and structure the data, like grouping or clustering of data points. The algorithm learns from test data which is not labeled, classified, or categorized. Unsupervised learning algorithms do not respond to the feedback instead they identify the commonalities in the data and react based on either the presence or absence of such commonalities in each new part of data. One of the most important applications of unsupervised learning is in the field of density estimation in statistics, though unsupervised learning encompasses other domains involving summarizing and explaining data features. The assignment of the observed set of values into subsets known as clusters is the cluster analysis process. The values are grouped such that the values within a cluster show high similarity and the values in different clusters show dissimilarities based on some predefined criteria. The assumptions made on the structure of the data differs for each clustering techniques. Often, they are defined and evaluated based on some similarity matrices. There are also methods based on estimated density and graph connectivity used for clustering.

3\. Reinforcement Learning

Reinforcement learning (Kaelbling et al., 1996) is one of the important areas of machine learning. It is mainly concerned with how software agents take actions in an environment to maximize the cumulative reward. It is a general area of learning and is used in a variety of areas such as game theory, control theory, operations research, information theory, simulation-based optimization, multi-agent systems, swarm intelligence, statistics, and genetic algorithms. In machine learning, the environment is typically represented as a Markov Decision Process (MDP). Many reinforcement learning algorithms use dynamic programming techniques. Reinforcement learning algorithms do not assume knowledge of an exact mathematical model of the MDP and are used when exact models are infeasible. This type of learning method is used in autonomous vehicles or in learning to play a game against a human opponent.

PROBLEM DEFINITION

Due to a large increase in email spamming, there is always a need to efficiently detect and predict email spam detection. Many traditional methods, as described in the above section, were used for email spam detection. Most of the, above mentioned, methods faced some limitations in detecting the spam emails efficiently. Here, it is aimed to analyze the content information of e-mails using machine learning models. The emails written in English were considered. In this study, the emails were analyzed and then classified as spam email or legitimate email with the help of machine learning models. Three machine learning models, Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), Long Short Term Memory (LSTM), and Bidirectional LSTM (BLSTM) were used here.

MACHINE LEARNING MODELS USED

There is a huge variety of machine learning models available today. A simple Artificial Neural Network (ANN) is the basic machine learning model. The other models are Support vector machines (SVM), Decision Tree, Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), Recurrent Neural Network (RNN), Bayesian Networks, and so on. In this study, three machine learning models are used.

1\. Recurrent Neural Network (RNN)

The recurrent neural network (RNN) (Mikolov and Karafiát, 2010) belongs to the class of artificial neural network in which connections between nodes form a directed graph along a temporal sequence. As a result, it can exhibit temporal dynamic behavior. RNNs can use their internal state (memory) to process sequences of inputs, unlike the feedforward neural networks. Basic RNNs are organized as a network where the nodes are neurons arranged into successive “layers” as shown in figure 1. Within a given layer, every node is related to a directed connection, which is a one-way connection, to every other node in the next successive layer. Each node or neuron is associated with a time-varying real-valued activation function. Each connection is associated with a modifiable real-valued weight. The nodes can be either input nodes, output nodes, or hidden nodes.

The input vectors arrive at the input nodes. The input vectors are real-valued vectors and they reach the input node as one vector at a time. At a given time in a step, each non-input unit computes its current activation (result) as a nonlinear function of the weighted sum of the activations of all units that connect to it. For some output units at certain time steps, supervisor-given target activations can be supplied.

Recurrent Neural Networks has a wide set of applications which includes machine translation, robotic control, time series prediction, speech recognition, etc.

2\. Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM)

Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) (Sundermeyer and Schlüter, 2012) is an artificial recurrent neural network (RNN) architecture mainly used in the field of deep learning. The feedback connections in the LSTM network makes it an ideal candidate for general-purpose computations. Also, the same makes the LSTM outstand the standard feedforward neural networks. Single data points like images and entire sequences of data like videos can be processed by an LSTM network efficiently. A common LSTM unit is composed of a memory cell, an input gate, an output gate and a forget gate and is given in figure 2. The cell will remember the values in all the time intervals and controlling of flow of values into and out of the network is done by the three gates.

One of the responsibilities of the memory cells in the LSTM is the tracking of the dependencies between the elements in the input sequence. Each gate are used for specific purposes. The flow of new values into the cell is controlled by the input gate, the time period of value in a cell is determined by the forget gate and computation of output using activation functions are controlled by the output gate. An activation function is used which is often a logistic function. Some of the connections into and out of the LSTM gates are recurrent in nature. The weights of these connections are learned during training. This information is used to determine the operations of the gates. Using an optimization algorithm like gradient descent, an RNN using LSTM units can be trained in a supervised fashion, on a set of training sequences. The algorithm is combined with backpropagation through time to compute the gradients needed during the optimization process. This is in order to change each weight of the LSTM network in proportion to the derivative of the error (at the output layer of the LSTM network) with respect to corresponding weight.

| Figure 2. Long Short Term Memory Network |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch011.f02](i/ch011.f02.png) |
| --- |

LSTM networks are considered to be one of the efficient methods for the classification, processing, and prediction of time series data. This is because of the presence of lags of unknown duration between important events in a time series. The LSTM method addresses and solves the problems in the training of traditional RNNs such as the exploding problems and vanishing gradient problems. The advantage of LSTM over RNNs and other sequence learning models is the relative insensitivity to gap the length. LSTM has a wide set of applications which includes the robotic control, prediction of time series data, speech recognition, learning of rhythm, music composition, grammar learning, recognition of handwriting, recognition of human actions, translation of sign languages, protein homology detection, predicting subcellular localization of proteins, time series anomaly detection, etc.

3\. Bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (BLSTM)

LSTM in its core preserves information from inputs that have already passed through it using the hidden state. The Unidirectional LSTM preserves only the information from the past because it has seen the inputs from the past only. Apart from this, the bidirectional LSTM (Schuster and Paliwal, 1997) can have input from the future also as shown in figure 3. This approach differs from unidirectional LSTM is that this is an LSTM that can run information backward, ie; information from the future is preserved. The two hidden states used and combined so as to preserve information from both past and future.

SPAM EMAIL DETECTION USING MACHINE LEARNING MODELS

In this study, the authors propose a system that aims to analyze the emails and classify them as spam email or legitimate email. This classification is done with the help of machine learning models.

The emails categorized as spam and ham are given as the input. A total of 6000 emails are given to this system. Initially, the dataset is split into training and testing sets. 80% of the data is used for training. This is to get maximum efficiency in training by avoiding the underfitting problem. The dataset is shuffled for each iteration for maximum training efficiency.

The inputs are processed initially. The emails are vectorized using the ‘Tokenizer()’ API provided by Keras library. Text tokenization is used to vectorize the words. This vectorization is done by the integer encoding of the words. The integers represent the index of that word in the corpus or dictionary. The words can also be vectors with binary coefficients based on the count of that word. This word count uses the term frequency-inverse document frequency method. In this model, the API provided by Keras, Tokenizer API, is used for text tokenization. This is an efficient API for large documents and can be reused for multiple text documents. Also, this works well for the deep learning approach. The tokenizer takes the raw text as input and converts the words in the text as vectors. The training set is initially given to the tokenizer. Once the Tokenizer has been fit on training data, it can be used to encode documents in the train or test datasets.

The dense vector representation approach for representing the words and documents is known as word embedding. The embedding of a word is the position of that word in the learned vector space. Here, an embedding layer provided by the Keras is used. This layer can be used efficiently for text data in neural networks. The input to this layer is integer encoded data, ie; each word should be represented using a unique integer. The integer encoding of input data can be done using the Tokenizer API which is also offered by Keras. The integer encoded data along with some random weights are fed as input to the embedding layer and the layer is initialized with this input. This is done for all the words in the training dataset. This flexible layer can be used in different ways like:

*   • It can save the learned embedding for a word and can use it in the future.
*   • The learning is integrated along with the model in which it is used.
*   • It can be used to load a pre-trained word embedding model, a type of transfer learning.

The Embedding layer is considered as the first hidden layer in a network. The “Sequential” model in Keras is used in all the models. It is a linear stack of layers. The expected input shape of the model is the prerequisite for a sequential model. This information must be passed to the first layer of the sequential model. The activation function used is the “sigmoid” function. Activations can be done either by using the Activation layer or by using the activation argument. Output values in the range (0,1) are produced by a sigmoid logistic function. The “rmsprop” optimizer is used for optimization. An optimizer is one of the two arguments required for compiling a Keras model. This optimizer is considered as a good choice for recurrent neural networks. The loss function used is the “binary cross entropy” function. With binary cross entropy, the outputs are classified into two classes. The model is compiled and trained using the “fit” function provided by Keras. The model is trained for a fixed number of epochs or iterations on the provided dataset. The model can save the history of the training in an object. This object can be used to retrieve the values of loss values and accuracy values of the training and testing of the model.

Three layers are used in all three models. An embedding layer and a dense layer is common to all the models. A simplernn layer, an lstm layer, and a bidirectional lstm layer is used in RNN, LSTM, and Bidirectional LSTM models respectively.

Different recurrent layers such as RNN, LSTM, and BLSTM were adopted for feature engineering. Experiments were conducted for evaluating the performance of each deep layer. Most of the employed architecture is not too deep, so the batch normalization mechanism was not used. All experiments have used a learning rate of 0.2 and a batch size of 60. Batch size indicates that the model parameters update is done once it trains the 60 data samples through the backpropagation mechanism. The Recurrent layer has used different layers such as RNN, LSTM, and BLSTM. Through domain knowledge, the hidden units were set to 32. A hyperbolic tangent within the range of \[-1,1\], \[1,1\] was used in the RNN unit and LSTM memory cell, respectively, as an input and output activation function. A logistic sigmoid for gates and other neurons within the range \[1,0\] was also used in the LSTM memory cell. The BLSTM also uses the same as that of LSTM but with a bidirectional motion. As recurrent structure layers capture the dependencies for the received matrix from an embedding layer and pass its last output 32 to dropout layer with 0.2. Dropout layer with 0.2 characterized as regularization parameters. This is interleaved with deep layers such as RNN, LSTM, and BLSTM. Dropout is a mechanism widely adopted to remove the neurons randomly along with their connections during training a deep learning architecture. Dropout layer interleaved dense layer with units as 1 in distinguishing emails as ham and spam. Additionally, a dense layer has followed an activation layer with sigmoid non-linear activation function and loss function as binary cross-entropy. The dense layer is typically called as a fully connected layer. It sums the received features from recurrent layers. Thus, a hierarchical feature representation is constructed for the final stage of classification.

The three models are trained on the same dataset for 10 epochs. The performances of each model are evaluated and compared. The performances in terms of precision, recall, F1-score, and support of all models are represented in the below Table 1.

Table 1. Comparison of Performance of the Three Models

|  ||  || Precision (%) || Recall (%) || F1-Score(%) || Support |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| RNN || Ham || 0.97 || 0.99 || 0.98 || 1019 |
| Spam || 0.96 || 0.82 || 0.88 || 181 |
| LSTM || Ham || 0.99 || 0.99 || 0.99 || 953 |
| Spam || 0.98 || 0.93 || 0.96 || 162 |
| Bidirectional LSTM || Ham || 0.99 || 0.99 || 0.99 || 953 |
| Spam || 0.98 || 0.93 || 0.95 || 162 |

Source: Author’s calculation based on the experiment conducted  

The interpretation of the inner workings of these deep learning networks remains a black box for both novices and advanced users. These deep layers can store a lot of information and this can be seen by unwrapping them. Inevitably, the deep architectures such as RNN, LSTM, and BLSTM are very complex. By unwrapping them, a huge amount of information can be extracted. Generally, the learned character representation in the embedding layer was transformed through the deep layers to capture the semantic similarity of them. The non-linear activation in each deep layer supports to learn the best features. Using the learned feature representations, the last layer in deep architecture should maximally separate the emails as spam and ham. To use this in this experiments, 4187 ham emails and 1813 spam emails were randomly selected from a sample of 6000 emails. The model trained is then given sample input data. The model predicts it as a spam email or a ham email.

The classification accuracy of the three models was also calculated. It was seen that the bidirectional LSTM achieves a higher accuracy of 98%. The other models, RNN and LSTM attained the accuracy of 96% and 97% respectively.

FUTURE RESEARCH DIRECTIONS

This study analyzed a set of emails from a dataset and applied machine learning models to classify them as spam and not spam. This study can be extended to other advanced and hybrid machine learning models. The accuracy of this model can also be checked on other datasets.

CONCLUSION

Email spam is considered to be the most important and attention-seeking issue in today's world of internet communication. Since the issues of spam emails are increasing tremendously, there is always a need for the detection of spam emails. Machine learning approaches are efficient in the detection and prediction of spam emails. The machine learning approach in the detection and prediction of spam emails is discussed in this chapter. This chapter has reviewed the effectiveness of using various deep learning mechanisms towards the analysis, detection, and prediction of emails. The models are trained with spam and ham emails in character level by extracting features automatically. Thereby, avoiding the manual feature engineering method and thereby itself serves as a robust method. The embedding layer followed by the other deep networks layers extracts features implicitly and these optimal features are fed to other layers of the deeper network for analysis and classification. The machine learning models such as RNN, LSTM and Bidirectional LSTM were considered for this study. The results obtained from the evaluation of the classifiers show that the bidirectional LSTM achieves a higher accuracy of 98%. The other models also show a good percentage of accuracy.

KEY TERMS AND DEFINITIONS

Email IMAP: The internet message access protocol (IMAP) is a mail protocol that can be used from a local client machine to access emails on the remote web server.

Innocuous: Not harmful or offensive.

Knowledge Engineering: A field of artificial intelligence that tries to collect the judgment and behavior of a human expert in a given field.

Malevolent: Having a harmful influence or malicious.

Overfitting: A condition when a model learns the detail and noise in the training data to the extent that it negatively impacts the performance of the model on new data.

Swarm Intelligence: A concept in artificial intelligence which considers the collective behavior of decentralized, self-organized natural and artificial systems.

Trojan: A type of computer virus in the form of computer software such as utilities, games, and sometimes even antivirus programs.

The dataset used for this study was the set of emails taken from the SpamAssasin and spam base datasets. The dataset contained a total of 6000 emails categorized as spam and ham. The dataset is distributed as Spam 1813 (30.2%) and Ham 4187 (69.8%).
