# Chapter 12

*   Sanjeev Rao  
    [![Orcid Image](i/orcid.svg)https://orcid.org/0000-0001-7338-1930](https://orcid.org/0000-0001-7338-1930)  
    Thapar Institute of Engineering and Technology, India
*   Anil Kumar Verma  
    Thapar Institute of Engineering and Technology, India
*   Tarunpreet Bhatia  
    Thapar Institute of Engineering and Technology, India

ABSTRACT

Online social networks (OSNs) are renowned powerful web tools that allow worldwide users to connect with their friends, families, professional groups, and social circle through social interaction for sharing common interests. With the proliferation, ease, and efficacy of OSNs, these are becoming an essential tool for communication. But many OSN users innocently uncover their personal information such as their home address, phone numbers, email id, etc. that can be used by the malicious user to perform various kind for cyber-crimes like cyber-bullying, spamming, click-jacking, identity theft, phishing, distrust, fake profiles, spreading malicious content, etc. This chapter presents a review of various privacy and security threats/attacks associated with OSN users and recommended combating techniques based on data-mining and machine learning algorithms. Also, the future directions for upcoming researchers in this field are suggested.

INTRODUCTION

From the last few years, the usage and popularity of OSNs have increased at a tremendous rate. It becomes a necessary tool to facilitate communication for every online social user (Boyd & Ellison, 2007). Some of the very popular OSNs are Facebook, Twitter, Google+, Myspace, Tumblr, Sina-Weibo, Snapchat, Pinterest, and Instagram, etc. have millions of daily active users. As of the first quarter of 2020, Facebook has a maximum, i.e., more than 2.5 billion monthly active users (Statista, 2020). The preliminary characteristics of social networking are based on 3C’s, i.e., creation, curation, and consumption. OSNs generally have synonyms like Online Social Media (OSM), Social Network Sites (SNS) that were used interchangeably in many research papers. Social media is like a vehicle for communication. It’s a place that can be used to transmit information to other people like newspaper agencies publish and spread the news in the form of a newspaper to many people. But with the advent of the internet, media is no longer static and can be used as blogs, apps, websites, videos, etc. Social media is a broader term, and the OSN is part of Social Media. OSN allows users to connect with their friends, families, professional groups and social circle through social interaction for sharing common interests by first connecting with other members through sending and receiving friend request, later in the form of posts, comments, likes, dislikes, tags, sharing posts, followers, following, etc. OSNs are helping many other business sectors like marketing, advertising, promotions, product reviews, knowing public opinion in political elections, online learning, growing business reputation, disaster management, healthcare, professional network, and recommender systems, etc. (Fire, Goldschmidt, & Elovici, 2014; Penni, 2017). The challenges associated with OSNs are an ever-increasing amount of users’ leads to the accumulation of Bigdata in the form of textual data, data related to their connections, multimedia data that they share, and personal information (Persia & D’Auria, 2017). These further give rise to issues such as data storage, data management, and data analyses. Users trust these OSNs and users within these social networks that lead them to make their social network by sending and receiving friendship requests from people whom they know and don’t know or but having some friends in common. By accepting these friend requests, users innocently reveal their personal information (age, religion, income, relationships, location, phone numbers, sexuality, habits, financial details, etc.) and professional in-formation like (company, project, work-culture, team, reports, earning, etc.) to strangers. This information could be exposed and abused maliciously and hurting the users both in the cyber and in the real world (Bilge, Strufe, Balzarotti, & Kirda, 2009; Gangavarapu, Jaidhar, & Chanduka, 2020). The vast Number of OSN users and huge volumes of personal details have attracted malicious people, hackers, computer criminals, and third-party companies, etc. These malicious users conduct illegal practices such as data stealing, ransomware, false accounts, spamming, invading viruses, phishing, cyber-bullying and sexual assault, and fake reviews, etc.(Persia & D’Auria, 2017). These challenges give rise to new research directions to secure the privacy of OSN users that is at stake due to misuse of personal information, spreading viruses, fake news, rumors, and spam by malicious users and hackers. The success of any OSN is influenced by the number factors like Number of active users, design, privacy and security of users, other useful features like searching, profile tagging, messaging, calling, photo and text editing options, etc. OSN developers give much emphasis on design and features, and decidedly less focus is given to the security and privacy of OSN users. So studying, analyzing, and combating OSN’s privacy and security issues have now become a wide area of research. The motive of this chapter is to provide useful information regarding privacy and security threats/attacks in the OSNs. In this chapter, a survey of some paramount cyber threats associated with Social Networking Sites, the primary reasons behind these threats and counter-measures to combat the security risks to users have been presented.

Evolving Cyber Threats in OSN

OSNs are the best tools used by masses for communication and transferring information. At the same time, it is misused by spammers or malicious users, for spreading spam campaigns, wrong information, fake news, rumors, unwanted messages, and phishing URL’s, etc. in OSNs. In figure 1, the classification of threats and attacks associated with OSNs is shown.

| Figure 1. Classification of threats and attacks associated with OSNs |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch012.f01](i/ch012.f01.png) |
| --- |

The various types of attacks/threats related to Online Social Networks are classified into the following categories:

*   1\. Classic Attacks
*   2\. Social Attacks
*   3\. Contemporary Attacks
*   4\. Hybrid/ Combinator Attacks

1\. Classic Attacks

*   a) Malware Attack: Malware is software used to take control of user’s private information by collecting and manipulating their identification details. Malware is used to broadcast wrong information or spam messages to users and their friends using their OSN network. Example Koobface was known to be the first malware propagated successfully through OSNs. Malicious links are used to harm or deceive the user once the link is clicked. Also, the malware gets downloaded into the user’s systems to steal their personal information (Brown & Hermann, 2020).
*   b) Compromised accounts: When instead of an authentic person, a fake person is accessing his/her online account, then the account is said to be compromised. Attackers try to trap users into fake websites that look like the original website to collect user login details and later use this information for criminal purposes by masquerading as a trustworthy body. OSNs are more prone to Phishing attacks due to their social and trustworthy nature (Adewole et al., 2017; Ravneet Kaur et al., 2018).
*   c) Phishing Attacks: Phishing is the fraudulent attempt to gain sensitive information such as usernames, passwords, bank account numbers, and credit card details, often for malicious reasons, by masking as a trustworthy person in an electronic communication. Phishers can easily explore the freely available information given on social sites to raise the success rate of a phishing attack (Selvaganapathy et al., 2018; Smadi et al., 2018).
*   d) Cross-Site Scripting (XSS) Attack: The XSS attack usually found in web applications like websites, blogs, e-mail, Instant Messenger in the form of the malicious script. The XSS exploits the client’s trust to execute malicious code on the user’s web client to collect their details. But in OSN, XSS worm can be easily transmitted without human intervention among social network users (Faghani & Nugyen, 2017; Rodríguez et al., 2020).
*   e) Spammer’s Attack: A Spammer is a person, organization, or bot that uses electronic messaging systems to send irrelevant or unwanted messages on e-mail, social sites, and mobile phones using Internet services to a large number of users. Spam content is used for advertising, phishing, pornography links sharing, and for spreading mal-ware purposes. Generally, Spammers use fake profiles to send advertisement messages, add fake comments, or fake reviews on social network sites as well as in online shopping websites. Due to the explosive growth of the Number of users in OSNs, spammers use to spread spams rapidly and widely on OSNs to produce traffic overload. Therefore distinguishing users as spammers or legitimate users has become a crucial and severe issue in OSNs (Fu et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2018).
*   f) Internet Fraud or Cyber-Crime: To perform internet/cyber-crime attackers first establish an in-person bond with potential victims on social networks to acquire the victim’s details. Then they use victim's details mentioned in their social network profiles to do fraudulent activities like fund transfer, stealing personal data, etc. (Apte et al., 2018; Ramalingam & Chinnaiah, 2018).
*   g) SQL injection (SQLI) Vulnerability: SQL injection attack is a famous security risk to database-driven web applications, and mobile apps such as banking, healthcare, social networking sites, gaming etc. It is a web application vulnerability in which cybercriminals apply Structured Query Language (SQL) commands to web-forms input text objects to obtain access to sensitive data and other database services secretly. The purpose of the SQL injection attack is to access the database remotely to alter data, perform a denial of service (DoS) attack, access database schemas, unauthorized database access, fingerprinting etc. Some of the famous SQL injection techniques are piggybacked queries, union queries, stored procedures, inference attacks using timing attacks and blind injections, tautologies etc. (Sadeghian et al., 2013). In the year 2017, companies such as NextGEN, Airsoft GI were attacked by cyber-criminals using SQL injection to steal registered users sensitive data and their e-mail accounts (Almarabeh & Sulieman, 2019).

2\. Social Attacks

Social Network Aggregator (SNA) vulnerability: Social Network Aggregator (SNA) like Snag, ProfileLinker extract content from many Social Network Sites to a single site, in that way helping users belonging to multiple social networks in managing their profiles efficiently. Once login into the SNA account, users can access their social network accounts through a shared interface without having to log in to each OSN site individually. A two-level real-time HTTP is used to establish the connection. Initially, the connection is established between the user and Social Network Aggregator site, later between SNA and linked OSN sites. The communication is done using Open API’s provided by the different OSNs. Vulnerability will be increased if the authentication of such an application is weak (Wang & Ma, 2014). Social Aggregator gives rise to many risks like identity theft, loss of privacy, and giving cyber-criminals a broader base of data to act on (Kamran, 2016).

| Figure 2. Social Network Aggregator (SNA) |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch012.f02](i/ch012.f02.png) |
| --- |

*   a) Espionage: Espionage can be of many types of industrial or corporate espionage and economic espionage. Corporate espionage occurs among companies and big corporate houses using social engineering methods like hacking, spreading malware, spyware, etc. to gain access to companies’ confidential data, customers’ information, plans, trade secrets, etc. whereas economic espionage is done by governments at the international level to detect attacks by terrorist groups, adversary foreign governments, etc. (Herrmann, 2019; Libicki, 2018).
*   b) Stalking by online Predators: OSN users reveal their personal information like phone number, home address, current location, some activity schedule, etc., that can be used by Online Predators for giving threats to OSN users using Instant Messenger, Social Walls, e-mails, phone calls, etc. In some cases, they lure innocent children and teens for sexual and violent purposes by masquerading of being the friend. Online predators are cybercriminals that are involved in activities like physical harm, bullying, kidnapping, rape, threatening, online harassment, and unwanted exposure of OSN users personal data such as textual data, pictures or videos, etc. (Fazil & Abulaish, 2018; Fire et al., 2014).
*   c) Cyber-Bullying/Abuse: Cyber-bullying generally affects children and teenagers. Cyber abuse involves the use of Internet and communication technologies (ICT) to harass others. The cyber-bullying attack can be done using e-mails, chat, mobile phones or on OSNs by posting bad comments or rumors about the victim, sending threatening messages, harming someone ’s public image by publishing wicked or forged pictures or videos, etc. (Herrmann, 2019; Kumar et al., 2018).

3\. Contemporary Attacks

*   a) Ransomware: Ransomware is malicious file-encrypting software/malware. Ransomwares are used to perform extortion-based attacks i.e. it locks data on victim’s machine and shows ransom/money notifications to be charged for the device to run again. These can be of two types i.e. Screen-locker ransomware or Crypto-ransomware (File-locker). The screen locker ransomware locks the victim’s screen or showing a pop-up window that never closes, and on the other hand, file-locker ransomware make files inaccessible by encrypting them with some password (Bijitha et al., 2020). One commonly used ransomware is Scareware used to threaten the victim with issues and viruses in the system and asks for online payment to fix the problems. A ransomware WannaCry was used to target British Health care system and demanded massive payment in the form of bitcoin cryptocurrency.
*   b) Click-jacking: In such an attack, the attacker forces users to click something that the user was not intended to click. In OSN, attackers hack user’s account once the user clicked on the malicious link in the form of advertisement or article or text to further spread the advertisement to their friends through the social network (Nalinipriya & Asswini, 2016; Rathore et al., 2017)
*   c) Fake/Clone Profiles or Social-Bots: Social bots are used to gather victim’s private data by sending them friend requests (Kantepe & Gañiz, 2017; Xiao et al., 2015). Once the victim accepts the friend request, all its private data is exposed to fake profile/user, i.e., otherwise not visible to the external user. Often malicious user generates many fake accounts for these purposes of reaching a more significant number of trustworthy users and communities. Fake profiles can be used to manipulate user profiles, sending spam messages, profile browsing, commenting, messaging, and for advertisement purposes, etc. In online shopping sites, fake profiles can be used to post fake reviews in bulk to increase the product’s sale revenues or service offerings (Persia & D’Auria, 2017; Ramalingam & Chinnaiah, 2018). Some of the possible risks involved are leakage of private and personal information, phishing, spamming to spread malware for advertising marketing campaigns (Yassein et al., 2019).
*   d) Identity Clone Attacks: In such attacks, the attacker makes a duplicate user profile in the same network or in different OSNs to collect personal information about the user’s friend. Later the collected data can be used to do fraudulent activities like mislead original user’s friends, sending spam messages, friend requests, and advertisements, etc. by forming a trust relationship with duplicate user profile, known as Profile squatting attack (Bilge et al., 2009). Attackers can damage the social image of a person or affects the brand value of a product that results in humiliation and financial losses (Gangavarapu et al., 2020; Persia & D’Auria, 2017; van der Walt et al., 2018).
*   e) Inference Attacks: Attackers in the form of data Analyst use data mining techniques on publically available OSN data or stealing from OSN profiles to detect user’s interests like their taste, preferences, geographical information, etc. for direct marketing and product recommendations (Heydari et al., 2015; Zheng et al., 2011).
*   f) Click-baiting and Like-jacking: Click-baiting is a form weblink or headline titles used by attackers to entice users to click over the content to generate online advertising revenue. It is usually used in blogs, news, videos, comments, reviews to gain users attention, often the link is to divert the online traffic and has no concern with the headline or weblink (Guo et al., 2018; Satya et al., 2016; Thejas et al., 2019).
*   g) De-anonymization Attacks: De-anonymization identifies unknown data sources, profiles by cross-referencing them with other sources using data mining techniques. To protect their identity and privacy, OSN users use pseudonyms or false names. These attacks reveal the real identity using web techniques like tracking cookies, user group memberships, and network topology, etc. Some researchers have also discussed OSNs vulnerabilities of personal identity information leaked using cookies and another tracking mechanism (Ratandeep Kaur et al., 2019; van der Walt et al., 2018).
*   h) Face Recognition: Huge Number for profile pictures and other photographs are uploaded and shared on any OSN every day and freely accessible to attackers. One OSN website Faces of Facebook has given the privilege to users to view Facebook profile pictures of billions of users, which can be used to build a biometric database. This biometric database help attackers to identify and use the profile pictures to find other personal information without OSN user approval. Face recognition software can also be used by attackers to extract useful features from profile pictures that are freely available to gain user interest. These extracted images can be used for face authentication and become an essential threat to biometric systems and mobile applications (Korshunov & Marcel, 2018; Sabir et al., 2019).
*   i) Location Leakage: Many users share their own and their friend’s current and future location information while posting any activity, photos, videos, comments on OSNs like Twitter, Foursquare, Flickr, etc. using mobile phone devices. Some OSNs allow the user to post pictures along with geo-tag, which gives the location where that picture was taken. Such information can be used by attackers and stalkers to perform a fraudulent activity that may cause substantial damage to OSN user in terms of blackmailing, burglary at home or offices, physical attack, etc. (Costa et al., 2013; Nalinipriya & Asswini, 2016)
*   j) Socware: Socware is referred to as a third-party mobile app or the website that is linked or posted on OSN in the form of posts and messages, to perform criminal and parasitic activities (Xu et al., 2015). OSN users come across socware advertisements or links in the form of attractive question-answering content, once the user visited or installed that socware, it automatically perform activities like sending malware, spam, etc. to another user without users consent. Studies mentioned that around 49% of users and 40 million posts were exposed to socware. Most of the third party malicious applications linked with OSNs are responsible for spreading socware (Thejas et al., 2019).
*   k) Political Manipulations and propagandas: The unverified news sources and fake accounts are used to create fake news into the OSNs to change the public consciousness. The artificial intelligence-based social bots automation help to spread deceptive content in social sites to masses (Qi et al., 2018). If such automation is combined with political propaganda, it can significantly affect public opinion during elections, debates, and political emergencies. Fake news and other spam content are used to perform attacks like click-baiting, spreading misinformation, and political propagandas (Grimme et al., 2017). Fake news has become a public concern after the 2016 US presidential election (Howard et al., 2018). It was a great scale spam act that happened to affect American Political Twitter. People behind political propaganda initiated the process by posting fake content or news on OSNs rest of the propagation work is done by online users. Nowadays, spam activities campaigns are being carried out in the form of advertisements supporting public health, stock market, gaming, and lottery, etc. Spambots and phishing attacks using short/tiny-URLs are also proven to be harmful by stealing personal data of OSN users (Fazil & Abulaish, 2018; Patil & Patil, 2018).

4\. Hybrid / Combinator Attacks

A hybrid attack is a refined form of attack that attackers performed by combining existing and recent attacks. For Example, a Click-jacking attack can be achieved by first performing a phishing attack to steal the username, password of OSN user. Cloned profiles to extract information related to OSN user’s friends, combined with a spamming attack by embedding a spam link in the personally tailored message, e-mail, etc. prepared by the attacker. Similarly, combining existing attacks, new attack strategies are built and performed by attackers.

Combating Techniques

The above section mentioned the various attacks/threats associated with OSN that may be directly or indirectly responsible for damaging the security and privacy of OSN users. Many authors have suggested different solutions for OSN attacks. In this section of the chapter, authors provide some data mining and machine learning-based solutions to combat various attacks such as phishing, spamming, cloned profiles, fake profiles, and socware, etc. for proving better privacy and security to OSN user. In table 1, the various existing combating techniques is given in-terms of tools, methods, techniques, algorithms and frameworks etc.

*   a) Phishing Detection: Anti-phishing methods are used to detect and prevent phishing attacks. Many researchers have suggested various solutions to detect phishing URL in OSN like WarningBird URL detection system (Lee & Kim, 2013), PhishAri technique (Liew et al., 2019), Blacklists (Wu et al., 2017), Rule-based heuristics (Apruzzese et al., 2018), Visual similarity (Fu et al., 2018), etc. Some researchers have mentioned feature extraction techniques and machine learning algorithms for detecting phishing attacks. The supervised algorithms such as KNN (K Nearest Neighbor), SVM (Support Vector Machine), C4.5, etc. and unsupervised algorithms such as K-means, DBSCAN, etc. (Gangavarapu et al., 2020; Liew et al., 2019).
*   b) Spam Detection: Most Popular OSNs like Facebook, Twitter, Instagram, and Sina Weibo platforms are used by billions of people worldwide for communication and sharing information (Zhu et al., 2012). Due to a massive number of users connected, spammers took advantage of spreading spam content on these platforms. Spam can be detected using existing techniques such as honeypot, list-based filtering methods such as Blacklist, Whitelist, Greylists etc. But these techniques are not efficient enough to deal in OSN environment. In recent works, Machine learning and deep learning based methods are used to analyze the content, behavior, malicious links etc., that are far better than existing filtering techniques for spam detection (Lalitha et al., 2018; Wu et al., 2018). The main challenge for such methods is the changing behavior of spammers (Guzella & Caminhas, 2009; Wu et al., 2017). Some other researchers have proposed new machine learning and ensemble-based approaches to improve the performance of algorithms (Mehmood et al., 2018).
*   c) Cloned Profile detection: Profile cloning is a severe threat to OSN users’ security since it uses people's trust to steal personal information for doing fraudulent activities. Attackers copy the profile picture and other useful information of the legitimate user from one OSN and create a duplicate profile on some other OSN to gain the trust of valid user’s friends on this network later can be used to spread spam or other malicious content (Bilge et al., 2009). Researchers’ have developed various methods to investigate cloned profiles by analyzing the same profiles in terms of same attributes, the similarity of relationship networks, node similarity, Graph similarity measures that can be drawn from structural and non-structural iterative measures (Devmane & Rana, 2014; Kamhoua et al., 2017). A technique CloneSpotter was developed using the user’s login IP addresses for detecting cloning attacks (Shan et al., 2013; Zare et al., 2020).
*   d) Fake profile or Sybil’s detection: Fake accounts are one of the favorite methods to spread spam, malicious content, cyber-bullying, and other illegal activities on OSN (Adewole et al., 2017). Researchers have developed new techniques, methods, algorithms, and tools to deal with fake profiles. The main methods given in the literature for Fake Profile detection are classified into three categories, namely Crowdsourcing, Graph-based, and Machine learning (Singh et al., 2018). Researchers have used various features that are specified under network structure-based features, content/behavior-based features, and network-based features. SybilGuard protocol, SybilLimit protocol, SybilInfer defense algorithm, SumUp Sybil defense system, SybilRank tool, and SybilRadar were some of the successful protocols, methods, and tools for detecting Sybil/fake profile detection (Al-Qurishi et al., 2017; Ramalingam & Chinnaiah, 2018).
*   e) Socware detection: Socware is a recent form of attack to spread spam and malware on the social walls of OSN. Facebook OSN is more prone to such attacks as compare to other OSNs. Significant contributions for socware detection was given by as MyPagekeeper secure Facebook application that rigorously examines the subscribed user’s OSN wall and news feed to detect socware (Ramkumar et al., 2016). FRAppE (Facebook’s Rigorous Application Evaluator) was used for detecting malicious applications on Facebook. They also gave literature related to the socware ecosystem and socware propagation features that would be of great help to future researchers for the detection and prevention of Socware (Rahman et al., 2012).
*   f) Cyber-bullying Detection: Cyber-bullying attacks are used by an attacker to insult OSN users by sending those threatening messages or posts. Part of speech (POS) tagging, Sentiment analysis, and text mining techniques are used to analyze OSN posts, messages to detect cyber-bullying content (Vyawahare & Chatterjee, 2020). In corpus taken from Formspring.me OSN to analyze the cyber-bullying content using supervised machine learning techniques with a scoring scheme (Fazil & Abulaish, 2018; Ioannou et al., 2018) Higher is the score higher is the cyber-bullying content. Some researchers have used Machine learning classifiers, Natural language processing (NLP), the fuzzy rule set to extract relevant data and genetic algorithms for obtaining optimizing factors and output results (Vyawahare & Chatterjee, 2020).

FUTURE RESEARCH DIRECTIONS

After a detailed literature review on cyber challenges to OSNs, authors have established several primary work avenues that can be explored further, such as the privacy and security of mobile OSNs, crowdsourcing methods, trust computation and management, decentralized OSN schemes, security and access control mechanisms, and resource management, etc. Also, analyzing OSN’s user behaviors, information diffusion models, detection and prevention of spam, spammer, social-bots, sentiment analysis, trend analysis, optimization of existing OSN functionalities, recommender systems, and big data analytics, etc. are some of the vital open research topics that need to be explored.

CONCLUSION

OSNs are the platforms that provide exciting new prospects for communication. But it also opens avenues for hackers and spammers to perform fraudulent activities. Authors have highlighted many privacy and security threats and attacks that are done on OSN Platform, later they have also mentioned various techniques and methods to combat against multiple types of attacks. The information given in chapter will be an excellent help to the OSN users for understanding numerous attacks on OSNs and roadmap for the upcoming researchers for building better security and privacy techniques to tackle such attacks.

KEY TERMS AND DEFINITIONS

Crowdsourcing: Crowdsourcing is a marketing strategy in which an organization outsources part of its operational activities to an ambiguous group of many individual contributors for advertisements, spamming, influencing people by increasing number of followers, friends, etc.

Machine Learning: Machine Learning is a subdivision of artificial intelligence. Machine learning is the study of computer algorithms which, through experience, automatically improve.

Natural Language Processing: It is a sub-discipline of linguistics, computer science, information engineering and artificial intelligence involved with computer and human language interactions, in specific to how computers can be programmed to process and examine huge volumes of natural language data.

Online Social Networks: It is an online platform which people use to build social networks or social connections with others to share similar personal or career interests, activities, experiences, or real-life relations.

Part-of-Speech (POS) Tagging: The part-of-speech (POS) tagging is to assign grammatical categories (noun, verb, adjective, etc.) to words in a natural language sentence.

Sentiment Analysis: Sentiment analysis is the interpretation and classification of emotions (positive, negative, and neutral) within text data using text analysis techniques. Sentiment analysis allows businesses to identify customer sentiment toward products, brands or services in online conversations and feedback.

Social Bots: A social bots are automated programs/agents who interact on social networks to influence the course of conversation/discussions and their readers' opinions.

Social Network Attacks: The attacks performed on Online Social Networks by cyber-criminals is known as Social Network attacks.

Socware: Socware as malicious software links propagated by cyber-criminals through malicious URLs embedded in posts and messages to perform illegal activities such as phishing, compromising accounts, etc.

Spam: Spam in social networks refers to undesirable, malevolent, unsolicited content or behavior, exhibiting in different ways, comprising microblogs, tweets, malicious links, fake contacts, false reviews, etc.

Sybil Attack: In the sybil attack, a single entity imitates several user activities and attempts to cause complications for users on online social networks.
