It also emphasizes, secondly, that the right to the protection of personal data “is not an absolute right, but must be considered in relation to its function in society and be balanced against other fundamental rights, in accordance with the principle of proportionality”, a balance that “is likely to vary significantly around the world”. In other words, both the sovereignty of third States and the modulation of essential rights in view of their constitutional texts, organization and regulations, as well as the different break even points that can be reached when balancing and making different rights compatible, justify that the EU Court of Justice establish territorial limits to the application of the new right now positively endorsed by the RGPD (Moura, 2020, p. 234).

Subjective and Objective Scope of the Right to Be Forgotten: Diversity of Agents Involved, Content and Interests at Stake

The right to be forgotten can be defined, in general terms, as “the right of all interested parties to have their personal data deleted from the network once the purpose that initially justified its collection and processing has disappeared” (Casino, 2012, p. 202). Its raises fewer problems when referred to personal information that would have illegally reached the network, as the right to informational self-determination involves demanding protection from the national authority for data protection or, when appropriate, to claim judicial justice for the fundamental right violated by the publication, usually to intimacy, privacy, personal reputation or self-image. Once the content has been declared illegal, the competent authority will order the publisher of the web page to withdraw the corresponding information, and the data subject may request the erasure of results, links or other forms of access to such, under penalty of personally responding for its publication. Internet search engines admit this type of request without the need to wait for an administrative resolution or a judicial sentence in those cases in which the illegal nature of the content uploaded to the internet is manifest.

The claim to oblivion is more complex with respect to publications on the internet that were, in principle, innocuous, or even required by a legal norm, but referred to a data subject who, over time, would prefer to see them removed from the network (Terwangne, 2012; Villaverde, 2013). Often the content refers to past information and its publication was then justified and lawful, but it is considered to have lost relevance over time, so that its immediate availability on the Internet is considered excessively burdensome from the perspective of the personal right to informational self-determination (Palacios, 2012). Even more so when said content may appear as the first results offered by one or several internet search engines when collecting information about a certain subject using their name and personal data as search criteria.

And so, publications that most frequently prompt erasure applications are press news contained in electronic newspaper archives, as well as administrative or judicial resolutions and notifications published in official bulletins, often as a mandatory measure. Saura, Palos and Navalpotro (2017, p. 225) refer to the “growing case-by-case motivation” in the matter, referring to “weariness, change of ideology or habits” as new causes to elicit requests. The indefinite permanence on the internet of the information that someone has decided to voluntarily share on the network has also been subject to debate, either because he or she wishes to exercise the possible right to be forgotten, or because it affects third parties who are cited or affected by the publication in question. To what extent can users actually consent to voluntarily yield part of their privacy in exchange for being able to use certain services that, despite being voluntarily subscribed, constitute essential tools in current daily life to be socially connected? Can their users really compromise with personality rights that are inherent to their dignity and, precisely by definition, non-transferable and inalienable (Pazos, 2016; Sancho, 2018)?

In any case requirements to cancel or erase harmful data or information from the past is not a new issue in our legal systems, which include instruments such as the cancellation of criminal records or the anonymization of judicial decisions and other administrative resolutions before being published, with the aim of guaranteeing the fundamental rights to privacy, reintegration, free development of personality, etc., although the emergence of new computer technologies and the spectacular development of the network have intensified the debate and encouraged its expansion to new premises (Guichot, 2012), demonstrating the ineffectiveness of traditional legal tools of protection in the virtual world of no temporal or spatial barriers (Chéliz, 2016, p. 269).

The most problematic cases refer, however, to contents referring to a natural person, lawfully published on the internet by an editor and accessible through a list of links offered by an internet search engine based on his or her name. Such engines involve a particular risk as a result of their own characters and operational mode. They allow searches to be carried out at high speed, tracing all the information existing on the network to offer a practically exhaustive list of links to pages related to the key word or data on which information is requested. All this in real time, free of charge, without having to reveal one’s identity and without the need to motivate or process a previous administrative procedure to justify the search. These features together with the perpetuity of the information contained in the network allow access to all kinds of personal data outside their original context, turning them into “eternally present past characteristics”, sometimes damaging to the data subject. Pérez (2016, p. 176) speaks in this sense of “digital hypermnesia”, following Metallinos (2016, p. 38).

In short, subjects involved in the possible conflict caused by the right usually fall into one of the following four categories. Firstly, the publisher responsible for uploading in the past the information that now bothers, the opinion that hurts, that the affected person would like to see, ultimately, suppressed from the network. Secondly, the search engine that crawls the web to index its content and display it in an orderly manner to its users, through a list of results with the link for each specific outcome. Thirdly, the internet user who browses the network either directly or through a search engine. And, finally, the data subject on whom the published message reflects, pursuing that their data or certain personal information is no longer available on the internet, either by deleting the content, or by deleting the corresponding links from the search engine results.

Such a variety of subjects translates, in turn, into a great diversity of rights, freedoms and interests affected (Cobacho, 2019). Thus, to cite the most important, communication rights, in both their active (broadcasting) and passive (reception) dimensions, free enterprise or fundamental rights to the protection of personal data, to intimacy, honor, and self-image, to privacy, to physical and mental integrity, to dignity and free development of personality. As jurisprudence has reaffirmed at all levels, there are no absolute rights in our legal systems, so when there is a collision of subjective rights due to a potential exercise of the right to digital oblivion, all rights in dispute must be weighed to determine precisely which of them should prevail over the others. The only exception in this regard is that expressly recognized in article 17.1 f) of the RGPD, concerning personal data that has been collected in relation to the offer of information society services directly to a child, in which case the erasure of personal data will proceed without undue delay, even if the right is exercised when he or she is no longer a child.

Judgment of the EU Court of Justice of May 13, 2014, Case C-131/12, stipulates that “in the light of the potential seriousness of that interference, it is clear that it cannot be justified by merely the economic interest which the operator of such an engine has in that processing. However, inasmuch as the removal of links from the list of results could, depending on the information at issue, have effects upon the legitimate interest of internet users potentially interested in having access to that information, in situations such as that at issue in the main proceedings a fair balance should be sought in particular between that interest and the data subject’s fundamental rights under Articles 7 and 8 of the Charter. Whilst it is true that the data subject’s rights protected by those articles also override, as a general rule, that interest of internet users, that balance may however depend, in specific cases, on the nature of the information in question and its sensitivity for the data subject’s private life and on the interest of the public in having that information, an interest which may vary, in particular, according to the role played by the data subject in public life.”

The balance changes, in any case, with the development of technology itself. If the first search engines already multiplied the presence and effect on personal reputation of information published by an editor, this megaphone effect is now further enhanced as a result of the evolution itself experienced over time by the internet. The processing of information reaches considerable commercial value, exploiting personal data available on the network through multiple applications and the development of computer programs (data mining and big data) which allow individualized commercial prospecting at low cost (Pérez, 2016). Also notable is search engine marketing or search marketing, divided into organic or natural positioning, SEO (Search Engine Optimization), and sponsored or paid, SEM (Search Engine Marketing) (Saura, Palos & Navalpotro, 2017). In short, technology, which is not neutral, has been put at the service of marketing, leaning towards the commercialization of personal data and preconfiguring smart electronic devices to monitor user activity (Sancho, 2019).

These are issues that should be taken into account when weighing the rights and interests at stake in a particular case in which the right to be forgotten is intended. They are in line, moreover, with the warning itself launched by the founder of the internet on the network’s 28th birthday. In his open letter, Berners-Lee (2017) shares his concerns about the three fundamental challenges that the internet will have to face in its evolution, highlighting, in the first place, his appreciation that we have lost control of our personal data, due to the offer of free content in many websites in exchange for personal information and the adoption of increasingly stringent national legislation to allow greater government control of online content, and also, secondly, how extremely easy it is to spread misinformation across the network using little transparent algorithms that determine the links and the content to be shown to each internet user based on their own personal data, collected continuously on the web.

In short, oblivion is not so much about erasing information as it is about obscuring it, hindering immediate access to it through personal data, without having the information disappear from the original source. A complex operation that does not allow simplistic solutions. There is concern that it should not establish in any way a right to censor or edit a false digital profile to accommodate an artificial reputation. But in the same way, there is no denying the right to one’s own personal data, to protect it, to safeguard and self-determine one’s own image and reputation on the internet. These are also fundamental rights, recognized in the highest European and national regulatory instruments as well as in the RGPD.

Its article 5 lists the principles relating to processing of personal data that are common in the entire EU, specifically, those of lawfulness, fairness and transparency (in relation to the data subject), purpose limitation (collected for specific, explicit and legitimate purposes and not further processed in a manner that is incompatible with those purposes), data minimization (adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purposes for which they are processed), accuracy (and, where necessary, kept up to date, so that every reasonable step must be taken to ensure that personal data that are inaccurate, having regard to the purposes for which they are processed, are erased or rectified without delay), storage limitation (so that the identification of data subjects is allowed for no longer than is necessary for the purposes for which the personal data are processed), integrity and confidentiality and, in a very significant way, of accountability, falling on the controller -in this case, both the publisher of the original source and the search engine- the duty to comply with all the aforementioned principles not only at the time of data collection but throughout its processing and, in addition, demonstrate it.

The Procedure to Exercise the Right to Be Forgotten: Weighing Criteria

The RGPD does not design a specific procedure to exercise the right to be forgotten, sanctioning the right of the data subject “to obtain from the controller the erasure of personal data concerning him or her without undue delay” where any of the following applies:

*   a) Personal data is no longer necessary in relation to the purposes for which it was collected or otherwise processed (principle of lawfulness, fairness and transparency).
*   b) The data subject withdraws consent on which the processing is based without it resting on another legal basis and regardless of whether or not it affects special categories of personal data (purpose limitation).
*   c) The data subject opposes to the processing and no other compelling legitimate grounds prevail for the processing which override the interests, rights and freedoms of the data subject or for the establishment, exercise or defense of legal claims, and, in any case, when the right to object is aimed at processing for direct marketing purposes (purpose limitation and conservation period).
*   d) Personal data has been unlawfully processed. In this case, it would be a clear violation of the first principle stated in this regard by article 5.1 a) of the RGPD, possibly linking, even, with the inaccuracy of the data, if “every reasonable step” has not been taken to ensure that inaccurate personal data are erased or rectified without delay, or with probable breaches of their integrity and confidentiality, if it has not been possible to guarantee “appropriate security of the personal data, including protection against unauthorized or unlawful processing and against accidental loss, destruction or damage, using appropriate technical or organizational measures”.
*   e) Data must be erased for compliance with a legal obligation in Union or Member States that is applicable to the controller (territoriality and unlawfulness). If the controller is subject to the law of the Union or one of its Member States, even if it is based in a third foreign state, it may have to erase the personal data of a data subject due to application of the right to be forgotten in its new formulation ex article 17 of the RGPD.
*   f) Personal data has been collected in relation to the offer of information society services to minors.

In any case, where the controller has made the personal data public and an effective cause of oblivion applies, “taking account of available technology and the cost of implementation”, he shall “take reasonable steps, including technical measures, to inform controllers which are processing the personal data that the data subject has requested the erasure by such controllers of any links to, or copy or replication of, those personal data”, that is, informing internet search engines. The “multiplying effect” of the internet is thus contended (Chéliz, 2016, p. 262). In accordance with article 83.5 of the RGPD, infringements of the rights of data subjects, specifically the right of erasure recognized by article 17, will be sanctioned with administrative fines of a maximum of 20,000,000 euros or, in the case of a company, of an amount equivalent to a maximum of 4 percent of the total global annual turnover of the previous financial year, opting for the largest amount of the two. This reinforces the right to be forgotten online (Álvarez, 2016).

Furthermore, for these purposes the right to compensation is of particular interest. It has been recognized by article 82 of the RGPD to any person who has suffered material or immaterial damages as a consequence of an infraction of the Regulation. Joint liability where more than one controller or processor, or both a controller and a processor, are involved in the same processing and responsible for any damage caused by processing, in accordance with the provisions of the precept itself, so that each one shall be held liable for the entire damage in order to ensure effective compensation of the data subject (Biurrun, 2017). Liability which could derive not only from the cases in which the data subjects are deprived of their rights and freedoms or they are prevented from exercising control over their personal data but, significantly, from the unauthorized reversal of their pseudonymization as defined by article 4.5.

However, article 17 itself establishes a series of exceptions to the recognition of virtual oblivion in which the right of erasure cannot be applied to personal data because it would affect an essential processing due to a superior and preeminent public interest. And so, the following stand out to the extent that processing is necessary:

*   a) For exercising the right of freedom of expression and information.
*   b) For compliance with a legal obligation which requires processing by Union or Member State law to which the controller is subject or for the performance of a task carried out in the public interest or in the exercise of official authority vested in the controller.
*   c) For reasons of public interest in the field of public health in accordance with the provisions of the Regulation itself, in particular, for the purposes of preventive or occupational medicine, for the assessment of the working capacity of the employee, medical diagnosis, the provision of health or social care or treatment or the management of health or social care systems and services on the basis of Union or Member State law or pursuant to contract with a health professional, or for reasons such as protection against serious cross-border threats to health, or ensuring high standards of quality and safety of health care and of medicinal products or medical devices, on the basis of Union or Member State law which provides for suitable and specific measures to safeguard the rights and freedoms of the data subject, in particular professional secrecy. Likewise, personal data may be processed when its processing is carried out by a professional subject to the obligation of professional secrecy, or under his responsibility, in accordance with Union or Member States law or rules established by national competent bodies, or by another person also subject to an obligation of secrecy in accordance with the aforementioned regulations.
*   d) For archiving purposes in the public interest, scientific or historical research purposes or statistical purposes in accordance with Article 89.1 in so far as the right referred to in paragraph 1 is likely to render impossible or seriously impair the achievement of the objectives of that processing, in short, that adequate technical and organizational measures have been provided to guarantee respect for the principle of minimizing personal data, giving priority to those that guarantee the satisfaction of these purposes through subsequent processing that no longer allows the identification of the data subjects.
*   e) Or the establishment, exercise or defense of legal claims.

Added to these exclusions are the possible limitations that in application of article 23 of the GDPR Union or Member States law may adopt to the scope of article 17, as long as such restrictions respect in essence other fundamental rights and freedoms and are necessary and proportionate measures in a democratic society to safeguard certain legal-public goods, among others, notably, prevention, investigation, detection and prosecution of breaches of ethical standards in regulated professions, or the protection of the data subject or others.

Moreover, article 85 forces Member States to reconcile by law, with the exemptions and exceptions that may be necessary, “the right to the protection of personal data pursuant to this Regulation with the right to freedom of expression and information, including processing for journalistic purposes and the purposes of academic, artistic or literary expression”. Does everything that reaches the network in a lawful way necessarily have to remain in it without a time limit? With the passage of time the public interest initially present in the information and personal data published may become irrelevant or, at least, weaken to the point of not justifying the complete suppression of the right to informational self-determination of the data subject.

A paradigmatic case of this new social demand for erasing legal content from the internet lacking in current interest is precisely that of Mr. Costeja. In 1998, the newspaper La Vanguardia published -by order of the Social Security- two announcements regarding the auction of real estate owned by him to face certain defaults with Social Security Treasury. Even though uncomfortable for the individual, the publication was fully legal at the time. However, when entering the name of the entrepreneur in Google more than ten years later, the auction ads for non-payment still appeared among the first results related to his identity, which obviously affected his privacy and honor. With the idea of ​​eliminating these links, referring to an issue already resolved and devoid of any public interest more than a decade after the embargo, Mr. Costeja requested both the newspaper and the internet search engine to remove the content and links, respectively. His request was ignored by both, he then filed a claim with the AEPD that upheld his claim in relation to Google, while rejecting it, however, in relation to the newspaper.

The conflict will eventually lead to the Judgment of the EU Court of Justice of May 13, 2014, Case C-131/12. It maintains that the mere economic interest of the search engine manager does not justify the potential seriousness of its interference with the data subject’s right to data protection. In short, rather than conflict, we must speak of the concurrence of rights that must be balanced according to the circumstances of each specific case. Although it is true that the aforementioned Judgment of the EU Court of Justice in the case also known as Google Spain provides some key elements for this, it still leaves questions to be resolved (Sarrión, 2015). For example, regarding the determination of the time to be considered adequate or sufficient to understand that a significant reduction of the public interest initially present in the publication has been consummated. Can it be regulated or should it always refer to the assessment of each particular case? Also, who should carry out this weighing? The task presents, without a doubt, certain inherent subjectivity that will be approached in a different way, in principle, depending on whether it is carried out by those responsible for the processing of personal data -depending, in turn, on whether it is the media, social networks or internet search engines-, by the independent authority articulated in each Member State for the protection of personal data or, finally, by the judicial authority itself in case of non-compliance with regulations applicable in this regard.

The judgment of the Spanish Supreme Court of October 15, 2015 went further to rule precisely on some of these unresolved issues and, in particular, on the limits to the new right to be forgotten, considering that it should be applied in practice even if the treatment of personal data is proved to be truthful as long as it is revealed inadequate for the purpose for which it was initially collected and processed, seriously distorting the perception of the affected person, causing a stigmatizing effect that prevents his or her full insertion in society (Aberasturi, 2016).

Indeed, the role of the press is different when reporting on current events or when preserving information and news. The first is presided over by the freedom of press and information, much stronger regarding the rights to privacy, intimacy, honor, own image or protection of personal data. The second is more about preserving the collective memory for historical, archive and research purposes. This has also been emphasized by the European Court of Human Rights, which extends the protection of article 10 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms, relating to freedom of expression, to digital newspaper libraries, among others, in its Judgments of 10 March 2009, case of Times Newspapers Ltd (Nos. 1 and 2) v. the United Kingdom, paragraph 45, and of July 16, 2013, case of Węgrzynowski and Smolczewski v. Poland, paragraph 59, affirming the network’s substantial contribution to preserving and making available news and information, as well as its role in relation to education and historical research as a source of easy public access and usually free, although underlining, at all times, the main function of the press as a public watchdog compared to its merely secondary role as keeper of the public archives that contain the news on which it has previously reported. Although the custody of digital newspaper archives on the Internet is a critical aspect of this role, the Court maintains in view of the different significance of the two essential functions entrusted to the press that the margin of appreciation granted to the States to achieve the balance between eventual competing rights, in particular informative freedoms and protection of personal data, is likely to be greater with regard to archives relating to news of past events than to current information. Moreover, it intensifies in relation to information that could be classified as historical or ancient, as the press’s duty to act in accordance with the principles of responsible journalism by demanding greater precision increases in these cases precisely due to the absence of any urgency in the publication of the material.

Not surprisingly, the Court emphasizes the capital distinction between the written press and the internet, which as an information and communication tool is fundamentally meant to store and disseminate information. Hence the difficulty, the real impossibility, of subjecting the network to the same rules and control as the written press. Hence also its greater potential as a weapon capable of causing serious damage to some human rights and fundamental freedoms, especially to privacy and intimacy. To that end, the Communication from the Commission, Shaping Europe’s digital future, COM (2020) 67 final, states that “citizens want meaningful answers to attempted manipulations of the information space, often in the form of targeted and coordinated disinformation campaigns. Europe needs greater transparency on the ways in which information is shared and managed on the internet. Trustworthy quality media is key for democracy as well as for cultural diversity.”

Furthermore, what criteria or elements must be weighed in when deciding whether the right to be forgotten has precedence over other rights affected by the claim? Although they can be systematized and subdivided, offering more specific guidelines (Aberasturi, 2016; Guichot, 2019), all of them basically break down into two, the offensive potential that the published information represents for the rights of the personality and the consubstantial public interest in having that specific information appear linked on the internet to the personal data of that same subject.

This is stated by the Spanish Supreme Court in its Judgment of October 15, 2015, specifying that:

This interest cannot be confused with a taste for gossip. As some author has said, what is relevant is not so much the ‘interest of the public’ (if you consider that the sector of the population that wants to know the miseries of their fellow citizens, even those that occurred a long time before is broad), but rather the ‘public interest’, that is, the interest in forming a well-founded opinion on matters of importance for the functioning of a democratic society. This interest may justify that, when it comes to people of public relevance, information about events that affect their privacy or reputation, even if they happened a long time ago, is linked to their personal data in automated process such as those of searches through internet browsers that index existing personal data in digital archives. Social relationships are largely based on the information we have from others, and the moral capital that each person has depends, in part, on the degree of confidence that their life trajectory inspires. For this reason, when this interest in information is present, it is justified that information harmful to privacy and reputation, linked to personal data, may be subject to automated treatment, as long as they are truthful, when dealing with people of public relevance, although the events have happened a long time ago. \[…\] This treatment of personal data can also be considered justified when the facts concerned and their connection with these specific people are of historical interest.

Regarding what should be understood as a person of public relevance, the Supreme Court refers to the Resolution of the Parliamentary Assembly of the Council of Europe, no. 1165, of June 26, 1998, on the right to privacy, in which it is held that “public figures are persons holding public office and/or using public resources and, more broadly speaking, all those who play a role in public life, whether in politics, the economy, the arts, the social sphere, sport or in any other domain”.

It seems exaggerated, if not unconstitutional, to affirm that “every person who voluntarily exposes himself to public attention lacks a reasonable expectation of privacy. Once that intimacy is lost, it is very difficult to argue why and how it should be recovered. And when a person is exposed to public attention through a dishonorable act, there does not seem to be enough to argue that others are obligated to give him a good reputation” (Pazos; 2015). These overwhelming statements raise many doubts as the person in question must also be recognized a right to remake, to rebuild, to reintegrate his or herself. Is dignity not recognized to every human being and the free development of their personality guaranteed as a fundamental right throughout their lives (Pérez 2016; Sancho 2019; Torres 2018)? Do they both not require, in some way, measures of social or collective forgiveness when someone commits an act that could harm their own reputation (Aberasturi, 2016)? Does it make sense to direct prison sentences and security measures towards reeducation and social reintegration, to recognize the person sentenced to prison the constitutional right to the full development of the personality, to legally establish the possibility of cancellation of criminal and police records and, nevertheless, deny digital forgetfulness and not allow a data subject to truncate the link between their personal data and the list of results shown by an internet search engine on the basis that once they committed a dishonorable act truthfulness must prevail at all costs (Pazos, 2015, p. 29)? Doesn’t this mean digitally reissuing the theory of the eternal return (Cobacho, 2019, p. 201)?

In any case, the High Court points out that the so-called “right to digital oblivion” does not assure that each citizen can construe a custom-built past, preventing the dissemination of information on events that are not considered positive, nor does it justify that those who expose themselves publicly demand that a curriculum be built to suit them, “controlling the discourse about themselves, removing negative information from the internet,” positioning “the results of internet searches as they please, so that the most favorable occupy the first positions. If this thesis were accepted, information mechanisms necessary for citizens to make their decisions in the democratic life of a country would be seriously disrupted.”

Thus, continues the Supreme Court, at the request of the affected, those responsible for digital newspaper libraries should adopt technological measures, such as the use of robots.txt codes or no-index instructions, etc., so that the web page of the digital newspaper library in which the obsolete and seriously harmful information appears cannot be indexed by internet search engines, without, however, sanctioning the elimination of personal data from the information collected in the newspaper archive itself, or the impossibility to index it by its internal search engine. These last measures would suppose an “excessive restriction” on the freedom of information itself in regard to the very existence of digital newspaper libraries (Aberasturi, 2016; López, 2015; Rallo, 2014; Simón, 2015). In sum, it makes sense to require media to proactively apply effective technological solutions to prevent personal data from being indexed from outside their web domain by internet search engines when the conditions concur for the right to be forgotten, that is, if the subject and/or the information are not of public relevance and sufficient time has elapsed for this purpose (Angulo, 2019).

SOLUTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

The so-called right to be forgotten does not imply the automatic suppression of all personal information on the legal basis of the right of everyone to informationally self-define, but rather an assessment of the various interests at stake and of the rights in conflict to guarantee their coexistence. A task complex as any legal assessment aimed at balancing fundamental rights. It seems excessively simplistic to resort to “the extreme difficulty of weighing respect for data quality in the framework of freedom of expression and information”, to conclude the absence of “objective legal criteria to determine when the inclusion of personal data in the transmitted message is excessive and when not” and to criticize that this decision “depends entirely on the personal opinion of each individual faced with the issue” (Pazos, 2015, p. 41). Is that not precisely the greatness and servitude of the Law as a system?

Law is not an exact science, it is made up of a set of principles and norms, not of mathematical formulas that can be applied to predefined cases repeated over time under laboratory conditions. Rather, Law is life, continuous flow, not final destination. It is inherent to the human being and its gregarious nature, imbued with its virtues but also afflicted with its hesitations. As a human system it aspires to regulate interpersonal connections and to express the ideas of ​​justice and order socially acceptable at a given moment. As Duguit has stated, the rule of law is a line of conduct that is imposed on individuals living in a society, a rule whose respect is considered at any given time, by a social group, as the guarantee of the common interest and whose breach brings the collective reaction against the perpetrator of the infraction.

In this context, those who take refuge in the formidable problem represented by the weighing of rights to which oblivion necessarily leads to in order to reject the recognition of the right itself without further ado, are caricaturing the issue, since the whole theory of human rights and fundamental freedoms has been precisely built and marked by similar frictions and tensions. No rights are absolute. All of them are limited by definition, as Hegel underlined by sustaining that true tragedies do not result from the confrontation between a right and an injustice, but from the clash between two rights. Balance exists and its subsequent weighing, is essential to the recognition of any right. This is highlighted in the Judgment of the Spanish Constitutional Court 58/2018, of June 4, emphasizing that the express recognition of oblivion as a fundamental right “supposes the automatic application to it of the jurisprudence regarding the limits of fundamental rights”, specifically, “in the remaining fundamental rights and constitutionally protected legal assets, as this is required by the principle of unity of the Constitution”.

The difficulty of the task should not lead to abandoning it without even undertaking it. The weighing implies, in short, the concretion of criteria and elements that try, from the objectivity, to clamp casuistry inherent in particular cases and subjectivity proper to the social valuation of each historical moment when deciding which right prevails in each case or what limits apply to one to the detriment of another. To this end, the list of common criteria for the handling of complaints by the European Data Protection Authorities provided by the working group for analysis of article 29 of Directive 95/46/EC offers a list to evaluate each case as a flexible working tool to help in decision-making processes:

*   • Does the result of the search have to do with a natural person -that is, an individual-? And does the search result occur when performing a search on the name of the data subject?
*   • Does the person concerned play a role in public life? Is the subject a public figure?
*   • Is the subject a minor?
*   • Are the data accurate?
*   • Is the data relevant and not excessive? In other words, are the data related to the person's working life? Does the search result link to information that is excessive or that allegedly constitutes hate speech / defamation / libel or similar crimes in the area of ​​freedom of expression against the complainant? Is it evident that the data reflects the personal opinion of an individual or does it appear to be a proven fact?
*   • Is the information within the meaning of Article 8 of Directive 95/46/EC sensitive?
*   • Is the data up to date? Are the data being made public for longer than necessary in relation to the purpose of the processing?
*   • Is the data processing causing harm to the data subject? Does the data disproportionately negatively affect the privacy of the data subject? Does the search result link to information that puts the person at risk?
*   • In what context was the information published? In other words, did the subject voluntarily make the content public? Was the content intended to be made public? Could the data subject have reasonably known that the content would be made public? Was the original content published in a journalistic context?
*   • Does the publisher of the data have legal authority - or legal obligation - to make the data publicly available?
*   • Is the data related to a criminal offense?

To affirm, to this purpose, that the “only objective aspect available is the decision of the original publisher of the message, that is, if with his conduct he has reflected that identifying a person was important to him”, reason from which it would be possible to advocate, in short, for “a greater preference for freedom of expression and information” (Pazos, 2015, p. 41), is flawed in its own approach. As objective or subjective, where appropriate, the decision of someone who appreciates that the transmission of information is more important than harmful, based on their freedom of expression and information, than that of those who consider it more harmful than socially relevant, taking a stance, in the opposite direction, for their dignity and free development of personality or their rights to private life, intimacy, their own image or the protection of their personal data. All of them are constitutionally recognized rights, present in international treaties. Therefore, none of them should be sacralized to the detriment of others.

CONCLUSION: TECHNOLOGICAL SOLUTIONS FOR THE RIGHT TO ERASURE

The preceding pages testify how the construction of the new right to be forgotten rests on the cornerstone of its jurisprudential creation. The jurisprudence of the EU Court of Justice, as well as that of the constitutional interpreters and judicial bodies of its Member States, in particular, Spain, has allowed, based on international treaties, decisions of the European Court of Human Rights and the corresponding constitutional texts, its recognition. It defined its outlines and, in attention to the particular case object of each dispute, its limits in relation to other fundamental rights and interests equally legitimate.

In view of its evolution, positive reception in the RGPD and different national regulations, we must question the opportunity of preserving the expression “right to be forgotten” in itself. It has been used from the outset to describe radically different claims, almost always much broader than those that have finally found accommodation in the jurisprudential configuration and legal regime of this newly recognized right. As it has been made clear, it does not suppose, in the majority of occasions, suppression of any information or content on the network (Pazos, 2015). In this sense, the reference to forgetfulness moves to confusion.

Not only that, oblivion cannot be truly guaranteed. It is an impossible task or aspiration. It seems illogical that the legal system affirms the right of a data subject to obtain something that, in reality, cannot be fully achieved (Sancho, 2019). This reference might lead the data subject to a certain degree of frustration, as he or she will not be able to find oblivion despite the fact that the applicable regulations on data protection have granted him a right so called, somewhat illusory (Abril & Pizarro, 2014, p. 13).

These contradictions, highlighted before the new positive regulation on data protection by the RGPD, would have advised opting for a different and more illustrative name of the actual content of the new right, of the faculties that it entails in practice. To this end, different options for a right that ultimately seeks to recover or reinsert the digital reputation of its owner based on its ability to negatively self-determine the personal information that is available on the internet about him or herself allow us to speak of a right to de-listing of data, to the expiration of negative data, to the protection of personal data online, to cyber forgetfulness or oblivion, to digital disappearance or to digital darkening or darkness, thus placing the emphasis on the practical effects of its recognition, specifically, the blackout or blocking of the multiplier information effect that would derive from its application (Pazos, 2015; Torres, 2018).

Despite the fact that freedom of information or of expression are usually referred to as immovable boundaries to reject oblivion, the intention of the person who exercises this right is really to digitally obscure certain information for objective reasons, specifically, due to the passage of time, the loss of public interest or the damaging nature of its publication, deleting not the information itself, but the links of the internet browser engines that allow it to be found using personal data for the search. And in that process, it is not who initially exercises freedom of expression or information who decides the withdrawal, but large multinational companies with a direct economic interest in the matter (Arenas, 2014), with little public scrutiny and with a transparency that has only been gradually achieved, but which is still today largely voluntary (Guichot, 2019). As a sample, the letter addressed to Google on May 13, 2015 by 80 international academics in order to demand greater clarity about the procedure by which the company would have to evaluate the requests received for the exercise of this right after the Judgment of the EU Court of Justice in the case that confronted the search engine with Mario Costeja. Initially published on Medium, they denounced that it was impossible to rigorously evaluate Google’s application of the right to be forgotten, since its transparency was very scarce regarding the type and amount of information de-listed, sources de-listed and to what extent, requests rejected, in what proportion and criteria used by the search engine in its balance between the right to intimacy and private life, on one hand, and freedom of expression, on the other. They were also concerned about the absence of mandatory formal involvement of original sources or public authorities in the decision-making process.

In any case, the debate does not affect new legal assets that require protection or suppose substantial change in principles and values ​​in force in our legal systems. Rather, it is a matter of assessing a conflict that is already known in light of the current indiscriminate expansion of the internet, of the dizzying succession of capital technological innovations that have changed the way in which we interrelate and obtain our information (Wittes & Liu, 2015), and therefore, the exponential increase in possible right violations and the appearance of new and various forms of injury, so that the Law can modulate legal mechanisms capable of reacting proportionally to the magnitude of the collision of rights (Cobacho, 2019). All this as a form of reaction against the “liquid modernity” that has submerged us in a “permanent sensation of volatility” and, precisely for this reason, of “uncertainty and, of course, legal insecurity” (Sancho, 2019, p. 180). A reality that is well synthesized in the words of Umberto Eco (2015) when he affirms that he is not sure “that the internet has improved journalism, because it is easier to find lies on the internet than in an agency like Reuters”.

Legal deliberation must lead, in any case, to solutions that will necessarily have to be technological if the essential content of all the rights involved is to be preserved and the number of conflicts in the matter to be minimized. There has been talk, for example, of possible normative predetermination of the expiration period of the public interest in relation to the dissemination of certain information, so that after the indicated period the indexation of the corresponding personal data is automatically blocked without the need for the data subject to personally exercises his right to informational self-determination. The content would be kept on the network although it could not be found through global search engines based on names and surnames (Aberasturi, 2016; Sancho, 2019). This solution has made its way in some areas, for example, in the publication of official bulletins, although there have been voices that have also questioned whether such an expiry date would not become a merely pro-forma, unrealistic requirement (Abril & Pizarro, 2014, p. 51). In any case, the advances in favor of automatic deletion or the recognition, in short, of automatic expiration periods are in accordance with the provisions of article 25 of the GDPR and with its promotion of privacy by design ab initio. Once the recognition of the right has been requested, the technical measures that subsequently prevent the indexing of personal data by search engines, robots.txt protocols or the like, called exclusion protocols, which prevent web crawlers used by search engines, are also appropriate for this purpose (Cobacho, 2019).

All this, however, without ignoring the need for realistic and truly preventive policies and administrative solutions that promote initiatives for the responsible and safe use of new technologies, enhancing what the Basque Ombudsman, the Ararteko, has called “digital maturity”, with the objective to educate in order to avoid risky practices (Lamarca, 2014). The recent Communication from the Commission, Shaping Europe’s digital future, COM (2020) 67 final, emphasizes how “trusting the digital world also means helping consumers to take greater control and responsibility for their own data and identity.” This is the great paradox of the internet, an essential public service in our day (Arenas, 2014, p. 557), and of the current technological society. Is it really a knowledge society or just a society of indiscriminate expansion of (mis)knowledge? We are, without a doubt, in “an unconscious society that enthrones the causes while condemning the consequences” (Cobacho, 2019, p. 223). Nonetheless, “much more information spreading, much more official education, much more divulgation actually matches with an intact (rather, not naïve anymore, but corrupted) ignorance made of irrationality, of prejudices, superstition, lack of understanding, instrumentality. The serious lack of a rational attitude reflected in the issues of life, of society, etc. It does not seem a society of knowledge at all, but rather one of technics and of information” (Castelfranchi, 2007, p. 2).

Without minimizing the rights guaranteed to citizens in the field of personal data protection, each one must take responsibility for their behavior in society, a requirement that also undoubtedly applies to this new liquid modernity promoted by the omnipresence of the internet. Only in this way will the unwise use of new technologies be discouraged with success, avoiding a false sense of protection and security (Pazos, 2015, p. 44), given that, as Mario Benedetti (2000) reminds us, “it happens that the past is always a dwelling but there is no forgetfulness capable of demolishing it”.

KEY TERMS AND DEFINITIONS

Geoblocking: Suppression in all network domains of access to search results obtained by internet seach engines from personal data but only in relation to attempts and search requests made through IP addresses located within a specific territory.

Informational Self-Determination: the right that assists citizens to protect their personal data and, in exercise of this right, to self-define and modulate their public image and reputation.

Intimacy: the sphere in which the most singularly reserved facets of the person’s life are developed, such as the home where daily life is carried out or communications, for example.

Personal Data Expiration Period: Normative predefinition of the expiration period of the public interest in relation to the dissemination of certain information after which the indexation of the affected personal data is automatically blocked.

Privacy: Broader than intimacy, it includes a set of more extended and global facets of the personality that isolated may lack intrinsic meaning but coherently linked cast a portrait of the personality that the individual has the right to keep reserved.

Pseudonymization: According to article 4.5 of the GDPR, it is the processing of personal data in such a manner that it can no longer be attributed to a specific data subject without the use of additional information, provided that such additional information is kept separately and is subject to technical and organizational measures to ensure that it is not attributed to an identified or identifiable natural person.

Right to be Forgotten: The right of data subjects to have information that refers to them obscured, hindering immediate access to it on the network through their personal data once the purpose that initially justified its collection and processing has disappeared.

Weighing Criteria: Key elements to consider when deciding whether the right to be forgotten has precedence over other conflicting rights which must be balanced according to the circumstances of the specific case.
