# Chapter 28

Cyber Security Developments

*   Jelena L. Pisarov  
    Doctoral School of Safety and Security Sciences, Óbuda University, Budapest, Hungary
*   Gyula Mester  
    Doctoral School of Safety and Security Sciences, Óbuda University, Budapest, Hungary

ABSTRACT

Even the behavior of a single driver can have a dramatic impact on hundreds of cars, making it more difficult to manage traffic. While the attempts to analyze and correct the traffic patterns that lead to congestion began as early in the 1930s, it wasn’t until recently that scientists developed simulation techniques and advanced algorithms to create more realistic visualizations of traffic flow. In experiments conducted by Alexandre Bayen and the Liao-Cho, which included several dozen cars in a small-scale closed circuit, a single autonomous vehicle could eliminate traffic jams by moderating the speed of every car on the road. In larger simulations, the research showed that once their number rises to 5-10% of all cars in the traffic, they can manage localized traffic even in complex environments, such as merging multiple lanes of traffic into two or navigating extremely busy sections.

INTRODUCTION

Challenges of fully-automated driving require vehicles that are able to recognize the limitations of their machine perception, as well as the functional limitations of their processing modules, since with fully-automated driving mode, a human is not expected to give any backup. To achieve this level of autonomy, the autonomous vehicle needs to perceive its surroundings, interpret them accurately, and be able to execute relevant decisions over and over again. This is achieved by individual processing modules that are both dependent on and upgrade each other (Figure 1).

| Figure 1. Structure of the information processing for automated vehicle driving |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch028.f01](i/ch028.f01.png) |
| --- |

The machine perception is achieved by various sensors, like cameras and radars which are part of the vehicle systems, but also by information from highly accurate digital maps. If a vehicle knows its position, it is able to self-localize while the environmental model displays the vehicle and other road users as individual dynamic motion models. This representation also contains the elements of road infrastructure, such as traffic signs, traffic lights, curb stones, traffic islands, and road markings. Using this vehicle environmental model, all the individual elements are in relation to each other while the vehicle processors generate a machine interpretation of the scene. Different possible developments on the road are called episodes and are continually calculated in advance and evaluated on the basis of probability. For example, the module can execute driving around an obstacle or overtaking a slower vehicle, calculating the optimal trajectory, the time horizon of 3-5 seconds, and the passengers’ safety and comfort (Rodic, Mester, & Xu, 2019).

However, if the machine perception fails, uncertainties in the situation evaluation might make it impossible for the vehicle to safely plan and execute actions. The question remains whether limitations in the machine perception operation can be detected or predicted, and if so, how early. The following section will discuss the technological possibilities and known methodical approaches that may provide the answer.

SCOPE AND CHARACTERISTICS OF THE MACHINE PERCEPTION

Machine perception uses cameras and radar/lidar technology. Cameras provide a 2D interpretation of a 3D scene as a high-resolution grayscale or colored images, from which processing modules can extract individual objects based on the contrast or differentiation in the texture. However, determining distance with cameras alone often leads to errors, based on the assumption that all objects are flat. Although stereo cameras can theoretically calculate the object distance, their accuracy decreases with the distance.

Conversely, radar and lidar sensors provide accurate distance measurements which are distance-independent in terms of the error margin. Still, their low-angle resolutions make them less accurate in capturing contours as well as any texture information. This is why different sensor types need to be used in combination to create a reliable machine perception module. Data that is typically taken into account includes the dimension of an object used as a box model, its position in the static world or relative to the vehicle, and in case of moving objects, their speed and acceleration.

However, without vehicle-to-vehicle communication, the yaw rate and angle of other road users is difficult and unreliable to determine. The module also needs to determine the object class, as, for example, a pedestrian and a motorcyclist differ greatly in their possible dynamic and degrees of freedom of movement. While humans are able to interpret visual perceptions with semantic accuracy relatively quickly, with the current state of technology, it is still a comparatively difficult task for the machine perceptions. To support machine perception, highly accurate digital maps are used as a support, where the automated vehicle can quickly recognize the infrastructure objects and markings as they are acquired in the sensors’ field of vision, as sensors only verify that the object is in its place (Stepanic, Mester, & Kasac, 2013).

A disadvantage of this approach is that standard GPS localization is not accurate enough, and the map must be updated more frequently than it is the case with available GPS maps.

FEATURES OF ENVIRONMENT MODELS

When the machine perception is used to create a dynamic environmental model, two principal representations are used – object-based and grid-based type.

An object-based environment model has a dynamic data structure, where all relevant objects and infrastructure elements around the vehicle are represented accurately in space and time. The object acquiring and tracking are performed continually, by fused on-board sensors with an aid of a highly accurate digital map (Figure 2).

| Figure 2. Schematic diagram of the object-based vehicle environment representation |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch028.f02](i/ch028.f02.png) |
| --- |

A grid-based representation relies on raster maps to divide the stationary environment into localized cells of the same size. The vehicle moves across the localized 2D or 3D grid and the onboard sensors only provide information whether specific cells are free, and allow for a free pass, or whether the respective cell is occupied by an obstacle. This type of representation is more suitable for interpreting static scenarios and infrastructural elements. As it does depend on a model hypothesis about the object class, it is considered very resistant to model errors (Figure 3).

| Figure 3. Schematic diagram of the structure of a grid-based representation of the vehicle’s surroundings |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch028.f03](i/ch028.f03.png) |
| --- |

OVERCOMING UNCERTAINTIES OF MACHINE PERCEPTION

The machine perception needs to detect static and dynamic objects and physically measure them as precisely as possible, but also assign correct semantic attributes to the detected objects. In this respect, there are three uncertainty domains for machine perception – state uncertainty, existence uncertainty, and class uncertainty.

State Uncertainty

As the environment module estimates static road variables such as the vehicle dimensions, their state uncertainty is received by means of repeated measurements. If there is no systematic sensor error, the estimated value progressively converges with true values. On the other hand, for the estimation of dynamic, time-dependent states, such as the object position or speed, there is no convergence with a true value, because the object changes its position between the measuring times. State uncertainties are handled through the general Bayes filter where the estimated state of an object and the related uncertainty are represented by a multi-dimensional probability density function p (PDF):

![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch028.m01](i/ch028.m01.svg)

Where it depends on all the measurements ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch028.m02](i/ch028.m02.svg) that are available at the time k+1.

Existence Uncertainty

Existence uncertainty refers to the probability that the object in the representation of the vehicle’s surroundings actually corresponds to a real object. For example, an autonomous vehicle should engage in automated braking only if a detected obstacle has a high existence probability. The existence probability in today’s systems is expressed on the basis of a heuristic quality measure – if the quality measure exceeds a sensor-application-dependent threshold, an object is confirmed. While in some cases, all real objects are considered existent, the object existence can also depend on their relevance in the current situation. The current object existence probability is calculated similarly to state estimation, through the Kalman filter in a prediction and innovation step

![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch028.m03](i/ch028.m03.svg)

Where the probability p[S] stands for the persistence probability of the object and p[B] the probability for the occurrence of an object in the sensor capture area. The probability for the disappearance of the object is given by 1 – p[S]. In the innovation step, the a posteriori existence probability ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch028.m04](i/ch028.m04.svg) is calculated.

Class Uncertainty

Classification procedures used to determine the object class, including the determination of semantic information, are increasingly sensor specific. With a high information content, image-based procedures are more commonly used for classification. In learning procedures, the classifier module is trained offline to recognize positive and negative examples and recognize the trained object class to a greater or lesser extent. A more traditional but also effective approach is to use sensor data to specify as many deterministic characteristics as possible for the different classes, e.g. length, width, or speed, and to determine the class-specific statistical variation areas for all of them. The mean value of the individual characteristics, such as the variation range, is approximated using a normal distribution. These procedures, are, however, less capable than learning procedures, and are expected to lose importance in the future development of autonomous systems.

Table 1. Uncertainty domains of machine perception and their methodical handling

|  || State uncertainty || Existence uncertainty || Class uncertainty |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Characteristic || Uncertainty in the state variables such as object position, object speed, etc. || Uncertainty whether an object captured by a sensor really exists || Uncertainty of class membership (e.g. passenger car versus truck) |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Cause || Stochastic measuring error of the sensor technology used || Detection uncertainties of individual sensors, e.g. camera, lidar or radar || Classification uncertainties of the algorithms/limitations of individual sensors |
| Modeling || Probabilistic; expected value with variances/covariances || Probabilistic by means of detection probabilities || No persistent method; at present mainly heuristic |
| Methods || Closed theory via general Bayes filter (e.g. Kalman filter variant) || Closed theory coupled with estimate of state uncertainty (e.g. JIPDA filter) || Feature-based:  
Bayes, Dempster-Shafer  
Learning-based:  
Neuronal networks, cascaded procedures (Viola Jones, etc.) |
| Prediction of the future || Generally no; limited possibility using trend indications || Generally no || Generally no |

Both classification procedures have a disadvantage in that no theoretically substantiated probabilities can be determined for the current quality of the classification. With no comprehensive theoretical basis for this, the classifiers’ output is currently only an individual reliability measure that can be standardized for the 0-1 range. Besides, image-based trained classifiers are so different from characteristic-based procedures that rely on radar and lidar sensors that standardized comparison of them is not easy to achieve (Mester, Pletl, Nemes, & Mester, 1998).

The problem with future uncertainty on higher levels is that it is impossible to predict in time. The currently available methods for estimating state and existence uncertainties (Table 1) allow for a current estimation of the machine perception capability, yet they cannot predict degeneration in the capability of individual sensors or failure of components. What remains is a trend indication only.

The Capability Prediction of Machine Perception

The future development of the machine perception capability of autonomous vehicles is difficult to predict with sufficient accuracy. The perception capability for the period of 5-10 s required to transfer driving duties to a human driver cannot be predicted as a backup option on the highly automated driving regime. In addition, a fully autonomous vehicle would have to be able to reach an intrinsically safe state autonomously, for which even a longer period of time would be required. Predicting the future limitation of the perceptional capability also depends on external conditions such as camera glare, as in the case of low sun position, as well as weather-related sensor limitations like rain, snow, and fog banks.

However, theoretically substantiated methods and procedures for continually monitoring the current machine perception already exist, and they are able to reliably detect system failures and deterioration of individual components. In this way, machine perception modules must be developed with sensor redundancy, which ensures that sufficient perception capability is active until either the driver takes over or, in case of a fully-autonomous vehicle, until an intrinsically safe state is achieved. For example, if both radar and lidar supply measurement data, they still operate in different sensor capture areas and are differently affected by the weather. Also, if one camera in a stereo camera system breaks down, the remaining camera is still capable of classifying objects and detecting road markings, while distance estimate measurements are taken over by radar or lidar sensors (Mester & Rodic, Modeling and Navigation of an Autonomous Quad-Rotor Helicopter, 2012).

THE MASS-INTRODUCTION OF AUTONOMOUS VEHICLES

Autonomous driving is expected to significantly change the road traffic in the future, especially once large-scale automation is implemented. This will be possible only when previously defined technical requirements have been fulfilled. One of the biggest motivations for vehicle automation is public road safety, as with all active and passive safety systems available today, the vast majority of present-day accidents are attributed to the human factor. The principal requirement of vehicle automation is that substituting the human driver with an autonomous driving module does not compromise the safety of public road traffic.

Considering the total number of accidents for conventional driving, represented by blue and green fields in Figure 4, the report from the German Federal Highway Research Institute assumes that a substantial number of accidents (green field) can be avoided by vehicle automation. On the other hand, automation could also cause new accidents, specifically related to vehicle autonomy. For fully-automated driving to be considered safe and approved, not only a reduction in the number of accidents is necessary, but also an acceptable ratio V[acc] between avoided R[avo] and additionally caused risks R[add].

![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch028.m05](i/ch028.m05.svg)

| Figure 4. Theoretical potential for avoiding accidents with vehicle automation |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch028.f04](i/ch028.f04.png) |
| --- |

If the ratio were greater than 1, the system is expected to reduce traffic safety. However, it is possible that even a ratio of less than 1 is needed for approval. Even today, there are examples where added benefits make additional risks acceptable. For example, for many motorcyclists, the experience of freedom and increased mobility evens out the considerable additional risks of motorcycling when compared to other modes of road transport.

Present-Day Test Concepts in the Automotive Industry

The safety validation concepts currently used in the automotive industry recognize four separate automation levels.

The first level includes driver-only vehicles with no automation capabilities. Apart from the reliability of the used components, the test relies on the abilities of the driver, as the reliability of the vehicle with test drivers is expected to be transferred to future users. This concept has proven itself to be a successful proof of safety – in spite of the increasing mileage driven in road traffic, the number of fatalities has fallen, even if the number of accidents remains constant.

The second level of automation are vehicles with the assisting systems such as Adaptive Cruise Control (ACC) and Lane Keeping Assist (LKA), the functions of which are added to the standard testing. According to the Code of Practice, although Advanced Driver Assistance System (ADAS) supports driving, increases comfort, and reduces fatigue, responsibility for vehicle behavior remains with the human driver.

The third level refers to partially automated systems, where depending on the speed, ACC and LKA can take over the lateral and longitudinal control for the driver. In this category, the driver is also responsible for the vehicle behavior, so vehicle testing counts on the possibility that the driver takes over in an emergency situation. This level presents an additional challenge for safety validation due to the conflict between relieving the driver and the necessary situation awareness of the lateral and longitudinal motion.

The fourth category of tested systems is expected to automatically intervene in both vehicle control and dynamics, compensating for the driver’s loss of control over the situation. Electronic Stability Control (ESC and Emergency Brake Assist (EBA) are components that engage additional or reducing braking force without any intervention of the driver, thus autonomously impacting the vehicle dynamics. The goal of validating these system safety requirements is to prove that emergency intervening systems should engage only in the case of loss of control and severely increased risk. The principal focus in developing the fourth level systems is to allow the driver to retain controllability or to restore it. Validation of current vehicles regarding safety thus depends on the driver as a backup.

This controllability for the driver is developed and verified by the procedure model shown in Figure 5 – the downward branch of the V-Model represents development and design, and the upward branch stands for verification and validation.

Test Concept Requirements

To explain why full automation presents a considerable challenge for safety validation, we need to describe the test concept requirements that assess safety.

Effectiveness Criteria

The test case generation needs to guarantee the test coverage required, for example, a vehicle should be tested in other than ideal weather conditions as well and in many realistic scenarios, taking into account vehicle limit samples. On the other hand, the test execution must provide the option to include all the test cases defined by the test case generation. Parameters of test execution also need to be observable, as only the situation that can be described can make a statement test “passed” or “failed”.

Efficiency Criteria

The economical aspect of the test concept means that the test execution needs to be prepared and carried out as quickly as possible and provide feedback on the test object immediately, and at the lowest cost possible. The test concept also needs to be reproducible, for example in case of an error during the test, the object under testing should be subjected to a test in the same conditions as before. A product should be tested in all stages of the development process, so fewer development steps need to be repeated in the case of an error. Finally, the test execution should consider the risk for all participants.

Current Automation vs. Full Automation

Considering the previously described safety validation of the four levels of automation currently available, the focus is on the vehicle and its ability to be controlled by the driver. Representing the three-level model of human target-oriented behavior and the three-level hierarchy of the driving task (Figure 6) this validation corresponds to the elements in the green field.

In full automation, the abilities of the driver are omitted, and the human no longer functions as a backup – all driving tasks are taken over by the driving robot. This leads to the conclusion that for autonomous driving there is no need for a controllability test, only a test of the technical system operation. For the safety validation of current systems, resulting safety results must be sourced from the driver and the vehicle combined, but for the production release of the vehicle, currently, the focus is only on the vehicle.

Comparison of the Technology Impact on Air Travel, Road Traffic, and Rail Travel

Apart from road traffic, automation has established itself in other traffic systems. In civilian air travel, currently, there are no examples of full automation, as even if pilots rarely perform real flying tasks, they are still present in both supervising and operating roles. Table 2 displays an overview of the differences in traffic systems, where the safety concept of the traffic flow best shows the differences between air travel and road traffic.

The railway traffic provided examples of full automation, for example, there is an automated underground railway operating in Nuremberg. Still, according to Table 2, the traffic system safety concept clearly differentiates between road traffic and the railway, as it is, much like air travel, a legally self-contained traffic space with an abundance of logic-based systems and external monitoring that prevents accidents.

As a mixed system, road traffic does not meet the criteria of a self-contained traffic space and external monitoring, with differences between these travel modes explaining why automated solutions for the production release cannot be applied directly to autonomous driving.

The Problem of Releasing Fully-Automated Vehicles for Production

The functions of autonomous driving as an object under testing are fundamentally different from current road vehicles, so it is necessary to determine how meaningful the current test concepts would be if applied onto autonomous driving. Every test concept consists of test case generation and test execution.

Test Case Generation

The three procedures for test case generation that have been discussed in 2.2 are contrived on the assumption of the driver’s driving capability, which is certified by the driver’s license, which is generally issued if the applicant has attained a minimum age, is suitable for driving a motor vehicle, has received training, and has passed a theoretical and practical examination. It is assumed that if the test driver has mastered example situations, every other driver’s license holder will also master the other relevant non-tested situations when driving. These situations include those in which the driver is actively driving, as well as those when they are supervising the system and take control when necessary.

Table 2. Comparison of the conditions in the traffic systems

|  || Air travel || Road traffic || Rail travel |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Movement options || 3-D (space) || 2-D (area) || 1-D (line) |
| Operator |
| Responsible vehicle operator || Usually redundant || Not redundant || Not redundant |
| Professionalism of the vehicle operator || Almost completely full-time occupation || Small proportion full-time occupation || Almost completely full-time occupation |
| Training |
| Theory || \> 750 h || \> 21 h || ~ 800 h |
| Practice || \> 1500 h || \> 9 h || ~ 400 h |
| Training for vehicle type || Yes || No || Yes |
| Further training || Required || Not required || Required |
| Safety concepts of the traffic flow |
| Traffic space self-contained || Legally defined boundaries || In special cases || Legally defined boundaries |
| Driving by sight || No, only in special cases || Yes || No, only in special cases |
| Technical equipment (examples) || Collision warning systems mandatory || Road markings, traffic lights, traffic signs || Automatic vigilance device, intermittent train control, automatic driving and braking controls |
| External monitoring || Yes, air traffic control || No || Yes, centralized traffic control, operation center |
| Technical framework |
| Documentation of tours/operating hours || Yes || No || Monitoring of operating performance, automatic tachograph |
| Servicing, repairs || Only by certified companies || Workshops, DIY || Only by certified companies, and then also small workshops |
| Accident analysis || Every accident/serious malfunction, by independent state-run body || In individual cases, by certified assessor || Every accident/serious malfunction, by independent state-run body |
| Number of vehicles  
(in Europe) || 10³ (decreasing) || 10⁶ (increasing) || 10³ (decreasing, with increasing kilometric performance of each traction unit) |
| Change of model || Approx. 20 years || Approx. 5–7 years || Approx. 20 years for traction units |

If the driver is absent, the currently existing metric is no longer valid and the test case generation for autonomous driving must include the driving capabilities which the human driver originally brought to the driver-vehicle system.

Test Execution

The test execution relies on a range of methods, from software-in-the-loop (SiL) and hardware-in-the-loop (HiL) to real driving. Currently, real driving is the most important approval method, however, autonomous driving remains a systematic challenge for the known methods. In autonomous driving, using a test driver would be a non-real behavior of a user, as the whole purpose of vehicle automation is to relieve the user from supervising the vehicle and the environment, let alone intervene. Besides, the vehicle could participate in the road traffic without passengers, and a test driver would again represent a non-real component in the vehicle – he or she could influence the other road users and alter their behavior, leading to unrealistic test results.

Approaches to Solving the Testing Challenge

Autonomous driving requires a new approach to testing which questions the classic test concepts. This is why approved test functions need to be remodeled and used along with an evolutionary approach to safety validation.

Repurposing Approved Functions

If we use a system in the same way as before, we can take an already issued release study. On the other hand, if the scope of functions is expanded, this must be re-evaluated. One way of overcoming the testing challenge is to apply an evolution across all parameters, such as the speed, the area of use, and the degree of automation. In selecting the evolution steps we need to differentiate between the perspective of a function developer, for example starting at an interstate during a traffic jam, and the perspective of the previously presented statistical considerations, where for example, the driver would make as many errors as possible.

Reducing the Testing Duration

The evolutionary approach aside, the safety of new functions still has to be validated and to accelerate the process, there are two adjustments to be made – what test cases can be changed, and how these tests will be executed.

Test Case Generation

The vehicle systems currently in use are based on the capability of humans and their options for controlling the vehicle. This leads to a significant reduction in the test cases that are theoretically required. This reduction, however, does not apply to autonomous vehicles, so new methods must be found that will reduce the number of test cases for autonomous vehicles. The test drives and large-scale field studies are valuable for defining potential critical situations, however, a valid measure of risk that enables an evaluation is the first step, and the selection of critical situations in the second step is still missing.

Test Execution Tools

Apart from the possibility to reduce the test cases during the test case generation, the test execution also has the potential to speed up the process (Figure 7).

Here, the testing tools are divided into nine classes, which are differentiated on the basis of representation for the vehicle and the environment. In this representation, the passenger is present in the vehicle, but they do not actively intervene in autonomous driving.

| Figure 7. Classification of testing tools for testing autonomous vehicles |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch028.f07](i/ch028.f07.png) |
| --- |

A real environment is not controlled, so test situations that result from it are based on the randomness of reality, but it is devoid of reproducibility of complex situations with other road users. This testing tool can be used only with first roadworthy prototypes, which means by the end of the development process.

Another approach is to test real vehicles in an artificial environment, where situations are created artificially, while the road users are aware of being involved in a test. For the benefits of safety, variability, observability, and reproducibility, the reality is significantly simplified.

For autonomous driving, the testing metric that relies on real driving and the driver’s license test is not valid. The resulting loss of the reduction in the test cases implies that current test concepts are not economically justified for assessing the safety of new autonomous driving systems. Only the evolutionary approach with step-by-step adjustments of parameters such as speed, scenery, and degree of automation, allows for existing components to be taken over and reduce the range of tasks for the following releases. The necessary test cases must be reduced on the basis of field experience and statistical procedures, while alongside real driving, alternative testing tools need to be used.

CAN AUTONOMOUS VEHICLES LEARN?

The idea behind autonomous vehicles is for the automotive industry, universities and large IT companies to develop and implement technological solutions that could substitute a multitude of human tasks in vehicle operation. These include perception, cognition, decision-making, and carrying out immediate actions. However, apart from the capability to drive a vehicle, humans possess other abilities, like for example, learning, which directly changes the way we tackle different tasks. In this sense, the biggest challenge of vehicle automation still remains, whether the new technological system will also have the capacity to learn.

Replicating human learning in the machine environment is an area of research in itself and focuses on examining the processes of human learning for a better understanding of how those processes could be applied to machine-learning methods. In this chapter, machine learning will be understood as a human-generated algorithm. Without comparing human learning with robot learning, let us discuss why and whether machine learning is possible in its current form in autonomous driving (Mester, Massive Open Online Courses in Education of Robotics, 2016).

Vehicles, Infrastructure, and Drivers Who Learn

A driver driving a vehicle in any environment shows target-oriented behavior which is based on three principles – skills, rules, and knowledge.

*   • Skill-based behavior is described as stimulus-response automatic, which people tackle in everyday situations without engaging intensive cognitive capacities.
*   • Rule-based behavior is more cognitively demanding, as it requires associative classification besides mere perception and motor actions. People learn rules purposely and identify similar situations, applying their “rules” to them.
*   • In the case of new situations that people have no trained behavior for, human drivers show knowledge-based behavior – where they rely on their knowledge to generate and evaluate alternative ways to act.

With each new piece of experience that a driver gains, their behavior transits from knowledge-based to rule-based, and from rule-based to skill-based. In human behavior patterns, training allows for increased efficiency.

Road traffic is an open system that includes static and dynamic objects, where a number of environmental factors such as light levels and rain pose a constant challenge for drivers. Even experienced drivers may encounter unknown situations that need to be solved using a knowledge-rule-skill approach. It is exactly these three human capabilities that developers of autonomous vehicles strive to replace with corresponding capabilities in driving robots.

Learning Technical Systems

Machine learning is usually described as a research area that deals with designing algorithms. An important feature of those algorithms is the automatic improvement of technical systems that relies on experience – the automatic improvement follows rules and measures pre-set by the human developer. With machine learning, we need clearly defined tasks, the accompanying metrics, and training data. According to Mitchell^((1)):

A computer program is said to learn from experience E with respect to some class of tasks T and performance measure P, if its performance at tasks in T, as measured by P, improves with experience E.

Machine learning is especially useful in case:

*   A. There is a large amount of data that contains valuable information that can be extracted automatically.
*   B. People have a limited understanding of a certain area and lack effective algorithms.
*   C. The test demands dynamic adjustments to changing conditions.

Supervised Learning

Also known as learning with a teacher, supervised learning is conditioned by pre-assessed training data or experience that machine learning builds on. For example, in determining whether airbags need to be deployed in an accident, training data would include acceleration values and the corresponding assessments which are made by an expert/teacher. In transferring of empirical values onto new input values, we differentiate between lazy learning (memory-based) and eager learning (model-based).

In lazy learning, the training data is saved during learning and a similarity measure is defined, while in eager learning, a global model based on training data is constructed during the training phase (Pisarov & Mester, Programming the mBot Robot in School, 2019).

Unsupervised Learning

In unsupervised learning, training data is also used, but in this case, there are no assessment or output values. Here, the aim is to find a structure in the data and classify the data according to the structure. The training data here is used to reveal these structures and classify newly acquired input values.

Reinforcement Learning

Unlike both previous processes, in reinforcement learning, there is little or no training data available, to begin with. The training data required is collected by an agent (anything that perceives its environment through sensors and acts through effectors) itself by carrying out the task that is to be optimized through a fixed scheme.

Batch Learning

Also known as online learning, in batch learning a set of training data is applied at a point in time to exploit different learning methods. If the learning method produces a model, this model does not need to be updated by further experience collected during its use.

Online Learning

Online learning is an iterative process in which new experiences are incorporated in the learning process. With continuous optimization of the way a task is approached, the process incorporates experience from the operation, resulting in system behavior changing as a result of experience and time (Pisarov, Experience with mBot-Wheeled Mobile Robot, 2019).

Automation Instead the Learning Driver

In automotive industry, machine learning and artificial intelligence are of particular interest for vehicle automation which is currently understood as:

*   1\. Perception of the environmental and vehicle state variables,
*   2\. Cognition of these state variables in order to make a representation of the world,
*   3\. Behavior planning,
*   4\. Execution of selected behavior.

What these four components have in common is the intervention in the actual behavior of the vehicle. To further discuss the deployment of machine-learning processes in vehicle automation, we need to classify different safety-related systems (Pisarov, mBot kerekeken gördülő mobil robot írányítása, 2019).

Safety Systems

By ISO26262, safety is defined as the absence of unreasonable risk. A car system impact on safety can be determined in the following ways:

*   A. Not safety-relevant, when a system error does not lead to dangers for a person or the environment.
*   B. Safety-relevant, when a system error may result in danger to a person or the environment.
*   C. Safety-critical, when an error directly leads to a person or the environment that is being endangered.

Autonomous driving is often categorized under unsupervised automation category within a safety-critical system, as machine-learning processes currently cannot be transferred from the two less critical levels to safety (Mester, Rang lista robotičara Srbije, 2020) (Mester, Pisarov, & Zilahy, Magyarországi robotikai kutatók ranglistája, 2019).

Measures of Safe Driving

The vehicle’s driving in safety terms needs to be evaluated for both the machine-learning process and verification and validation during operation. The goal is to derive an evaluation that classifies a journey as unsafe even before it exceeds physical driving limits. In this, we differentiate between deterministic and stochastic procedures in hazard assessment (Mester, Academic Ranking of World Universities 2009/2010, 2011).

Deterministic Procedures

The limits for lateral and longitudinal, acceleration and yaw rate are the easiest values to determine. In a study that included 100 cars, longitudinal accelerations greater than 0.7 g were used as triggers for detecting unsafe situations, however it is also evident that a vehicle’s safety is affected by the surrounding traffic in the immediate environment.

If the environment is observed as parallel traffic on one lane in each direction, time-to-collision (TTC) indicates the safety of a situation in forward vehicle collision mitigation systems,

![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch028.m06](i/ch028.m06.svg)

defines the time until the ego-vehicle collides with an object at distance, if the relative speed remains constant.

Deterministic procedures are valuable for ex-post safety assessments of an executed maneuver or situation. Uncertainties in these cases imply that the development of a situation over time not only has a potential deterministic procedure, but that many different situations can occur. For example, when calculating the TTC to diffuse a critical situation, the autonomous car in front could accelerate instead of slowing down. In order to include these uncertainties into the hazard assessment, we need to consider stochastic procedures as well.

Stochastic Procedures

In a situation when we need to assess a hazard of two vehicles passing each other as in Figure 8, we need to use stochastic procedures. Assuming deterministic behavior and an extrapolation of speed, such passing would pose no danger, as their trajectories do not cross. If we take uncertainties into consideration, the situation changes. If a human-driven vehicle in the lower lane does not stay in its lane, it creates an immediate hazard for the autonomous vehicle in the upper lane and its surroundings. Both the probability of an accident and its potential severity involve unknowns that need to be estimated as accurately as possible.

| Figure 8. Comparison of predictions in a passing situation: deterministic (above) and stochastic (below) |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch028.f08](i/ch028.f08.png) |
| --- |

Considering the uncertainties that involve human drivers, automation sensors and actuators, as well as the interaction between objects, we cannot project only one trajectory but a probability distribution of the states of all involved objects over time. If the potential areas that the objects occupy happen to overlap, there is a high probability of an accident (Mester & Rodic, Navigation of an Autonomous Outdoor Quadrotor Helicopter, 2012).

Automation in a Learning Collective Group

Although the analysis of learning vehicles in this chapter focused mainly on the system life cycle of a particular vehicle, vehicle automation as a whole implicitly brings the duplication of hardware and software within a whole group of vehicles. This means that while on one hand, driving errors, breakdowns, and accident types would impact a whole group of vehicles, on the other, this would provide adaptive systems an additional degree of freedom.

Considering the exchange of data and collective learning, two approaches can be differentiated – agent-based machine learning and machine learning with agents. The first approach, often called agent-based swarm intelligence, presents a learning collective system that consists of numerous networked agents with limited cognitive capacity, similar to ants or bees. In machine learning with agents, the learning system consists of several agents which, however, employ machine learning procedures described above (Pisarov & Mester, Rang lista fizičara Srbije, 2020).

Still, the question remains from which position of a group is relevant information gathered from the data and applied in learning and performance measurements. Apart from vehicle robots, there are other agents, such as smartphones or personal assistants which will gather data from completely different areas to those available to the autonomous driving module.

AUTONOMOUS VEHICLE SAFETY CONCEPT

The main focus in the development of autonomous vehicles is the vehicle guidance system. However, if the experimental vehicles are tested in traffic on public roads, there is always a safety driver who monitors the technical system and is ready to intervene if a technical defect occurs and if the situation is beyond the capabilities of the vehicle itself. The necessary monitoring of the technical system makes these test drives on public roads semi-automated. Still, the purpose of future vehicle guidance systems is to achieve higher levels of automation, including safety functions that can achieve or maintain a so-called safe state.

Safe State

Since safety is a relative concept that depends on the individual perception of the observer, the use of the term safe state is somewhat ambiguous. According to the ISO 26262 standard, in a system or an arrangement of systems, an operating mode is safe if there is no unreasonable risk. In other words, a state is safe only when the current and future risk is below a society-acceptable limit. Risk, on the other hand, is perceived as a combination of the probability of occurrence and the severity of the personal injury (Mester, The Evaluation of the Impact Factor of the Journal Acta Polytechnica Hungarica, 2011) (Mester, Baza podataka Madjarskih naučnika i publikacija, 2020) (Mester, Pisarov, & Németh, Óbudai Egyetem rangsorolása a Webometrics 2019-es ranglistákon, 2019).

When using the term safe state, the principal challenge of an acceptable level of risk for passengers and other road users is to identify the threshold under which the risk level is acceptable. In autonomous driving, the level of acceptable risk depends on the current situation of the vehicle that includes:

*   • Stationary and driving object relevant to decision-making
*   • Intentions of the dynamic objects including the vehicle itself
*   • Relevant legal conditions
*   • The autonomous vehicle missions
*   • The current power capability of the vehicle

The conclusion is that with autonomous vehicles, the current risk needs to be continually determined on the basis of the current situation, as well as compared with the threshold value that is considered acceptable.

Safety Concepts Adopted in Series-Production

Apart from autonomous vehicles and driver assistance systems, functional safety is widely used in other areas.

Track Vehicles

Automation technology has already been introduced to track vehicles. On public transport vehicles, the role of a train driver is mainly to monitor the system functions. However, we must note that unlike autonomous road vehicles, safety functions of track vehicles are integrated into the infrastructure. The central control system makes sure that the track sections are occupied by only one train at a time, to avoid collisions.

On driverless trains, such as the RUBIN underground system in Nuremberg, the vehicle speed is regulated automatically, and apart from monitoring track occupancy, the vehicles also have on-board monitors that allow for wireless communication between the control center and the vehicle.

Actuator Electric Controls

The actuators on autonomous vehicles are triggered and controlled by electrical signals. This so-called X-by-Wire technology is not yet available for series-production vehicles, although some components like electromechanical steering and electrohydraulic brake systems are already in use.

With autonomous vehicles, the actuators must have several redundant control circuits, similar to airplanes. All communication systems, actuators, control devices, and operating elements need to be installed multiple times so that in the case of a fault, the redundant systems can take over.

Robotics

Mobile robots can become a danger to themselves and their surroundings due to collisions with objects, persons, animals, as well as by underestimating ledges, steps, and ditches. Stationary manipulators, on the other hand, can endanger people by moving their jointed arms and injuring nearby persons with tools they are using. For both mobile robots or stationary manipulators, the safe state is the instant abatement of all actions or movements and coming to a standstill.

Robot control systems need a safety-oriented architecture that contains a safety-layer, which allows the robot to effectively transition to a safe state. When applied to autonomous vehicles, this means that although driving decisions can be made according to different criteria, such as traffic rules, efficient driving, and comfort, a collision-avoidance system must have the ability to override all other criteria and take action as the highest level authority.

Safe State of Use Cases

An important criterion in the autonomous vehicle operation is whether the passengers are on board or not. For example, when an occupied autonomous vehicle is choosing a parking space, a safe exit for passengers must be taken into consideration. Without passengers, for example, comfort plays no role, which means that a different driving style is possible. The same applies to the treatment of other loads, especially hazardous goods. Here we investigate the four cases and the respective properties of their safe states.

Use Case 1: Interstate Pilot with Safety Driver

By restricting autonomous vehicles to freeways, the number of possible and probable situations is much lower than compared to urban traffic. The safety driver has a fallback role and can take control whenever they estimate it necessary. In this case, the vehicle is in a safe state when:

*   A. Standing still on the stopping lane, on the curbside, a parking lot, or an emergency stopping bay.
*   B. Driving on a lane at a prescribed or greater distance to other road users.
*   C. The vehicle guidance system reacts according to an event to reduce the current risk, for example by handing over control to the human driver.

Use Case 2: Autonomous Valet Parking

In this case, transferring control to a human driver is not possible, as the vehicle can operate without a driver. The safety of passengers is not important either, as no passengers are on board in a valet parking procedure. The route must be planned, however, so that the vehicle does not drive on any road it has no command of, for example, streets with level crossings. In this case, the vehicle is in a safe state if:

*   A. It is at a standstill in a location where it poses no threat as an obstacle to other vehicles or blocking emergency vehicles and escape paths.
*   B. It is driving in a lane on the road as described in use case 1. However, since there is no safety driver on board, in the case of a fault, vehicle control is transferred to a remote operator.
*   C. It is driving over a crossing or roundabout or turns off, provided that the vehicle has command of the situation and the applicable traffic priority rules.
*   D. It is in a parking lot.

The biggest challenge in this use case is the absence of a safety driver. One solution is the remote operator who can take control of the vehicle in an event of a fault, and remotely bring it to a safe state.

Use Case 3: Full Automation with Safety Driver

In this use case, both the safety and risks are similar to a combination of use cases 1 and 2. With a safety driver on board, it is possible to hand over control, while the driver can also secure the vehicle in the case of a breakdown. The vehicle can be used on interstate connections, while the maximum speed is restricted to 240 km/h, but the maximum speed must be maintained within the performance capability of the vehicle guidance system.

For achieving the safe state, the same terms apply as in use cases 1 and 2.

Use Case 4: Vehicle on Demand

This use case is the most challenging in terms of safety technology, as the autonomous vehicle is expected to overcome every situation that a human driver may have to handle. The risk, on the other hand, needs to be below a threshold that is reasonable for the passengers and other road subjects. In this use case, the vehicle is in a safe state if it:

*   A. Is standing still as in use cases 1, 2, and 3. In each situation, in addition to potential passengers, there are other persons who need to be informed of the vehicle state.
*   B. The vehicle is driving on a traffic lane is in use cases 1, 2, and 3. While driving, however, the vehicle must be capable of autonomously maintaining and attaining a safe state.

The on-demand availability means that the autonomous vehicle must be able to handle all traffic situations.

Safety-Relevant Events

While the vehicle is in road traffic, there are different events that can occur that impact the risk in the current situation and its future development. Technical defects and faults in the vehicle guidance system may reduce its performance capabilities, but there are also changes in environmental conditions, as well as irregular behavior of other road users. Higher levels of risk are particularly attributed to a combination of reduced capabilities and increased demands.

Technical faults and defects on the vehicle and its guidance system are difficult to predict as they can occur suddenly. Adverse light and weather conditions increase demands on sensors used to detect changes in the environment, directly affecting the driving dynamics.

On the other hand, the behavior of other road subjects does not always follow the rules, and in some cases, an autonomous vehicle can never be safe because other road users act in an irresponsible manner.

Measures that Reduce Risk Levels

If we assume that an autonomous vehicle always operates under an acceptable level of risk, and at the same time maintains a wide scope of functions, its actions should be perceived as a reaction to safety-relevant scenarios that reduce or maintain the risks on an acceptable level.

The examples of measures that reduce the risk include a reduction of driving speed, an increase of distance to the vehicles in the immediate vicinity, safety-focused planning of driving maneuvers, etc. In certain situations, even these actions cannot reduce the risk to an acceptable level, so stopping the vehicle or leaving the traffic flow remains the only option.

In the case of faulty technical components, restarting and restoring the functionality of individual components can also be a risk-reducing measure. Sensors and actuators can be re-calibrated to regain their measured values while system restore points can be implemented to reconfigure the mechanisms after risk-increasing events (Mester, Stanic Molcer, & Delic, Educational Games, Computer Games as Educational and Management Tools: Uses and Approaches, 2011).

The Anticipation of Degradation Cases

Having the highly dynamic nature of road traffic in mind, as well as the properties of electric and electronic systems, safety-sensitive events can occur in a matter of seconds and demand a fast response from the vehicle systems. However, in a more favorable scenario, high levels of risk can be anticipated and at least taken into consideration when planning driving actions. Anticipatory driving of human drivers can be transferred in an even more comprehensive manner into a vehicle guidance system, as numerous measurable values can be monitored and processed directly from the vehicle.

The vehicle collects and measures values to predict how situations will develop, detecting problems even a few tenths of a second before the event can mean a safer situation outcome.

By communicating with the road infrastructure and other vehicles, autonomous vehicles can increase their safety potential even more. The sooner the information on road hazard (damaged surface, ice, traffic jams, etc.) is available, the sooner a response can be planned and executed.

Dilemmas

There are situations where a chain of events can lead to a situation where personal injuries cannot be avoided. When faced with a dilemma, as the automated vehicles must choose a possible course of action, the one which will cause the minimum damage, although personal injuries are unavoidable (Mester, Modeling of Autonomous Hexa-Rotor Microcopter, 2015).

In these situations, material damage and road traffic rule infringements are secondary priorities. When evaluating possible uncertainties, the vehicle needs to take into account the type and dynamics of other traffic participants, as well as the number of passengers on board (Mester & Rodic, Simulation of Quad-rotor Flight Dynamics for the Analysis of Control, Spatial Navigation and Obstacle Avoidance, 2013).

RISKS AND OPPORTUNITIES RELATED TO COLLECTING AND EXPLOITING ADDITIONAL DATA

Although cars have become a symbol for the freedom and autonomy of their owners a long time ago, now autonomous vehicles raise the question of how the data flows associated with autonomous driving impact the privacy of their owners. In this chapter we focus on new or additional data that is being collected and processed as a part of the autonomous driving infrastructure, what types of data are particularly vulnerable, how data can impact privacy, how architecture can solve privacy problems, and what other considerations need to be made in the long term.

Between Cars, Freedom, and Privacy

The whole purpose of owning a car is the ability to choose where to drive, which route to take, as well as to plan the time of arrival, breaks, etc. On the other hand, a car provides its owners a protected sphere of privacy, as people from the outside cannot overhear the conversation nor can easily join the company inside.

Autonomous vehicles could also become an extension of the traditional concepts of freedom, autonomy, and privacy; however, autonomous driving requires a much higher degree of interaction with the outside than a person-driven car. Beyond the data exchange with nearby entities, there are plans to integrate autonomous cars into synchronized traffic centers that would optimize their behavior (Pisarov & Mester, The Impact of 5G Technology on Life in 21st Century, 2020).

Like any centralized data-collecting entity, this raises privacy and security concerns, especially if we know that autonomous cars do not only collect and process data but also store them for a long time and communicate it to other entities on the road.

Additional Autonomous Driving Data

Before we can assess the opportunities and risks associated with collecting and processing additional data, we must first identify them. Some examples of sensitive personal data that non-autonomous cars collect, process, and even transmit include:

*   • All kinds of location and navigation data. When a car is tracked by a dispatching system, its own navigation system, a theft control system, or a road pricing infrastructure, a lot of information is collected and transferred to the respective central entities.
*   • Driving dynamics data – for example, acceleration, that gives information about the behavior of the driver and their driving style.
*   • Driving behavior data, which can be sourced from location data over a time span. For example, comparing the location of the car on a highway with the location of 15 minutes earlier can tell whether a speed limit was possibly violated.
*   • Data on the environment. The car can collect data from the environment to document the ride or specific traffic situation which may be used later as evidence. Dashboard cameras can gather other people’s personal data, such as license plates or their faces.

While the question remains what kinds of data are actually personal, it is undeniable that there are no guarantees that vehicle data cannot be related to persons and potentially misused.

Use Case 1: Interstate Pilot with Safety Driver

In this use case, the automated driving module takes over the driving tasks but only on interstates and similar expressways. For the duration of the autonomous journey, the driver becomes a passenger who can pursue other activities. If needed, the driving robot coordinates a safe transition to the driver and even stops the car at a safe place. In this case, the car can collect the following additional data:

*   • Driver capabilities, like whether the driver is able to take control from the robot or not, and how much time the transition takes.
*   • Driving behavior, like under which circumstances the driver delegates control and takes it back.
*   • The environment – additional road environment data can document specific traffic situations that may prove helpful in solving potential conflicts. Environmental data, however, may contain a mix of personal data of several individuals such as their faces, license plates, etc.

Use Case 2: Autonomous Valet Parking

In this use case, the driving module parks the vehicle at a remote or nearby location after the passengers have exited and unloaded their baggage. This saves the driver the time of finding a parking spot as well as walking to and from a remote parking spot. The new and additional data that the autonomous car can collect in this use case include:

*   • The duration of stay, or how much time do users spend on different destinations.
*   • The area of interest – where do users spend most time.
*   • The travel itinerary – when do users make breaks as well as how long they leave the car alone.
*   • Circumstances under which the car is left unattended.
*   • Visiting habits – how often do users visit a particular place and on what schedule.
*   • The environment – while the principles from the Use Case 1 apply, a car driving through a parking lot can collect additional data, such as more license plates, indicating that multiple car owners are localized together at the same time.

Since there is no direct interaction between the driver and the car, no data on driving behavior can be collected in this use case (Pisarov, 5G i samovozeći automobili, 2020).

Use Case 3: Full Automation with Safety Driver

As in Use Case 1, the driving robot performs the driving tasks while the driver can take the role of a passenger who pursues other activities. In Use Case 3, however, the driver can delegate the driving task to the autonomous module in many permitted areas in addition to expressways. The new and additional data that the car can collect is the same as in Use Case 1, but due to the driver’s ability to take control, it can lead to more data being collected on driver behavior (Nemes & Mester, 2017).

Use Case 4: Vehicle on Demand

The automation module drives the vehicles autonomously in all scenarios and makes it available for passengers or cargo at any requested location. From the perspective of autonomous driving, this scenario is the most demanding, but there may be less additional data collected than in Use Case 3. In this use case, it includes:

*   • Travel behavior, for example when passengers make breaks.
*   • General behavior and misbehavior of all passengers in the vehicle.
*   • Data collected on the environment as in previous use cases.

Responsibilities for Control Over Data and Potential Misuse

The storage of any kind of data opens possibilities for any kind of misuse and processing under circumstances that the user was not originally aware of. Data stored in a car is of particular interest to (Mester, Backstepping Control for Hexa-Rotor Microcopter, 2015):

*   1\. Law enforcement agencies that often take the approach that the user data stored for commercial and technical purposes should also be made available for law enforcement purposes.
*   2\. Internet companies such as Google, that subside on connectivity and transmitting data. Commenting on the attempts to contain the spread of connectivity, Director of Google Ideas said that information will always find its way through.

Risks of Data Transfer to Other Parties

When data is transferred to third-party entities, outside of the domain of the car owner and driver, those entities may use it to pursue their interest, which may or may not conform to the interests of the parties involved.

Car Manufacturers

They may be interested in learning about vehicle behavior to receive feedback on the performance of their complex autonomous software solutions. This data, at the same time, delivers sensitive information about the driving habits of the owner.

Insurance Services and Fleet Operators

Insurance providers are always interested in learning more about their customers, to assess the level of risk associated with individual clients or gain other customer insight. While on one part, these assessments may benefit instance customers, for example by awarding cost-reducing behavior, they put users under more tracking without a clear description of the related risks and opportunities.

Commercial Location-Based Services

The aim of advertising campaigns is to deliver the right message to the right target group. This includes placing advertisements at critical locations, such as near the highway exits or at places where traffic jams are frequent.

Government-Authorized Parties

Government-licensed parties such as law enforcement or intelligence agencies can use the surveillance data to detect behaviors they want to sanction or prevent. For example, traffic police might be interested in unsafe behavior on the road, while crime police and intelligence agencies may be interested in learning about the navigation patterns and whereabouts of suspicious individuals. Some municipalities are considering using crowd-sourcing to collect pollution data, where a car would literally spy on the emissions of the car in front.

Privacy Requirements

There needs to be a clear justification with regard to relevant privacy principles whenever any personal data is collected and transmitted beyond the data subject domain. These privacy principles depend on the respective national and industry-specific legislation, so it would be impossible to make a complete analysis.

On the other hand, there is the international standard ISO/IEC 29100 Privacy Framework that lists eleven privacy principles:

*   1\. Consent and choice
*   2\. Purpose legitimacy and specification
*   3\. Collection limitation
*   4\. Data minimization
*   5\. Use, retention and disclosure limitation
*   6\. Accuracy and quality
*   7\. Openness, transparency, and notice
*   8\. Individual participation and access
*   9\. Accountability
*   10\. Information security
*   11\. Privacy compliance

Under this framework, any data usage that absolutely needs to provide the service for which the data was collected requires explicit consent. In other words, for any personally identifiable information (PII) collected and transferred beyond the PII principle, there must be a valid and convincing rationale in regard to these eleven principles.

Architectural Considerations

Data architecture characteristics derive from privacy principles discussed earlier, where the principles of collection limitation, data minimization, and information security are especially relevant for architectural considerations. An architecture that stands behind a service that collects, uses and transmits less PII, not only reduces the risk of information misuse but makes the securing of information easier.

In this sense, three architecture characteristics are recommended:

*   1\. A decentralized approach where PII is not transferred to central entities such as traffic centers, automatically reducing the risk of misuse. 
    *   • In any case, as the situation is resolved directly between two vehicles or identifying the other vehicle individually against a central registration database.
    *   • A user-owned “Private Data Vault” is used to store PII of respective individuals and protect it against unwanted access.
    *   • If other than just personal data of the car user needs to be stored, but also environmental data of other parties, the four-or-n-eye principle should be used for access control.
*   2\. Anonymization, where information that needs to be collected for a justified purpose is collected in ways that do not identify the respective individual. This includes information needed only in aggregated form, like: 
    *   • Traffic and congestion analysis.
    *   • Interaction with peers, like exchanging data for traffic safety with other vehicles.
    *   • Generating access to parking spaces.
*   3\. Systematic deletion of PII, where architectures need to include concepts for systematic data deletion and consideration how long which data need to be kept for which purpose.

While there is a popular opinion that a higher degree of autonomy in driving could lead to more data processing and consequently more surveillance, this might not be the case.

An autonomous vehicle does not need to interact with the driver and does not need to collect more data from the driver than any other conventional car. If the vehicle is able to autonomously navigate traffic and reach its destination, it will hardly communicate more data than any other vehicle and even fewer data than a conventional car using a centralized navigation system.

On the other hand, scenarios, when the driver has to take over, combined with centralized surveillance, can lead to more surveillance and privacy issues, so an approach that would tackle autonomous driving scenarios on personal privacy principles is needed.

In order to prevent problems or breaches in data security domain, a Risk Management Framework (RMF) has been developed, which can be applied for these instances. This framework can be implemented in organizations and information systems, for its ability to provide a disciplined, structured, and flexible process for managing security and privacy risks. It addresses security and privacy risk from two perspectives – an information system perspective and a common controls perspective. Finally, RMF is purposefully designed to be technology neutral so that the methodology can be applied to any type of information system.

Regarding these characteristics, this framework could be applicable in self-driving robotics cars information system as well, with appropriate modifications and adjustments for this domain.

The flexibility of RMF suggests and propagates the maximization of automation wherever is possible, in order to increase the speed, effectiveness and efficiency in execution of the data security system. This characteristic also implies the minimization of human error impact in the assessment and monitoring – the intelligent decision making can be performed in real-time, or near real-time manner.

Self-driving robotics cars depend a great deal on their information system – to perform and carry out the activities which are required by the passengers. The successful execution of these actions depends on protecting the data flow, processed, stored, and transmitted information by both – the system itself, and the individuals driving in the car. In this regard, there is a complementary objective with respect to managing the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of PII.

There are many threats to such information systems, which include equipment failure, environmental disruptions, human or machine errors, and also purposeful attacks on information systems. Each of these can cause serio/us and even catastrophic damage to assets and individuals.

RMF is a general framework for data security and data protection, which describes the necessary actions and steps to be taken in order to achieve efficient risk management.

These steps are the following:

*   • Preparation to execute the RMF from a system-level perspective by establishing a context and priorities for managing security and privacy risk.
*   • Categorization within the system and the information processed, stored, and transmitted by the system itself based on an analysis of the impact of loss.
*   • Selection of an initial set of controls for the system and development of the controls as needed to reduce risk to an acceptable level based on an assessment of risk.
*   • Implementation of these controls and describing how the controls are implemented within the system.
*   • Assessment of the controls to determine if the controls are implemented correctly, operating as intended, and showing the desired results in order to satisfy the security and privacy requirements.
*   • Authorization of the system or common controls based on a determination that the risk to organizational operations and assets, individuals, other organizations, is acceptable.
*   • Monitoring the system and the associated controls on an ongoing basis to include assessing control effectiveness, documenting changes to the system and environment of operation, conducting risk assessments and impact analyses, as well as reporting the security and privacy posture of the system.

Each of these general steps compile further partitions which describe the tasks to be solved. They also include more detailed assignments for every participant in the organization. These assignments comply to the appropriate sector.

The purpose of the each given step in RMF is to specify every element and to predict all possible risks and to prevent them, as well to develop an appropriate reaction in cases when a breach or damage happens.

However, although it is quite detailed and flexible, this framework implementation, could be quite demanding, and requires constant monitoring, which involves a presence of individuals who will make decisions in cases when they are needed. This suggests that the self-driving car is not that self-sufficient and autonomous.

There are several segments which should be reviewed when it comes to cars and driving in general, which makes the issue of data security in this domain even more complex, since it includes the privacy of the passengers, as well as the data concerning the vehicle itself. Some of these were mentioned in the previous passages.

The car is one of the mass consumer products that has impacted society as a whole. Cars have become more than just a means of transportation. They represent a private area in which people can enjoy a form of autonomy of decision, without encountering any external interferences. However, with IT development, these circumstances have changed as well, so vehicles and drivers and passengers are also becoming more and more connected. Many car models developed over the past few years, especially self-driving cars, integrate sensors and connected onboard equipment, which may collect and record, among other things, the engine performance, the driving habits, the locations visited, and potentially even the driver’s eye movements, their pulse, or other biometric data for authentication or identification purposes. This large volume of various data inevitably generates potential risks, so the management and protection have created an industry which deals with these issues. In order to efficiently address the whole sphere of possible problems, some global guidelines – RMF and similar – have been developed, but also the legislation had to be modified as well, to preserve the rights and privacy of individuals and every other participant in this domain. This development requires the implementation of specific safeguards in order to prevent surveillance of individuals and misuse of the data (Kasac, Milic, Stepanic, & Mester, 2014).

Self-driven cars naturally require a certain number of sensors that can create an excessive data collection compared to what is necessary to achieve the purpose. The development of new functionalities and those based on machine learning algorithms may require a large amount of data collected over a long period of time. This collected information needs to be categorized, assessed and processed, and the whole process requires certain guidelines, as RMF suggests. The data can be divided into several groups, such as geolocation, biometrical, vehicle, manufacturer, etc.

There are two main groups of personal data to be considered:

*   • commercial and transactional data: passengers’ identifying information, transaction-related data, information relating to means of payment, etc.
*   • usage data: personal data generated by the car itself, location, velocity, etc.

All this information needs to be sufficiently protected. Therefore, the recommendation is to design and develop technologies to minimize the collection of personal data, provide privacy-protective default settings and ensure that data subjects are well informed and have the option to easily modify configurations associated with their personal data. This also implies that vehicle and equipment manufacturers, service providers and other data controllers should, wherever possible, use processes that do not involve personal data or transferring personal data outside of the vehicle – the data should be processed internally. This possibility offers the advantage of guaranteeing to the passenger the full control of their personal data, and it presents fewer privacy risks, especially by prohibiting any data processing by other parties without the passenger’s knowledge. It also enables the processing of sensitive data such as biometric data, as well as detailed location data which otherwise would be subject to stricter rules.

Basically, in order to provide the best privacy and data protection, local data processing should be considered by the self-driven car constructors and service providers, whenever possible to mitigate the potential risks of cloud processing (Mester, Cloud Robotics Model, 2015).

There is also an important issue to be addressed, and that is the data transfer outside the vehicle, to a certain control center, or elsewhere. This data transfer is also needing to be well protected, since it is more sensitive, not for its content but because of the fact it is not being processed locally, in the car, but outside.

In the spirit of RMF, there are several recommendations, which can ensure the data protection.

Self-driving car constructors and equipment manufacturers, service providers and other data controllers should develop and implement measures that guarantee the security and confidentiality of processed data and take all useful precautions to prevent control being taken by an unauthorized person. This means that all participants should adopt the following measures:

*   • encrypting the communication channels by appropriate algorithms
*   • placing an encryption-key management system that is unique to each vehicle
*   • when stored remotely, the data should be encrypted by unique algorithms
*   • regular renewing of encryption keys
*   • protection of encryptions keys from any disclosure
*   • authentication of data-receiving devices
*   • ensuring data integrity
*   • making access to personal data subject to reliable user authentication techniques (password, electronic certificate, etc.)

Nowadays, almost every country has a set of rules and appropriate legislation which covers privacy and data protection. They all suggest certain general guidelines how to perform and provide a required level of data security. This chapter describes one possible manner to achieve a certain level of security, based on the risk management framework guidelines.

So, regarding the above described instances, it is fair to say, that in order to create a safe self-driving car, many aspects should be taken into consideration. In the current environment, data security is a very significant issue, regarding the prompt development of internet technologies, and the passengers’ demands. Beside this aspect, autonomous cars need a connection for their purposes, which also needs a high degree of protection.

All of this dictates a necessity for a separate department which has to deal with the risks, risk assessment, information collection and review, decision-making based on the collected information. Although a great part of information collection can be done automatically, even a part of information categorizing, the final decision must be made by human supervision, and this implies that self-driven cars need a remote “driver”.

KEY TERMS AND DEFINITIONS

Autonomous Vehicles: An autonomous vehicle (AV), also known as a self-driving car or a self-driving robotic car, is a vehicle that is capable of sensing its environment and moving safely with little or no human input.

Machine Learning: Machine learning is described as a research area that deals with designing algorithms. An important feature of those algorithms is the automatic improvement of technical systems that rely on experience – the automatic improvement follows rules and measures pre-set by the human developer. With machine learning, we need clearly defined tasks, the accompanying metrics, and training data.

Machine Perception: Machine perception is the capability of a computer system to interpret data in a manner that is similar to the way humans use their senses to relate to the world around them. The basic method in which the computers take in and respond to their environment is through the attached hardware, that allows computers to take in sensory input in a way similar to humans.

Safety: The state of being away from hazards caused by natural forces or human errors.

Security: The state of being away from hazards caused by the deliberate intention of a human to cause harm.

Sensor: A sensor is a device that responds to a physical stimulus (such as heat, light, sound, pressure, magnetism, or a particular motion) and transmits information (used for measurements or operating a control).
