# Chapter 29

*   Joshua Ojo Nehinbe  
    Federal University, Oye-Ekiti. Nigeria

ABSTRACT

Fake news and its impacts are serious threats to social media in recent time. Studies on the ontology of these problems reveal that serious cybercrimes such as character assassination, misinformation, and blackmailing that some people intentionally perpetrate through social networks significantly correlate with fake news. Consequently, some classical studies on social anthropology have profiled the problems and motives of perpetrators of fake news on political, rivalry, and religious issues in contemporary society. However, this classification is restrictive and statistically defective in dealing with cyber security, forensic problems, and investigation of social dynamics on social media. This chapter exhaustively discusses the above issues and identifies solutions to challenges confronting research community in the above domain. Thematic analysis of responses of certain respondents reveal three new classifications of fake news that people propagate on social media on the basis of mode of propagation, motives of perpetrators, and impacts on victims.

INTRODUCTION

Fake news is an interdisciplinary problem that is dated back to ancient times in contemporary literature (Lazer et al, 2018; William, 2009). However, the recent dimension of the problem on social media and the depth of its impacts on legitimate news, news’ publishers, victims and senders of fake news are serious concerns across the globe. Besides, fake news is seriously threatening the mind-set of people and genuine news on televisions, rmedia and social media. Crime studies have revealed that fake news has been used to commit serious cybercrimes like extortion, character assassination, misinformation, swindling and blackmailing of highly dignified personalities on social media (Kohei, 2017; Dominic, 2017). Hence, the quality of the news that young and aged people originate and spread on social media platform is frequently criticized and significant numbers of them are suspected to be unreliable news.

Fundamentally, fake news is a complex issue to foretell, detect and stop for a number of reasons (Pennycook and Rand, 2019; Joshua et al, 2019). Fake news may signify a sequence of logically and deliberately fabricated lies that perpetrators spread among their group members (Allcott and Gentzkow, 2017). Findings suggest that perpetrators can circulate fake news on outbreak of epidemic diseases, vaccines, scientific innovations, technological breakthroughs, insurgency, products and services to cite a few. Consequently, feelers begin to contemplate whether the recipients of fake news on social media endeavour to ponder and consider the ontology of the news before they continue to spread the news to other people. Apart from the discrepancy in the underlying motives of perpetrators of fake news, it is unfortunate that several studies have failed to clarify the hierarchical and logical relationships of the entities that encourage fake news to widely spread on social media (Lazer et al, 2019). For these reasons, fake news on social media is an emerging problem across the globe in a recent survey.

Furthermore, research has also identified brands of fake news that are due to unintentional mistakes, overzealous in journalism and errors inherited from the secondary sources and originator(s) or primary source(s) of the news (Joanna, 2017). Fake news has also been correlated with misconception, rumor, anticipated and incorrect personal views of the sources and originators of the news (Kohei, 2017). Unfortunately, Lazer et al (2018) and Joshua et al (2019) have shown that fake news on social media quickly spread to distance audience but all the underlying motives of its perpetrators and the severity of its impacts on the victims are often contestable in most studies. According to Watts (2018), some perpetrators create fake news to confuse, allure and manipulate readers, certain audience and laypeople. Specifically, Dominic (2017) and classical social anthropologists believe that intruders, propagandists, corporate firms, agencies, activists, terrorists and politicians have disseminated fake news via social media at different occasions in the last two decades.

Moreover, the conceptualization of the significance of capturing in-depth stories, the need to deeply research into public records and the challenges in conducting face-to-face interviews with primary sources of information have led to the development of a paradigm shift in the method, assessment, interpretation, organization and writing of investigative reporting in journalism across the globe. From experience, founders of social media generally designed them for information sharing. Facebook is designed for sharing photos, videos and messages, Twitter is designed for sharing breaking news such as political news, sports and other forms of entertainment, YouTube is designed for downloading and sharing of videos and music with friends. Instagram is designed for video-sharing while WhatsApp is designed for fast sharing of messages and calls. For these reasons, Joshua et al (2019) further submit that most journalists derive their stories from social media platforms of some celebrities, reputable politicians and corporate websites to complement the conventional methods of using face-to-face, interviews and eye witness to explore scenes and events. Nonetheless, the above approaches can lead to serious legal tussles between the victims and the publishers of news that derogate governments and high profile nationalities especially if the stories eventually turn out to be counterfeit and fallacies.

Social and forensic experts have argued that some intruders deliberately create fake news on social media to ridicule, destroy, degrade, expose, humiliate, impoverish and ruin their targets or competitors. Consequently, the central issue is that studies on the impacts of fake news have described fake news as a kind of cybercrime that demands urgent attentions. Some journalists and reputable organizations have incurred huge fines and libel from court cases on deformation of characters for reporting and publishing incorrect information on governments and highly dignified personalities.

In Wang (2017), datasets that can be used to benchmark data mining models for detecting fake news are grossly inadequate. Another problem with fake news on social media is that the rate at which some swindlers adopt it to carryout deceitfulness; extortion of countless victims and manipulate the intelligence of philanthropists and sympathizers often calls for urgent attentions to curtail them (Allcott and Gentzkow, 2017). Consequently, contemporary studies have suggested that several victims of fake news have incurred severe material, mental and psychological damages like bankruptcy, depression, cognitive imbalance, phobia and aggression that beyond immediate recovery (Allcott et al, 2019). The above issues have raised serious doubts concerning the actual motives of perpetrators of fake news, the factors that promote the spread of fake news on social media and suitable measures that can enable online users to promptly discern and stop the spread of fake news on social networks. Some measures have been notably undertaken to address some of the above concerns.

| Figure 1. Traditional classifications of fake news |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch029.f01](i/ch029.f01.png) |
| --- |

The diagram in Figure 1 explicitly presents five categories of fake news that was proposed by Watts (2018). The scholar classified fake news on the basis of the traditional motives of perpetrators. Besides, classical studies on social anthropology have profiled motives of perpetrators of fake news on the basis of political, rivalry and religious issues in contemporary society (Lazer et al, 2018). Nevertheless, the above classifications obviously restrict the menace of fake news to textual information. Hence, they are less effective to conduct critical exploration of the ontology of fake news on social media.

Secondly, most of the existing classifications of fake news are statistically defective in dealing with cyber security, forensic problems and investigations of social dynamics on social media. Studies suggest that these classifications often lack the capability required to determine the degrees of predictability and similarity of fake news that is circulated through social media networks. Another classical issue is that some political actors, agencies and propagandists frequently use social media to deliberately propagate fake news to gather political supporters, campaign for votes and hypnotize people. With the current limitations of fact-checking services, it is difficult for the recipients of fake news on social media platform to accurately detect the validity of the news and isolate perpetrators that intentionally meant to deceive people from people that craft news to cover their misdeeds by misinforming the public (Asr and Taboada, 2019; International Society for Technology in Education, 2020).

Besides, in crisis management, it is difficult to segregate politicians and propagandists that are liars from motivational speakers that merely seek to gain media popularity, dowse tension or reduce emotional outburst of the masses. Thus, the efficacies of forensic and legislative measures that have been designed to reduce various problems that are associated with fake news continue to generate strict criticisms from country to country especially if intruders, opponents and competitors adopt fake news to attack governments, agencies, public figures, ruling party and social media.

Therefore, the main objective of this chapter is to exhaustively discuss the ontology of fake news and challenges that are confronting research community in the domain of fake news on social media. Furthermore, the chapter proposes Category utility and Gini Index to statistically explore categorical datasets on fake news. One of the significant contributions of this chapter is its ability to identify and suggest solutions to major challenges that are confronting research community in the domain of fake news on social networks. The chapter statistically illustrates how to cluster fake news over social media on the basis of hoax pictures (HP), hoax video clips (HVC), hoax text/messages (HTM), hoax audio clips (HAC) and hoax newsprints (HN). The remainders of this chapter are organized to include discussions of related work on the above issues and the ontology of fake news on social media. The chapter will further identify research challenges in the above issues and methods to resolve them. A section of the chapter will discuss new classification of fake news and statistical methods to examine the above problems. The chapter will end with a concluding section. This section will also offer suggestions together with research direction that can be carried out to extend model that is proposed in this chapter.

BACKGROUND

Studies have suggested six methods for detecting fake news on social media. Allcott and Gentzkow (2017) agree that recipients of news on social media should manually and comprehensively review the content, source and purpose of the news before they would spread the news. Similarly, the International Federation of Library Association (IFLA) in 2016 has evolved eight guidelines for detecting fake news. Accordingly, media users should verify the sources, authors, dates, fairness in the reports, references, confirmation and conduct critical review on online news to ascertain whether the stories are jokes or realities before they disseminate the news. In addition, an automated algorithm has been suggested to verity sources of information on digital media (Pennycook and Rand, 2019). However, fact-checking outlets are often unreliable to verify political misinformation across the globe (Walter et al, 2019). Skilled criminals may adopt some toolkits to erase or update the recording dates of fake pictures and fake audio tapes before circulating them on social media.

Fact-checking websites such as Snopes, Politifact, Emergent, AllSides and Media Matters have been established (International Society for Technology in Education, 2020; Asr and Taboada, 2019). The International Fact-checking Networks (IFCNs) has published a code of principles that can be adopted to vet and validate the originality of information before it is printed. In addition, media literacy has been proposed to complement IFLA’s guidelines on media education and on how users of online resources can discern fake news from genuine news.

Additionally, modeling techniques that adopt visualization frameworks to detect fake images have been proposed over the years (Asr and Taboada, 2019). However, one of the major weaknesses of visualization is its inability to separate fake news with blurred images from genuine pictures that are indiscernible, vague and invisible to naked eyes.

Essentially, the time it requires for the recipients to adopt manual method and searching algorithms to evaluate the news on a daily basis and the possibility that the sources of the news may be offline and inaccessible as at the time the recipients want to verify the news often limit their capacities. With the diversity and weaknesses of some cyber laws across the globe, most of the existing methods for detecting fake news on social media are ineffective for combating its indiscriminate circulation and related cybercrimes on social media.

THE ONTOLOGY OF the FAKE NEWS ON SOCIAL MEDIA

Ontology often describes the relationship between a concept and its entities (Pundt, 2007). In this paper, the ontology of fake news intends to explain the hierarchical and logical relationships that exist within the attributes of fake news on social media. With the new paradigm shift in cultural anthropology, this chapter premises that digital culture and criminal skills can be acquired and shared during social interactions.

Simple Propagation of Fake News on Social Media

Pedlers of fake news on social media can disseminate and promote fake news through small groups of participants.

| Figure 2. One-to-one sharing of fake news |

| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch029.f02](i/ch029.f02.png) |
| --- |

The model presents in Figure 2 illustrates how fake news can migrate from an originator and how the news is subseqently spread to one recipient.

| Figure 3. One-to-few sharing of fake news |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch029.f03](i/ch029.f03.png) |
| --- |

The model presents in Figure 3 illustrates how fake news can migrate from an originator and can subsequently be spread to many recipients. The ontology of the above possibilities conveys different threats for a number of reasons. Fake news that is disseminated to a terrible recipient may harm the victims more that similar news that is spread to less dreadful recipients. The recipients may or may not further disseminate the news. Thus, fake news must definitely terminate with recipient(s) that will not share it with other social members.

Furthermore, the risk and impacts of fake news on the above scenarios usually depend on social platform, news, orginators of the fake news, the recipients and the actions that the recipients would take with the news they have received. The impacts of fake news are not often determined by the number of recipients involved in spreading the news. The reactions of members of the society that is pre-occupied with economically bouyant people might be different from the perceptions and reactions of people living in ghettos. Fake news on sudden reduction of wages of employees might impact on downtrodden proletariat that are noted for resisting social injustice in developed countries in different ways if compared to their counterparts that possess insignficant labour-power in underdeveloped countries.

Complex Propagation of Fake News on Social Media

Pedlers of fake news can be adolescents and adults. Each group of users of social media has areas of life that interest them. Some young people are interested in specific celebrities, sports, movies and news about relationships. Contrarily, adults are most likely to be gravitated to news on politics, health, scientific discovery and leisure. Some pedlers of fake news on social media usually aim large audience so that they can maximally disseminate the news across large groups of adolescents and adults.

| Figure 4. Complex sharing of fake news to all group members |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch029.f04](i/ch029.f04.png) |
| --- |

The model presents in Figure 4 is a complex way of spreading fake news on social media. The originator of the news may decide to circulate the news to all recipients in his/her chating groups on social media. Furthermore, some recipients repeatedly receive the old news they had previously disseminated to other people. Hence, the underlying motives and quality of the news are susceptible to modification; distortion and misrepresentation as the news is being received and propagated by different people.

The implications of fake news that depicts radicalism and widespread of ideology through interractions of recipients on social media can be grave in some cases. The risks can encompass enormous cyber crimes and threats to the medium of its propagation, the victims, participants and information privacy in general. The model has the tendency to leak online information.that can affect several millions of recipients and victims. This can further heightened the concerns and suspicion that users of social media may develop about their security and in the disclosure of their personal information online. Furthermore, dissemination of fake news across all members of social groups can potentially jeopardize international and bilateral relationships. The news can impact more on trust on social media companies as well as the peace and security of two or more countries that are noted for frown relationships. Social media that encourage circulation of obsolete news that eventually turn out to be fake news can annoying many users especially if the news provokes wrong emotional expressions.

Incessant incidence of massive dissemination of fake news can underscore the fragility of Cyber Physical Systems (CPS). Cyber criminals that attack critical infrastructure by leaking and disseminating the procedures of incident reporting with competitors may have different motives compare to cyber criminals that are spreading distorted news about the same victims. Investigations, litigations and closure of cases of cybercrimes in the above context can be complicated if detectives must interrogate lots of suspected peddlers of fake news. People may begin to develop discomfort; sentiment and strong criticisms against international governance on the ways social media are operated and regulated across the globe if they continue to deveop bad feelings about the above issues.

| Figure 5. Complex sharing of fake news to some group members |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch029.f05](i/ch029.f05.png) |
| --- |

Contrarily, the model of fake news presents in Figure 5 exemplifies how an originator of fake news on social media may decide to circulate the news to some recipients in circles. There are three emerging issues whenever fake news is spread through complex groups of social members. Firstly, classification of recipients of fake news on socia media becomes complex because there will be different ways to categorize them. For instance, some recipients (such as recipient-5, recipient-7, recipient-9 and recipient-10), may be categorize as hesitants. They are users that are reluctant and unwilling to spread the news they receive with other people. This model also demonstrates tthat some hesitants (like recipient-5 and recipient-10) can be grouped together. These are people that will not spread fake news to their group members irrespective of the numbers of instances they have received it. Similarly, some recipients (such as recipient-1, recipient-4, recipient-5, recipient-6 and recipient-10) can be grouped together. They represent users of social media that repeatedly receive the old news they had previously declined or spread to other people. Some recipients (such as recipient-8 and recipient-12) can also be classified together. They symbolize users of social media that may resend the fake news to some people that had previously spread the news to their group members.

Secondly, the underlying motives and quality of the news are susceptible to modification; distortion and misrepresentation as the news is being received and propagated by different people. Thirdly, the above ontology of fake news further advises that the mode of dissemination of the news can alter the patterns of users of social media and Internet users from regular users to selective users of cyber resources. Users of social media may decide to close their accounts to dispel fake news. Therefore, social and legal interventions that will curb the widespread of fake news on social media should be taylored towards increasing the numbers of hesistants that will be unwilling to spread the news they receive with other people.

Concept, Scope, Problems, and Solutions to Fake News on Social Media

The objectives and scope of research on fake news on social media are broad. Investigators can focus on countless areas of the subject matter in relation to cyber security and information privacy. Some researchers may explore fake news that target digital tools (such as computers and networks) that victims of cyber attacks use in private or corporate setting. Researchers may investigate cyber criminals or intruders that adopt fake news to attack actions and operations of their victims in a specific setting. Similarly, some investigators may be interested in conducting studies on cyber criminals that fabricate and circulate fake news with authentic news to deceive masses in a given society. Nevertheless, most of these domains are difficult to explore in many countries.

Inability of research community to freely explore fake news on social media can generate some background issues. New models to protect against circulation of fake news that appear to be leakages of classified information and detection of cybercrimes on social media may suffer major setbacks if researchers are unable to conduct informative studies in the above domain. Hence, efforts of stakeholders must focus on potential solutions that can lessen challenges in exploring the above domain of fake news.

Research Challenges With Fake News on Social Media

Researchers in the domain of fake news on social media face contoversial challenges in the last two decades. Some researchers face difficult challenges to develop security and privacy models that founders and business owners of social media can adopt to achieve strong security and resilient of cyber system. Currently, some young researchers constantly experience difficulties to maximize and harmonize limited resources available to them to participate in international collaborative studies on the above domain. Thus, this section further discusses other important issues and problems confronting researchers in the areas of fake news on social media.

Grouping of Fake News on Social Media

Fake news across Facebook is different from fake news that migrates across Twitter. Employers of labour that advertise fake services on social media are different from users that fondly use fake news to fight cyberwarfare on social media. Hence, it is often difficult for researchers to cluster fake news and the above issues on the basis of location, purpose, type, time of occurrence and impacts of the news. The present circumstances of issues with fake news on social media may easily exchaust capabilities of most researchers to progress through the required milestomes. Sometimes, young researchers may exchaust years of laborious efforts to achieve insignificant results in the explorations into categories of fake news on social media due to jurisdictions, verdicts by courts and discripancies in cyberlaws across the globe.

Some community may not perceive fake news on social media as a serious cybercrime. In a dictatorial caliphate and some religious society, researchers may begin to ponder on how to discern fake news that is intentionally created to limit freedom of speech of their subjects or subordinates from fake news that originates from unapproved sources. Some researchers are restricted by international laws and practice. Local iinvestigators may face restrictions to evolve models that can isolate cyberterrorism from cybercrimes that were aided by fake news on social media especially if the scope of the research extends to fake news that is spread across different international boundaries. It is plausible that some actors may outsource and monitized cybercrimes over social media. However, recruitments of participants and volunteers needed to conduct empirical studies to examine these new possibilities have many constraints. For example, it might be very difficult to recruit perpetrators of fake news across all categories of social media. Hence, the validity and reliability of the data and main themes that are deduced from the research are often criticized by experts over the years.

Issues With Datasets for Investigating Fake News

There are no universally acceptable datasets to evaluate research models on fake news that people specifically propagate on social media. Apart from the fact that most of the existing datasets are restricted to specific originators of fake news, findings have shown that they do not comprehensively reflect all forms of fake news, For instance, the scope of the available datasets like Liar (Wang, 2017), FEVER (Thorne et al, 2018) and evidence that fact-checking service providers can verify are limited in scope.

The integrity of some online datasets is subjective. Some countries have placed limit to the quantity of datasets that researchers can generally gather to achieve their research objectives. Sometimes, public relation officers may decline requests from fact-checking service providers to confirm the validity of news specific to certain politicians, scientific and military claims (International Society for Technology in Education, 2020). Besides, the usage of most of the above datasets is limited because they have insufficient documentations.

Issues With Databases Of Fake News

One of the central issues here is that it is practically difficult to create and develop valid databases of fake news that researchers can adopt to benchmark their findings. It is plausible that some perpetrators of fake news can suddenly deny and retract their past statements and actions that they subsequently realize could trigger hostility in the society. Some public relations' experts can openly apologize or denounce fake news they thought could be detrimental and inimical to the moral responsibilities that the society usually accept from public office holders as symbols of good leadership and best corporate governance.

Additionally, researchers on text classifications have observed that most of the available datasets on the above domain are unsuitable for evaluating and modifying models on Natural Language Processing (NLP) (Asr and Taboada, 2019). It has also been reported that the efficacies of some models on deep learning begin to decline whenever they are evaluated with some of the available datasets on fake news. Essentially, the domain of fake news on social media continues to face numerous criticisms and challenges that subsume lack of suitable datasets, lack of standard data donors, limited scope, insufficient documentations and poor legislations in the last two decades.

Exploring Impacts of Fake News on Social Media

Research community faces big challenges on how to design models to identify victims of fake news on social media that may not aware of cyber attacks on them. Fake news on social media is an example of qualitative studies. Selecting suitable scientific models that can conform to social behaviour is an additional setback. Filtering algroithms that freely work with underlying concepts are usually based on Neural Networks (NN), Linear Programming (LP), Genetic Algroithm (GA), Support Vector Machine (SVM), Electroencephalography (EEG), Discrete Fourier Transform (DFT) and data mining. However, most of these paradigms are not directly suitable for explicating inadequacies of classifiers that extract, filter and cross-correlate fake news on social media.

Researchers that intend to carryout exploration on the discriminative features, perceptions of law enforcement agencies and legal luminaries regarding impacts of fake news on social media across underdeveloped, developing and developed countries may end up depleting their financial resources due to sensitivity of this research domain. In some cases, researchers must spend additional time to secure approvals before they can be allowed to analyze the above issues. Unfortunately, it is a common practise to observe some researchers that would have waited for approvals for several months before some agencies would evenntually deny their requests without genuine reasons.

Fighting Fake News on Social Media

Researchers may face strict challenges to secure grants in other to explore models that governments and corporate individuals can adopt to fight against pedlers of fake news on social media for two reasons. Studies have suggested that some firms, governments and their agencies are pedlers of fake news on social media. Lack of trust and professional ethics can conflict with security and privacy of empirical studies. In this regard, the investigators might waste their efforts and limited resources without achieving the objectives of the studies. The outcomes of research to fight fake news on social media concorted and circulated by agents of governments and corporate bodies may eventually be harshly criticized as hateful, misleading and falacies. Such research's proposals stand the likelihood to be rejected, unpublished and summarily carpeted by the people in the positions of authority.

Another core issue is that cybercrimes due to fake news on social media are clearly different from other categories of cybercrimes. Hence, researchers do not often receive cooperations of private and public individuals required to conduct and design robust expert systems that can massively reveal cybercrimes committed against them with fake news on social media. Corporate individuals and celebrities that are constant victims of fake news often shy away from disclosing the severity of the impacts of the news on them.

Developing Hesitant to Fake News on Social Media

Real news on social media should convey information about recent and important events. It could signify interviews and commentary echoed on radios and broadcasted on televisions. News can be a sequence of information reported in newspapers, news bulletins or news magazine. However, it is difficult to design models that can discriminate and establish information of any kind that is not news and information that will not be interesting to prospective hesistants in all social groups on social media.

Developing measures to encourage hesitants on social platforms require multi- disciplinary methods. Getting the required expertise and implementation of this concept across all social platforms are time consuming. The intentions of hesistant can vary from one person to another. Some group members may decline to participate in circulating fake news because of workload, fatigue and hatred. Group members may report, delete and block nuisance's users for sending unwanted messages to them. Accordingly, researchers are presently facing tough challenges to explore, aggregate and correlate motives of the above group of users on Facebook, Twitter, YouTube and in other types of social platforms.

Controversies With Social legislation

Usually, social media should be newsy and most social media possess functionalities that support dissemination of news and trivial or informal conversations. In terms of quality, modern news on social media should focus on current events that are enlightening or educative, consultative or advisory, interpretative, illuminating, informatory or elucidative, demonstrative and instructive. News with the above qualities can help audience to increase their knowledge and dissipate ignorance. Unfortunately, significant numbers of social legislations are weak in regulating qualities of good news in most countries.

In adddition, with the new threats to social media, it is very hard to adopt quantitative research to model and sequestrate naive peddlers of fake news. Presently, significant numbers of research models on fake news on social media are rarely used for reducing the numbers of users that may wish to join chat groups of stealthy cybercriminals. Furthermore, models are not designed to discriminate users that are not obviously identified with dramatic information intended to lure or give the illusion of unfeigned reflections to naive audience. The underlying fact is that social media users that seek for daily news or news update about recent, important and fundamental events must be prudent in shmoozing, reading and acting on online chats to avoid embarrassment, sudden detection and interrogations by detectives.

Multifarious Nature of Cybercrimes on Social Media

Comprehensive findings on all areas of cybercrimes on social media are insufficient. The main reason is that the scope of cybercrime is generally wide. A few examples of cybercrimes on social media include circulation of a recorded attack in video and audio event. Signficant numbers of cybercrimes on social media involve attacks in writing. These include circulation of falsified instrument of payment (cheques) or falsified information with intention to smear or defraud victims; illegal disclosure of official matters on social media, online sharing of news that undermines sovereign authority or governments; and wilful and unlawful circulation of crippling images or mutilated drawings of another person.

Some cybercrimes on social networks are gross violations of professional ethics. Infringement is one of the commonest examples of violation and disregards to corporate agreement. Breach of corporate agrement can occur in many ways. Employees can be guilty of this crime if they involve in chatting and sharing of immodest personal pictures. Some employers of labour may sanction or penalise employees displaying wealth and personal assets like buildings, exotic cars and jewerries that depicts misdemeanour. Some employers of labour may overlook that behaviours while corporate settings like banks may believe they are gross violations of ethical standards or inappropriate of public figures or role models to safeguard their corporate image and employees from being targets of online swindlers.

Online thuggery is another kind of cybercrimes committed on social media. Online thugs can incite or provoke well-mannered users to engage in violent or brutal activities in clever ways. Thugs can share online news that bear false witness, news that convey breach of national peace; news that derogate ruling party as incompetent; news that breach the peace of a person and news that incites and fuels crisis between two rival communities. In essence, inability of research, government and data donors to collaborate is militating against rapid growth of research in the above domains. For these reasons, little is known about the fact that cybercrimes embrace all forms of activities that unknowingly and deliberately violate accepted principles of right and wrong usage of computers, mobile devices and the Internet. Above all, adaptability of research findings on fake news on social media has generated series of controversies in recent years. One of the controversial arguments of social critics is that fake news has limited pragmatic applications from one country to another.

SOLUTIONS AND RECOMMENDATIONS

There are several solutions and recommendations that can be adopted to deal with the above issues and controversial problems. For instance, suitable datasets that researchers can adopt to investigate models on fake news over social media should conform to the formats of categorical data. Fundamentally, attributes of both the synthetic and real datasets in the above domain should include source, short description and timestamp of the news. For instance, the timestamp of fake news should indicate the time, date and year at which the fake news occurs. It is imperative that data donors should endeavour to improve on the documentations and details they provide on their datasets to enable research community to perfectly understand the variability of attributes that form the datasets.

Harmonization of cyberlaws, policies and legislations across the globe can help researchers to lessen multifarious challenges on the above domains. Stakeholders must create online platforms to dialogue, share and delibrate on cyber legislations and cybercrimes relating to fake news on social media. Researchers intending to explore any of the above issues should be granted permissions to access such online platforms. Furthermore, instances whereby some perpetrators have used fake news on social media to proficiently acquire market dominance, defeat warfare or redeem dwindling reputations have been identified in business, military and scientific arena over the years. Therefore, data donors should publish the genuineness, strengths and weaknesses of their datasets to assist scientific claims. Donors of online datasets should explicitly state the conditions at which their datasets are valid or untrue for pragmatic evaluations of research models. Data donors should also state the methods they have adopted to extract their datasets. Above all, online datasets should be accompanied with strong disclaimers.

Forensic aspects of fake news suggest that originators of fake news are storytellers. The basic fact is that forensic methods to separate someone who tells a story from someone who tells lies are scarce. Storytellers can fabricate literary work based on their power of imaginations without necessarily concentrating on factual implications of their narrations. Some stories may deliberately or erroneously contain improbable or false account of events that aim to attract lots of audience in the society. Journalists may interview literary writers based on their famous or new novels. Globalization and socia media are major threats to social anthropology. Without doubt, newsflash on some novels or interviews may signify fake news especially if the literary work is on dystopias. Literary work of fiction that describes an imaginary race, slum or community where poverty is pandemic and life is extremely bad for inhabitants may get diverse interpretations from different settings. Investigators of cybercrimes should aware that aggressive reactions may be observed from activists, social critics and non-governmental bodies especially if the story attributes the suffering of the people to pandemic outbreak of disease, oppression and social deprivation.

Social media should increase users’ understandings and awareness about legitimate cyberculture and how to frequently conform to ethical expectations on social media. There should be educative functionalities in social websites that will enable online users to chat from the perspective of networks' forensics: The reason is that cyberculture is a peculiar and dynamic society and it is mostly favoured by different social groups. People with the same or different economic, social and educational status can belong to the same social groups. Group members have the tendency to be reserved and cautious to chat if they belong to highly reputable strata in the society. Therefore, the assumption is that rich or educated people are likely to avoid excess group members while using computers for business communication and entertainment. However, famous assumptions are not always coherent with social groups that should be suspects and victims of cybercrimes in network's forensics.

With the existence of rootkits and new waves of manwares, features that can discriminate cybercriminals are difficult to forestall by technical methods. Hence, fundamental assumptions about any social class on cyberculture are weak in the investigation and establishment of criminal evidence in courts. As a result, valid conclusions can not be drawn from all cases of cybercrimes on social media without thorough investigations of the motives, impacts and mode of each incident. Finally, investigators should endeavour to differentiate datasets they extract from websites that are well-known for deliberate usage of fake news to attract readers, promotional ratings, revenues and online advertisements from synthetic datasets that they download from online repositories.

New Classification of Fake News on Social Media

In Kothari (2004), qualitative methods are used to investigate the underlying reasons behind human behaviour in the society. In exploring the above problems, this chapter adopts qualitative methods to gather the opinions of undergraduate students and computer operators that are familiar with Facebook, Twitter, YouTube, Instagram and WhatsApp. In addition, 92 of the above correspondents were interviewed while 14 of them participated in a focus group. The two groups agreed that fake news is a common menace on social media. The participants were asked to express their critical opinions on the categories of fake news that people have received on social media in recent time. Giving an attribute, category utility is a measure that determines the expected value of correct attributes that a predictor can accurately predict in a set of clustering schemes that the attribute belongs and to compare them with the expected values of correct attributes the predictor can make with any other attribute (Gluck and Corter, 1985; Fisher, 1987, Scott, 2012, Nehinbe, 2011). Suppose C[1], C[2]….C[k]….C[N] are clusters of attributes A[1], A[2], … A[j] of a given dataset. FUTURE RESEARCH DIRECTIONS

Fake news on social media is an extensive research opportunity within the domains of cyber security and forensics. Further research directions should focus on cybercrimes on social media, Fake news that is used to blackmail and extort kind people, camouflage, conceal the truth and promote fallacious ideas are alarming on social media. Investigators can also explore these new trends to lessen the problems in due course.

Importantly, lacks of suitable categorical datasets that have been identified above is limiting further evaluations of the model proposed in this chapter. Research community can further explore suitable datasets that can be used to implement and evaluate Category utility and Gini Index. Future research can also focus on how to create effective legislation and databases of fake news on social media to extend the quality of this chapter.

CONCLUSION

The pervasive nature of Internet resources often encourages people to speedily spread substandard information and publish it on social media without undergoing pair-reviewing processes. Hence, significant numbers of news on social media lack comments from independent experts that are necessary to thoroughly verify the quality and veracity of online information. Impacts of sending and receiving fake news on social media can endanger, implicate and incriminate the victims, originators of the news and people that receive it. In this chapter, fake news on social media, how to discover the underlying motives of the perpetrators and predict the desires of its perpetrators are seen as classical issues that are gathering serious momentum across the globe. This chapter subsequently observes that social media is changing politics, scientific claims, business and the mode of practicing journalism in the last two decades in the developed and developing countries.

Fake news may emerge from the reactions of originators or radicals to literary work on dystopias. Literary work of fiction that describes an imaginary race, slum or community where poverty is pandemic and life is unbelievable can trigger emotional problems from sympathizers and social critics. In this era of modern journalism, the ideas of using conventional methods such as eye witness, face-to-face-interviews and live commentary to achieve direct coverage of events are gradually fading away. Most often, fact-checking procedures are doubtful. Thus, some journalists and corporate firms continue to rely on the news they gather over social media websites such as Face book, Twitter, YouTube, Instagram, WhatsApp and LinkedIn. Stories obtained from social media tend to be readily organized in the required news’ formats, published and even broadcasted within short intervals. With this, social media is indirectly promoting active press by enabling journalists to promptly insert late news into the newspapers that are already scheduled for printing. Journalists that extract news from social media have indirectly avoided the risks of being eye witnesses. They have avoided brutality and common attacks on reporters such as assault, lynching, unlawful arrest; illegitimate detention and kidnapping of reporters at the scenes of the events. Affront on the media can lead to tyrannical behaviour, cruelty and barbaric tactics with the intention to suppress media. Besides, the expected operational costs that the reporters should have incurred for them to witness and report the scenes have also been minimized in this context. But then, the intelligence required in analyzing and transcribing the news printing so that news program, news show and news editing will conform to newsworthiness are prone to human errors.

This chapter has also shown that the quality of information that is recently reported in the newspapers, bulletins and news magazine are not often exonerated from fake news. It is plausible that some journalists will erroneously adopt news that is an abstraction of reality. Accordingly, they tend to garner, propagate and recycle news with technical mistakes that may be intentionally or unintentionally committed by the original news’ casters. Reporters and publishing firms may face different range of penalties for reporting fake news depending on the victims and the impacts of the news. Thus, this chapter has also explored the ontology of fake news and its impacts on victims and social media. It is observed that the perpetrators of fake news on social media recently adopt Hoax pictures (HP), Hoarse video clips (HVC), Hoarse text/ messages (HTM), Hoax newsprints (HN) and Hoarse audio clips (HAC) to misinform, deceive, hypnotize, radicalize and defraud masses.

We suggest that social media that is noted for hoax news may suddenly record low patronage by their online users. We have identified that fake news on social media is associated with serious cybercrimes such as character assassination, misinformation, fraudulent practices and blackmailing of corporate and private individuals. Some private victims may express emotional breakdown like weeping, depression and attempt to commit suicide while significant numbers of them may suffer symptomatic expressions like heart attacks and bewildering. Consequently, this chapter extends the existing classical studies on the above issues with three different classifications of fake news on social media.

The chapter categorizes fake news on the basis of the underlying motives of the perpetrators. The premise is that experts can statistically adopt the proposed model to handle cyber security, forensic problems and investigation of social dynamics on social media. We also empirically proof that fake news on social media can endanger economic growth, lives and properties of people. We point out that fake news that is embeded in health and safety issues can trigger serious economic and political crisis across the globe. Fake news can also cause public reactions that may include loss of job, loss of market dominance, cyberphobia, stigmatization, emotional breakdown, hatred; unlawful arrest, breakdown of laws and orders; mutiny and civil unrest.

Technically, social media websites have inbuilt features for security and privacy control. Users can block, delete, report and quit nuisance's groups. With the prevalence of how systemic partners are adopting fake news to fight themselves on social media, business owners should enhance existing functionalities on routine basis. Incorporation of algroithms that can extract; cross-correlate and filter suspicious sequence of statements on social media websites can help to reduce migration of fake news.

Fake news must originate from a source. Therefore, it is imperative that investigators of cybercrimes should properly prove the validity of sources, treding and all recipients of information (or accusations) levied against suspects of cybercrimes. Finally, the chapter suggests areas of focus to data donors. Additionally, legislative interventions including cyber laws and stiff penalties are needed to punish offenders. These should target five key modes and attributes of fake news identified in this chapter. Government should collaboratively setup experts that are saddled with the responsibilities to monitor and regulate social media. Above all, suitable cyber legislations to protect victims and cyber courts that will empower victims to prosecute and sanction perpetrators of fake news on social media must be enacted or established across the globe.

KEY TERMS AND DEFINITIONS

Category Utility: Category utility is a concept that measures similarity of two items in the same cluster and their differences with items in other clusters.

Clustering: Clustering uses attributes to group similar objects or items together to succinctly represent a collection of objects or items.

Cybercrime: Cybercrime is an activity that a user performs with computer, mobile device and the Internet that is punishable by law. Examples of cybercrimes are online fraud, character assassination, misinformation, and blackmailing.

Fake News: Fake news signifies hoax news that people may deliberately or unintentionally disseminate to people.

Gini Index: Gini index estimates the statistical dispersion or the degree of similarity in attributes of a categorical dataset.

Hesitant: Hesitant is a person that disinclines to take part in the spreading of fake news on social media.

Ontology: Ontology describes the relationship between a concept and its attributes or entities.

Social Media: Social media is used to describe interactive websites that enable users to share information such as multimedia and texts. Examples of social media are Facebook, Twitter, YouTube, Instagram, WhatsApp, and LinkedIn.

ABSTRACT

Stuxnet is a malicious code used to exploit multiple unpatched Windows vulnerabilities and infect end devices. It was very sophistically used by attackers to infect computers that are connected to specific models of Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs) manufactured by Siemens. The stuxnet worm alters the PLCs' programming and raises a false alarm to machines, which leads to an accident. The worm uses zero-day vulnerabilities in the Windows operating system, and because of that, it remains undetected by the antivirus programs. The attacker attempts to breach the vulnerabilities in hardware systems and breaks the infrastructure, which leads to a watering hole attack. Thus, this chapter explores the different possibilities of the stuxnet-based cyber-attacks and their risk factors. The chapter represents an analysis that is performed on the different patterns of attacks, and its preventive measures are also proposed.

INTRODUCTION

Currently cyber warfare is a technology that generates harmful operations to victim nations which leads to increase cyber war situation. Many nations are trying to prevent and fight against cyber-attacks to save human lives, economy and geographical assets. Cyber operations are creating crucial condition for entire world because it directly effects on human lives. As per researcher Taddeo definition: Warfare based on certain uses of ICTs within a state-sponsored offensive or defensive military strategy aimed at the immediate disruption or control of enemy resources and carried out in the information environment, with agents and targets ranging from physical to non-physical, and the level of violence of which may vary according to circumstances. Here we are focus on how one malware change the prospect of cyber security and cyber warfare. There is open security challenge to entire cyber world how could malicious things/objects change behavior to hide themselves from security measures and impacts more than expectations. Cyber Story began in 2010 when security company VirusBlokAda detected one malware that was Rootkit.Tmphider. Afterwards Symantec title as w32.Temphid and later changed the title as W32.Stuxnet. Stuxnet worm has three execution phases: i) It uses worm-script to sequentially load all payloads to perform successful attack ii) Link file automatically propagate worm script file and makes multiple copies and iii) Rootkit file hides all contents and supportive processes which is helpful to avoid the detection of stuxnet malware (Duqu, 2011).

Compare to other categories of malware objects, stuxnet did not affected computer and networks also it did not require any software requirements. Attacker identify target and only hit that target rather than releasing impact on network or computers. Attacker needs few layer of system to make an attack successful that are suspected windows operating systems, Siemens PC7, step7 and WinCC software and Siemens S7 PLCs.

Stuxnet is a malicious computer code that was first time detected in 2010. Basically, it is designed to infect the Supervisory Control and the Data Acquisition system (SCADA). The Siemens SCADA system is used to manage the working of many industrial equipment’s. The Stuxnet as a cyber worm infects Programmable Logic Control system which allows the automation of electromechanical processes that are used to control machinery and industrial processes including centrifuges for spreading nuclear material. The Stuxnet is designed to exploit the Windows operating system vulnerabilities that are not auto patch. The study mainly focuses on which kind of vulnerability is susceptible to attempt cyber-attacks (Resource207, 2012).

Stuxnet worm basically explores a network via an infected USB device which goes through different steps: i. Malware or worm that executes the main signature or payload ii. An LNK file or service file (SVCHOST.exe) that automatically executes the propagated malware copies. iii. Genuine digital certificate by authenticated service provider that remains undetected by antivirus. iv. The rootkit used to hide all malicious codes and processes to bypass detection mechanisms (cv2, 2012).

In addition to this, Stuxnet also exploits a print spooler vulnerability in the Windows operating system to spread and infect all computers that use a shared printer. Other exploits attack vulnerabilities in a Windows keyboard file and Task Scheduler file through which the attacker gets control over the infected machine with administrative privileges. Stuxnet could exploit static password or default password that was hard coded by Siemens in its Step7 software. Stuxnet was able to obtain access using this password and also infect the database hosting server of Step7 which in turn infected the users and hosts connected with it. The attackers continuously try to intent on spreading infection of their payload or worm without getting detected by security applications. Stuxnet worm spreads via USB and infects the connected local area network (Hamdouni, 2017).

Unfortunately, Stuxnet was rapidly growing with the same or different format but the spreading speed is wider rather it continuously reported in different ways to get a major impact on operational programming and hardware too. From its origin to the victim it travels in a very silent situation but the impact of the attack is very dangerous. It was many time used to affect the economic zone, power plants, disaster equipment, etc. (ICS, 2017).

Zero-Day Attack

Today’s Cyber security is facing unintended security flaws in application software and OS platforms. Software vulnerabilities occur due to misconfiguration of application software, unattended bugs and ignored programming warnings, etc. This kind of security flaws are used by an attacker to exploit and generate massive security attack. When any vulnerabilities are not identified and before auto-patching that is used by an attacker then it leads a zero-day exploitation.

Cybercriminal tries to penetrate firewall security including IDS and IPS. But good thing is that they always leave some digital footprints on hardware and software too. So, it’s quite relief thing to find attackers using footprint and protect data and device from massive damage.

*   Step 1: Attacker compose .DLL (Worm Script) file which contains information about targeted software, date of trigger, auto patching and many more. Stuxnet is derived from mrxnet.sys file which is use for installed rootkit in target system. This composition is also carrying digital certificate of authenticated certificate provider.
*   Step 2: Attacker compose it in USB drive and physically try to attach it with any computer which is connected in industrial network.
*   Step 3: After entering into the network worm propagated with multiple copies using .LNK file. This is specially crafted file to duplicate replicas of worm and creates an icon like internet explorer, etc. There is no any interaction by human. The worm is highly adaptive and spread very calmly in different operating system. The worm infected the operating system with 32-bit versions such as: 
    *   • Windows 2000
    *   • Windows Server 2000
    *   • Windows XP
    *   • Windows Server 2003
    *   • Windows Vista
    *   • Windows 7
    *   • Windows Server 2008
*   Step 4: Until it gets any target system worm spreads ideally and does not perform any activity or breaching. After finding target system the rootkit code is executed and taking update from available network. Rootkit is installed in system and dropper code is executed with two different files -mrxnet.sys and mrxcls.sys. These files are installed in device driver with Realtek or JMicron digital certificate. -mrxnet.sys file is responsible to hide the Stuxnet worm file and mrxcls.sys file is taking care from behavioral antivirus and monitoring system to avoid the detection. Following are targeted application software’s: 
    *   • Siemens PCS 7
    *   • STEP7
    *   • SIMATIC WinCC 6.2
*   Step 5: Stuxnet replicated themselves using following Zero days Vulnerabilities and exploit target system using print spooler server service, Server Service Vulnerabilities (such as RPC handling remote code execution), shortcut files with malware signature, vulnerable STEP7 software, etc.
*   CVE-2008-4250 Microsoft server 2003 SP1 SP2, Microsoft server 2008, Microsoft Windows XP, Windows 7, SP1 and SP2, Window Vista Gold and SP1 allows control to an attacker over the server services via remote login which executes arbitrary code by using special RPC request that susceptible to trigger the overflow attack such kind of vulnerability titled as Server Service Vulnerability. MS08-067 Vulnerability in Server service susceptible to allow remote code execution with which gives control privilege to an attacker to exploit this vulnerability using RPC by the unauthorized way and execute exploited code. If exploitation could fail then it leads to crash server services such as svchost.exe. This issue is responsible to provide public access to a file system, printer, etc. over the internet (cv2, 2012).
*   CVE-2010-2568 Windows Shell in Microsoft server 2003 SP1 SP2, Microsoft server 2008, Microsoft Windows XP, Windows 7, SP1 and SP2, Window Vista Gold and SP1 allows all users including attackers to trigger the malicious code using concealed .LNK or .PIF extension shortcut files, etc. These files basically use windows basic application icons so it is not recognized/identified by a normal user. And they blindly click on it and trigger the exploitation code/ malware signature. This was recorded the incident on Siemens WinCC SCADA software which was released in CVE-2010-2772 (cv2, 2012).
*   CVE-2010-2729 In Microsoft server 2003 SP1 SP2, Microsoft server 2008, Microsoft Windows XP, Windows 7, SP1 and SP2, Window Vista Gold and SP1 are having print spooler server service to enable to share a printer in a network but it lacks privileges scheme setting which allows hackers/attackers to insert a malicious file in the system directory and triggers it for infection. This kind of vulnerability used to spread a crafted RPC file which is known as Print Spooler Service Impersonation Vulnerability (cv2, 2012).
*   CVE-2010-2743 In Microsoft Windows XP SP3 and Windows 7 have vulnerability at kernel mode drivers. So, it does not support perfectly to perform indexing of a function pointer table to load keyboard layouts from disk. This bug allows users to gain control over administrative privileges on many software applications which allows local users to gain privileges. The same vulnerability is used by Stuxnet worm (Win32k) to gain control over STEP7 software to infect PLCs functions/Operations. This is called a keyboard layout vulnerability also noted in CVE-2010-3888 /CVE-2010-3889 (Falliere et al., 2011).
*   Step 6: After doing the exploitation Remote Procedure Call (RPC) server services gets start by the worm. Through this step it searches the connections with other infected machine in the respective industry network. Stuxnet uses some similar features that are also there in infected machine and paired with it. These features are i) the worm dropper is downloaded which has mrxnet.sys and mrxcls.sys files. ii) find the malware version iii) running targeted application such as STEP7 software iv) privileged file such as read, write and delete file. Every RPC server which is installed by Stuxnet has one unique software identifier that is GUID (for example 001200e1-0000-0000-r000-000000000067). This GUID infected system are able to detect each other and communicate with others. Because of this unique ID malicious objects are enabling to find the updates and upgrade themselves using target network. Next task towards attack get successful is find siemens WinCC software. If WinCC is installed in windows operating system means that machine is able to control an industrial Programmable Logic Controller (PLC). The worm finds WinCC is installed or not by searching window system file such as S7DOS block administration file (s7otbxdx.dll). Stuxnet worm get modified the code with respect to some event handler (s7b\_open, s7blk\_findfirst, s7blk\_findnext, s7\_event, s7blk\_delete, s7ag\_link\_in, s7db\_close, s7ag\_bub\_cycl\_read\_create) and functions (s7blk\_write, s7blk\_read, s7af\_test, s7ag\_read\_szl, s7ag\_bub\_write\_var s7ag\_bub\_read\_var, s7ag\_bub\_write\_var\_seg, s7ag\_bub\_read\_var\_seg) (Mueller & Yadegari, 2016). Such a kind of functions and event handling instructions are coded in PLC to delete, access, read and write operations to control industrial devices. The worm added few more functions to intercepting communication between target device (like centrifuges chamber) and PLC. So Stuxnet is ready to call functions contained in S7DOS block administration file.
*   Step7: Now, Stuxnet communicates with command and control server via local area network. It tested HTTP request response state. After that with the WinCC and vulnerable STEP7 software it sends controlled instruction to target device and false negative alarm generate and check configuration of PLC with CPU details. If PLCs are having 6ES7-315-2 or 6ES7-417 CPU then verified that which type of devices are connected via PLC’s SDB (system data block). Stuxnet is alone capable to trigger their own script on programmable logic controller. If PLC’s are connect with fararo paya frequency driver converter than the worm records the frequency configuration data in PLC to start penetrate commands and change false operations/ instructions. It observes that stuxnet sometime change driver converter’s frequency for some period of time that is 1410 Hz to 2 Hz and return back to 1064 Hz. It is a very crucial thing that little bit frequency change in industrial automation systems and operation fields create lots of pressure on centrifuges. This situation leads to failure and disaster condition.

Now attacker ensure that attack get successful and generate replay attack to PLC to send false negative (Attack didn’t happened and generates an alarm). This task played by rootkit file to clear track of attack.

Local Behavior of the Stuxnet

When the worm enters the local computers, it sits ideal until it gets the target software or an application for spreading infection. If it doesn't detect target software it resides in idle condition and when that computer connects with the Internet, first it searches updated Stuxnet signature and updates it immediately and this thing is not detected by any antivirus or detection software because worm uses authenticated parties’ digital certificate.

After getting target windows OS with above listed software the sample code loads the DLL module that executes the assigned behavior. The DLL sample copies remain undetected and unnoticed by being moved into the memory of the system and behaves as a regular DLL loading style, rather than dumps the DLL module into a file and loads it (Thabet, 2011).

*   Step 8: Generate False Negative Alarm to clear track of attack.

HOW DOES INDUSTRIAL CONTROL SYSTEM WORKS?

Industrial Control Systems (ICSs) are essential part of infrastructure development and safe communication in industrial devices. ICSs are maintaining controlled instructions and also a safety to handle a device. Previously ICSs were not design for security purpose but know it has a concern of security measures too. They are mainly configured with open architecture link with open ended software. Most communication protocols for ICSs are planned without taking cyber security into consideration. Physical attacks due to cyber-attacks became a reality with the appearance of Stuxnet in 2010. In contrast to attacks directed solely against information systems, cyber-attacks against ICSs can directly affect physical objects or devices. We are also at high risk of causing incidents that are directly linked to disasters and impact human lives (Azarcon, 2017). The accidents may occur not only in ICS-controlled processes but may also stop the services they provide and supply products that do not meet the requirements of the product. Cyber-attacks on chemical plants, for example, may cause serious incidents like explosions and chemical substances use beyond the limit. In particular, incidents such as with a loss of wealth due to production disruption and delivery of products that contain toxic chemicals may exist. Improving Defence towards cyber-attacks which impact human health is indeed a serious issue in mitigating certain incidents. Prevention and cyber security will need never be treated independently. Cyber security always needs to be recognized dependent on countermeasure in order to avoid unsafe situations. To cope with such an issue, safety risk analysis for enterprise systems needs to be expanded (Iasiello, 2013). The emphasis is on keeping the process going rather than cyber-safe. Cyber-safety can attach a fault point, interrupt the operation, and complicate repair.

Industrial Control Systems are categorized to control multiple instruments and controller which are used to manage operations in the automation industry. These kinds of systems can handle small modular panel mounted controllers to big scale interconnected distributed systems that have thousands of operational field connections. The system collects data or input signals from a remote sensor using process variables and compare data with Set Points and generate command function to control a process through the final control elements.

Such kind of distributed systems are implemented by using supervisory Control and Data Acquisition system (SCADA) and Programmable Logic Controllers (PLCs). These systems are used in the telecommunication industry, chemical processing field, electricity power plant, oil and gas processing plants, and many automation industries (Azarcon, 2017).

Process Controller in ICS Environment

These old forms of communication always had their place, even though they allow quick and safe interconnection in between product lines of the a specific provider. Communication is an option for simple systems with no plans to expand or connect to other components, and will remain for quite some time to come. Most PLC vendors also support these older physical, wired connections most often based on RS-232C, RS-422 and RS-485 connectivity and the associated proprietary communication protocols. For example, many Automation Direct control systems use a serial RS-232C or RS-422 medium access connection with the Direct NET inter process communication. Using standard PLC instructions, this mechanism can be used for Siemens-to-PLC communications over a point-to - point or multiple access network, or to connect with C-more HMIs from Automation Direct. If the control device needs a step while in a single operator, interface standards come into focus, originating at the lower layer (Polley, 2019).

Nowadays complex system uses network-based controller that communicates with some standard protocol such as Pofinet, Modbus RTU, Modbus TCP / IP, EtherNet / IP. Such a Network based system allows to use local or remote SCADA interface and enables to use of local or remote SCADA operational interfaces, and enables the cascading and interlocking of controller system. But such kind of system is very costly and time consuming. Modbus RTU, developed by Modicon, was the most popular industrial serial communication protocol that usually ranges on an RS-485 network. That and other prominent serial protocols are sponsored by a network of suppliers, and a high proportion of engineering experts are very recognizable. But performance is low, making high speed serial protocols not a good option. Ethernet has emerged as the dominant standard for the physical layer of many industrial protocols such as EtherNet / IP, Ethernet TCP / IP, Modbus TCP / IP and Profinet, due to consistency and other advantages. And unlike serial protocols, multiple Ethernet protocols will work on a protocol stack of same Hardware (Kushner, 2013).

Some, like Siemens PROFIBUS, Allen Bradley Information Highway^®, Westinghouse WDPF^®, using any variety of a network provider. Also, through node by exchanging and forwarding a virtual token applicable to provide better network connectivity.

To minimize the cost and computational efforts programmable logic controllers (PLCs) (Figure 4 shows the architecture of PLCs) are used. A PLC is a machine designed specifically for efficient service in harsh industrial environments such as high temperatures, muddy, dry and/or dusty conditions. This is used to automate industrial processes such as the assembly line of a production facility, a mining facility for coal or a wastewater treatment system. PLCs share lots of personal computer apps that you have at home.

They also have a power supply, a CPU (Central Processing Unit), inputs and outputs (I / O), memory, and operating software (although it is a different program to operate). The main differences are that a PLC can perform discrete and continuous functions that a PC cannot do, and a PLC is much better suited to harsh industrial environments.

PLC allows to give the sensor information to application software and on basis of that dataset, the software generates an instruction and PLCs are responsible to perform an action. Using Ethernet, interconnecting multiple devices like PLCs, HMIs, field I / O, and valve banks isn't too difficult. Moreover, connectivity maintains fast while communicating to many other various devices along the same cable, so the Ethernet is having very high connectivity speed compare to other old network techniques.

| Figure 4. The architecture of Programmable Logic Controller |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch030.f04](i/ch030.f04.png) |
| --- |

Steps to perform functioning by PLCS:

*   • The operating system begins running and time control.
*   • The CPU starts reading input module data and checks the status of all inputs.
*   • The CPU starts running the user or application program written in relay-ladder logic, or some other language of PLC programming.
*   • Then the CPU performs all the functions of internal diagnosis and communication.
*   • Based on an Input signal and collected data output signal gets generated.
*   • Above processes have continuously happened until the PLC works

Distributed Control System

In DCS, multiple process control devices are connected together through the SCADA system. SCADA manages working instructions for all programmable devices likewise many SCADA system work together to handles distributed connections. SCADA system also enables alarm whenever any false instructions are generated. But which is susceptible to a different category of a cyber attack. These all SCADA systems are configured to avoid looping and controlled interface with the computer system using the production controller following Figure 5 shows the layered architecture of the distributed control system (Hieb J et al., 2007).

The adaptive control system is closely connected to the SCADA system. The variations between a SCADA device and a DCS are very minimal, and over time, the two are almost indistinguishable. While SCADA systems have historically been used for automation tasks covering a wider geographical region, this means that parts of the SCADA system are located in individual buildings

| Figure 5. Layered architecture of distributed control system |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch030.f05](i/ch030.f05.png) |
| --- |

A Distribute Control System (DCS) main attribute is its reliability, due to the system's distribution of control processing across nodes. That mitigates the malfunction of a multiple processors. Whenever a processor fails, only one part of the production plant would be impacted, as opposed to a central machine failure which would impact the entire operation. This allocation of local computational resources to the Input / Output (I / O) link rack domain also provides fast processing speeds for both the dispatcher by eliminating potential errors in network and central processing.

Figure 5 provides description as follows:

*   • Level 0: This requires equipment in the field such as flow and temperature sensors and final control elements such as control valves.
*   • Level 1: It includes the modules of automated input / output (I / O) and their related electronic processors distributed.
*   • Level 2: It includes supervisory computers that collect information from processor nodes on the system and provide control screens for the operator.
*   • Level 3: It is the level of production control which does not control the process directly, but is concerned with monitoring production and tracking targets
*   • Level 4: Not a level but it is the level of output scheduling.

DCS used in many of applications such as chemical processing plant, oil refineries, nuclear power plant, water treatment and purification plant, and many more.

SECURITY ISSUES IN PROGRAMMABLE LOGIC CONTROLLER

Following are specific categories to provide an overview of the types of threats that the organization may face and the kinds of harm that they will encounter during operations:

*   • Incorrect and insufficient policy: Access, maintenance procedures, testing and downtime could render you vulnerable to attacks.
*   • Internal Threats: Organization employee has lack of training, simple human error and lack of security knowledge leads a organization at risk every day.
*   • Poorly deployed and configured hardware / software: Once a supplier deployed the PLC that company uses, security measures had to be priority based from bottom to top level security. Furthermore, any bugs or suspected vulnerabilities should be reported and timely handled (Hieb J et al., 2007).

Using security flaws attackers try to intercept organizational network and attempt to affect the target systems.

| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch030.f06](i/ch030.f06.png) |
