ABSTRACT

Supporting a mechanism to authenticate members in electronic health record (EHR) is a fundamental procedure to prevent different threats from penetrating patients’ identities/data. Existing authentication schemes still suffer from security drawbacks. Exchanging medical-related information/data between clients and the servers leaves them compromised to breakthrough by intruders as they can transmit over an unreliable environment. To guarantee the protection of patient records, this chapter proposes a new scheme that provides authentication of patients/providers in EHR depending on the legitimate member identities and the device information. The scheme utilizes an elliptic curve cryptography and lightweight hash function to accomplish robust security with satisfying performance. Moreover, it depends on a set of techniques such as multi-pseudonyms to authenticate legitimate members. Additionally, concentrated theoretical and experimental analysis proves that the proposed provides elevated performance and security compared to existing research.

INTRODUCTION

An insufficiency of privacy and security of medical records applied by healthcare applications (HCA) stays the major drawback that reduces the prevalence of these applications. The healthcare (HC) systems demand reliable protection techniques to validate HC members via accomplishing the security requirements (He & Zeadally, 2015) and the obedience of the Health organizations standards to secure patient records from being modified and tampered. Protection procedures (confidentiality, integrity, and availability) should be achieved during exchanging medical records between clients (users) and server applications, as any alteration to this data affects both the patients' condition and medical decisions (Al-Zubaidie et al.,2020). Authentication is the most critical security procedure that performs the main role in constructing proper protection before the exchange of patients’ records in HCA (Das et al., 2017; Li et al., 2016; Rajput et al., 2016). First, authentication can limit fatal/malicious errors caused by permeation threats on the authentication requests. Second, it mitigates errors in specifying dose, drug, timing, or procedure. Consequently, authentication protocols are significant countermeasure to prevent different threats. Commonly, the server should block all illegal and fake authentication requests (Shen, Gui, et al., 2018). It should safeguard personal identities (IDs), medical data, and physiological records such as blood pressure and sugar. Nonetheless, the authentication information can be simpler to penetrate if the information and data kept on the same server. Moreover, a sending of authentication requests in an unreliable channel (Internet/wireless sensor network (WSN)), can subject patients’ records for destruction/alteration (Li et al., 2016). Many examples of real-world security threats implemented against user authentication in HCA as follows:

*   • In 2017, a patient’s personal information was compromised at the AU Medical Centre, Children’s Hospital and Clinics of Georgia. However, information database attacks were not detected until 2018 (Donovan, 2018).
*   • In 2018, according to the proofpoint report, more than 100 million authentication attacks were carried out around the world against clinics, hospitals and insurance companies (Proofpoint, 2018).
*   • In 2019, the Oregon Department of Human Services indicated that cyber-threats breached users’ credentials (625000 patients’ records) (Jessica Davis, 2019).

The conventional signature/encryption performs complex operations that exhaust server resources such as memory and time to process with big data of HC (Manogaran et al., 2018) and hence, which may cause them infeasible. The digital signature is utilized to verify the safety of the members’ IDs within the authentication message (Giri et al., 2015). Many lightweight hash-function (PHOTON and ARMADILLO) are preferred to apply a digital signature that performs lightweight processes to reduce consumption of the server resources. HCA require encryption and signature secure, and high-speed techniques (Liu & Chung, 2017). To build an authentication scheme, many mechanisms, such as Rivest Shamir Adleman (RSA), Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC), hash-function and fuzzy extractor (Chandrakar & Om, 2017), are implemented in HCA projects. Many modern HCA are depending on RSA and ECC, both supply the same protection strength, but ECC has performance better compared to RSA. The HCA authentication protocols should include countermeasures to various threats plus the efficiency of high-performance.

Threat to Authentication Scheme

The threat model has presented to determine the security holes in security protocols. This model is applied to the proposed depending on the Dolev-Yao (dy) (Dolev & Yao, 1983) model to establish a correct process for authentication in unreliable channels such as Internet/WSN. For the real-world, the dy is an efficient manner to interpret authentication schemes. Proposed threat model assumes that an intruder can carry out an internal, external, active or passive threat such as man in the middle (MITM) and eavesdropping. The intruder can:

*   • Theft the user application and its files to extract the secrets.
*   • Listen for authentication requests and execute interception, replay and MITM threats.
*   • Breakthrough the authentication protocol by a forgery/masquerading threat.
*   • Execute a privileged insider threat relying on user legitimacy in the HCA.
*   • Analyze of many authentication requests to guess the real information for users.

CHAPTER OBJECTIVES

The objectives of the proposed are as follows:

*   • Using lightweight encryption (ECIES) and signature (PHOTON) in HCA.
*   • Applying an OTP, timestamp and random nonce to authenticate members in their first registration in the HCA network.
*   • Using a multi pseudonyms technique to protect real information for users.
*   • Integrating the login request with the MAC address to verify that these legitimate devices.
*   • Improving mutual authentication (MA) to prevent impersonation and spoofing threats.
*   • Using security-proofing methods and tools such as automated validation of Internet security protocols and applications (AVISPA) and Burrows, Abadi and Needham (BAN) logic.

BACKGROUND ON AUTHENTICATION SCHEMES

This section investigates the design of authentication schemes to secure HC users in the health networks as suggested by related existing studies and highlights their shortcomings.

Authentication scheme becomes insecure when using the same IDs with unreliable key size in all authentication phases. He & Zeadally (2015) designed an authentication protocol using advanced encryption standards (AES) and ECC cryptography. The drawback with their protocol is that controller and member IDs are fixedly transferred to all network parties. If the intruder could break through the cryptography, he/she may obtain that the controller and member IDs related. Then, the intruder can generate a nonce, message security code, timestamp and temporary key. After that, he/she encrypts the controller and member IDs and produce the request authentication code. Then, the intruder forwards a request to the server to become an authenticated and legitimate member. Their scheme also used ECC key 160-bit, which is considered untrusty by reliable organizations, such as NIST.

The storage of medical records (information and data) on a single remote server represents a serious risk in terms of performance and security. Farash et al. (2016) suggested authentication procedures depending on ECC for HC networks. Authors claimed that their authentication supported secrecy-forward. Unfortunately, their scheme describes that the data and information (IDs) are deposited on the same server. When the server is infiltrated, the members’ data and information are exposed to the modification and tampering. Jiang et al. (2016) also proposed authentication scheme utilizing a password, biometric and smart card (3-factors) in order to secure HC repositories. They depended on ECC and fuzzy extractor to provide the authentication and confidentiality of HC members. However, their scheme relied on a single remote server to validate members, which is an intruder’s goal. Moreover, it performs seven hash-functions that could consume the lonesome server resources if the institution has a large group of HC members, particularly if it is not using an efficient function.

Leakage of legitimate members' information or using unnecessarily large keys destroys the authentication process. An authentication scheme was suggested to safeguard users’ passwords using RSA against secret guessing threats (Giri et al., 2015). The big drawback in their scheme is that the researchers applied RSA-1024 key. Their algorithm impacts the throughput of large HCA networks. Recent research recommends using ECC (AbdAllah et al., 2018) as the RSA-1024 is equivalent to ECC-160 with the same protection strength. Also, their scheme sticks transferring IDs plainly from source to destination at the registration phase. This case reveals authentication parameters to be leaked for analysis threats, leaking any information that an intruder could use to disclose authentication information. Furthermore, the Petri Nets model and ECC were suggested to perform authentication procedures to secure HCA for the mobile cloud (Kumar et al., 2016). However, authors did not declaim the concern of loss/steal of device or tag and internal threats that are more earnest than external threats to penetrate patient records. They gave no hint of the signature's algorithm type that implemented to ensure accuracy-information. The other problem is that the tag’s ID plainly transmits from server to tag.

HCA are continuously expanding and become vulnerable to failure if they are not able to offer scalability. Utilizing a shared key to execute authentication procedures was proposed to block various threats, particularly the denial of service (DoS) threats (Li et al., 2016). Nonetheless, the registration request of their scheme is untrusty if the users' IDs is transferred in an unsecured network. Their research also requires expandability because it used the singular shared-key technique that requires safeguard from all entities. Das et al. (2017) presented member authentication mechanisms for HCA depending on the Secure Hash Algorithm 1 (SHA1) and AES. They utilized user biometrics and the anonymity feature to prevent threats. However, symmetric encryption suffers from the scalability, plus the obstacle of preserving the only shared key. Their scheme will lack key administration if implemented to a huge HC organization with members hundreds whose accounts must be managed during data changes such as additions and deletions. Additionally, the intruder may perform a counterfeit threat on the login request if it reveals the shared key.

MA and pseudonym are significant techniques to establish robust authentication. Cloud-assisted conditional privacy-preserving authentication (CACPPA) (Rajput et al., 2016) has been designed to validate a network’s entities. CACPPA scheme utilized the elliptic curve integrated encryption scheme (ECIES) and ECDSA algorithms with a timestamp and pseudonym to apply the authentication procedures. The CACPPA drawback was that it did not support MA to repel a forgery attack. Neither did the researchers demonstrate the length of the algorithms' keys to guarantee their scheme was able to prevent known threats. Moreover, a singular pseudonym may not detach the engagement to real parameters to rein analysis threats for authentication information. Chandrakar & Om (2017) suggested a remote authentication depending on hash and ECC. Their authentication was assigned on multiple servers in member authentication with 3-factors. Also, the researchers did not assign the length of the message digest (MD)and hash-function type that were applied. These procedures are essential to repel threats, i.e., preimage, second preimage and collision. Utilizing multiple servers indicates that the same of members' parameters are deposited on more than one server. Consequently, penetrating any server can cause user identities to be detected or alternated. Moreover, their scheme did not apply a technique to hide real member information within an authentication message, such as pseudonyms.

Recently, Nizzi et al. (2019) proposed the address shuffling algorithm (AShA) method to protect devices’ MACs when these addresses transferred from sender to recipient. They used keys and hashes to shuffle MAC addresses in the network and prevent intruders from executing collisions or privacy breaches. However, their method is vulnerable to security threats especially as it does not provide resistance against the second preimage. Similarly, El-Tawab et al. (2019) relied on MAC addresses to protect users’ privacy. They used techniques such as MAC randomization and SHA-256 to prevent the penetration of users’ devices. But these techniques are still weak in ensuring the authenticity of MAC addresses.

PRELIMINARY CONCEPTS OF AUTHENTICATION TECHNIQUES

This section describes the basic concepts of authentication techniques.

*   • Encryption technique Elliptic Curve Cryptography (ECC) has been utilized to supply security requirements such as confidentiality. It relies on the discrete logarithm problem (DLP), which is impervious to various threats when selecting parameters strictly (Al-Zubaidie et al., 2019a), i.e., difficulty obtaining an ephemeral key from curve's points. Small parameters utilized in ECC help to proceed computations rapidly. These computations are significant in large/constrained-source networks that demand fast execution, memory or energy. ECC supplies exchange keys (Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH)), encryption (Elliptic Curve Integrated Encryption Scheme (ECIES)) and signature (Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA)). Many procedures are completed in ECC approaches (shown in five layers) as displayed in Figure 1 (Al-Zubaidie et al., 2019c). ECIES has presented confidentiality and assured to be significant performance efficient, as it utilizes small keys; hence, the calculation costs are small compared with other public-key approaches, such as Elgamal (Shen, Chang, et al., 2018). Table 1 (Harkanson & Kim, 2017) provides a comparison of key lengths for public-key algorithms.
*   • Signature technique A hash function has utilized to produce signatures for authentication messages. PHOTON is lightweight hash-algorithm and significantly convenient for schemes that need a reliable signature. Table 2 presents a comparison among the lightweight functions (the latest version of hash functions) in terms of efficiency and security (Guo et al., 2011; Bogdanov et al., 2011; Aumasson et al., 2010). Although traditional hash-functions are still utilized in platforms such as SHA1 (5527 GE, MD 160-bit) and SHA2 (10868 GE, MD 256-bit), lightweight-functions such as PHOTON (2177 GE, MD 256-bit) supplies the most effective manner for dealing with complicated signatures in huge HCA environments.

Table 2 presents that the PHOTON-256 (2177 GE) has the best performance compared to all lightweight hashes and provides a high degree of security through the achieving of signature features: first preimage resistant (FPR\[224\]), second preimage resistant (SPR \[128\]), and collision-resistant (CR \[128\]). Differential and linear threats are the strongest threats in the MD analysis of hash-functions. Compared to PHOTON-256, SPONGENT-256 and ARMADILLO also provide signature features, but both are vulnerable to threats, where ARMIDLLO2 has been penetrated by local linearization (practical semi-free-start collision threat) (Naya-Plasencia & Peyrin, 2012) and SPONGENT has been penetrated by linear distinguishers (23 rounds) (Abdelraheem, 2012) and (13 rounds) (Zhang & Liu, 2017) for all SPONGENT versions; and furthermore, they require the most calculations (3281 GE and 8653 GE) compared PHOTON-256 (2177 GE). PHOTON is a robust function against differential and linear threats (Guo et al., 2011). It has a high level of efficiency and security; consequently, PHOTON is appropriate for the proposed as a verification technique.

*   • One-time password technique One-time password (OTP) is a technique to authenticate rightful members by generating nonce/passcode only once in a specified time. It will not be useable the subsequent times for validation. OTP is an operative way of verifying members in HCA if implemented with reliable signature/encryption approaches. Utilizing a static password/nonce without other authentication techniques is unsafe with respect to threats.

Thus, OTP presents worthy support to the authentication protocol. It blocks many threats such as guessing and replay (Al-Zubaidie et al., 2020). The intruder cannot utilize this nonce/passcode to communicate to the HCA later. The client transfers OTP as part of an authentication message. If the authentication request is righteous, the server will remove OTP from the repository and will not permit it in the subsequent times. OTP is a vigorous technique to alleviate the threats of intruders’ connection with the server.

*   • Mutual authentication technique Mutual authentication (MA) represents a prerequisite for blocking deceitful authentication messages. The conventional ways of authentication (such as name and password) are not convenient for HCA (Liu & Chung, 2017). Generally, there are two manners of authentication, simple and mutual. In simple authentication, one entity applies the authentication mechanism, e.g., the server validates the authentication message for the client. This manner of authentication is vulnerable to threats, i.e., impersonation/spoofing. An intruder can employ his device as a counterfeit server to obtain all users’ messages. MA supplies a security solution to repel various threats (Liu & Chung, 2017). In this manner of authentication, each entity authenticates the other entity and hence, blocks forgery threats by both server and client.
*   • Physical address technique MAC address has utilized to identify rightful members’ devices in a network during the accomplishment of the authentication. All devices of various kinds have a hardware card to communicate with the local/global network. Each wire/wireless card contains a physical or media access control (MAC) address (a unique identifier with a 48-bit). It can be changed programmatically in different operating systems, i.e., Windows/Linux. The main problem with this address is that the intruder can implement an eavesdropping threat to access the MAC addresses of rightful devices in the network and next choose a rightful MAC to utilize it. For example, an intruder could implement an ARP spoofing/poisoning threat by utilizing a counterfeit ID of the MAC (for a rightful device) to obtain illegitimate permissions that will authorize it to implement other threats such as DoS/MITM (Xiao et al., 2016). Moreover, randomization processes for the physical address have fallen worthless in the security against traceability threats (Vanhoef et al., 2016). Hence, if the server does not apply a technique to reveal MAC alternation, the intruder becomes a rightful member and can access to network services.

Entities and System Model

Figure 2 shows the proposed that consists of 4 entities:

*   1\. Client (C[i]): This entity includes HC providers, patients and patients’ relatives.
*   2\. Central Server (CS): This entity works as a gateway to authenticate members with the Attributes Server.
*   3\. Attributes Server (AS): This entity has members’ real IDs and multi pseudonyms to achieve user authentication.
*   4\. Data server (DS): This entity has members’ data and multi pseudonyms.

Overall, C[i] creates an authentication request fundamentally depending on PHOTON and ECIES. C[i] transfers a message to CS to validate encryption, signature, and security parameters (i.e., OTP[i], MAC and pseudonyms). Next, the CS resurrects a message to the AS to validate the link between the real information, pseudonyms, PW[i] and signatures. Then, the AS sends the response to the CS that validates the parameters and signature, then the CS sends the response (authenticated or not) to the C[i]. If the member is authenticated, proposed supposes that the member can then send an authorization message to access the server data (DS) and gain the authorization response from the CS, AS, and DS.

The Security Requirements of the Proposed Scheme

The proposed embraces the following security requirements:

*   • Confidentiality: This service is used to conceal authentication information and to maintain member privacy from disclosure by attackers.
*   • Integrity: This is to secure the authentication parameters information from tampering by attackers (Al-Zubaidie et al., 2019b).
*   • Non-repudiation: This service curbs clients/server from denying their authentication messages.
*   • Anonymity: This requirement is to camouflage the clients/server of the authentication messages (Rajput et al., 2016).
*   • Pseudonym: This service indicates to hide/connect the real user attributes with non-real attributes.
*   • Forward secrecy: This service is achieved when HCA members utilize temporarily new parameters/keys without depending on old ones.
*   • MA: This service is applied in HCA to relieve the risks of external threats. With this requirement, each entity guarantees that it connects with a rightful entity.
*   • Scalability: HCA managed in a scalable environment in terms of users/data. Hence, these applications need authentication protocols capable of handling/adapting to the ever-increasing number of members of HCA (Kumar et al., 2016).
*   • Freshness: This service denotes that the authentication message is updated/new.

Protocols of Proposed Scheme

The proposed consists of five protocols, as follows:

Protocol 1: System Setup

In this protocol, all entities are prepared to begin connecting with each other as in the next steps:

*   • Each rightful member receives a client application from the authorized system provider.
*   • Each rightful member receives a PW[i] and a random OTP[i] to be used in the first registration.
*   • C[i], CS and AS should generate public and private keys (C[i] (CK[pui], CK[pri]), CS (CSK[pui], CSK[pri]), and AS (ASK[pui], ASK[pri])) to validate the authentication information.
*   • All entities broadcast the CK[pui], CSK[pui], and ASK[pui] to implement in ECIES’s encryption (Enc[i]) and decryption (Dec[i]) procedures.

Protocol 2: Registration and Login

HC providers (C[i]) and patients should perform the registration and login protocol with CS to be rightful members of HCA. Without this protocol, the member cannot perform the authentication protocol in the proposed. Member registration is completed once, i.e., the member does not require to perform the registration protocol the subsequent times (only the login protocol), Figures 3 and 4 display registration and login protocol, and login protocol. This protocol performs the next steps:

C[i] side:

*   • The user enters UID[i] (i.e., her/his name), MID[i] (i.e., medical centre name), PW[i] and OTP[i] for registration and login while only entering UID[i], MID[i], and PW[i] for the login protocol the subsequent times to the client (C[i]) application. C[i] replaces UID[i] with user’s pseudonym (![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m05](i/ch032.m05.svg)), and MID[i] with medical centre pseudonym (![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m06](i/ch032.m06.svg)) to secure the authentication parameters when transferring from C[i] to CS. C[i] generates timestamp (TS[Ci]) to be utilized to validate the sending time of the registration/login request in CS.
*   • C[i] gets a MAC address (GM) by using its Internet protocol address (IP). The operation of checking MAC (CM) is executed by C[i] to check the credibility of the MAC. In the Linux, the proposed implements the command “ethtool -P interface name” (such as “ethtool -P wlo1”) in the C[i] application. If the result is identical to GM, it denotes that the MAC is organic (CM = “Real\_MAC”). In Windows system, C[i] searches for string value “NetworkAddress” in the path of the system registry (“HKEY\_LOCAL\_MACHINE\\SYSTEM\\CurrentControlSet\\Control\\Class\\{4D36E97-E325-11CE-BFC1-08002BE10318}\\”). If “NetworkAddress” = null, CM = “Real\_MAC”; otherwise CM = “Fake MAC”. The GM send is encrypted with a registration/login request while CM is implicitly sent with the signature value (C[i]Sig[1]). If only login protocol, C[i] requires to extract the C[i]K[pri] from a tmpC[i]K[pri], MAC, PW[i], and N[Ci]. C[i] generates a new N[Ci] to change signature and encryption data and provide anonymity to the registration/login request.
*   • C[i] implements two signatures utilizing the PHOTON-256 to secure information from tampering. The first signature hashes the parameters: check MAC, nonce, and timestamp (CiSig[1]\=h(CM || N[Ci] || TS[Ci]). The second signature hashes all the authentication information of the get MAC, nonce, timestamp, first signature, pseudonyms, one-time password, and password (CiSig[2] = h(GM || N[C] || TS[C] || CiSig[1]|| ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m07](i/ch032.m07.svg)|| ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m08](i/ch032.m08.svg) || OTP[i]|| PW[i]). In the login protocol, OTP[i] is not included in the signature.
*   • C[i] calculates a temporary value (tmpPW[i] = PW[i]⊕ N[Ci]⊕ GM⊕ C[i]Sig[1]) of PW[i] when transferring from C[i] to CS.
*   • C[i] utilizes ECIES to hide/encrypt all the data of the request (Enc[i]). In the login protocol, OTP[i] and GM are not included in the encryption as in Figure 4. Next, C[i] sends the registration and login request/login to CS. Then, C[i] hides the C[i]K[pri] by tmpC[i]K[pri]\=C[i]K[pri]⊕ PW[i]⊕ C[i]Sig[2].

CS side:

*   • Upon receiving a registration and login request/login request, CS decrypts this request utilizing ECIES’s C[i]K[pui] and CSK[pri]. It tests timestamp (TS[CS]\-TS[Ci] ≤ ∆T) to ensure that this message arrived without delay.
*   • In the registration and login protocol, CS tests the random OTP[i] in the database. If OTP[i] is found, then the member is legitimate for the registration protocol. Next, CS removes OTP[i] from the database to block it from being utilized the subsequent times. If OTP[i] is not found, it rejects the communication. If the login protocol, CS tests the ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m09](i/ch032.m09.svg) and ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m10](i/ch032.m10.svg) and then checks their correlation with the MAC in the database. If GM is found, CS performs the steps of this protocol; otherwise, it declines the communication.
*   • CS requires to guarantee that the member’s device is rightful within the network. CS calculates the signature value to ensure that the MAC is original and non-modified (CSSig[1]\= h(“Real MAC”||N[Ci]||TS[Ci]). It checks the result of the calculated signature (CSSig[1]) with the C[i]’s signature (C[i]Sig[1]). If the result of the signatures is identical, then the device is rightful, and the MAC did not modify. In the registration and login protocol, CS stores this MAC in the database for use/check the subsequent times in the login protocol.
*   • CS implements the computation process the tmpPW[i] ⊕ N[Ci]⊕ GM ⊕ CSSig[1]to retrieve the PW[i] value and then utilize this value to compute a second signature (CSSig[2]).
*   • CS calculates a second signature (CSSig[2]) to ensure that all the encrypted parameters is not modified. Next, it compares the calculated signature (CSSig[2]) with the received signature in the message (CiSig[2]). If the signatures are identical, then the parameters for this request are not modified. In the login protocol, OTP[i] and GM are not included in the signature. In this stage, CS prepares to send the member’s authentication message to AS.

Protocol 3: Authentication

In this protocol, the proposed needs to link pseudonyms and passwords with real information for members in AS’s databases. Note that, the members’ information (i.e. name, address, phone number, age, and passwords) are stored in a separate server (AS) and multi pseudonyms utilized to block disclosure and tracking of members’ parameters, Figure 5 displays the authentication protocol. This protocol performs in the next steps:

CS side:

*   • CS generates a new timestamp (TS[CS]) to ensure the fresh authentication request.
*   • CS uses ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m11](i/ch032.m11.svg) and ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m12](i/ch032.m12.svg) pseudonyms to prevent intruders from tracking the authentication request. It generates random nonce (N[CS]) to guarantee an anonymous authentication message.
*   • CS signs authentication information by PHOTON-256 (CSSig[3]) to block alteration of authentication parameters.
*   • CS calculates temporary PW[i] by the calculation of PW[i]⊕ N[CS]⊕ CSSig[3].
*   • CS encrypts information of authentication (Enc[i]). It sends an authentication request to validate member’s parameters in AS.

AS side:

| Figure 5. Authentication protocol |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.f05](i/ch032.f05.png) |
| --- |

*   • After receiving the authentication request, AS decrypts that request utilizing ECIESs’ CSK[pui] and ASK[pri] to extract the authentication information.
*   • It tests timestamp by (TS[AS]\-TS[CS] ≤ ∆T) to guarantee that the authentication request is not replayed. AS examines the pseudonyms (![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m13](i/ch032.m13.svg) and ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m14](i/ch032.m14.svg)) sent from CS and links them with the member’s real ID (UID[i] and MID[i]) in the databases. AS retrieves member’s password from PW[i] = tmpPW[i] ⊕ N[CS] ⊕ CSSig[3]. Then, it tests to match PW[i] in the database. AS calculates the value of the signature-based on authentication parameters (ASSig[1]\=h(TS[CS]||N[CS]||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m15](i/ch032.m15.svg)||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m16](i/ch032.m16.svg))) by PHOTON-256. AS compares the computed signature value (ASSig[1]) with the received signature value (CSSig[3]). If the signatures values are identical, the member’s information is not changed. In this stage, AS considers this member to be rightful.
*   • AS creates a response to authenticating the request of that member. It calculates new TS[AS] to block replayed/delayed messages at subsequent times. AS utilizes new pseudonyms (![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m17](i/ch032.m17.svg)and ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m18](i/ch032.m18.svg)) to hide information. It generates a new N[AS] to add anonymity and prevent threats from signature/encryption analysis.
*   • AS computes a signature (ASSig[2] = h(TS[AS]||N[AS]||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m19](i/ch032.m19.svg)||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m20](i/ch032.m20.svg))) to block alteration of response parameters.
*   • AS encrypts authentication parameters (Enc[i]) and sends this response to CS.

CS side:

*   • CS decrypts the response (Enc[i]) received from AS. It tests the timestamp (TS[AS]) to block late responses. It checks that ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m21](i/ch032.m21.svg)and ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m22](i/ch032.m22.svg) in databases to perform the process of correlating multi pseudonyms to the member.
*   • CS calculates the signature (CSSig[4]) for authentication response information. It compares the calculated signature result (CSSig[4]) with received signature value (ASSig[2]). If the results of the signature are identical, then the response information is not changed.
*   • At this stage, CS creates a login response request. It calculates the value of new TS[CS]. It utilizes new pseudonyms (![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m23](i/ch032.m23.svg)and ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m24](i/ch032.m24.svg)). It generates a new N[CS] to hide signature/encryption information.
*   • CS computes a new signature (CSSig[5]) to secure login response information from alteration.
*   • CS encrypts login response information (Enc[i]) and sends this response to C[i].

C[i] side:

*   • C[i] extracts his private key (CiK[pri]) from the tmpCiK[pri]⊕PWi⊕CiSig[2], and decrypts the login request (Enc[i]) received from CS.
*   • C[i] tests timestamp (TS[CS]) to guarantee that the login response is not delayed.
*   • C[i] tests that CS’s pseudonyms (![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m25](i/ch032.m25.svg) and ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m26](i/ch032.m26.svg)) are received in the database and correlated with ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m27](i/ch032.m27.svg) and ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m28](i/ch032.m28.svg). In this stage, the proposed implemented multi pseudonyms among model 's parties (C[i], CS, and AS) to repel traceability in correlating the real IDs of the member with pseudonyms.
*   • C[i] calculates the value of the signature (CiSig[3]) for login response. It compares the calculated signature result (CiSig[3]) and the received signature value (CSSig[5]). If the signatures match, i.e., the login response information is not modified, C[i] accepts the login response; otherwise, C[i] rejects the login response. Next, C[i] conceals its private key by C[i]K[pri] ⊕ GM ⊕ PW[i] ⊕ N[Ci] after generating a random nonce to block the disclosure of the private key if the device is penetrated. In this stage, if all operations are performed properly, then all requests are considered reliable through the execution of MA.

Protocol 4: Password Change

The protocol of changing PW[i] is significant in any HCA for two reasons. First, preventing the utilize of PW[i] statically for a long period reduces the guessing threats. Second, updating PW[i] gives members more resilience in selecting the suitable PW[i]. Figure 6 describes password update protocol, if the member wishes to update his/her PW[i], the next explanation provides the new PW[i] protect procedures in a secure way.

*   • C[i] side: C[i] enters UID[i], MID[i], old PW[i], and new PW[i]. It replaces UID[i] and MID[i] with pseudonyms to conceal the member’s real information. C[i] fetches MAC, then extracts the private key from the tmpC[i]K[pri]⊕GM⊕oldPW[i]⊕N[Ci] to utilize in the encryption operation of the password update request. C[i] generates three random numbers (N[C1], N[C2] and N[C3]) and calculates a new timestamp (TS[Ci]). C[i] calculates the signature value (C[i]Sig[1]\=h(TS[Ci]||N[C1]||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m29](i/ch032.m29.svg)||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m30](i/ch032.m30.svg)||oldPW[i]) by PHOTON-256 depending on the information of the update request. It performs an anonymity technique to old PW[i] and new PW[i] (tmp\_oldPW[i]\=oldPW[i]⊕N[C2]⊕CiSig[1] and tmp\_newPW[i]\=newPW[i]⊕N[C3]⊕CiSig[1]) to hide passwords and not explicitly send it in the PW[i] change request. It encrypts the PW[i] change request (Enc[i](TS[C]||N[C1]||N[C2]||N[C3]||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m31](i/ch032.m31.svg)||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m32](i/ch032.m32.svg)||tmp\_oldPW[i]||tmp\_newPW[i]||C[i]Sig[1])) and sends it to CS, C[i] then conceals its private key by C[i]K[pri]⊕GM⊕newPW[i]⊕N[Ci].
*   • CS side: CS receives and decrypts an update request (Enc[i]). It tests timestamp to block delayed requests and examines ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m33](i/ch032.m33.svg) and ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m34](i/ch032.m34.svg) in databases. CS extracts old PW[i] and new PW[i] from tmp\_oldPW[i]⊕N[C2]⊕CiSig[1] and tmp\_newPW[i]⊕N[C3]⊕ CiSig[1].Then, it calculates signature value (CSSig[1]) relying on TS[Ci], N[C1], ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m35](i/ch032.m35.svg), ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m36](i/ch032.m36.svg), and oldPW[i] to check the matching between CSSig[1] and CiSig[1]. Similarly, in the authentication protocol, CS computes TS[CS] and replaces pseudonyms. CS generates three nonces N[CS1], N[CS2] and N[CS3] and then CS calculates signature value (h(TS[Ci]||N[C1]|| ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m37](i/ch032.m37.svg)||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m38](i/ch032.m38.svg)||oldPW[i]) and hides old PW[i] and new PW[i] by oldPW[i]⊕N[CS2]⊕CSSig[2] and newPW[i]⊕N[CS3]⊕CSSig[2]. It encrypts update request with security information (TS[CS], N[CS1], N[CS2], N[CS3], ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m39](i/ch032.m39.svg), ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m40](i/ch032.m40.svg), tmp\_oldPW[i], tmp\_newPW[i], and CSSig[2]) and sends to AS.
*   • AS side: AS receives a password update request, and decrypts (Enc[i]) this request with ASK[pri], and CSK[pui]. It examines time delay and then, it examines correlating pseudonyms with real information for members. It extracts old PW[i] from tmp\_oldPW[i]⊕N[CS2]⊕CSSig[2] and then, it examines old PW[i] in the database. It computes the signature value ASSig[1]\=h(TS[CS]||N[CS1] ||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m41](i/ch032.m41.svg)||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m42](i/ch032.m42.svg)||oldPW[i]), and then, it compares the calculated result (ASSig[1]) with the result of the received signature (CSSig[2]). If identical, the signature is correct; otherwise, AS rejects the PW[i] update request. AS executes the computation tmp\_newPW[i]⊕N[CS3]⊕CSSig[2] to get the new PW[i] value. If all previous tests are validated, AS updates old PW[i] to new PW[i].

Protocol 5: Revocation

Revocation in HCA uses when a member finishes a task or to prevent an attack. This protocol can be achieved by C[i], or AS. If C[i] intends to revoke his account from the HCA after accomplishing his/her duties, i.e., a research doctor who utilizes the HCA for a limited period and then cancel his account after the accomplishment of his duties. Moreover, AS can cancel the account of any member who implements suspicious actions (internal threats) that are not within his/her privileges, i.e., a nurse who wants to access the personal information of a specified doctor or patient. Additionally, the member can demand from the authority’s provider (AS) to cancel his/her account information that is correlated with his/her data. The proposed involves a revocation protocol to supply rigorous protection processes in securing members’ authentication information, Figure 7 displays the revocation protocol in C[i] side:

Revocation from C[i] side:

*   • C[i] enters UID[i], MID[i], and PW[i] and then replaces UID[i] with ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m43](i/ch032.m43.svg) and MID[i] with ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m44](i/ch032.m44.svg).

| Figure 7. Revocation protocol |
| --- |
| ![Figure978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.f07](i/ch032.f07.png) |
| --- |

It chooses the revocation reason (RR[i]) from the drop-down list (i.e., ending the researcher’s study, ending a satisfactory condition, resigning a professional, changing a health institution, and the unwillingness of a patient to utilize the HCA). These reasons have converted to signatures utilizing PHOTON to get MDs with a 256-bits in the database. C[i] calculates new TS[Ci], N[C1], N[C2] and N[C3]. Next, C[i] performs the process of RR[i]⊕N[C1] to add randomness for RR[i]. Utilizing this process is helpful in tightening authentication and distinguishing the roles of members (professionals or patients) in CS. It computes the signature C[i]Sig[1]\=h(TS[Ci]||N[C1]||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m45](i/ch032.m45.svg)||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m46](i/ch032.m46.svg)||RR[i]||PW[i]||”delete”). C[i] performs a computation to hide the RR[i] (tmpRR[i]\=RR[i]⊕N[C2]⊕C[i]Sig[1]). C[i] computes the temporary PW[i] value of PW[i]⊕N[C3]⊕C[i]Sig[1] to hide the PW[i] value. Furthermore, it computes encryption (Enc[i]) and sends a revocation request to CS. After that, it conceals a private key, in the same manner, in the password update protocol.

*   • CS decrypts (Enc[i]) and calculates timestamp and checks ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m47](i/ch032.m47.svg)and ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m48](i/ch032.m48.svg) in the databases. It obtains the RR[i] from the computation equation RR[i]\=tmpRR[i]⊕N[C2]⊕CSSig[1]. It extracts PW[i] from tmpPW[i] ⊕N[C3]⊕C[i]Sig[1] and checks PW[i] matching in the database. CS calculates the signature (CSSig[1]) and then compares the result of the signatures. CS calculates operation RR[i] ⊕N[C1] to use RR[i]’s signature in order to compare the RR[i] with the member’s R[i]. If all operations are validated properly, CS sends a request to AS to examine the pseudonym’s correlation with real information and examine PW[i]. AS deletes correlation between pseudonyms and information and deletes member’s PW[i] from the database. AS sends MAC delete request to CS. After receiving MAC delete request, CS decrypts this request, then examines signature and security parameters. If all parameters are validated properly, CS deletes MAC from the database. In this stage, this member cannot execute an authentication protocol in the proposed.

Revocation from AS side:

*   • AS deletes the correlation between member’s information and pseudonyms and PW[i] in databases. It sends an encrypted request (Enc[i]) to CS to remove the device’s MAC for this member. Upon the accomplishment of this protocol, the member is considered illegitimate and cannot access HCA repositories.

DISCUSSIONS AND SECURITY ANALYSIS

In this section, analysis of a theoretical (attacks analysis and BAN), an experimental (AVISPA) and security comparison have been provided.

Theoretical Analysis

This section will show the security analysis of the proposed by providing assumptions and proofs.

*   • Resist against a privileged insider attack.

Proof 1: The internal intruder (II) needs to eavesdrop authentication requests between C[i] and CS. Then, he/she attempts to execute an analysis of these requests depending on his/her access privileges to the HCA. First, the analysis of these requests to gain the private key or password is infeasible because the authentication request is encrypted by the ECIES-256 bits; II cannot decrypt these requests with his private key. Second, if II penetrated the encryption (which is impossible), he/she cannot extract the PW[i] value (tmpPW[i] = PW[i] ⊕N[Ci]⊕GM⊕C[i]Sig[1]) in the login protocol because it is hidden and relies on the values of GM, C[i]Sig[1], and N[Ci] where II does not know the GM value of the rightful member’s device, and the C[i]Sig[1] value relies on the CM value that is also not known to II. Hence, the proposed resists a privileged insider threat.

*   • Resist against resistant to stolen attack.

Proof 2: In the first scenario, the intruder (I) steals a rightful member device (i.e., a laptop) that has a client application. In the proposed, the member’s PW[i], and IDs are not stored on the member’s device, or in the client application. Moreover, the private key is concealed and random for each authentication by C[i]K[pri]⊕GM⊕PW[i]⊕N[Ci]. Furthermore, Proof 1 shows that the PW[i] value cannot be extracted from the tmpPW[i]. If I is II, he/she also cannot utilize his/her IDs and PW[i] to access information or other member data because both CS and AS implement matching IDs, and PW[i] to check member-related information and data. In the second scenario, the intruder steals only client application. I cannot utilize the application on another device because it does not have OTP[i] or original MAC, which prohibits the application from being utilized on another device even if I knows the IDs and PW[i]. The original MAC technique (C[i]Sig[1] = h(CM||N[Ci]||TS[Ci]) blocks the fake authentication request from being validated in the server because I cannot generate an original MAC (CM) in C[i]Sig[1]. Thus, the proposed is resistant to stolen attack.

*   • Resist against replay attack.

Proof 3: I attempts to obtain a login/registration/authentication request for a rightful member to send it later and hence, acquires access to the network. This scenario is infeasible in the proposed because all entities (C[i], CS, and AS) utilize timestamp (such as TS[CS] -TS[Ci]≤ ∆T, where T is the maximum transfer delay rate) that blocks the intruder from sending the authentication request at a later time. Additionally, random nonces/signatures are not applicable the next times. Therefore, the proposed strongly withstands replay threat.

*   • Resist against the MITM attack.

Proof 4: Suppose that an I tries to intercept encrypted login/authentication requests (i.e., Enc[i](TS[Ci]||N[Ci]||CiSig[1]||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m49](i/ch032.m49.svg)||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m50](i/ch032.m50.svg)||tmpPW[i]||CiSig[2])) among network entities and then alters/changes these requests with his/her messages to send to network entities. However, the intruder cannot replace exchanged messages among C[i], CS, and AS for two reasons. First, he/she does not know the private keys (C[i]K[pri], CSK[pri], ASK[pri]) and thus, the decryption operation is computationally infeasible with 256 bits key length and difficulty in solving ECDLP. Second, MA with PHOTON-256 signatures blocks the modification of requests between the proposed entities. Consequently, the proposed gracefully overcomes the MITM attack.

*   • Resist against guessing attack.

Proof 5: Suppose that an external intruder (EI) was able to hack the encryption (Enc[i]) between C[i] and CS (from Proof 4, this assumption is infeasible). This EI attempts to guess PW[i] in a login request to utilize it to access the HCA as a rightful member. EI cannot get PW[i] for any authorized member (either off-line or on-line) because he/she does not know the configured process to secure PW[i] (tmpPW[i]\=PW[i]⊕N[Ci]⊕GM⊕CiSig[1]) and does not know the MAC for that member and thus, the process of deriving PW[i] is infeasible (Proof 1). It is an extremely difficult process to guess PW[i] from the tmpPW[i], which is 64 hex (256 bit). Furthermore, EI cannot get UID[i] and MID[i] for any rightful member because of the utilize of multi pseudonyms technique for members and medical centres instead of sending real information to rightful members. Therefore, the proposed is safe against a guessing threat.

*   • Resist against client impersonation attack.

Proof 6: Suppose that an intruder attempts to impersonate a login request (such as Enc[i]\=TS[Ci]||N[Ci] ||CiSig[1]||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m51](i/ch032.m51.svg)||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m52](i/ch032.m52.svg)||tmpPWi||CiSig[2]) for a legitimate member. This I can create TS[Ci] and N[Ci] but does not know PW[i] and CiKpri (Proofs 1, and 4) for the rightful member, namely, I cannot impersonate the member IDs. Additionally, I attempts to impersonate the legitimate member’s device by programmatically changing the MAC to a rightful one to gain access to the network. This scenario is infeasible because the original MAC check (CM) in CiSig[1] = h(CM||N[Ci]||TS[Ci]) detects the hacker’s attempt to impersonate the rightful member’s device (as in Proof 2). As a result, the proposed withstands against cases of impersonating the member’s ID and device.

*   • Resist against server impersonation attack.

Proof 7: Suppose that an I traps login requests from C[i] to CS. The intruder tries to deceive C[i] by sending fake requests to C[i] to inform them that he is a rightful server. I needs the private key for CS to decrypt and to execute the threat. MA blocks I from impersonating CS’s requests (such as Enc[i](TS[CS]||N[CS]||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m53](i/ch032.m53.svg)||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m54](i/ch032.m54.svg) ||CSSig[5])) and sending them to C[i]. This technique guarantees that C[i] deals with legitimate CS. Consequently, the proposed effectively resists server impersonation attack.

*   • Resist against DoS attack.

Proof 8: In order for I to implement a DoS threat against CS and AS, he/she needs to decrypt the login request and modify its data or send the same request repeatedly for destroying servers. However, in the first scenario, decryption and modify of signatures are infeasible as in Proofs 2 and 4. CS checks signature validity and rejects login requests containing fake signatures, and I cannot perform a preimage/collision threat because PHOTON-256 provides PR, SPR, and CR. In the second scenario, the intruder sends the same request frequent times. This case is infeasible because CS or AS examines timestamp (TS[Ci], TS[CS], TS[AS]) for each login/authentication request and cancels all late requests (Proof 3) without testing the other security parameters, i.e., PW[i], CM, and multi pseudonyms. In case I can penetrate the encryption, he/she can modify timestamp and nonce but cannot tamper with the signatures. The proposed prohibits this condition during CiSig[1] and does not need to examine the rest authentication parameters. Thus, the proposed meritoriously resists DoS threat.

*   • Resist against password change attack.

Proof 9: Suppose that an I intercepts a request to modify PW[i] between C[i] and CS. When I gains an encrypted password update request (i.e., Enc[i](TS[Ci]||N[C1]||N[C2]||N[C3]||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m55](i/ch032.m55.svg)||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m56](i/ch032.m56.svg)||tmp\_oldPWi||tmp\_newPWi ||CiSig[1])). If I can decrypt (this case is infeasible as in Proofs 1, and 4), he/she will find temporary passwords and cannot retrieve new PW[i] because it relies on the CiSig[1]\= h(TS[Ci]||N[C1]||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m57](i/ch032.m57.svg)||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m58](i/ch032.m58.svg)||oldPWi). The signature operation (CiSig[1]) is based on the old PW[i] which is not explicitly sent to CS in this protocol. I does not know old PW[i] and hence, he/she cannot make a signature to complete the PW[i] change process. Thus, the proposed presents a reliable solution against password change threat.

*   • Resist against eavesdropping attack.

Proof 10: Suppose that an I eavesdrops login/authentication requests to obtain information about member authentication and access to the network. However, in this proposed, I will not benefit from requests that are intercepted because the proposed utilizes ECIES algorithm with key 256 bits to encrypt authentication information. The I can only decrypt requests by deriving private keys and this process is infeasible (as in Proofs 1, and 2) due to key length, and random encryption with anonymity. Hence, the proposed prevents eavesdropping threat.

*   • Resist against traceability attack.

Proof 11: I tries to collect as many login/authentication requests as possible and next implements an analysis of those requests that assists him/her to execute member IDs tracing. When an I succeeds in tracking member requests, he/she can detect and distinguish patients’ data. All exchanged requests among proposed entities do not contain direct members’ information (i.e., PWs). The proposed replaces the real member IDs (UID[i] and MID[i]) with pseudonyms. This scheme utilizes multi pseudonyms (![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m59](i/ch032.m59.svg), ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m60](i/ch032.m60.svg), ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m61](i/ch032.m61.svg), and ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m62](i/ch032.m62.svg) for members and ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m63](i/ch032.m63.svg), ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m64](i/ch032.m64.svg), ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m65](i/ch032.m65.svg), and ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m66](i/ch032.m66.svg)for medical centres) to block intruders from tracking member requests and revealing their IDs when sent between entities (C[i], CS, and AS). Hence, the proposed resists traceability attack.

*   • Resist against revocation attack.

Proof 12: Suppose that an I attempts to hack a revocation request. This I attempts to analyze the request and utilize it to block members from accessing the network’s repositories. Relying on Proofs 1, 5, and 11, the I cannot distinguish/extract UID[i], MID[i] and PW[i] from the revocation request. The I does not know and cannot retrieve a reason from the tmpRR[i], which is based on the values of RR[i], N[C2], and CiSig[1]. In Proofs 2 and 8, I cannot execute collision, preimage, and second preimage threats against the PHOTON-256. Thereupon, this scheme resists breakthrough of revocation request.

*   • Resist against verifier attack.

Proof 13: Suppose that I attempts to infiltrate the databases in CS. If the I is EI, he/she cannot penetrate databases because he/she does not have a Kpr[i], UID[i], MID[i], OTP[i], and PW[i]. If the I is II, when he penetrates databases in CS and wants to impersonate another member’s ID, first, he/she cannot distinguish this information for a specified member because the real information for members is stored in AS. Second, since CS does not have passwords’ database, II will not benefit from penetrating databases (i.e., pseudonyms) and cannot make a request and send it to AS because it does not know members’ PWs. Thus, the proposed prevents successfully verifier threat.

*   • Resist against leakage attack.

Proof 14: Suppose that I listens to some exchanged requests among C[i], CS, and AS and attempts to find any information that assists him/her to hack authentication (i.e., sending an ID explicitly or sending a password with weak encryption). Exchanged requests between network entities (i.e., a password update request) offer that I does not receive any leaked real information for members during transmissions, such as IDs and PW[i] (all information is concealed and anonymous) that could be helpful in hacking the HCA. Consequently, this scheme withstands leakage threat.

Proposed with BAN Logic

In this section, the proposed security will prove by BAN logic. To validate the legitimacy of an entity, message source and freshness, the proposed has used Burrows, Abadi and Needham (BAN) logic. BAN is widely utilized to perform authentication processes in distributed healthcare systems. It relies on a set of rules (R), i.e., seeing (SR), message meaning (MMR), nonce verification (NVR), jurisdiction (JR), freshness conjuncatenation (FCR) and shared secret (SSR) (specifics of BAN’s rules and notations are obtainable in (Burrows et al., 1989; Al-Zubaidie et al., 2019b)). The logic rules confirm that each party in the proposed connects with another rightful party when sending the message (M) from the member to the CS/AS/DS or conversely. BAN's sections include goals(G), idealized form (IF), hypotheses (H) and proofs (P) of goals by achieving hypotheses and rules.

Experimental Analysis

This section will provide the experimental security analysis of the proposed utilizing the AVISPA tool.

AVISPA Tool

Authentication scheme must be tested, and its accuracy validated under a test model, i.e., the Dolev-Yao (dy) to theoretically analyze, detect and trace the potential of threat. Nonetheless, this analysis requires to be simulated in a factual way such as AVISPA to detect mistakes and concealed traces of the authentication scheme designer, statistics and accurate outcomes.

The AVISPA tool is a push-button, testing/proofing model and is relied on HLPSL language. This language utilizes expressive terms and directives to perform security features. It is incorporated with a set of backends such as the On-the-Fly Model-Checker (OFMC) and the Constraint- Logic-based Attack Searcher (CL-AtSe) to perform the simulation in AVISPA (Team, 2006). To demonstrate authentication and establish simulation framework, HLPSL utilizes roles, including basic roles, i.e., clients and servers (clients, centralServer, and attributesServer), and composition (session and environment) roles that regulate the sending and receiving operations between clients and servers. Moreover, communication channels between HCA entities are controlled by the dy model. In HLPSL, many basic types utilized to declare constants, variables and algorithms (symmetric/asymmetric/hash), i.e., public key, message, text, nat, const, hash func and agent. Table 4 shows some symbols and terms, more details are provided in (Team, 2006). Each protocol has a set of goals (secrets and authentication) in authenticating each entity with the other. In secrecy, the goals are to confirm that secrets are not penetrated/exposed to non-intended parties. In authentication, the goals are to confirm that strong authentication has been implemented between parties depending on witness and request.

Using AVISPA with Proposed

In this section, the simulation of the proposed relies on HLPSL language in the AVISPA. This scheme relies on three core roles: clienti, centralServer, and attributesServer played by C[i], CS and AS respectively. Moreover, it consists of the supporting roles such as session, and environment, goal specification section. Each role has parameters, variables, and local constants. Each basic role has a transition section that offers the sequence of connections among parties.

Each supporting role has a composition section that specifies the linking of sessions and roles. Asymmetric encryption has been applied between scheme entities (C[i], CS, and AS) during public-key exchange (KC[pu], KCS[pu], and KAS[pu]) to perform confidentiality. Additionally, MA has utilized to guarantee the legality of linked entities in the proposed protocols (initial setup, registration, login and authentication). Furthermore, it has used nonces (N[c], N[cs], N[as]) and timestamp (TS[c], TS[cs], TS[as]) to support the features of freshness and anonymity. Figure 19 shows that this scheme achieves six authentication goals and ten secrecy as noted in the goal section.

The authentication scheme starts by sending requests from clients to the server. Figure 16 shows the clienti role includes the start signal. Ci receives the start signal and changes the state flag (State variable) from 0 to 1. It replaces UID and MID with UPc and MPc and computes the timestamp (TSc’) and new nonce (Nc’) by the new() operation. Then, it computes the signatures (CiSig1 and CiSig2), plus the password hiding operation as computed in the TmpPW variable. It encrypts the registration and login request (TSc’, Nc’, GM’, CiSig1’, UPc’, MPc’, OTPi, Tmp\_PW’ and CiSig2’) by the public-key (KCSpu) to build a robust connection with CS. Ci sends the request to CS where the transmission is applied by the SND() process. It accomplishes secrecy goals (sec1 to sec6) with both CS and AS; these secrets have been only known and protected by the specified entities. For example, in sec1, PW, UID and MID have been known and protected only to Ci, and AS. While in sec3 GM, and CM have been known and protected only to Ci and CS, since this information is not sent directly during the transition of requests between network entities such as PW implicitly is in the calculation of TmpPW and CM is implicitly in CiSig1. Furthermore, Ci accomplishes the goal of authentication utilizing statement (witness) with parameters (Ci, CS, ci\_cs\_auth2, Ncs, TSc). Namely, Ci is a witness that the security parameters (Ncs, TSc) are correct and fresh. CS utilizes a statement (request) to verify parameters with the strong authentication goal (ci\_cs\_auth2) specified in the goal section (Figure 16). Ci receives the authentication response by the RCV () operation and that transferred from AS by CS. Next, Ci decrypts the response utilizing its private key to validate the authentication information. If all authentication parameters are validated properly, Ci reliably achieved the MA requirement.

As shown in Figure 16, CS receives a registration and login request by RCV () process in state 0. It decrypts request with its private key and then tests the signatures and parameters to achieve goals of secrecy and authentication.

CS achieves strong authentication with AS during witness (CS, AS, as\_cs\_auth4, TScts’, Ncts’) to achieve the authentication goal (as\_cs\_auth4) depending on fresh nonce and timestamp that verified in AS by statement (request). In state 1, CS receives an authentication response from AS and tests the security parameters after decryption with its private key. It updates the state signal to 2 and next creates the authentication response to Ci. CS sends a response with two strong authentication goals (cs\_ci\_auth1 and cs\_ci\_auth5) depending on the security parameters (Nc, TScs, TmpPW, and OTPi).

Figure 18 shows that AS receives the authentication request and decrypts it with the private key. It achieves 2 authentication goals and 5 secret (as\_cs\_auth4 and as\_cs\_auth6) based on TScs’, Ncs’, and PW’. It creates the authentication response and builds strong authentication when verifying parameters (TSas, Ncs’, and PW’) in CS. Figure 19 shows the roles of session, environment, and goal section. In the session role, a composition process has been applied for the three roles (clienti, centralServer, and attributeServer). This role assigns the receive/transmit channels in the dy model. In the environment role, the security information, the goals specified in the goal section, and the known parameters for the intruder (intruder knowledge) have been defined. In this role, one or more sessions are composed.

The proposed checked with sessions for threats of impersonating, MITM, and replay. The simulation supposed that an intruder (I) generates a public key (ki) and has knowledge of the public keys (kCpu, kCSpu, and kASpu) of rightful entities in the HCA. The intruder tries to resend the registration/login/authentication requests later, intercept/altered these requests, or impersonate the HCA entities utilizing i\_ci, i\_cs and i\_as constants rather than ci, cs and as.

Security Comparison

This section compares the proposed with the existing research and presents the superiority of the proposed in terms of authentication.

The authentication schemes in He & Zeadally (2015); Giri et al. (2015) suffer from a leak of authentication information when transferring user requests between network entities. Compared with the proposed, all real user information is not transmitted through the network exchanges and therefore does not leak information. Farash et al. (2016) and Jiang et al. (2016) designed authentication schemes but these researches lacked the management and protection of user information/data on the server. This scheme stores information on the AS and uses signatures and multi-pseudonyms to disguise user information on the AS. It also uses CS as a gateway to check requests before sending them to the AS. In Kumar et al. (2016), the authentication scheme suffers from internal attacks. If the intruder uses a sniffing program to steal user information such as MAC addresses, he/she becomes authenticated in the network as a legitimate member. In comparison, the proposed uses CM and GM to prevent internal attacks.

Li et al. (2016) and Das et al. (2017) utilized a symmetric algorithm that relies on a single key and therefore runs the risk of key detection. In contrast, this scheme relies on an asymmetric algorithm that supports scalability. Rajput et al. (2016) proposed an authentication scheme that suffered greatly from impersonation attacks. An I can use his/her device as a server and deceive users. The proposed uses robust MA to prevent impersonation attacks. In Chandrakar & Om (2017), the authentication scheme suffers from collision and preimage attacks, and it handles real user information when requests are transferred to the network. Compared to the proposed, it uses PHOTON to prevent collision and preimage attacks as well as using multi-pseudonyms to prevent the exchange of real information between network entities.

The schemes in Nizzi et al. (2019) and (El-Tawab et al., 2019) suffered from several problems, such as spoofing the coordinator/server by shuffle (AShA)/randomization of fake addresses sent from intruders, key detection, breaking the integration process/vulnerability to preimage/second preimage attacks, and a single technique that does not provide security for online devices. This scheme does not suffer from these problems because it uses CM to prevent MACs change, the public key algorithm to prevent key breaking, PHOTON to provide signature principles, and it uses a set of techniques to protect authentication processes. DISCUSSIONS AND PERFORMANCE ANALYSIS

This section analyzes and compares the proposed performance with existing related works to test the computation and communication processes.

Theoretical Analysis

The authentication scheme should perform lightweight processes to support the reliable communication of users in healthcare applications. If the authentication process is vulnerable for attacks, network performance will be greatly affected by the fact that the servers will perform additional complex computations.

The proposed uses algorithms and techniques to support performance-efficient authentication. It uses the ECIES to encrypt user information only. This algorithm performs lightweight operations and produces small keys compared to public-key cryptographic algorithms as described in Table 1. Additionally, this scheme uses the hash function (PHOTON) that performs hash operations compared to lightweight hash functions as described in Table 2. The use of robust security algorithms against attacks such as ECIES and PHOTON is a major cause of performance stability. In this scheme, new users use OTP only once at the registration phase. They do not need to use this technique in subsequent times. This technique reduces the burden on the server processor to perform complex computations. If the intruder tries to connect to the network with a fake or previously used OTP, the server would reject this request early without having to examine other authentication techniques. This contributes significantly to reducing the depletion of server capabilities.

Furthermore, the proposed relies on multi-pseudonyms that perform lightweight operations in protecting user information rather than using k-anonymity, which consumes the server’s time and power needed to search and explore real information for legitimate users. Moreover, it supports the authentication process via the MAC address technique. This technique is extremely efficient in verifying legitimate devices connected to the network. The other solutions also rely on IP to authenticate users’ devices. IP does not prove the identity of the legitimate device when connected to the network because it is the address of software and not hardware. Also, if the intruder uses a legitimate IP, he/she can perform malicious threats on the EHR repository that will significantly affect network performance. This scheme uses lightweight operations (GM and CM) as part of the authentication processes in the examination of legitimate devices. Thus, the aforementioned proposed scheme features enable it to perform lightweight and efficient authentication.

Experimental Analysis

In this section, the proposed performance in HCA is shown. It provides tests on the hash function (PHOTON 256-bit) and encryption algorithm (ECIES 256-bit). In addition, communication costs (storage overheads) and computation (execution time) are calculated to extract the proposed performance. Applications codes (C[i], CS and AS) are written in Java Programming Language. Also, the results are implemented on Ubuntu 16.04 LTS, CPU Intel Core i5 2.6GHz, OS type 32-bit, RAM 4 GiB and disk 32.0 GB.

To compute the cost of communication, this proposed computes the bits of all security parameters. Hash’s MD (PHOTON) is 256-bit and the ECIES encryption key is 256-bit. The number of messages transmitted through the authentication and login protocol is 4, the password update protocol is 2 and the revocation protocol is 3. On the C[i] side, it produces a 6-line file (TS[Ci] =8, GM =17, C[i]Sig[1]\=64, ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m67](i/ch032.m67.svg)||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m68](i/ch032.m68.svg)\=5, N[C] =8, tmpPWi\=64 and C[i]Sig[2]\=64). The total size of the parameters is 230-byte. Then C[i] converts the plaintext file to an encrypted file with a size from 210-byte to 255-byte (the minimum value is 1680-bit) and the number of bits inside the encryption file is 253-bit. When C[i] receives the authentication response from CS, the size of the decryption file is from 93-byte to 99-byte (the minimum value is 744-bit). The total size of encryption and decryption files in C[i] is 2424-bit.

On the CS side, it produces a 4-line file (TS[CS]\=8, ![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m69](i/ch032.m69.svg)||![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch032.m70](i/ch032.m70.svg)\=11, N[CS]\=8, tmpPW[i]\=64 and CSSig[3]\=64). Performance Comparison

This section shows the superiority of the proposed performance over the authentication schemes.

The authentication scheme in (He & Zeadally, 2015) relies on ECC 512-bit plus AES to generate a session key, while the proposed relies on ECC 256-bit which is NIST certified and sufficient to encrypt and secure the authentication request. As a result, this scheme uses ECC with the best performance and has no need to use symmetric encryption that increases computation expenses. Schemes in (Farash et al., 2016) and (Jiang et al., 2016) are depending on a single server performing all complex operations with users’ devices. These processes consume server resources while this scheme divides computations on servers CS and AS which dramatically improves performance. Additionally, it performs the lowest number of hashes compared to these schemes as shown in Table 6 (T[h] is the time complexity for hash function, T[s] is the time complexity for symmetric encryption and T[H] is the time complexity for bio-hash function). This makes the proposed performance suitable for the HCA environment.

Compared to this proposed, both authentications in (Jiang et al., 2016) and (Das et al., 2017) utilized a fuzzy extractor that requires additional operations to consume an execution time of 0.442s, while the proposed does not need these additional operations. Furthermore, the scheme in (Giri et al., 2015) is based on RSA 1024-bit which is expensive in encryption and decryption while this scheme relies on ECIES 256-bit which uses small keys and is suitable for high-performance security. The CACPPA scheme in (Rajput et al., 2016) suffers from storage overheads. It requires 76-byte per pseudonym as well as other storage requirements such as keys, encryption by ECIES 256-bit and signature by ECDSA 256-bit. With increasing numbers of users, this scheme will be extremely costly for server memory (communication and computational overheads). The proposed uses only 5-17 bytes per pseudonym which saves significant memory storage. Moreover, the scheme in (Chandrakar & Om, 2017) stores the same user information on multi-servers which consumes storage resources as well as the computation cost to store this information. This scheme does not deplete storage sources by repeating the same information on servers.

The scheme in (El-Tawab et al., 2019) suffers from costly processes due to the use of SHA256, while this scheme uses PHOTON which has lightweight processes. Additionally, impersonation attacks of legitimate MACs on schemes in (Nizzi et al., 2019) and (El-Tawab et al., 2019) cause low network performance due to increased network-connected fake devices. The proposed prevents the use of legitimate MACs addresses in more than one device by using the CM technique and thus maintains network performance.

FUTURE RESEARCH DIRECTIONS

Future directions for further the advancement of the proposed are:

*   1\. To support the proposed authentication scheme, it should addition users’ biometric properties such as fingerprint, iris, or sound recognition to the authentication procedures. This procedure strengthens security precautions that prevent external intruders from accessing network services. However, adding these features requires performance evaluation in the login and authentication protocols.
*   2\. The proposed uses lightweight and efficient performance algorithms. It should evaluate the proposed in terms of other performance standards such as throughput, error rate and request delay.
*   3\. From other future works, supporting this scheme with shuffle MAC to support the exchange and management of public keys. Broadcasting public keys in general needs more attention to prevent various attacks. Public-key storage on users’ devices can also be a source of compromised authentication.

CONCLUSION

In this chapter, this study investigated that existing HCA were unreliable against a range of various threats. Hence, a reliable authentication scheme proposed to prohibit threats on EHR's records that are transferred or stored on servers. This scheme applies multi pseudonyms for both members and health institutions to block the exchanging of real IDs in the authentication messages and physical address to block forgery devices from communicating to the EHR repository. The lightweight cryptography is implemented to guarantee efficient performance for the proposed with the member messages. Moreover, the intensive security analysis is provided to manifest the effectiveness of this scheme in preventing various threats. The proposed provides high-level protection that secures authentication information for members from known threats. Furthermore, a theoretical and experimental performance evaluation is provided plus a comparison of the proposed performance with researches in the literature review. These analyzes indicate to this scheme outperformed on existing research.

KEY TERMS AND DEFINITIONS

Authentication Protocol: A set of communication rules and agreements to ensure the connection of legitimate members within the network.

Electronic Health Record: A technology allows legitimate members to exchange patient data and information over the Internet and store them in a central server repository based on a set of standards and rules.

Lightweight Hash-Function: An algorithm that produces a fixed message digest from arbitrary size data faster than traditional hash-function.

Medical Record: The paper record is a conventional manner applied to check and record patient information/data.

Public-Key Cryptography: A technique used to encrypt/sign data based on a pair of public and private keys also called asymmetric cryptography.

Security Evaluation Tool: A method used by researchers to apply threat models to security schemes in a real-world simulation such as AVISPA and Scyther.

Security Scheme: A set of security protocols (authentication, authorization, and data collection) that regulate networks connectivity.
