# Chapter 33

The Role of Automated Affective Content Screening of Neuro-Response Plasticity

*   Jonathan Bishop  
    Crocels, UK
*   Darren Bellenger  
    Crocels, UK

ABSTRACT

This chapter proposes automated screening of internet and multimedia communications through a combination of neuroeconomics to measure neuro-response plasticity through forensic phonetics, EEG monitoring, and EigenFaces. These measure neuro-response plasticity through facial differences, including through the eyes, differences in EEG pattern, and prosody in the form of tone of voice. Through describing the ‘Distress in the Mind Test’, a computer program is proposed that can be implemented on any device with a camera and microphone and can therefore also be used to diagnose social orientation impariments, such as autism and social phobia. Further development would prevent people with social orientation impairments or whom are otherwise at risk from online harms being exposed to them through automated content filtering.

INTRODUCTION

The convergence of media content is posing challenges in terms of protecting the vulnerable while also protecting free speech (Wright & Javid, 2019) . Government film rating agencies are inefficient and overly bureaucratic. Regulating abusive online media content, such as Internet trolling, has not been suited to this 'before-the-fact' model. Basing rating on subjective judgements of age appropriateness is also ineffective for the online world, as people will have different maturity for different content at different ages. Internet trolling as a concept has transformed in definition in recent years from classical trolling, which was the posting of messages in a friendly way, to Anonymous Trolling, which is posted to harm others (Bishop, 2014b). Internet trolling messages posted to entertain others can be seen as 'kudos trolling' and that designed to harm others can be seen as 'flame trolling' (Bishop, 2012). But this does not mean all flame trolling is 'bad' and should be punished, nor does it mean all kudos trolling is 'good' and should be allowed. In some forums on the Internet, flame trolling is encouraged, such as the criticism of politicians, bankers, or other people who may be part of a group with dislikeable qualities. The consensual nature of these forums it could be argued should not mean their abusive comments should be prosecutable. Equally not all kudos trolling is designed to be in the interests of people. For instance, a type of online community user called a chatroom bob, will often post friendly comments in order to seduce others, such as a pervert looking to coax naked pictures out of the person, or a sex predator trying to groom a child or other young person (Bishop, July 19 2012).

It is therefore necessary to have a more technical way of looking at online harms through means such as Internet trolling, which could make it easier to regulate online content, so that mature users know what to expect, and Internet security software providers can better produce software with parental controls to avoid the corruption of the minds of those lacking in maturity, or those at risk adults with social orientation impairments such as autism and social phobia. Such people may or may not have been exposed to severe or traumatic content in the past, but either way they less able to cope with it.

The Role of 'Knol' in Calculating the Risk of Harm to People with Social Orientation Impairments from their Attitudes and Affective Responses to Media Content

The extent to which someone can withstand or effectively use media sources can be measured in ‘knol.’ In the context of the human mind, knol technically refers to the amount of pressure on parts of the brain that acts as a restriction to synaptic flow and thus the plasticity of the mind to efficiently process the requests made of it consciously by the actor, or forced on them by the environment. Those pressures, or 'impressions' imposed on the actor may include traumatic event such as abuse of violent videos on television, which have the effect of reducing their ability to process information, measured as a 'knol.' The most researched part of the brain in relation to the calculation of knol is the prefrontal cortex (Bishop, 2019; Bishop, July 19 2012; Bishop, September 10 2011). This part of the brain it is believed is responsible for many of the social interactions humans have with one another. It is hypothesised that if the prefrontal cortex has a high or optimal knol of 0.81 then the flow of information, or neuro-response plasticity, is likely to be greater than the level of involvement required to utilise that part of the brain. To explain how attitude to media content, in this case the arts, have an impact on knol, the remainder of this section will apply nuroeonomic equations (Bishop, 2019; Bishop, July 19 2012; Bishop, September 10 2011) to show the variation in knol and how to calculate it.

Equation 1 presents the means by which a phantasy is calculated. A phantasy can be defined most easily as a memory that has an effect on how quickly the brain can perform certain tasks. It can have an inhibiting effect, such as if it is a traumatic memory, or an enabling effect, such as if it is the memory of a loved one. A phantasy is made up of two 'cognitions,' which are essentially the meanings we have attached to those phantasies, which are both linked together in some way by us.

![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch033.m01](i/ch033.m01.svg) (1)

In the case of this study, phantasies were computed through the use of a type of cognition called a detachment (rated from 0 to 6) and a plan (rated from -2 to +2). A detachment is an attitude towards a person that makes one anxious and which the mind tries to suppress. A plan is a willingness or lack of, to perform a particular action.

The detachments were calculated through linking six regions in the UK where data on reports of electronic messages faults between 2009 and 2011 were known. This was done by the region with the lowest number of EMF incidents being 0 and the highest number of incidents of flame trolling being 6. This resulted in Yorkshire and the Humber being ranked 0, with 42 incidents and the East of England being ranked 1, with 114 incidents. Wales was ranked 2 with 135 incidents, Scotland 3 with 174 incidents, and South West England 4 with 578 incidents. Northern Ireland was ranked 5 with 1485 incidents and South East England 6 with 1903 incidents.

The three plans used in the study were, 'People like me don't get involved in the arts and culture,' 'There are other things besides arts and culture that I prefer to do in my leisure time,' and 'It's expensive to get involved in arts and culture.' Using the lookup table for the x[1] and y[1] variables (Bishop, September 10 2011), Equation 1 was used to produce three phantasies from combining the detachment with the associated plan for each participant.

![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch033.m02](i/ch033.m02.svg) (2)

The next stage was to compute the 'Pression' for each participant using Equation 2. The Pression (P) is the extent to which a number of phantasies inhibit or enhance performance at a particular point in time. In this case it would be when engaging with media in general or art in particular. In Equation 1 the variable F reflects the normal force a human can handle in an average week, measured in hours, which is taken to be 48, based on the European Union's Working Time Directive \[2003/88/EC\].

![Mathtype978-1-7998-5728-0.ch033.m03](i/ch033.m03.svg) (3)

The final stage was to calculate the knol, which is the level of possible brain productivity for each person in performing a particular task where certain phantasies become activated using Equation 3. Essential to this is the baseline (B) figure. The B figure reflects the number of hours a person is working or is comfortable working. Participants were asked to state whether they worked full-time, part-time, were a homemaker, registered unemployed, a full-time student, or not working at all. The number of hours worked were harmonised based on official government figures to reflect the 'potential' as opposed to 'actual'. Those working full-time were assigned to 30 hours and those working part-time were assigned to 24 hours. These are the hours required for the respective rates on the UK's Tax Credits system. A homeworker was assigned 35 hours, which is the number of hours required to claim Carer's Allowance and a person who was not working or seeking work was assigned 0 hours. Someone registered unemployed and seeking work was assigned 15 hours, which is the maximum one can work and still receive out-of-work benefits, and a full-time student was assigned 21 hours, which it the number of hours one needs to be studying to qualify as a full-time student to receive a reduction in council tax.

The baseline figure, which is a person's individual production possibility in terms of workable hours is then added to the maximum a person can work in an healthy environment, which is 48 hours as signified by F. Adding the baseline and the force together and dividing them by the Pression calculated by equation 2 then produces a persons speed and performing in a particular setting. In terms of phantasies containing detachments, 0.81 is an ideal figure for someone achieve as they are likely to be able to withstand most abusive content due to media content of a GOIOM nature being suppressed. A knol based on a detachment phantasies of 0.98 or over is not ideal as this could put a lot of pressure on the prefrontal cortex of the brain which is quite vulnerable. And a knol of below 0.5 is below also ideal as the phantasy is likely to be affecting the person's mental wellbeing and participation in society. Where this reaches around 0.6 then there is an increasing chance the person would not be as productive as they would be at either 0.81 or 0.50. Further details on this can be found other publications (Bishop, 2019; Bishop, July 19 2012; Bishop, September 10 2011).

Determining the Appropriate Means to Restrict Access to Media Content

The rating of media content has a different regime in most jurisdictions in the world. In the United Kingdom it is the British Board of Film Classification (BBFC) that is responsible for the rating of media content, such as TV, DVD, video games, etc. (Smartt, 2011). They say that each year the BBFC rates over 10,000 media sources and in 2010 alone, of 407 films censored there were five that were cut (1.2 per cent), which compared to 1983 where 123 out of the 514 (24 per cent) were cut. The BBFC have the competence to rate a piece of audio-visual media content where it falls into a number of categories. These include where the content is; criminal behaviour, illegal drugs, violent behaviour or incidents, horrific behaviour or incidents, human sexual activity (Smartt, 2011).

The fact that the BBFC has censorship powers over this explicit content does not mean it always will censor it, even if the content is of a ‘grossly offensive, indecent, obscene or menacing’ (GOIOM) character. One notable example of discrepancies between the regulation of film and Internet content is the case of DPP v Collins. In this case the defendant made what were deemed racist comments to their local Member of Parliament’s staff. These comments included their view that ethnic minorities, who they called “foreigners”, should “go back to their own country.” One should ask therefore, what is the reason why racism exposed in an imaginary world through film, which causes offence to the same magnitude as that by public communications networks, any more acceptable? Why is hearing something reposted on Twitter for instance more prosecutable than equally bigoted representations of the same vile language shown in films? On this basis, one might argue that the BBFC to be one of the most highly regarded and trusted non-governmental organisations in the world (Smartt, 2011), should be given the remit to rate Internet-based media content. It is likely that BBFC, who have a lot of experience balancing what is simply offensive and what is a GOIOM in the case of film, could add a lot to regulating online media content, but the stronghold of basing ratings on age, are totally unsuited to the information age we are in. Today, young people, or digital teens as they are sometimes called, are able to mature in their use of media content a lot faster than some of their ancestors were able to (Bishop, 2014a). There therefore needs to be a new rating system that goes beyond age, as it should perhaps be considered unacceptable to expose vulnerable people to certain content, just because they happen to be of an arbitrary age where most people have greater maturity. Indeed, the case of DPP v Connolly found that even among adult professionals, some are likely to find certain images (in this case aborted foetuses) to be GOIOM (in this case by pharmacists), whereas others, such as abortion surgeons, would be unlikely to see it as a GOIOM message. The regulation of media content therefore needs to adapt to go beyond age and provide greater information to the public on the actual content of the file or other media content they are accessing, and not simply assume if they are at the age of majority that it is unlikely they will find it to not be of a GOIOM nature.

The trolling magnitude scale was made relative to the number of hours spent on the Internet (Bishop, 2013a). A trolling magnitude (TM) of 1, which is Playtime, where people are more likely to act in the heat of the moment, was assigned to all the participants who used the Internet 0 to 1 hours. A TM of 2 (i.e. Tactical) was assigned to people who used the Internet for 1 to 3 hours. A TM of 3 (i.e. Strategic) was assigned to people who used the Internet for 3 to 5 hours, and finally, a TM of 4 was assigned to people who used the Internet for between 5 and 7 hours, or greater than 7 hours. Using a One-Way ANOVA, the data was then analysed to see whether there was a significant difference between those knols of those assigned to the 4 groups, to make it worthwhile proceeding with further analysis of difference between the groups.

| TM || N || Mean k || L Bound k || U Bound k || Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 || 90 || 0.7265 || 0.6926 || 0.7604 || The prefrontal cortex is operating nearing its most optimal (0.81), mean a person is likely to act in the heat of the moment when their knol is at is greatest. |

Table 1 shows the number of persons assigned to each trolling magnitude, the Mean knol (k) for each group and the upper and lower knol for those groups. As can be seen, there is a negative relationship between trolling magnitude and knol. That is, as trolling magnitude increases then knol decreases. As shown in Table 1, this can be interpreted as meaning that in order to troll at a higher magnitude, more effort is needed in the brain. It could also mean that those who have been traumatised to the extent their knol is very low, may be at more risk of trolling at a higher magnitude. This may explain why Sean Duffy, who keeps vandalising memorial pages no matter how many times he is convicted, may be doing so because of his social orientation impairment (diagnosed as Asperger syndrome), which could equally result from abuse of him by others, as much as it could neurological differences, which whilst not psychiatric produces the same mental vulnerabilities as mental disorders.

In terms of detailed statistical analysis, these findings are confirmed. The degree of freedom numerator for the dataset of 975 participants was 3 and the degrees of freedom denominator was 971. This gave a CV of 2.08380. As the F for the dataset was 1.145 (0.9388) this was not an ideal outcome, but further inspection of the dataset showed it was the best outcome possible. An eight-factor model gave an F of 0.568 and CV of 1.71672 (a difference of 1.14872) and a five-factor model, as currently used by the police gave an F of 0.891 and CV of 1.94486 (a difference of 1.05386). This shows the four-factor model to be most appropriate for determining media ratings based on knol and number of hours spent on the Internet.

Measuring Neuro-Response Plasticity Through Automated Affective Content Screening Using ‘Forensic Phonetics’, ‘Neuroeconomics’ and ‘EigenFaces’ to Caculate ‘Knol’: The Role of the Distress in the Mind Test

The length of time on the Internet – exposure to the media – is linked someone’s neuro-response plasticity, which can be measured to calculate knol and cross-referenced against the trolling magnitude scale. This makes it possible to suggest intervention and methods for assessing someone’s risk of being exposed to online harms in the form of distressing media content.

Forensic phonetics involves the comparison of two voice sources in order to assess their differences or similarities (Elliott, 2000). An important part of forensic phonetics is monitoring given voices over a period of time (Eriksson, 2005). Whilst forensic phonetics is usually used to distinguish one person from another (Taitechawat & Foulkes, 2011), this paper extends it from the perspective of wanting to distinguish each person’s affective states through continuous analysis. An important consideration in affect recognition where forensic phonetics is concerned is the sincerity of the voices sampled (Fraser, 2009). The uncertainty that comes from not knowing whether a voice sample is genuine can cause problems in affective computing.

The approach, which is still under development, provides many advantages for at-risk educational environments through the use of “EigenFaces,” which are the basis vectors of the eigenface decomposition (Turk & Pentland, 1991). These “eigenvectors” are used by many in the computer vision problem of human face recognition (Kshirsagar, Baviskar, & Gaikwad, 2011) .

The concept of EigenFaces has commonly been used for visual face detection, but its use in visual facial emotion detection is not widespread. The advantages are that it is quicker and requires less computation, although conversely its accuracy in poor lighting and poor camera situations is something that needs to be improved upon. A possible auditory/facial data decoding component can be seen in . This algorithm involves the acoustic properties of the amplitude, pitch and spectral profile of the stimuli being measured (Sauter, Eisner, Calder, & Scott, 2010). The basis on which this algorithm is designed is that emotional states, cues associated with voice quality, loudness and pitch give the emotional speech its affective quality (Sauter et al., 2010). The spectral centre of gravity and the standard deviation of the spectrum component are computed on the basis of fast Fourier transformations (Sauter et al., 2010). Amplitude cues in the algorithm are included measurements of intensity, aspects of the amplitude envelope and duration (Sauter et al., 2010). Initially the development of the system involved creating a series of prototypes that demonstrate each part of the complex functionality required, such as facial recognition, video/audio emotion recognition, speech recognition (Bishop & Reddy, 2003; Bishop, 2011b) . The app was among the first to tackle the developing of a mobile app for facial and emotion recognition and recommendation.

Using Table 2, it is possible to easily distinguish between that which could be grossly offensive, indecent, obscene or menacing at a TM of 1 and that of a TM of 4. Equally it shows which content could cause harassment, alarm or distress, and how this differs with a TM of 2 compared to a TM of 4. If one considers a child that has been told by their parent that they will see them at their school play. There is nothing explicit in what their parent said. However, if that parent did not turn up at that play the child may be grossly offended. This could be quite traumatic for them if they feel their parent has betrayed them. If the parent keeps missing school plays or similar events where the child wants to make them proud, their phantasy from the original ‘betrayal’ will strengthen and their knol will increase, which will make them not only less able to be grossly offended over ‘minor’ upsets, but also less able to notice the positives in situations where they may be upset in a similar way. The level of strategic thinking ability also relates to Trolling Magnitude. Table 2 shows the lower and upper bounds of knol and how they relate to the maturity of different audiences to consume and otherwise use content without suffering HAD or perceiving it as GOIOM. Someone who is at the Playtime level of strategic thinking, will be like an infant, who could be easily led astray even though they think they are being clever. It also includes people who would get caught up in the moment, such as people who were intellectually challenged, or regularly victimised. The Tactical level of strategic thinking applies to those who are able to understand concepts like intertextuality and be able to be humoured while also understanding when something humourous could be offensive in the wrong context. The Strategic category of strategic thinking relates to content where the person would have to be able to differentiate practices and behaviours that harm others and should not be adopted, from those which others might get gratification from whilst in other situations some people might be discomforted. Finally, the domination form of strategic thinking requires an advanced level of understanding so that it is possible to know what could severely harm others and also cause harm to oneself. Someone of this maturity in strategic thinking should be able to understand murder plots in media, or be able to see graphic scenes of sexual and other violence, without in any way being corrupted by them. People with a low knol, who are made anxious by this content should know in advance whether they would be at risk. This content is most suited to people who have a high knol in all situations, including violence, so that it in effect 'goes in one ear and out other other.' Such people have a clear value system and are unlikely to have suffered any serious abuse. While it is more likely such people will be over the age of 18, where most people will be at less risk of corruption form a high knol, it may not always be the case. Those people at 18 who may not have had any form of personal, social or health education, or citizenship education, may not be aware of the risks and dangers of the society in which we live. Developing a system of regulating media based on these levels of maturity are essential.

IMPLICATIONS AND FUTURE RESEARCH DIRECTIONS

A system has been developed during this chapter based on one able to read affective information in a person and recommend a particular course of action to another person (Bishop, 2011; Bishop, 2013). Using the rating system with this technology, it could be possible for cinemas to be installed with kiosks that assess the risk of viewing a particular film to a particular individual based on assessing their neuro-response plasticity through calculating knol from both EEG impulses and EigenFaces. By assessing their emotional responses in their eyes and face or through a brain-computer interface based on EEG, while watching clips from the film that trigger distressing emotions, their risk from online or other visual harms can be detected. In terms of online harms in particular, a web-cam or brain-computer device could be used by a parent or guardian to calibrate the Internet security software to only display websites which are suited to the maturity of their child, especially if that child has a social orientation impairment like autism or social phobia. It could also be used as a permanent Internet of Things device, which like an audio-video baby monitor, can warn parents or guardians when their children are viewing distressing content. The device could even act as a ‘chastity band’ to ensure that sex predators are unable to access content that could give them inappropriate thoughts or encourage them to perform undesirable acts. Future research in needed to assess these applications, particularly as they could help protect people with social orientation impairments like autism and social phobia from online harms and other media-based content that might be distressing in nature.

DISCUSSION

This chapter has investigated how measuring neuro-response plasticity through a variety of means – through facial expressions, tone of voice and EEG patterns – means it is possible to help people with social orientation impairments such as autism and social phobia avoid being exposed to online harms. The chapter has shown how the neuro-economic variable of knol can be a suitable means for calculating neuro-response plasticity so as to determine whether someone has a social orientation impairment that might put them at risk of being adversely affected by specific media content. A table is presented showing the different emotional states capable of being detected using the EigenFaces algorithm, EEG monitoring and forensic phonetics algorithm.

KEY TERMS AND DEFINITIONS

Automated Affective Content Screening: A means by which media, whether social media, new media or older forms of media, can be analysed to ascertain the effect they will have on an individual or group.

Fantasy: Subconsciously encoded responses to the neurotransmited and ingested substances that affect a person’s ability to achieve the things they want to achieve.

Flow: The extent to which a person’s fantasies and phantasies balance (i.e. their cognitions are consonant) to the point they lose track of time because they feel they are achiving what they want to achieve.

Involvement: The extent to which a person’s fantasies and phantasies are unbalances (i.e. their cognitions are not consonant) to the point they have to exert a lot of mental effort to achieve what they want to achieve.

Knol: The unit for measuring brain productivity calculated by divinding the number of hours a person is motivated to exert arduous labour by the capacity of their body to work those hours.

Neuro-Response Plasticity: The extent to which the brain can effortly produce a response to a stimulus based on the contents of the mind.

Phantasy: A lesion or other impression on the brain that increases the level of pressure a person has to deal with in performing a task, such as arduous labour.

Social Orientation Impairment: One of a number of conditions, from autism spectrum disorder to histrionic personality disorder that adversely affects the way a person perceives and respond to the people around them.

Maria Manuela Cruz-Cunha is a professor of Information Systems and Project Management in the School of Technology at the Polytechnic Institute of Cavado and Ave, Portugal. She holds a Dipl. Eng. (5 years) in the field of Systems and Informatics Engineering, an M.Sci. in the field of Computer Integrated Manufacturing and a Dr.Sci in of Production Systems Engineering. She teaches subjects related with Information Systems, Information Technologies and Project Management to undergraduate and post-graduate studies. She has authored and edited 25 books and her work appears in more than 250 papers published in journals, book chapters and conference proceedings. She is founder and conference chair of the “CENTERIS – Conference on ENTERprise Information Systems” and “ViNOrg – Conference on Virtual and Networked Organizations Emergent Technologies and Tools”. She is the editor-in-chief of the “International Journal of Web Portals”.

Nuno Ricardo Mateus-Coelho is a Professor of Information Security, Systems Intrusion, Cloud Security, Graphical Computing and Data Privacy at Polytechnic Institute of Management and Technology (ISLA) and at Polytechnic Institute of Cavado and Ave (IPCA), Portugal. He holds a BEng. in Information and Multimedia Systems Engineering, a MEng. in Computer Sciences Engineering by Polytechnic of Porto - School of Engineering (ISEP) in the field and subject of Cloud Security and Secure Operating Systems, and a DSc. Summa Cum Laude, in Computer Sciences by University of Trás-os-Montes and Alto Douro (UTAD) in the field and subject of Information Security and Secure Operating Systems. He is an Expert Accredited by the European Commission on R&I projects in the Horizon 2020, COSME and CEF programs in the area of information technologies. He is a TED and Keynote Technology and Security Speaker; GDPR & DPO Expert in several Portuguese companies, ISO 27K Expert, COBIT & ITIL Expert; Cybersecurity Certified Expert and CEO & Founder of NRMC.PT.

\* \* \*

Mishall Al-Zubaidie received the bachelor’s degree in computer science from Basrah University, Iraq, in 2004, and the master’s degree in the security of the wireless network from Basrah University, Iraq, in 2010. He is currently pursuing the PhD degree with the School of Agricultural, Computational and Environmental Sciences, Faculty of Health, Engineering, and Sciences, University of Southern Queensland, Toowoomba, QLD, Australia. His current research interests are public-key algorithms, authorising users in electronic health record (EHR), and both security and efficiency in the wireless sensor network.

Walaa Alnasser is a Ph.D student in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering at Arizona State University, Tempe, AZ. She joined Data Mining and Machine Learning Lab under the supervision of Professor Huan Liu. In general, her research lies in data mining and machine learning. Recently, she is focusing on privacy protections.

Soumi Banerjee is an Assistant Professor in Department of Information Technology, Ramrao Adik Institute of Technology, Nerul, Navi Mumbai and a Certified Ethical Hacker by EC Council. Completed Master of Technology and Bachelor of Technology from West Bengal University of Technology, West Bengal, India. Published 3 research papers in International Springer Conferences in the area of Cyber security, Cryptography. Guided 12 UG project groups in the domain of Cyber security, Cryptography, Machine Learning.

Ghazaleh Beigi is a Ph.D. candidate in Computer Science at Arizona State University. Ghazaleh obtained her master’s degree in Artificial Intelligence in 2014 and bachelor's degrees in Software Engineering in 2013 from Sharif University of Technology, Iran. The focus of her research is user behavioral modeling, privacy protection, trust/distrust prediction, signed network analysis and recommendation systems. As a result of her research work, she has published over 25 innovative works in major high-impact venues (including WSDM, SDM, TheWeb (former WWW), EMNLP, HyperText, ICWSM, ASONAM, SBP, ACM TIST, ACM TDS, and ACM SigWeb Newsletter), with over 300 citation count. She is also an author of 2 book chapters and 3 patents. Her research has been featured multiple times in the news including KDNugget, The Morning Paper, and ASU Now. Ghazaleh regularly serves on program committees for major international conferences and reviews for multiple journals and conferences. She has also interned as a Software Engineer at Google Inc., Sunnyvale, in 2019. Ghazaleh will join Google Inc., as a full-time Machine Learning Engineer in 2020. More information can be found at http://www.public.asu.edu/~gbeigi.

Tarunpreet Bhatia is working as an Assistant Professor in CSED, TIET, Patiala, Punjab, India. She received her Ph.D and M.E. degree in Computer Science & Engineering from Thapar Institute of Engineering & Technology and B.E. (with Honors) in Computer Science and Engineering from Kurukshetra University. She received the Gold Medal in Master of Engineering. Her research interests include Security in Social Networks, Network and Information Security, Mobile Computing, Cloud Computing, Internet of Things and Soft Computing. She has more than 30 research publications in reputed journals and conferences. She is member of various program committees for different International/National Conferences and reviewer of various International/National journals. She is Vice President, Computer Society of India (CSI), TIET, Patiala, Punjab, India.

Maria Teresa Borges-Tiago is Assistant Professor at University of Azores, Ph.D. in International Marketing, and has the MsC and MBA by the Portuguese Catholic University. She teaches marketing courses and she is a Research Fellow at the Centre of Applied Economics Studies of the Atlantic – University of the Azores and Advance/CSG, ISEG - Lisbon University. Her main research interests include Digital Marketing, Social Media, and Tourism. She has published several articles in internationals journals such as Tourism Review, Management Research News, Journal of Business Research, Business Horizons, Tourism Management, among others.

Gautam Borkar obtained his Ph.D and Masters form Sant Gadge Baba Amravati University, Amravati and received his Bachelors degree from National Institute of Technology, Jalandhar, Punjab, India. Currently he is working as Associate Professor in DY Patil Ramrao Adik Institute of Technology, Department of Information Technology, Nerul, Navi Mumbai 400706, Maharashtra, India. His current research interest includes network security, trust management and security in wireless sensor network.

Luiz Camolesi Junior is professor in University of Campinas (UNICAMP), Brazil. He holds a B.Sc. and a M.Sc. in Computer Science from the University of São Paulo (USP) and a Ph.D. in Computational Physics from the Physical Institute of University of São Paulo (USP). Since 1996, he is stakeholder of international scientific associations and active member of Brazilian Computer Society (SBC) acting such as, author and reviewer of conferences, workshops and journals. He has lectured courses on software engineering and database systems. His research interests and publications include data engineering, data quality, dynamic systems and security of systems.

Anabelen Casares is a Full Administrative Law Professor at the University of Leon (Spain). Currently Deputy General for the Ombudsman of Castille and Leon (Adjunta al Procurador del Común de Castilla y León).

Antonio Castro is a PhD Adjunct Professor at the Engineering Institute of Porto (ISEP) and a researcher at GILT (Graphics, Interaction and Learning Technologies) coordinating the Multimedia and Medicine research line. In recent years he has written several articles on e-learning and the use of technologies related to the production of multimedia educational resources. He co-authored a book on the subject published in Chile. He gave several lectures, by invitation, on Learning Technologies in several European and American countries.

Elizabeth Chang is Professor and Canberra Fellow at the UNSW at the Australian Defence Force Academy (ADFA). She has 30 years of work experience in both Academia and Industry. She has been a full Professor in IT, Software Engineering and Logistics Informatics for 14 years. She had been in senior positions in commercial corporations for 10 years, typically working on commercial grade large software development. Her key research strength is in large complex software development methodologies, requirement engineering, structure and unstructured database design and implementation, trust, security, risk and privacy. In the 2012 edition of MIS Quarterly vol. 36 issue. 4 Special Issues on Business Research, Professor Chang was listed fifth in the world for researchers in Business Intelligence.

Pallavi Chavan is working as an Associate Professor in department of information technology. Her area of research is Image processing and deep learning.

Michelangelo De Bonis has a degree in Computer Engineering at the Polytechnic of Turin (2000); IEEE member; Cisco certified Instructor; Computer Science teacher in high-school; Consultant on networks and information security; Computer Science professor in Engineering Department at University of Foggia, Italy.

Tharam S. Dillon received the Ph.D. degree in electrical and computer systems engineering from Monash University, Melbourne, VIC, Australia, in 1974.He has published over 750 papers in international conferences and journals. He has authored five books and edited five books. His current research interests include Web semantics, ontologies, Internet computing, e-commerce, hybrid neurosymbolic systems, neural nets, software engineering, database systems, and data mining. Prof. Dillon is a fellow of the Australian Computer Society and Institution of Engineers in Australia. He is the Editor-in-Chief of the International Journal of Computer Systems Science and Engineering and Engineering Intelligent Systems. He is the Head of the International Federation for Information Processing (IFIP) International Task Force WG2.12/24 on Semantic Web and Web Semantics, and the Chairman of the IFIP WG12.9 on Computational Intelligence, the IEEE Industrial Electronics Society Technical Committee on Industrial Informatics, and the IFIP Technical Committee 12 on Artificial Intelligence.

Pablo Philipe Do Nascimento graduated in Computer Networks from the University Center Maurício de Nassau. Specialist in Computer Network Security from Faculdade Estácio. He currently holds an Academic Master's Degree at the Universidade Federal de Pernambuco, at the Computer Center - CIn. Has a professional course in Game Development by C.E.S.A.R. Has experience in Computer Science, with an emphasis on Systems Performance Analysis, Information Security, Critical Systems Analysis, Linux Server Administration, Computer Network Administration and Monitoring, Vulnerability Analysis, Computational Forensic Auditing. Participant in the MoDCS Research Group - Modeling of Distributed and Competitive Systems.

Jorge Henrique Fernandes is a PhD and MSc in Computer Science. Biologist. Professor of Computer Science at the University of Brasília. Researcher working in computing, information, management, education, innovation and social studies.

Benjamim Fonseca is an Assistant Professor with Habilitation at the University of Trás-os-Montes and Alto Douro (UTAD) and researcher at INESC TEC, in Portugal. His main research and development interests are collaborative systems, mobile accessibility and immersive systems. He authored or co-authored over a hundred publications in these fields, in several international journals, books and conference proceedings, and participates in the review and organization of various scientific publications and events. He is also co-founder and CEO of 4ALL Software, UTAD's spin-off that works in the development of innovative software, implementing complex digital platforms and interactive solutions.

Josélia Mafalda Ribeiro da Fonseca is Assistant Professor at University of Azores, Ph.D. in Education - Philosophy Education -, and has the MsC by the Minho University. She teaches education courses and she is a Research Fellow at the Research Centre on Adult Education and Community Intervention (CEAD), Algarve University. Her main research interests include Education, Citizenship, Ethics and Values. She has published some articles in internationals journals in this mentioned fields.

Dušan Gabrijelčič is a researcher at Laboratory for Open Systems and Network, Jožef Stefan Institute. His main interests are in information and future communications system security, privacy, critical infrastructure security and application of modern machine learning techniques to cyber and physical security. His publication list includes a number of publications in books, journals and conference proceedings.

Crescenzio Gallo has a degree in Computer Science at University of Bari, Italy (1978); Degree in Information Science and Technology at University of Milan, Italy (2007); Software Consultant; System Engineer and Software Programmer; Manager of Information Systems division; Tenured teacher of Information Management, Commercial High School; Research Professor of Information Processing Systems, Department of Clinical and Experimental Medicine, University of Foggia, Italy.

Carlos Roberto Gonçalves Viana Filho has a specialization in Network Management Techniques from Centro Universitário Carioca (2001), a degree in Computer Science from Universidade Católica de Petrópolis (1994) and a Master's Degree in Computer Science from CEFET / RJ (2019). He is currently part of the permanent staff of PRODERJ Center for Information and Communication Technology of the State of Rio de Janeiro, exercising the function of Director of Information Systems. Has experience in Projects, Software development and computer network administration. He is a researcher in Information Security.

Paulo R. L. Gondim obtained a B.S. degree in computer engineering in 1987 and an M.S. degree in systems and computing in 1992 from the Military Institute of Engineering, and a doctorate degree in 1998 in electrical engineering from Pontifícia Universidade Catolica do Rio de Janeiro, both institutions located in Rio de Janeiro, RJ, Brazil. Since 2003, Professor Paulo Gondim has been working at the University of Brasília, Brasília, Brazil. He has authored over 80 papers in international periodicals and events and advised 29 master’s degree dissertations and 4 doctoral theses. He has been a member of Technical Program Committees of several technical-scientific events and a member of the Editorial Advisory Boards of three international journals. He has experience in Computer Science, particularly in wireless networking, information security, and performance evaluation. Paulo Gondim is a Senior Member of IEEE.

Steven Gordon's current research interests relate to the role of information systems in supporting corporate innovation and in fostering social movements. He has been published widely in the academic press and is the co-author of three text books and the editor of three research anthologies. He serves on the Advisory Board of the Journal of Information Technology Case and Application Research, where he was previously Editor-in-Chief. Before arriving at Babson, Dr. Gordon founded and served as president of Beta Principles, Inc., a developer and marketer of accounting software and reseller of computer hardware. He has also consulted to the airline industry at Simat, Helliesen & Eichner, Inc. He holds a Ph.D. in Transportation Systems from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology.

Florian Gottwalt is a Senior Research Associate at UNSW Canberra at the Australian Defence Force Academy (ADFA). He was awarded the Ph.D. degree in Computer Science from UNSW Canberra in 2019. His research focuses on anomaly detection in provenance-graphs and risk management in distributed systems. Before joining UNSW Canberra, Dr. Gottwalt obtained his Master’s degree in Cyber Security at Queens University Belfast, Northern Ireland and his Bachelor’s degree at the Hochschule Furtwangen University in Germany. Dr. Gottwalt’s research capability has been recognized by different competitive scholarships such as the University International Postgraduate Award (UNSW), Study Canberra Scholarship, ACT Government and the Centre for Secure Information Technologies (CSIT) scholarship, UK. His contributions as a researcher and technical lead of the National Vehicle Sampling project were recognised with the award of the 1st place in the Defence Capability and Sustainment Group (CASG) Innovation competition ($300k) in December 2019, Garden Island, Sydney.

Gueorgui Gotzev holds an LLM in International Economic Law from University Paris I Panthéon-Sorbonne. He is specialised in capital markets and microstructure of financial markets. He has expertise in EU financial sector licensing, regulatory and compliance: MIFID2, PSD2, Prospectus regulation, AIFM, AML/CFT/PF, KYC. He advises asset managers, investment firms, Fintechs, Regtechs and startups on financial sector licensing, business model and product definition, deployment and staging, structuring compliant smart contract structuring for assets dematerialisation on DLT for issuers and fund managers.

Felipe Henriques holds a PhD in Electrical Engineering from COPPE / UFRJ. He is currently a professor in the Graduate Program in Computer Science at CEFET / RJ, in addition to being a professor at the Petrópolis Campus of CEFET / RJ. Felipe is interested in areas such as Wireless Sensor Networks, Internet of Things and Signal Processing.

Edison Ishikawa is a Professor at Computer Science Department of the University of Brasília, Brazil. He received his Ph.D. degree in Computer and Systems Engineering from Federal University of Rio de Janeiro (COPPE-UFRJ). His current research interests include semantic computing, systems of systems engineering, command and control systems and distributed systems. He participates in research projects in those areas, with funding from several Brazilian government agencies, including CNPq, Brazilian Army, FAPERJ and FAP-DF.

Rogério Iwashita is Masters student in Eletrical Engineering at University of São Paulo (USP) and collaborator professor in University of Campinas (UNICAMP), Brazil, lecturing information security. He has a degree in Electrical Engineering with an emphasis in Computing and MBA in Project Management by Fundação Getúlio Vargas (FGV). He is certified CISSP and CISM and has lectured CISSP domains to CISSP candidates on ISSA Brazil. He has been working with Information Security for more than 15 years, implementing and managing efforts of network, governance, access control, risk management, and other domains related with information security on several companies in different sectors.

Dipti Jadhav completed her PhD in Computer Engineering from Ramrao Adik Institute of Technology, University of Mumbai, India in 2019. She received her ME (Computer Engineering) degree from Ramrao Adik Institute of Technology, Mumbai University in 2012. She received her BE (Information Technology) degree from Walchand Institute of Technology, Sholapur, Shivaji University, Maharashtra in 2004. She is currently working as an Associate Professor in the Department of Information Technology, Ramrao Adik Institute of Technology, Navi Mumbai. Her research areas of interest are image processing, pattern recognition, computer vision and genetic algorithms.

Vinita Jindal is an Assistant Professor in the Department of Computer Science, Keshav Mahavidyalaya, University of Delhi since August 2001. She was the Head of Department of Computer Science, Keshav Mahavidyalaya, University of Delhi from June 2017 till May 2019. Before joining the Department of Computer Science, Keshav Mahavidyalaya, University of Delhi, she worked as a Manager/ Sr. Faculty in the PCTI Ltd. from July 1999 to July 2001. She did her Doctorate in Computer Science from University of Delhi in 2018. She did her M.Phill. in Computer Science from Madurai Kamaraj University in 2007, MCA from IGNOU in 2000 and Bachelor in Mathematics from University of Delhi in 1997. She is mainly working in the area of Artificial Intelligence and Networks. Her area of interest includes dark web, deep learning, Adhoc networks, Recommender Systems and Vehicular Adhoc networks to name a few.

Ramanpreet Kaur received her Ph.D. in the Computer Science & Engineering from the National Institute of Technology, Jalandhar, India. She is currently a Postdoctoral Fellow in the Laboratory for Open Systems and Networks, Jozef Stefan Institute, Ljubljana, Slovenia. She has several years of experience in research and development. From 2012 to 2019, she held Assistant Professor position at Jaypee University of Information Technology, India. Her main research interests include network security, computer networks and machine learning with focus on protection from DDoS attacks, intrusion detection system and the algorithm design of networked and distributed systems. She has been involved in various European projects related to the security and privacy of networks.

Tomaž Klobučar is head of the Laboratory for Open Systems and Networks at Jozef Stefan Institute and an assistant professor at Jozef Stefan International Postgraduate School, where he is teaching on information security. He obtained his diploma degree in mathematics and doctoral degree in computer science and informatics at University of Ljubljana. Dr. Klobučar has years of experience in research, development, and project management in the field of security and privacy enhancing technologies. Lately, he has been involved in various security and privacy related EU projects, such as DE4A, SI-PASS 2.0, SI-PASS, eID4U, STORK 2.0, e-SENS, EmployID, SENTER and LIVE\_FOR. His scientific publication list includes around 100 items.

Sidney Marlon Lopes de Lima is currently Adjunct Professor of Department of Electronic and Systems, UFPE (Federal University of Pernambuco), Recife, Brazil. He received the B.Eng. and the M.Tech. degrees in Computer Engineering from the UPE (University of Pernambuco), Recife, Brazil. Sidney Lima received the Ph.D. degrees in Computer Science from the UFPE. Sidney Lima is Post-Doctor of Computer Engineering Program at UPE. The Professor is author of IEEE (Institute of Electrical and Electronic Engineers). In addition, he is author and reviewer of Science Elsevier. The professor is a reviewer of Science Elsevier in the following scientific journals: Expert Systems with Applications, Computer Methods and Programs in Biomedicine, and Computers in Biology and Medicine.

Huan Liu is a professor of Computer Science and Engineering at Arizona State University. He obtained his Ph.D. in Computer Science at University of Southern California and B.Eng. in Computer Science and Electrical Engineering at Shanghai JiaoTong University. Before he joined ASU, he worked at Telecom Australia Research Labs and was on the faculty at National University of Singapore. At Arizona State University, he was recognized for excellence in teaching and research in Computer Science and Engineering and received the 2014 President's Award for Innovation. His research interests are in data mining, machine learning, social computing, and artificial intelligence, investigating interdisciplinary problems that arise in many real-world, data-intensive applications with high-dimensional data of disparate forms such as social media. His well-cited publications include books, book chapters, encyclopedia entries as well as conference and journal papers. He is a co-author of a text, Social Media Mining: An Introduction, Cambridge University Press. He is a founding organizer of the International Conference Series on Social Computing, Behavioral-Cultural Modeling, and Prediction, and Field Chief Editor of Frontiers in Big Data and its Specialty Chief Editor of Data Mining and Management. He is a Fellow of ACM, AAAI, AAAS, and IEEE. More can be found at http://www.public.asu.edu/~huanliu.

Asmita Manna has submitted her PhD thesis recently at Jadavpur University, Kolkata, India. Prior to joining for PhD, she completed her Masters of Engineering in Software Engineering from Jadavpur University in 2009. Her primary research domains are Information Security and Privacy.

Suzana Maranhão Moreno is a co-founder of BNDES Blockchain Lab in the Brazilian Development Bank (BNDES). She was the vice-chair of ITU DLT focus group and now she is the associate rapporteur in a working to define blockchain standards in ITU. Suzana performed many roles in business process management and IT developing projects involving up to billions of USD in the last 15 years. She has a multidisciplinary education - Bachelor and Master degree in IT, additional Bachelor in Economics, MBA and blockchain certification by University of Nicosia in Cyprus.

Chandan Mazumdar is a senior professor in the Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Jadavpur University, Kolkata, India. His research interests include Big Data Analytics, Information Security, Risk Assessment, Insider Threat Assessment and Privacy.

João Mello da Silva is an Associate Professor in the Department of Production Engineering, Faculty of Technology, University of Brasilia (UnB). At UnB he is also member of the Risk Management concentration area in the Professional Master's Program in Applied Computing, responsible for courses of IT Project Management, and for the guidance of master dissertations. He holds a degree in Mechanical Engineering, School of Engineering of Sao Carlos, Sao Paulo University (EESC/USP), a Master in Systems Analysis and Applications by the Brazilian Space Research National Institute (INPE), a Master in Operations Research – Case Western Reserve University (CWRU), and a PhD in Operations Research – CWRU. As Production Engineering Undergraduate Coordinator for 5 years, he was one of the members of the team that implemented the Undergraduate Production Engineering Program at UnB. He has been responsible for Risk Management courses in UnB’s Specialization Course in Health and Safety at Work. As a professor at the Federal University of Sao Carlos, he was one of the members of the team that implemented the Undergraduate Production Engineering Program at that institution. As an engineer at Telebras, and Brasil Telecom, and as a managing partner of a consulting firm, he worked in Telecommunications Services Production Engineering, with an emphasis on Services, covering topics as business engineering, quality management, business relationships between telecommunications service providers, regulation and risk management. He has co-authored many publications, in terms of articles in technical-scientific journals, congress papers, books, and chapters of books. Research areas of interest include Maturity and Value Creation in Production Systems, particularly via sustainable and innovative projects for the poorer; Risk Management, emphasis on cybersecurity linked to personal data protection; and Education in Production Engineering, with a special focus on synthesis, integration and entrepreneurship activities. In coordination of research activities he was the General Manager of a project on retirement modeling for special working conditions, and Integration Coordinator in a cyber defense project.

Gyula Mester, D. Sci., PhD, Full Professor, Óbuda University, Doctoral School on Safety and Security Sciences, Budapest, Hungary. Orcid ID: 0000-0001-7796-2820, h-index = 30, researcher of Robotics, Self-Driving and Flying Cars, Scientific Metrics. Full member of the Hungarian Academy of Engineering, American Romanian Academy of Arts and Sciences. Member of the World Academy of Science, Engineering and Technology, New York Academy of Sciences. Man of the Year 1997 and 2011 by the American Biographical Institute. His CV was published in the Marquis ‘Who’s Who in the World 1997’.

Igor Mikhalevich is a PhD, Associate Professor, Department Control and Protection of Information, Russian University of Transport (Moscow Institute of Transport Engineers).

Subhankar Mishra received his Ph.D. from the University of Florida in 2016 and BTech from NIT, Rourkela in 2010. He is currently an Assistant Professor in the School of Computer Sciences at NISER. His general research area is Machine Learning and Privacy. He focuses on critical infrastructures such as Smart Grid, 3D Modelling, and Robotics and collaborates with Biological Sciences for bio-statistical analysis.

Joshua Ojo Nehinbe obtained Ph.D. in Computer Science at the University of Essex, UK in 2011. He has taught Undergraduate and Postgraduate students in the areas of computer security, data mining, database management, system modeling and simulation. He has actively published papers and book chapters on computer security, data mining, computer security and forensics.

Anita Patil is an Assistant Professor in Department of Information Technology, Ramrao Adik Institute of Technology, Nerul, Navi Mumbai. Completed a Master of Technology from RGPV university, Indore and Bachelor of Technology from Dr. B.A.T. University, Lonere. Published 13 research papers in International IEEE Conference, National Conference and Journals in the area of Network security, Information security and cyber security and cryptography. Guided 13 UG project groups in the domain of Artificial Intelligence, Network Security, Biometric Security, Machine Learning.

Sudipta Paul has received her M.Tech. In 2018 from the Department of Computer science and Engineering, University of Kalyani, WB, India, and B.Tech from the Department of Information Technology, Kalyani Government Engineering College, West Bengal University of Technology, WB, India in 2015. She joined as a Junior Research Fellow in the School of Computer Science, NISER Bhubaneswar, India under the supervision of Dr. Subhankar Mishra, Assistant Professor, NISER Bhubaneswar, India IN 2019, since then she is working there. Her fields of interest include Machine Learning, Security, Deep Learning, IoT.

Michele Perilli has a degree in Computer Science (1987); Degree in Information Technology (2005); Degree in TLC Technology (2006). Technical Manager in Telecom Italia S.p.A. (Italian TLC Carrier) from 1988 to 2001. Computer Science Engineering Consulting since 2001. Computer Science Professor at University of Foggia since 2006.

Jelena L. Pisarov is a PhD student at the Óbuda University, Doctoral School of Safety and Security Sciences, Budapest, Hungary. Working as a teacher of Physics and IT at Primary school Matko Vukovic, Subotica, Serbia. Her research is mainly focused on Robotics, Self-Driving Cars, Drones, Webometrics, and STEAM Education.

Sanjeev Rao is working as Assistant Professor in CSED, TIET, Patiala, Punjab, India. He received his B.Tech and M.Tech in year 2007 and 2012 respectively, majoring in Computer Science and Engineering. He is an Oracle Certified Professional (OCP) from Oracle University. He is also pursuing Ph.D. in the domain of security issues in Online Social Networks at CSED, TIET, Patiala, Punjab, India. His area of interests are data-mining, social network analysis and security in social networks. He has published and presented many papers in Conferences and Journals. He is also a member of IEEE, ACM, and IAENG.

Alexander Ryjov, Professor, Doctor of Sciences, has 30+ years of combined business, advanced research, and teaching experience. Alexander has Ph.D. in Mathematics, D.Sc. in Engineering, Executive MBA from Bled School of Management. He is professor at Lomonosov Moscow State University (mathematics) and head of the Chair at Russian Presidential Academy of National Economy and Public Administration (high-tech business), member of two authorizing PhD boards. He has 100+ scientific publications including 6 books and chapters in 14 books. More information on http://www.intsys.msu.ru/en/staff/ryzhov/.

Jean-Marc Seigneur has published more than 100 scientific publications worldwide in the field of online reputation, trust, security, and privacy. He is the director of the blockchain certificate of advanced studies at the University of Geneva.

Devaraju Sellappan received the B.Sc degree in Chemistry in 1997 from the University of Madras, Chennai, and the M.C.A. degree in Computer Applications in 2001 from the Periyar University, Salem, and the M.Phil. degree in Computer Science in 2004 from Periyar University, Salem and also received M.B.A. degree in Human Resource from Madurai Kamaraj University, Madurai in 2007. He received his Ph.D degree in Science and Humanities from Anna University, Chennai in 2017. He has 17 years of teaching experience and 2 years industry experience. He is an Associate Professor, Department of Computer Science and Applications, Sri Krishna Arts and Science College, Coimbatore, Tamil Nadu, India. Dr.S.Devaraju is a Reviewer for various reputed Journals and Conferences. He has published more than 20 papers in international journals and conference proceedings. His area of research includes Network Security, Intrusion Detection, Soft Computing, and Wireless Communication.

Anirban Sengupta is a senior research engineer in the Centre for Distributed Computing, Jadavpur University, Kolkata, India. His research interests include Information Security, Risk Assessment and Privacy.

Poushali Sengupta is doing her MSc. in Statistics from the Department of Statistics, University of Kalyani, WB, India and graduated with BSc. Honors in Statistics from Lady Brabourne College, the University of Calcutta in 2018. Currently, she is working on her MSc. thesis under the guidance of Dr. Subhankar Mishra, Assistant Professor, NISER, Bhubaneswar, India. Her fields of interests are machine learning, data science, security, deep learning.

Swapnil Shinde is an Assistant Professor in Department of Information Technology, Ramrao Adik Institute of Technology, Nerul, Navi Mumbai and a PhD Research Scholar at Symbiosis International University, Lavale, Pune. Completed Master of Engineering and Bachelor of Engineering from Mumbai University. Published 16 research papers in International IEEE Conference, National Conference and Journals in the area of Image and Video processing, Biometrics Security and Machine Learning. Guided 13 UG project groups in the domain of Medical Imaging, Biometrics Security and Machine Learning.

Divya Singhal is a Guest Lecturer in department of Computer Science, Keshav Mahavidyalaya, University of Delhi. She has a 4 years teaching experience. She is pursuing her P.hd in Information Technology from Amity University, Uttar Pradesh, Noida. She has qualified CBSE-NET and ICAR-NET in 2018. she has completed her MCA from GGSIPU in 2016 and B.sc(hons) computer science from University of Delhi in 2013. She is working in the area of network and information security.

Ramakrishnan Srinivasan received the B.E. degree in Electronics and Communication Engineering in 1998 from the Bharathidasan University, Trichy, and the M.E. degree in Communication Systems in 2000 from the Madurai Kamaraj University, Madurai. He received his PhD degree in Information and Communication Engineering from Anna University, Chennai in 2007. He has 20 years of teaching experience and 1 year industry experience. He is a Professor and the Head of the Department of Information Technology, Dr. Mahalingam College of Engineering and Technology, Pollachi, India. Dr. Ramakrishnan is an Associate Editor for IEEE Access and he is a Reviewer of 28 International Journals including 7 IEEE Transactions, 5 Elsevier Science Journals, 3 IET Journals, ACM Computing Reviews, Springer Journals, Wiley Journals, etc. He is in the editorial board of 7 International Journals. He is a Guest Editor of special issues in 3 International Journals including Telecommunication Systems Journal of Springer. He has filed one Indian patent. He has published 181 papers in international, national journals and conference proceedings. Dr. S. Ramakrishnan has published 12 books on Image Processing, Pattern Recognition, Soft Computing, Information Security and Wireless Sensor Networks for CRC Press, USA, InTech Publisher, Croatia and Lambert Academic Publishing, Germany. He has also reviewed 3 books for McGraw Hill International Edition and 20 books for ACM Computing Reviews. He was the convenor of IT board in Anna University of Technology- Coimbatore Board of Studies(BoS). He had successfully guided 5 PhD scholars and guiding 4 scholars. His biography has been included in Marquis Whos’s Who in the World 2012 & 2016 edition. His areas of research include digital image processing, information security, and soft computing.

Dauda Sule is a CISA with an MSc. in Computer Security. He is currently lecturing Cyber Security at Air Force Institute of Technology, Kaduna after being Marketing Executive of GGL Risk and Strategic Conulting - a training and consulting firm that is into organizing trainings and seminars pertaining to information management, security, assurance and control; finance; fraud prevention and detection; and anti-money laundering. A continuous learner with a passion for Information Security, Assurance and Control, he is an author for eForensics Magazine and have written articles for the magazine as well as ISACA Journal. He has also delivered workshops related to Digital Forensics and eDiscovery for eForensics Magazine among others.

Carlos Alberto M. S. Teles graduated in Economic Science from the State University of Rio de Janeiro, Brazil (2005). He holds a Master's Degree in Computer Science at CEFET/RJ-PPCIC, Brazil (2019). He is a researcher in Information Security and interested in areas such as Wireless Sensor Networks and Internet of Things. He is currently an employee of CLARO BRASIL S.A with over 15 years of experience in network management and systems development.

Vishnu Venkatesh is the CISO and VP of Digital at Vibronyx. He is a technology entrepreneur, business and thought leader with experience in multiple verticals focusing on cyber security, business intelligence and data analytics. Vishnu is also a Visiting Lecturer at Babson College, and is the college’s teaching expert on cybersecurity while also covering emerging technologies in AI and Blockchain. Prior to Babson, Vishnu worked at McKesson, Pfizer, Fidelity Investments and launched a cybersecurity startup. Vishnu is CISSP certified and holds advanced degrees of Master of Science from MIT and an MBA from Babson College.

Anil Kumar Verma is currently a Professor in CSED, TIET, Patiala. He received his B.S., M.S. and Ph.D. in 1991, 2001 and 2008, respectively, majoring in Computer Science and Engineering. He has published over 150 papers in referred journals and conferences (India and Abroad). He has chaired various sessions in the International and National Conferences. He is active member of MIEEE, MACM, MISCI, LMCSI, MIETE, GMAIMA. He is a certified software quality auditor by MoCIT, Govt. of India. His research interests include Security in Online Social Networks, Mobile computing, Wireless networks, Routing algorithms and Mobile clouds.

Eduardo Vianna has a Ph.D. in Information Science from the University of Brasília (2019). It operates in the public and private sectors, particularly in the areas of digital protection and strategic knowledge. Advised the Ministry of Defense in the planning and operations of security and cyber defense during the “Great Events”: Rio + 20 (2012), Confederations Cup (2013), WYD (2013), FIFA (2014) and Olympic Games (2016). Advisor to the Cyber Defense Command (2018-19). Acts as Researcher at the Superior School of War and Special Advisor to the Ministry Public of the Federal District and Territories.

Tawei (David) Wang is currently an Associate Professor and Driehaus Fellow at DePaul University. He received his Ph.D. from Krannert Graduate School of Management, Purdue University in 2009. His research interests are information security management and IT management. His papers have appeared in several leading journals, including Information Systems Research, Accounting Horizons, Decision Support Systems, European Journal of Information Systems, Information and Management, Information Systems Journal, International Journal of Accounting Information Systems, Journal of Accounting and Public Policy, Journal of Banking and Finance, Journal of Information Systems, Journal of Organizational Computing and Electronic Commerce, among others. He received several research awards and is currently the 2nd most productive researcher in AIS archival research based on the BYU ranking. His articles have been downloaded more than 36,000 times through Science Direct. He mainly teaches audit analytics and has been invited by universities and conferences to discuss curriculum design and analytics teaching strategies. He was a speaker of analytics at a CAE roundtable hosted by IIA. He was also a speaker of cybersecurity and analytics at the 2019 AAA AIS Bootcamp and involved in the development of cybersecurity curriculum guidelines by ACM. He was also a panelist talking about cyber risk in a workshop hosted by the Federal Reserve Bank. He was selected to be the KPMG James Marwick Professor in Residence in 2018.

Yen-Yao Wang (Ph.D., Michigan State University) is an Assistant Professor in Information Systems Management at the Department of Systems and Technology at the Harbert College of Business of Auburn University. His research interests include business analytics, social media, digital marketing, Economics of information systems, and IT management. His work has appeared in several academic journals and peer-reviewed conferences such as Industrial Marketing Management, Journal of Database Management, Information Systems and e-Business Management, International Conference on Information Systems (ICIS), among others.

Ricardo Zelenovsky graduated in Electronics at Military Institute of Engineering (IME), master’s degree in Parallel Computing at IME and Doctor Degree at Catholic University of Rio de Janeiro (PUC-RJ). Currently teaching in the Department of Electrical Engineering of University of Brasilia (ENE-UnB).

Ji Zhang received the PhD degree in computer science from Dalhousie University, Halifax, NS, Canada, in 2008. He served as the Principal Advisor for Research with the Division of ICT Services, University of Southern Queensland, from 2010 to 2013. He is currently an Associate Professor of computing with the University of Southern Queensland, Australia. His research interests include knowledge discovery and data mining, health informatics, and information privacy and security. He is an Australian Endeavor Fellow, a Queensland Fellow, and an Izaak Walton Killam Fellow, Canada. He has authored over 160 papers, some appearing in top-tier international journals, including the IEEE TRANSACTIONS ON DEPENDABLE AND SECURE COMPUTING, the Information Sciences, the WWW Journal, the Bioinformatics, Knowledge and Information Systems, the Soft Computing, the Journal of Database Management, and the Journal of Intelligent Information Systems, and international conferences, such as VLDB, ACM CIKM, ACM SIGKDD, IEEE ICDE, IEEE ICDM, WWW, DASFAA, DEXA, and DaWak.

Zhongwei Zhang has been a senior lecturer in the University of Southern Queensland since 1999. He received his B.S. from Harbin Institute of Technology, China, M.S. from the University of Amsterdam, the Netherlands. He was awarded a PhD degree by Monash University, Australia in 1998. Dr Zhang research interests lie in Computer Communications and Network Security, Wireless Sensor Networks and its Application in HealthCare. He has published more than 26 articles in prestigious journals and around 56 papers in IEEE international conferences, etc. Dr Zhang has been the chair for a number of research projects while he has been lecturing many Computing courses in USQ, particularly in network performance and security.
